New

## Critique of Reason

by

Jacob Friedrich Fries.

Volume One.

Heidelberg,

Mohr and Zimmer,

1807.

[scan 13]

### Preface.

The purpose of this work is indicated closely enough by its very title, and what is more particular I have said in the Introduction. I hand over to public judgment the fruit of long-tested and often repeated investigations. But how soon will anyone be found who cares to grasp such lengthy, dry and difficult investigations exactly? Perhaps sooner than it might now appear! We stand at a point of philosophical cultivation where the attractive manner of presenting philosophy has carried off all the greater a victory, in that it has managed at the same time to put on the mask of weighty and rigorous scientific character. This ornament, however, is no healthy property of our life, but everywhere a foreign imitation, and for that very

[p. II]

reason it cannot fail soon to dissolve into elegant superficiality and mystical nonsense.

My continuation, chiefly of the Aristotelian and Kantian investigations, has its worth only in the strictest and narrowest demands of truth. If there is no philosophy as rigorous science, distinct from all mythology, which becomes clear to us purely from speculation, in which all the individual principles and theorems can be counted off, where each has its determinate place and its own justification, as in pure mathematics, and if there is no proper interest in working out this science in such a way: then we must give up our efforts as wholly lost. But there is no real danger of that; the history of philosophy sufficiently guarantees us (even though I do not wish to dwell here on demonstrating the importance of a knowledge of scientific forms) that the thread of these investigations, however often it was dropped so as to reach merely for embellishments and applications, is nonetheless each time soon taken up again.

[p. III]

So let us not, any more than mathematics does, take piety or learning as a pretext for gaining a hearing, but aim solely at truth.

That motley, elegant talk about philosophy, by contrast, is like the seven lean kine in Pharaoh’s dream: however often it may devour the fat of fantasy, it still stands there in the end, again and again, as dry, lean logic. What good does it do to express the withered rafter-work of identity and difference in Latin, and to cover it with green garlands of flowers that cannot take root there, which the first glance of the sun withers and the next gust of wind scatters again? The effort is in vain to roof over a comfortable hut for human beings with it, let alone a temple for gods. This ornament in presentation and language can seem important only to one who does not quite trust dry truth and his own enthusiasm to stand the test. We do not fear that. Indeed: to the common crowd one may supply the bitter draught of its apotheosis with some syrup,

[p. IV]

so that he only brings it to his lips; let whoever finds it worth the trouble then take pains to let these people behold truth in the half-light of mystified feelings, like conjured spirits. But whoever is versed in science will want to see clearly everywhere, and will fear no clarity.

[scan 17]

### Introduction.

It is the spirit of the age that lives and transforms itself in our history; it is the mighty ruler of every individual, for only by it is each one nourished and brought up, only on it does it depend whether a small power shall accomplish the greatest, or the greatest remain unnoticed and crushed, and yet it is again in struggle with it that whoever wishes to work for the cultivation of the mind must measure himself. This holds above all for the self-activity of reason in philosophizing.

Everyone is formed by the public opinion of his time; it introduces his course of thought, and even afterwards foreign opinion continually presses him unconsciously, now because he wishes to flatter its interest or at least to follow it, now because he perhaps also wishes to impress it by contradiction, now finally only because he wants to be understood by it—partly always toward an end, as it lay prepared in the spirit of the times. Above all, however, the effect! Where at one time a spark sets everything far and wide in flames, at another time the strongest glow does not suffice to kindle further. The interest of the moment decides everything here.

[p. VI]

So in philosophy too there is a public opinion, as spirit of the age, which determines the interest of the moment and points every thinker his direction. In this spirit of the age lies a basic judgment about what philosophy is to accomplish; it bears the whole philosophical cultivation of the age with its merits and faults. It determines the basic prejudices of the time, which are inherited by everyone who does not free himself from them by his own power; and this liberation is the hard struggle that lies upon us if we wish to work for philosophy.

Public opinion about philosophy is formed at any time by that for which one just then considers philosophy good. All the interest of philosophy, however, hangs on the three ideas of truth, beauty and goodness, and what is decisive here is how an age grasps these singly or in their union, according to the practical need of the one and the theoretical need of the others.

The first moving factor that determines for an age the worth of philosophy lies in how necessary one holds it to be for the practical interest, how indispensable one deems it for one’s ideas of right and virtue and religion, or perhaps also for the aesthetic interest of beauty. Here, however, we see public opinion constantly changing. When in modern times thought became free again, people began to place confidence in philosophy for religion as well as for right. The law

[p. VII]

of hierarchy, and the letter of a positive faith first lost its undisputed power, until the godlessness of an empiricism that had become fashionable destroyed again the belief in the good cause of reason. Longer did public opinion hold for the philosophy of right; people hoped to make constitutions of states with philosophical theories, and laws with natural right; finally, in our own time only the physicians still hope to learn from it through natural science, and, without having taste and fine art, some think to win them back through philosophy. In the outcome, then, philosophy has drawn upon itself, through its practical side, more enemies than friends, since it too easily falls into conflict with the figurative and the positive. Indeed, people would probably long since have turned away from all speculation, if the theoretical interest of truth for truth’s sake alone, at first subordinate, did not always remain the same, even against our will constantly lead back to the old theme, and at least for the moment rouse every newly blossoming youth again; for it is the indestructible striving of the developing understanding to make the unity of its own essence valid as law in all its cognition; hence the ever living spirit of speculation, which everywhere seeks system and principle, and wants to ground and explain.

Here, however, we must distinguish this need that engenders philosophy from the actual attempts to satisfy it. A system once set up, with all its

[p. VIII]

consistency, is after all always only the final result of its creator’s basic opinions about the essence of philosophizing, and it is a hard task to follow the threads of reasoning into this depth of the mind, where the seeds of a new presentation actually develop. For the most part these first seeds are the more or less correct prejudices, taken over from past time, about the end and essence of speculation. What appears immediately, and is easier to notice, is then only the attempt to comply with these laws and to satisfy these needs. In that deeper level, however, lies the secret power of the spirit of the age.

For this reason the temporarily ruling fashion must not, even in philosophy, be confused with the spirit of the age itself; the latter sets the problems that are to be solved, whereas fashion only gives loud currency, for a time, to single, passing attempts to solve them. If these problems were solved, instead of by new fashion, by established science, then the history of philosophy, in the meaning in which we must now take it, would thereby have reached its end, and for that very reason there would no longer be any philosophical spirit of the age, since through science all opinion, in which alone it lives and moves, would be annihilated. Mere philosophical fashion is at first only stirred up by a more eminent independent thinker, and then lives in the opinions of the philosophizing public, and receives even

[p. IX]

their authoritative word only through the acclamations of the crowd that repeats after them; the spirit of the age, on the other hand, really lives in the independent thinkers of every age. Thus among us the fashions of Wolffianism, of French materialism, then of Kantianism have succeeded one another, until now the philosophy of the All, or the deification of the world, has come to be the order of the day. This fashion is easy to follow historically. But how the spirit of the age has gradually transformed itself under its cover is harder to unfold. For one who exerts himself for philosophy, this fashion, if only he has patience enough, is no particularly dangerous enemy, for, like all fashion, it destroys itself as soon as the charm of novelty is withdrawn from it; its errors are only errors in the results, which reveal themselves of their own accord as they are further peddled. The true errors of the spirit of the age, by contrast, lie in the first presuppositions, to which one usually does not even direct one's glance, which one either unconsciously goes along with, or according to which one is condemned unheard, because they are for the judge an unconscious and therefore wholly unsuspected rule of truth<sup>∗)</sup>.

∗) For this reason, as Leibniz once remarks, a great deal goes unseen precisely because it is too familiar to us; and those who have educated themselves for a science without teachers often discover the most. Thus in philosophy one will do well to turn from recent teachers to quite ancient ones, precisely because from the latter we

[p. X]

It is these prejudices, rooted deep in the public opinion of the independent thinkers of every age, with which we actually have to fight it out, if we wish to help speculation forward.

If, therefore, the question is raised: What are the needs of speculation in our time? How is our philosophy to develop further? then the answer to it can be found and made intelligible only if we show by a historical view what misleading prejudices still lie hidden here, and if, in view of this, we distinguish what is mere fashion of the *followers-after-thought* from what is the public opinion of the *independent thinkers* of the age. Such a historical view we wish to attempt here.

All philosophical riddles resemble Columbus’s problem of making an egg stand on the table: as soon as the riddle is completely solved, the pupil can hardly any longer find the place at which the problem was possible, because everything is so thoroughly clear. For everything here depends on regulated, sharp abstraction, which the first time is very hard to find, but afterwards is easy enough to learn

not so much learn as be pointed to ideas. But the rage of philological erudition and fashionable citations works only to harm, and stifles independent thinking, through learned pedantry and affected elegance, in thoughtless parroting of foreign words.

[p. XI]

It required many kinds of preparation in the history of philosophy, and then still years of long comparisons, before Kant succeeded in separating exactly the forms of intuition from the concepts of the understanding; his pupil now learns to understand and see into this abstraction in a few hours. So, as soon as we possess the most important abstractions with some completeness, philosophy will begin to form itself as firm science; only thereby will it actually become a school subject, like mathematics, and put an end to all pretentiousness, all bombast and all mysteriousness in it. All strife in philosophy turns on the one evident truth: human reason is finite and sensible, hence limited; consequently there is for human reason 1) *more than merely sensible cognition*, but our rational cognition is limited, there is for us 2) *insuperable ignorance* and no absolute cognition. With the development of this truth in its consequences all strife of the philosophers is to be settled and firm science obtained in it.

The final end of all philosophizing lies in its practical interest in the ideas of virtue, of right and of religion, but this final end is only the last result; we must pay little heed to it if we wish to get to know the philosophical spirit of the age. It is a purely speculative impulse which here determines the direction toward the higher, ideal, or toward the low and common. In respect of this practical interest there stand out

[p. XII]

two turning points in the history of philosophy. Socrates led Greek philosophy back from the empty logic of the sophists to its practical interest; and in our own time the struggle with positive religion has turned a natural science devoid of ideas and of religion into the fashionable excuse for the low, common way of thinking in the educated classes, which is anyhow so easily favored, in the confusing turmoil of a rising culture, by the need of every individual, which overpowers everyone. This our period, distinguished above all by Kant, began to oppose from the side of the school, and it gave idea and religion their esteem again before the educated understanding.

But with these last consequences we have nothing to do here, for in them the great thinkers of all times are at one in any case. An individually low and common view of the world can easily be united with political greatness and political genius of mind, but with truly philosophical genius of a deep thinker this idealess view of things is so much in contradiction that a philosophical genius would rather incur all the most incomprehensible inconsistencies than deny this faith. Hardly *a single* true philosophical genius can be named as an example to the contrary. Yet the moral conviction of the originator of a certain spirit in philosophy is a poor measure of the ideal worth or worthlessness of this spirit itself; for every spirit in the philosophical sphere lives immediately only in the

[p. XIII]

theoretical speculation; with the originator it depends on chance whether, consistently or only forced by inconsistencies, he combined his moral conviction with the speculative foundation; these inconsistencies will not be repeated uniformly in the spirit of his philosophy, and only his school can show in this what truly belongs to this spirit, and the most pious teacher will then often form the most godless pupils, and conversely.

The spirit of philosophy which we are seeking here will therefore show its true life and essence only in the properly speculative part of the science (the lofty aims and wishes of each individual in the matter we are glad to leave him). Here now the general demand on philosophy is what we now state: one is to exhibit the coordination of the finite beside the eternal, to unite nature and freedom, so that neither annihilates the other and the rights of both subsist together. This problem is common to all speculation and all times; the difference shows itself only in the supreme maxims by which one wants to arrive at its solution—maxims which, in the natural cultivation of the understanding, are at first unfailingly guided by prejudices. For all the difficulty is here always determined by the relation of sense to reason: the finite belongs to sense, the eternal to reason in its opposition to sense, and truth demands that the rights of sense and of reason both be allowed to stand, and that they be positively united with one another. This, however, is with the unprepared

[p. XIV]

ordinary way of thinking very hard; every individual falls either under the prejudices of the sense that holds itself alone sufficient, or of the self-sufficient reason, or else it comes finally to a negative union of both in skepticism.

To the cognition of the finite sense leads us immediately; for the eternal, however, we need a higher standpoint of properly speculative cognition, which belongs only to thinking reason on its own, and to which it is led when it wants to set up unity as the law of all its cognizing. The first gives us the cold, natural view of the things of knowledge and of common sense. The other gives us a, so to speak, exalted religious view of the things of faith and of the idea. Both, common sense and idea, then try in ordinary cultivation of mind their salvation either with an empirical basic prejudice of sense, or with a rationalistic basic prejudice of reason.

For common life we have two fundamental maxims according to which one philosophizes; the one belongs to the empiricism of common sense, and expresses itself: *I believe only what falls within intuition, what I see and hear*; the other belongs to the reasoning of common sense, is logical, and expresses itself: *I believe only what can be proved to me*. Both unite in a

[p. XV]

third: *I believe only what can be proved from what is seen and heard*. What is judged and inferred under the presupposition of these maxims is the commonly comprehensible and clear, on which people are usually agreed. But as soon as one begins to touch these maxims themselves, to call their validity in question, or merely to want to settle their relation to one another, common sense goes astray into the wavering, obscure and indeterminate; it has no firm judgment any more.

Over against these fundamental maxims of common sense, which wants to know about everything, there stands the religious view of things, which is taken under protection by a *party of faith*, which accuses this understanding of pride and presumption. To it belong again two opposed fundamental maxims; one belongs to the idealized empiricism, which is basically hostile to all speculation, however philosophical it may often appear, after the saying: *Yes, under the moon there are many things of which the dreamery philosophy dreams nothing.* Under the wings of this doctrine all sorts of faith and superstition then take refuge. The other maxim belongs to the idealized rationalism, which accuses the understanding of a one-sided pursuit of reflection without aim or end, after the objection: In the way you see things, you have after all only your view of things; who vouches to you that the essence of the world in itself is really as it appears to you,

[p. XVI]

is it not rather already in your conviction that you have only a limited, finite reason, that you will also have only a limited view of things? But hardly is this condemnatory judgment on the common view pronounced, when the very same reason, left to itself, ventures after all to raise itself again to the primal source of truth: *follow me*, it says, *and I will show you, beyond all the images of your seeing and hearing, the eternal unity and necessity in everything, before the transfigured gaze.*

In this way speculation has always played with us and with itself in history. Three prejudices unconsciously and involuntarily guide the judgment about truth in everyone who is unprepared. The prejudice of natural empiricism, or *of trust in intuition*; one of natural rationalism, or *of trust in proof*; and one of artificial rationalism, or *of trust in the idea*; for the fourth opinion, of idealized empiricism, consists only in opposition, without any positive property.

These we wish to compare more closely with the more recent history of philosophy.

Ever since the forms of the faculty of reflection had been developed on their own through Greek philosophy, according to concept, judgment, inference, proof and system, the rationalism

[p. XVII]

of common sense received a firm shape, in that, driven by the convenience of classifying and proving, it demanded theoretical science everywhere, and tried to form it according to the maxim: nothing is certain but what is proved from its grounds. There formed itself through scholastic philosophy, through that of Descartes and Spinoza down to the Wolffian, more or less unconsciously, the prejudice of the sufficiency of the logical forms and of proof, in order to secure truth and certainty in philosophy. One may call this the prejudice of the mathematical method, for what was understood in Wolff’s time by mathematical method is nothing other than the general logical method, i.e., the procedure of resolving all the concepts of a science into definitions, forming axioms from them, and deriving proofs from these. By subjecting everything, bit by bit, to proof in this way, the whole system of human wisdom in the end hung only on the single ring of logical identity, of contradiction and of sufficient ground; for here the thinking understanding was wholly left to itself, and the last ground on which it could rest was only the rules of its thinking itself.

On the other side there had formed itself, chiefly since Bacon of Verulam, in England, a more experience-based speculating, which had the empirical maxim at its ground: to trust only sensible intuition. These two parties came into conflict chiefly through Leibniz and Locke; but the dispute was

[p. XVIII]

only about the manner of application, and each let the fundamental maxim of the other, partly unconsciously, count along with his own: to the prover intuition was only confused, to the intuiter proof was mere derivation, hence empty in itself.

For this reason Hume succeeded in making the whole natural speculation doubt itself, solely by uniting both maxims decisively with one another. He lays as the fundamental maxim of his speculation the prejudice: only through proofs from what falls within intuition is certainty of knowledge possible. From this he showed, especially in the use of the concepts of cause and effect, that all so-called speculative knowledge could not be grounded at all in that way, and condemned the speculating understanding to an unavoidable skepticism.

Against this presentation nothing consistent could be objected in the traditional way; one had to abandon this manner of speculating, and was now driven back to mere self-cognition of reason, through which we received at first the treatment of empirical psychology by the English and the German eclectics.

For more speculative minds, however, there lay in past history a greater instruction. F. H. Jacobi discovered first with sufficient sharpness the ground of the failure of all Wolffian speculative attempts, by showing the mediacy of all proving and comprehending, and

[p. XIX]

demonstrating that something determinate must first be given, from which one proves, before one can begin to prove. He taught us that all determinism necessarily ends in fatalism, since the supreme ground, with its own inner necessity, nonetheless stands there only as fate, for the *causa sui*, the ground of itself, was a far too facile excuse for a conclusion of determinism within itself.

The same circumstances Kant grasped, and they led him to his *Critique of Reason*. He saw first that the evidence of mathematics does not depend on its strictly logical form, but on its own intuition; the latter is lacking in philosophy, and therefore one may not apply to it at all this method, then so highly esteemed, but can accomplish something in it only by a regressive, analytic method. Nothing could be gained by proceeding directly to the setting up of a speculative system; rather the outcome in Hume’s presentation shows clearly that reason in this way entangles itself in contradiction with itself; it is therefore unavoidably necessary that it first occupy itself with itself and arrive at self-cognition, as to how far it reaches in speculation with its own powers or not. In now conducting these investigations he discovered first the distinction of analytic and synthetic judgments, further in space and time the forms of a pure intuition, which become the source of mathematical universal and necessary laws, and which arise not from the

[p. XX]

understanding, but from productive imagination. Further he showed against Hume that not only the concept of cause and effect, but the whole table of concepts, which he calls the table of categories, arise in our mind independently of experience, yet would necessarily have to be applied even by every skeptic, because they are necessary conditions of the possibility of experience in general. Finally he showed that beyond the domain of experience, in the field of ideas, speculative reason on its own can accomplish nothing at all, that it has here no power at all toward positive cognition, yet that it justifies to itself the possibility of freedom, in that it acknowledges its conditioned sensible cognition only as a subjective appearance, only as its view of the world, which need not be acknowledged as a necessary law for the existence of things in themselves.

Thus through the infallible critical method the fact of speculation in our mind had to be determined decisively, namely that we unavoidably use categories as conditions of the possibility of experience, and that speculative reason on its own in the domain of reason can know nothing positive; but why this is so remained undecided in Kant. How are we entitled to experience itself and to its forms *a priori*? and whence comes our speculative incapacity? this was not shown here. In spite of the strict systematic form, and the regular completeness of the

[p. XXI]

system, the whole nevertheless lacked closure, rounding, and thereby inner stability and unity.

What became immediately clear through Kant was the insufficiency of all English and French empiricism, for he demonstrated in our mind, as a fact, a consciousness of universality and necessity, which according to those principles would have to be absolutely impossible. On the other side it was also clear, through Jacobi and Kant, against natural rationalism, that the logical forms of reflection, with their identity and their contradiction, the mere proofs, do not suffice to procure for us speculative certainty. People then became more or less agreed on the expression that the hitherto prevailing treatment of philosophy as *philosophy of reflection* is to be rejected, and felt the need, instead of the mediate certainty of proofs, to demonstrate an *immediate cognition of reason* as the proper source of speculative truths. In doing so, various people behaved very differently, but most agreed in this, to introduce an immediate cognition of the unconditioned, the absolute, the eternal, exalted above the finite, which some hoped to attain through a faith opposed to knowledge, others through an immediate highest knowledge of intellectual intuition.

These historical moments are sufficient to grasp and comprehend the purely speculative spirit of our time in German philosophy. What more or less loudly

[p. XXII]

in particular beyond this has been said is more a matter of fashion than the property of the spirit of the age.

Among the philosophers who were most heard, Reinhold, in seeking to add the missing unity to the Kantian system, brought the rationalistic prejudice again definitely into motion under the formula: it is the end of all theoretical science and speculation to derive all our knowledge from one highest principle. This principle was at first to be logically a basic principle, but soon turned around metaphysically, and became the idea of the universe or of the deity. Here, then, one grasps the problem of philosophy under the formula: to comprehend the essence of things from the essence of the deity. And however clear it is for every reflective speech that everything is through the deity as it is, if the idea of the deity has reality; but that man can neither grasp nor comprehend the essence of the deity, still less therefore the essence of things from it: yet this idea has become, for the moment, so widespread a matter of fashion in philosophy among us that one might almost call it the characteristic of the spirit of our speculation.

Fichte with his pure I; Bardili with his *prius*, Reinhold with his thinking as thinking, Schelling with his absolute reason, and the whole Schellingian school with its absolute science and its science of the All, agree in this, that their philosophy wishes to cognize the essence of things from the eternal unity

[p. XXIII]

Yet the error is here so openly in the daylight that this idea can never be more than a passing matter of fashion. For as soon as every school has sufficiently developed its language, it will result of itself that it merely confuses the ectypal human view of the world with the idea of an archetypal divine understanding, and in the problem of its philosophy has cast human reason over into that divine one.

If I now propose by the present work to lead the course of speculation a few steps further: the question arises, first, what prejudices lying in the spirit of the age I shall have to encounter here, and secondly, what demands this spirit of the age will make on me, what it should make on me?

First we wish to develop the former more exactly from the presentation so far. The progress of speculation in recent times may in general be characterized thus:

1) Completion of speculation from the rationalistic prejudice: all truth must be comprehended from one highest principle, through the systems of Spinoza, Leibniz and Wolff.

2) Counter-attempt of a speculation from the empirical prejudice of intuition, in Locke’s *Essay concerning Human Understanding*, in which he wants to make sensation the sole source of our truth.

[p. XXIV]

3) Completion of this empiricism in Hume’s presentation, in which empiricism assumes its proper standpoint for philosophy, through the denial of all speculative truth, if one may trust only intuition.

4) Union of the empirical and rationalistic view through Kant’s *Critique of Reason*.

We see, then, in this history a conflict between the prejudices of natural empiricism and rationalism, which ends with an attempt at reconciliation between the two. Our question is therefore really: what has actually been gained in the philosophical spirit of our time, through conflict and reconciliation, over the one-sidedness of those prejudices? and what may still remain of it?

Here we can easily be done with the pure Lockean prejudice; Kant has answered it so determinately and distinctly that no educated independent thinker can any longer fall into this error. The sole ground of the Lockean view was this, that every human cognition is determined by sense and sensation and begins with sensation. To this, however, Kant replies: although all our cognition begins with sensible sensation, it does not therefore all arise from it, but comes to consciousness in us only on the occasion of sensation. If we had only sensible intuition, the concept of necessity and universality

[p. XXV]

would thereby not even be possible in our understanding, even supposing that it could not be applied at all; now our mind possesses, even in mathematics and philosophy, necessary cognitions which according to Locke’s theory would have to be wholly impossible; this theory is therefore in any case one-sided.

Hume’s completion of this empiricism, however, has by no means been so cleanly annihilated as Locke’s presentation, because in it the rationalistic prejudice also finds expression.

This is the many-shaped thing which, when it is refuted on one side, nevertheless always communicates its errors again in another way. There goes the general saying: in the domain of philosophy there is somewhere its supreme and first beginning, in which from the *one unity* the source of all truth springs forth. To find this domain is said to be the true riddle of the philosophical stone of the wise. Many a one went out on this adventure, and believed he had made the find, but almost every one already imagined, under that which he sought, something else. It is supposed that from One highest thing everything individual, particular, manifold shall be now grounded, now proved, explained, deduced, made indifferent. Whereby the matter gets now a logical, now an obscure metaphysical meaning. Spinoza and Leibniz took the matter wholly metaphysically, and wanted to comprehend the essence of all things from the unity of one highest essence. If such a doctrine were really to be set up, however, it would have to appear under

[p. XXVI]

the logical form of a system; Wolff, then, actually set himself quite the same problem, only that he looked at it from its logical side: we are to arrange all our knowledge in a logical system, and so prove it from one highest principle.

Hume again presupposed the same problem, but made the objection: how then will you find a proof, with necessity, for the applicability of the concepts of cause and effect? and answered: from the sensible impressions, with which every cognition begins, the validity of these concepts does not follow, so you can procure for them no validity other than by custom.

Kant finally attacked the Wolffian prejudice from several sides: first, in the main matter, by rejecting the Wolffian method as dogmatic for philosophy, and declaring the critical investigation, which merely prepares the system, to be the most important; secondly, in that he shows that a universal material criterion of truth is a contradiction, since every universal principle of human reason is only formal; thirdly, in that he shows that speculative reason on its own is capable of proving nothing at all. With all this, however, he had not brought the proposition against this prejudice to its simplest expression; indeed, in the very way in which he treats his *Critique of Reason*, he falls again himself under the same prejudice. Kant concedes it to Hume tacitly

[p. XXVII]

as acknowledged truth, and presupposes with all others: what *pure* reason asserts, that it must first have subjected to a *proof*. This presupposition lies in *his* idea of the deduction of the categories; it seduces him into the contradiction that in the *Critique of Pure Reason* he sets up a system of the *principles* of the pure understanding, where he nevertheless, for each of them, although it is supposed to be a principle, still conducts a so-called transcendental proof from his allegedly supreme principle of all synthetic judgments *a priori*, the principle of the possibility of experience. (Especially from the *Crit. of Pure Reason*, Doctrine of Method, I. On the Discipline of Reason, it appears that Kant really confuses the aim of his deduction with proof.) The error of this transcendental proof has actually brought the appearance of incompleteness into the Kantian system, against which Reinhold began to work; its consequences have become the cause of all the later errors of his pupils, and only thereby did the good cause of his Critique not obtain clarity enough to be generally recognized with firmness.

We have, then, still to guard ourselves now, first against the *natural prejudice of rationalism in general*; secondly against a particular consequence of it, which I call the *Humean prejudice*, and thirdly against a *peculiarly Kantian prejudice* or the prejudice of the transcendental.

[p. XXVIII]

#### 1) The Rationalistic Prejudice in General.

In Euclidean geometry we have the example of a science under the strict form of the logical system: every derived concept enters here only through its definition, and every derived proposition finds its place only through the proof from preceding ones. The logical ideal of the state of our knowledge would be, then, that our whole knowledge be treated systematically in exactly the same way. That is indeed in form the goal of the cultivation of our understanding. From this idea, however, a rule of all philosophical judgments has been formed, according to which it is presupposed that there is a certain architectonic of the sciences, in which each individual science has its place in the whole so assigned that it stands under others in which its principles are proved, e.g. machine-science stands under pure mechanics, and this under pure mathematics, and so on until one arrives at a highest and first science that is the founder of all the others, which by tradition is to be philosophy. (Whoever has a mind to bring the pyramid wholly to a point, then goes on to assume with Reinhold and Fichte: the highest science again has only one highest principle, from which therefore all human wisdom flows.) Whoever now wishes to treat any science in a regular theoretical way must first look to see where it stands in this series, and may then at its beginning assume nothing further

[p. XXIX]

than what has already been established in the higher sciences. E.g. in pure geometry there may be no talk of motion, for that is a concept from applied mathematics; in logic one may presuppose neither psychology nor metaphysics, for these stand under it, in it there are as yet no causes, no laws of nature, and no productive imagination.

By this rule, however, we shall not at all let ourselves be bound; it is an erroneous prejudice arising from the correct logical idea. For we shall show, first, that the logical system of our knowledge is not a cone of light springing from its apex, but that it has quite a few starting points independent of one another, as already follows quite simply from this: that in the system only propositions are strung together through inferences, but every inference, besides its principle in the major premise, requires a minor premise given independently of it, merely in order that *one* conclusion may arise. From *one* principle, then, no science springs. Secondly, this rule is properly that of dogmatism, against which Kant so greatly warns. Only in a science in which one can begin dogmatically, without becoming unintelligible, directly with the most general and with the system itself, as in pure mathematics, can one also follow the classification of concepts in such a way that one never assumes as already known the subordinate concept in the case of the superordinate. But that takes place in no science that requires the regressive or critical method, as is the case with the empirical sciences and with philosophy,

[p. XXX]

for there the higher is made known to us only through the subordinate individual case. Whoever, for example, wished to follow that supposed rule strictly would be permitted, in the exposition of logic, to speak neither of understanding nor of thinking, for these are psychological concepts, which belong only in the preparation for logic, but not in the system of its laws.

The cause by which this prejudice maintains itself in such general esteem among views otherwise ever so different lies in the rationalistic basic demand, not thought out distinctly enough: *reduction of all our cognitions to unity*; whose claims one allows to hold too unrestrictedly. To this there then comes, for the logical systematic form, a misunderstanding of the logical principle of ground. This logical principle of ground is namely mostly expressed so generally that it demands approximately this: every cognition must have its sufficient ground; now one says further: to prove means to derive a cognition from its grounds—consequently every cognition must be able to be proved. In this inference, however, both premises are false, and with them the conclusion too.

First, logic has to do not with all cognition in general, but only with *thought cognition*, i.e. with judgment. The principle of ground can be applied to judgments alone, and at the same time easily proved, for every judgment is only the mediate consciousness of another cognition that in it again

[p. XXXI]

is repeated, the ground of its truth lies therefore always in this immediate cognition.

Secondly, the definition of proof that was given is worthless. To prove means only to derive a judgment from *other judgments*, which takes place in inferences. The principles of a science cannot be proved. One has indeed helped oneself against this with the hypothesis that what is presupposed in a science as a principle must still be subjected to proof in a higher one. This hypothesis, however, is wholly incorrect. Every science has its own basic judgments, and every whole system in our knowledge rests of itself on principles that can no longer be subjected to any proof. This can, to be sure, become wholly clear only through the removal of the transcendental prejudice. But every proposition, even every principle, stands under the condition of the logical principle of ground; it must have its further ground. The main thing is that we know how to distinguish properly the grounding of judgments and proof. Precisely there where the proof ends, where we no longer support a judgment on others, but state the principles as first judgments, the question arises: on what immediate cognition is the principle grounded? If this immediate cognition is an intuition, then the principle is grounded through demonstration, through exhibiting its worth in intuition, as in mathematics and in propositions of experience. If it is, as in philosophy, no intuition, then the grounding is called deduction.

[p. XXXII]

Here the transcendental prejudice arises from the confusion of proof with deduction, and this is the worst error that follows from that false rule of the systematic. Whoever attempts deductions under this presupposition finds them turning into logical *circles in the proof*; or if, on the other hand, important deductions are to be examined under this presupposition, the critic falsely takes them for such circles.

The former is the case, as far as the words go, with Kant’s deductions in the *Crit. of Pure Reason*. He wants to prove the principles of the pure understanding from the principle of the possibility of experience; but how can he want to prove the law of causality from this, since experience is grounded only in the interaction of our sensible and intellectual faculties of cognition? Or, to put it more distinctly: how does he want to prove the law of possibility in general from the law of the possibility of experience? That would indeed, against all rule of philosophical cognitions, make the universal law follow from one individual case of it.

As for the other, my philosophical deductions too have been charged with being a circle in the proof; but they are not, for they are no proof at all. They belong rather to a theory of these cognitions, and the case occurs constantly without any difficulty in all inductions in physics. E.g., from individual facts I get to know the phenomena of electricity, and trace them back to their most general laws; I then take these laws as the basic laws of a

[p. XXXIII]

theory of electricity, and explain from them in turn those facts with which I began. First, my reasoning takes the regressive course by way of preparation, and only then, as consequence, the progressive course of the system. In quite a similar way we proceed from the observation of our cognizing, show thereby how the *human power of cognition* is constituted, raise ourselves to a theory of it, show which principles must, in accordance with this theory, lie in our cognition, and only now derive in turn the individual cognitions and judgments from these principles. Should those principles be proved in any way by this procedure, the procedure would of course be wholly inconsistent, for we show from a theory of cognitions why they occur in our reason, and this theory of cognizing is only one individual part of inner natural science, as against which those principles are in part the first laws of all nature in general. Their truth is thus already presupposed among the grounds of their deduction.

#### 2) The Humean Prejudice.

The Humean prejudice is only a particular case of the foregoing. We must contradict it provisionally, only so that we may not be condemned *unheard* according to it. Hume presupposes with Wolff: if one wants to employ a cognition from mere understanding, e.g. the necessity of the law of causality, then one must

[p. XXXIV]

first have proved that this law holds, and then says: that cannot be proved, therefore we are not entitled to presuppose that law. Against this Kant shows *de facto* sufficiently: Hume’s final judgment is false, for in human cognition there are universal and necessary cognitions; but he does not deny Hume’s presupposition: *if we want to use these, we must first have proved them*; rather he himself attempts such a proof, which he calls the transcendental.

In this the inconsistency was soon noticed, that he, in order to prove those principles, always already presupposes their truth (as, for example, Aenesidemus and Maimon showed us); no one noticed clearly enough the falsity of the Humean prejudice, and so one came upon the hypothesis: there must be in our science a still higher domain of the immediately certain, in which there is as yet no talk of causality and the like, from which, rather, the validity of such laws can first be secured. This reasoning produced the absurdities of Fichte’s *Doctrine of Science*. His speculation directed him first of all to the I, which occurred in ordinary cognition as cause; he wanted to deny this out of existence by force, and asserted now that the I is an act, an acting without an agent, an effect without a cause.

We, on the contrary, say against the prejudice itself: proof is not the last founder of truth in our cognition. It is a fact that in our cognition

[p. XXXV]

sensible intuition and necessary and universal cognition are united, whether this union be sound or not, we want first only to observe how it actually comes about; we must therefore presuppose this cognition *as a whole*, and subject it to investigation *as we find it*, with its substances, causes and qualities; a further decision can then first become the result of our investigation.

#### 3) Kantian Prejudice.

In the Kantian *Critique of Reason* the concept of the transcendental is of very frequent use. Transcendental cognition he calls the cognition of the possibility and applicability of cognitions *a priori* (*Crit. of Pure Reason*, p. 80); he speaks of transcendental faculties of mind, and calls by that name those from which principles of cognitions *a priori* spring; these he vindicates for philosophy, and holds it, e.g., very important thereby to withdraw the feeling of pleasure in the sublime from mere empirical psychology. Finally, however, he also speaks of transcendental principles in opposition to metaphysical ones; here the former are such as subsist by themselves from pure cognitions *a priori*, whereas in metaphysical ones a concept *a priori* is always applied to a concept that is first to be given through experience. Whoever wants to compare this precisely will notice that Kant with his transcendental cognition properly means the psychological,

[p. XXXVI]

or better anthropological cognition, whereby we see which cognitions *a priori* our reason possesses, and how they arise in it. E.g. the principle that every alteration has a cause is metaphysical, but *the insight that this principle is found in our understanding, and how it must be applied*, is transcendental, and the critique of reason differs precisely in this from philosophy itself, that it contains the transcendental cognition, whereas the latter contains the logical and metaphysical.

Kant, however, made the great error of taking transcendental cognition for a kind of cognition *a priori*, and indeed a philosophical one, and of misjudging its empirical psychological nature. This error is an unavoidable consequence of that other, which we have just reproved, that he confounded philosophical deduction with a kind of proof, which he called transcendental proof.

Admittedly he also could not concede that his transcendental cognition is empirical, unless he wished to concede that Locke and Hume were entirely right. For if he proved his cognition *a priori* from the transcendental principle, e.g. of the possibility of experience, he would be grounding it on this, letting it spring from it; and if this were therefore empirical, his whole cognition *a priori* would after all rest again on an empirical ground, and would have *sprung* from perception.

For him who does not correct this mistake for himself, there lies in the Kantian system an insurmountable absurdity,

[p. XXXVII]

in that through the apriority of transcendental cognition inner perception itself is made cognition *a priori*, and so, instead of the Kantian transcendental idealism, an absurd empirical idealism would result, according to which the I would be not only the self-creator of its world, but even of itself.

This misconception is the cause that Kant never grasped the essence of reflection, and was unable to unite sense and understanding in *one* reason. It gave him the repugnance to empirical psychology and inner self-observation, which in some of his pupils, e.g. in Fichte, turned into a real aversion. Erhard Schmid noticed very early that the knot of the critique must properly be loosed in anthropology, but the general prejudice did not let him get a hearing. Every previous treatment of the critique of reason suffers from this prejudice, and the greatest errors were all made through its natural consequence, that one took inner perception for the source of cognitions *a priori*. Hence the *immediate consciousness* in Reinhold and others, hence the Fichtean *inner and intellectual intuition*, and the complete relapse into dogmatic rationalism in Schelling.

We shall seek to meet this error by making the subjective, empirical, anthropological essence of transcendental cognition quite distinct, and by stating more precisely the distinction of deduction and proof.

[p. XXXVIII]

So much, then, about and against the prejudices that we have to fear in the present spirit of speculation. We ask further: what task is now properly set us, in order to help the cause of speculation further? The answer lies in the historical presentation given. The history of philosophy drives us to the question: How is the immediate cognition of reason constituted, on which our philosophical conviction rests? and in what relation does it stand to reflection? I hold, therefore, my new development of the faculty of self-cognition, of how it develops itself from inner sense up to complete reflection, to be the most important and decisive point of my presentation, whereby we then at the same time obtain a new presentation of the grounds of the validity of all cognition.

Let us ask, then: what is the need of speculation in our time? the answer is still always the same as formerly: self-cognition in regard to cognizing, investigation of our faculty of cognition, investigation of reason. Locke, Leibniz and Hume called it the investigation of the human understanding, to the recent eclectics it was the task of empirical psychology, Kant called it the critique of reason, we will call it *philosophical anthropology*. If we see what lasting advances have been made in the history of philosophy through the efforts of a single man, these always lie in the domain of the investigation of our faculty of cognition, whereas everything else, like a mere matter of fashion,

[p. XXXIX]

moves now forward, now backward. This investigation is the true *philosophia prima* of Bacon and Descartes; the system of every philosopher proceeds, thought more darkly or more clearly, from a certain basic hypothesis about the origin of cognition in reason, and is itself only the consequence of the individual view of this first.

The need of all speculation can thus be expressed: We do not yet know the nature of our mind exactly enough to exhibit in it the origin of all our convictions. So much, however, is certain, that if we learned to know the essence of reason deeply enough, we should be able to judge from it all laws of speculation and all philosophy, for our cognition of the world is, as cognition, always only an activity of my reason, and can be investigated as such. For whoever understands the essence of philosophy even a little sees this: we create no world, and make no nature with our speculation, but we want only to learn to know the rules according to which the correct human view of the divine and the earthly of the world takes place in our mind. Everything thus depends on investigating the essence of our mind so far as is necessary in order to find in it the source of knowledge, and thereby to see whether we possess philosophy, and which philosophy is necessarily found in us.

Self-cognition is thus the demand, investigation of reason, knowledge of the inner nature of the mind, anthropology! Before this, philosophy has hitherto often

[p. XL]

shown a certain shyness; some, e.g. Kant, held it impossible, others dangerous, still others at least did not dare to treat it for itself as a separate science, but always mixed it with the physiology of the human body, and those who treated it best brought it therein only to an enumeration or classification of the faculties of mind, but never to a true *theory of inner life*.

It will therefore be necessary to set out the essence of our philosophical anthropology, and its relation to philosophy, still more distinctly.

By anthropology one understands either *pragmatic* anthropology, knowledge of men as knowledge of the world, as an art of judging men in their actions, or *physiological* anthropology, a natural science of man as a systematic science. This physiological anthropology receives in turn a threefold meaning. Man finds himself, as it were, in two different worlds. First, he recognizes himself at the summit of the organized formations in nature as an organized living body, but then a world of his own also opens to him in inner self-consciousness. This determines for us the object of three different sciences. The first considers the outer of man, his body, its natural functions, and is called *medical anthropology* or physiology. The second occupies itself with the inner of man, as he becomes the object of inner self-cognition, according to ordinary treatment

[p. XLI]

it is called empirical psychology, we want to call it *philosophical anthropology*. Finally, the third science is to compare the outer and inner of man and to exhibit the connection between the two; it is usually called philosophical anthropology, but for us it shall be called *comparative anthropology*.

The domain of philosophical anthropology is thus only inner experience, its object man as we know ourselves inwardly. This inner experience, to be sure, hangs together very closely with the outer appearances of our body; the movements of the body and the affections of the mind are throughout in a reciprocal dependence on one another; but notwithstanding this the domains of outer and inner experience do not mix at all, rather each rests on its own closed circle of perceptions, even though outer perceptions often come to the aid of inner observation. For the object of the former is made up by matter, that of the other by inner activities of the mind. However interesting, therefore, a general investigation is that compares the constitutions and states of the mind, as they are inwardly cognized, with the organs and movements of the body that correspond to them: yet the investigation of the nature of our mind is not in such a dependence on the investigation of the nature of the body animated by it, that the one could not also take place without the other.

[p. XLII]

Rather, each contains parts in which it is wholly independent of the other, and with regard to that which is only an object of inner experience, philosophical anthropology has an exclusive right of property. For just as the physiologist in his investigations of the nature of the organized body may take no account whatever, for his theory, of a mind animating it, so one can also in philosophical anthropology investigate the mind merely from inner experience, without yet bringing this into connection with the constitution of the organized body, for it is always advantageous for the correction and extension of our knowledge to keep what is separate separate, and to present separately also such investigations as take place independently of one another. Indeed, the most essential disadvantage for the science of which we speak was that one mixed its finer investigations so much with hypotheses with regard to the body; wanted to explain memory, imagination and much else materially, and thereby lost sight of the idea of an inner lawfulness of the mind, of a theory of reason, altogether. But only from this separated experimental physics of the inner can the great gain for philosophy be promised. Attempts at comparative anthropology could succeed only when the physiological theory of the human body and the anthropological theory of the human mind had advanced to a sufficient perfection, in order that the comparisons

[p. XLIII]

could be made sufficiently determinate, whereas up to now this science consists for the most part only of empty formulas, which, if fortune is kind, may perhaps someday be filled in.

We have to do here, then, only with physiological anthropology, in so far as this occupies itself solely with the human mind as the object of inner experience; we proceed here from an inner experimental physics, whose experiments and observations each makes only in himself, and seek thereby to arrive at an inner natural science as a theory of reason. That would then be the science that one usually called psychology; we depart, however, from this usage for several reasons. The word psyche, soul, is taken in philosophy for the metaphysical, persistent, simple and immortal essence of the mind, and thus becomes entangled with presuppositions which we may not take into account for the present. We are concerned only with a natural science of the human mind, as it is obtained through inner experience. We want to treat as little a doctrine of the soul as a doctrine of spirits, for we know no other mind than that which thinks, and no other thinking being than man; we have to do, therefore, only with inner anthropology. In this limitation to the human mind we should have as our theme the experiential doctrine of the soul, or empirical psychology. But also from this science differs

[p. XLIV]

our task. The experiential doctrine of the soul is an inner experimental physics that for itself always remains fragmentary; with this we do not want to content ourselves, but we want to raise ourselves to a theory of inner life, to an inner natural science; our idea is an analogue of that which, for inner spiritual nature, we now call philosophy of nature in the case of outer physics. Our philosophical anthropology is no history of reason, of how it develops in the child into the adult, into the old man, how it appears in waking and sleeping, how it is shaded according to sex and constitution, people and race, or how it is injured and destroyed in bodily and mental illnesses. These are tasks for empirical psychology; we seek, on the contrary, a description of reason, in order to arrive at a theory of it, as it lies, in healthy specimens generally, before the eyes of everyone’s inner observation.

This is precisely that about which hitherto commonly almost nothing intelligible is thought; the important thing that is to be observed here is rather mostly held to be impossible, and yet it is precisely this inner natural science that must be of the most important influence on all philosophy. It is the true fundamental investigation of all philosophy; its standpoint is the only *standpoint of evidence for speculative things*.

This its relation to philosophy will become clear through what follows.

[p. XLV]

Every individual fact, that I know this or that, that I cognize this or that individual object, is an object of inner experience. There is thus for every cognition a twofold standpoint of consideration: on the one hand an object belongs to each cognition, which is to be cognized in it, and then I must become conscious to myself of the cognition itself in turn, if I am to be able to judge about it. I can consider every cognition now subjectively, in so far as it is my activity, and then objectively, in regard to its object. E.g., I catch sight of a tree, I can distinguish it by its growth from many other kinds of tree, its less rough bark, its rounder, smoother leaves distinguish it from the elm, I recognize it by the scent of its blossoms for a linden, and can now extend my knowledge of it to the whole natural history of this kind of tree. On the other hand, however, I can ask: how do I arrive at this knowledge? and I see at once: underlying it are perceptions that contain the intuition of this tree, which reach me through touch, sight and smell. I find that an influence of the tree on my eye, on the nerves of smell or of touch takes place, that in a certain correspondence with this my mind receives sensations through a receptivity called sense, which however are still far from making up the whole cognition of the tree, not even the complete intuition of it, but only contain, e.g., in sight, a manifold of colors,

[p. XLVI]

without a determination of the mathematical in my representation of the tree, without a determination of the distance from me, of the parts among one another, etc. I see that these mathematical determinations come to be added to the representation only through activities of my imagination, partly voluntary, mostly guided by habit. Beyond these I then need further concepts and judgments of the understanding, in order to make the cognition complete, etc. etc.

Here, then, the inner history of cognizing itself is evidently, according to the second way of considering, an object of inner anthropology, the cognition may be of whatever kind it will. Our philosophical knowledge too will thus, in so far as we want to become conscious of it in turn, be able to be considered from an anthropological point of view. Indeed, this anthropological view of philosophical cognition is just of decisive importance for philosophy.

Experience, subjectively, first needs a foreign stimulation through sense in order to come into our mind; philosophical cognition, however, is to be the pure property of reason, to spring only from itself, to depend only on its self-activity. If we could therefore put ourselves in possession of an anthropological theory of reason, we should be by this exactly in a position to determine which philosophical cognitions we possess at all, which alone we can possess, and how they can be correctly applied. The complete problem that Locke wished to set for

[p. XLVII]

speculation, in that he says: it should first investigate the human understanding, in order to learn to know its powers, or the problem that Kant afterwards called a critique of reason, is nothing other than our philosophical anthropology.

We must at first leave the ordinary, merely objective view of considering cognitions, and limit ourselves solely to the subjective, anthropological one; the other will fall to us afterward of itself. Ordinarily we consider our cognition only through its object, and call it, e.g., true when it agrees with its object; this, however, is not the correct relation for a secure observation. Through this we must unavoidably come to doubt all our philosophical conviction and in the end all truth in our cognition. For in the case of the eternal truths, the universal and necessary laws, the cognitions *a priori*, or however else we may wish to call philosophical cognition, it strikes the eye at once that we cannot make them true through their object, in that we can think the object only mediately through them, and cannot compare it with them. We shall, on the contrary, bring this riddling necessity to another, quite anthropological expression, in that we characterize them as that cognitive activity of our reason which belongs to it constantly in every state of its activity, from which then its relations can be judged far more easily. For if I want to learn to know my cognitions securely,

[p. XLVIII]

I must only subjectively first observe the cognition itself; this is my activity, and belongs to me, whatever object it may have. The object may be outside me or in me, the cognition is always in me, and so I must first observe it, learn to know its laws and the laws of the faculties from which it springs, before I can judge with success about how it stands with the object that corresponds to it. In this, then, consists our proposal for philosophy, that we want to subject all our cognitions first to such an anthropological observation before we venture to judge about their truth and fitness. If we have arrived in this way at a theory of reason, then we shall also be able to speak with certainty about validity and truth.

That is to say, our task becomes philosophical anthropology as a theoretical inner natural science. Our investigation begins on the standpoint, to be chosen with circumspection, of empirical psychology or inner self-observation, where we must guard against clouding the pure fact right at the start with ideal metaphysical presuppositions, where, however, we also do not stop at the merely descriptive part of the experiential doctrine of the soul, with its this and that class of faculties of mind and their occurring varieties, but where we use this pure fact only as ground, from which a rational induction according to well-chosen heuristic maxims proceeds, in order to raise itself to the general laws of our inner life, and thus to

[p. XLIX]

a physical theory of this life purely according to its spiritual relations.

For this our purpose we find the most substantial preliminary works in the Kantian *Critiques of Reason*, those first philosophical masterpieces. Indeed, it might well be asserted that Kant was the first who, without seeing ghosts, and yet also without mixing himself up with the material, found the idea of our science with regard to an overview of the whole; he was indeed the first who rose thus above the merely describing psychology, even though this idea only dimly floated before him. In many parts his investigation has been brought to completion, in others we must improve it, and in several give it the missing completion. What, however, compels us to subject his work to a thorough re-working is in the end solely his misapprehension of inner sense and of the essence of reflection, whose consequences spread to the very smallest detail over the whole.

The course of our investigation would be simple, easy and clear (in that we only put together observations and derive universal laws from them), if the false pretensions of psychological fanatics and enthusiasts did not step into our way. Psychological fanatical enthusiasm, namely, mixes its own arbitrary reasoning with inner perception, and confounds imagination with inner experience; false psychological enthusiasm for the spiritual, and the freedom of the genial, wants, on the other hand, to entertain its hearers only with fine sound

[p. L]

and thinks its divinity and holiness already profaned if anyone wishes to subject poetizing, philosophizing and character to an explanation. In these two inner self-observation has two great enemies. Enthusiasm we can and must for the most part leave to its fate; one cannot easily argue with it, for it arises either from a lack of properly scientific sense, to which dry theoretical truth therefore finds no access, or only from a lack of cultivated judgment about the laws of inner life, and then it will lose its credit of itself without dispute when firmer judgments about these objects become more general. The confusion of reasoning with observation, on the other hand, we must never lose sight of; we must ourselves be on our guard against it, for it often misleads in inner observation the most practiced thinkers to the most obvious absurdities. In this inner observation the mind is absolutely left to itself alone; there it is often hard for it to distinguish the most diverse kinds of its activities; it will therefore easily take inferences from falsely presupposed impossibilities for pure observation of facts, and so deceive itself in a way in which it is extremely hard to find the error again once it has been committed.

[scan 63]

## Critique

of

## Cognizing Reason.

[scan 65]

### Introduction.

#### The Life of the Human Mind in General.

#### §. 1.

#### a) External and Internal Nature.

Like a flower closed in upon itself, which does not blossom toward an external light but comes into contact with what is external only through stem and leaf, our inner life is bound to the form of self-cognition. All our knowledge of the inner nature of our mind is, by its nature, only self-cognition, from which the mind can learn to understand itself only in itself, but according to no external relation at all. I can indeed observe in myself how I think and cognize, what and how I feel, desire and will, and for this an explanatory inner natural science can also be sketched. But how this life of mine is stimulated from without, how an object which I think and cognize comes into contact with my thinking and cognizing, how my acting will could work on something outside it; how the history of my life could begin, one mind arise through another

[p. 4]

or comes into community with the other, there can be, in human reason, absolutely no explanatory natural science, precisely because my mind is wholly isolated in its inner self-cognition, and hence no external relation can be observed through it. A philosophy of nature for the inner life of the mind therefore extends, with its theory, only to the inner history of a single human being and the organization of his mind. This remark reminds us of the supreme physical result of all speculation, in relation to which it first acquires its full significance. So as not to become disoriented in what follows, we wish to draw attention to it here in advance. The chief relations of theoretical natural science cannot indeed be new, but there are some that, the better known they are, are all the more easily overlooked, or at least have their consequences not duly heeded. To these belongs especially the most general relation of the inner and outer natural science.

The standpoint for nature in general is not the highest in our mind, but shows us the essence of things only in a subjectively limited way, above which we can raise ourselves only through ideas. In these subjective limitations, through which nature becomes for us mere appearance, there lies also the ground of an opposed inner and outer view of things. Matter and mind here stand over against each other, and are cognized according to wholly different laws.

With regard to the spiritual we cognize immediately only our own inner life and the organization of our own reason; thoughts and mind outside us we find only by analogies, mediately, through matter.

[p. 5]

Matter, however, we cognize immediately according to wholly different views. First, through sensation-representations such as color, sound and fragrance, we cognize it merely according to relations to our spiritual life; it has color, sounds and smells only for our cognizing mind; one matter in relation to another, by contrast, is the movable and moving in space only according to mathematical laws.

Now the principle of all explanations lies in the homogeneity of that which differs only in magnitude; there is therefore a twofold theoretical natural science, in which the explanations of the one part cannot reach over into those of the other; a theory of the inner spiritual life only for the one human mind, and a mathematical theory of outer nature, must be possible. But between outer and inner nature there is no theoretical contact at all; neither may matter be explained according to the laws of inner life, which are qualitatively wholly different from it, nor the mind according to the laws of the material. There is therefore, neither for matter nor for mind, theory or explanation with regard to external relations of the spiritual.

Motion and inner activity are two distinct modes of appearance of things; the former knows only a law of external relations, the other confines itself only to the inner side of *one individual life*; both run alongside one another on the two sides of a chasm which can be filled up by no philosophy and no theory. For the material relations of sensation there can be no talk at all of anything being explained, and for inner nature we must leave the body, with its organization and its motions, wholly out of

[p. 6]

play if we wish to become acquainted with the inner law. To be sure, down to the smallest detail the organization and the motion in it is the most exact correlate of the spiritual activity; but however exactly organ and expression of life may correspond to one another here and there, there can nonetheless be no talk at all of an explanatory theoretical connection between the two. For here wholly different qualities are apprehended, and whoever has rightly grasped what explaining means sees that no explanation can lead across from one quality to another.

#### §. 2.

#### b) The Mind.

We are here seeking a theoretical inner natural science, and can therefore draw only from the inner consciousness of ourselves. The characteristic of this inner perception is that in each single case it expresses itself through an: I think, I cognize, I feel, I desire, I will. So that in inner perception one of my inner activities each time presents itself to me as belonging to me, the I.

We distinguish in this source of inner experience and of self-cognition a pure self-consciousness, the “I am”, and then the single intuition of my activity, of which the former determines, as it were, only the form. This I of self-consciousness is now the one and abiding object of inner perception, whereby I distinguish its object from every thing outside me, and to which I must ascribe everything that occurs in inner perception as its activity. Careful linguistic usage calls this I as the

[p. 7]

ever self-same object of inner experience *the human mind*, in order to free itself from all the metaphysical secondary meanings of the words soul and spirit. We too, in what follows, wish to consider only the I as object of experience, setting aside all metaphysical disputes about the true essence of the thinking being; by *mind*, as by human spirit, human reason, we therefore always understand only this inner object of one’s own consciousness.

The most general relations of the self-cognition of the human mind we cannot survey better than under the following numbers, as Kant gives them:

1) I think; I am inwardly active.

2) I think as subject; immediately I perceive not myself, but only individual ones of my activities, to which I belong only as subject of the activity.

3) I think as a single, individual subject.

4) I think as the same subject of all my thinking. Even though I can become determinately conscious of the whole history of my life in time only through the external relation to the history of my body, still for the whole extent of my inner self-consciousness the I is determined as one and the same object.

But since we do not wish here to undertake, from these moments, metaphysical investigations of materialism and spiritualism, or of the simplicity and immortality of the soul, we need only examine more closely the first two determinations: what is inner activity? and what is the I as the subject of it?

[p. 8]

#### §. 3.

#### c) Inner Activity.

All investigations of inner activity are burdened, by the mere concept of it, with two difficulties, of which the one has been contrived by speculation, while the other lies naturally in the matter itself.

For we perceive immediately only the single expression of life, the action of the mind, and not the mind itself; the mind we add in thought to its action only through the concept of causality. Against this arise the difficulties of all speculation about causality. This first difficulty has recently, especially by Fichte, been declared important, and his view has had a wide influence on the whole new philosophy of nature.

Fichte asserted first: the I is a mere act, an acting without anything acting, a life without anything living, a deed without anything doing it. With this view Schelling went further into philosophy of nature, wished here too to proceed only from acting alone, from mere productivity without product and without substratum of being. This accorded very well with the wish to free philosophy of nature from the dead mathematical law of mass. The process in nature, according to its mere form, as magnetism, electricity or organization, was now sufficient to itself, without being bound to the underlying substance of mass; one imagined that one had transformed everything into life.

But the whole proposal is utterly untenable; here an abstraction is demanded which no human being is actually in a position to carry out. As little as we are able to intuit the color

[p. 9]

detached from the surface of the body, which we represent as colored, by itself alone, just as little will we succeed in actually thinking mere activity without a subject to which it belongs.

Fichte wished to satisfy the coarsest empiricism and the highest speculation at once, by singling out this mere acting without substratum, of which we are first of all conscious, and wishing to hold it fast for itself. But in this he could satisfy himself only through delusion.

Inner activity, the acting of the I, is here only a particular case; the general demand is to think all happening, all becoming, all alteration without a substratum which becomes and through which something becomes, but only naked becoming for itself. We have here, then, properly to do with the general speculative relation of becoming to being.

Whoever observes himself carefully enough in this regard will find that we can think becoming and a law of becoming only through activity, but that activity and acting are one and the same, and acting is that which belongs to the cause. Where we cognize activity, therefore, there we also cognize the cause of it. As Kant said: becoming is the schema of the concept of causality; where experience shows a becoming, the understanding necessarily adds in thought the relation of cause and effect. Skeptical scruples against the use of causes and effects cannot be removed by our thinking becoming without cause; rather, if they have ground, it would follow that the whole manner of representation, which cannot, without cause and effect,

[p. 10]

take place, that the whole manner of representation of becoming in general would have no reality.

How far this is right or wrong we need not investigate here; so much, however, is certain, that wherever we speak of activity, something active is already presupposed, and that only both together, activity and something active, acting and something acting, can have meaning or not.

So the outcome also shows it: the attempted improvement is not so seriously meant; afterwards one speaks again of understanding, imagination and other faculties of the thinking mind, and in outer nature one adds powers to mere happening.
