Thus the causal relation of the active I to its activity is wholly present in all our self-cognition, and determines the form of this, so that there is talk only of determinate faculties of the mind and their expression.

#### §. 4.

This relation of cause and effect, however, is the only wholly immediate one of its kind in our cognition, and for that reason is unavoidably difficult in its application. The second difficulty arises thus: if we wish to represent a thing distinctly to ourselves, we must compare it with others and perceive in this agreement and difference. Here now the case of the inner life and its activity is a wholly unique one, which no other in our cognition equals.

The essential of life consists in this, that here an acting occurs, as activity in itself, without relation to anything else, an acting without anything acted upon,

[p. 11]

an acting through which nothing becomes except the action itself, e.g. in representing and cognizing. All external causal relations consist in this, that a cause alters the state of another thing, that the accidents of a matter are altered by powers. Light warms a body or bleaches its color; one body alters the motion of another by attraction. In all these cases there is, besides the dependence of *acting*, *another thing effected* as the proper effect, not only an attracting of the attractor, but also altered motion of the attracted. In immediate inner living activity, e.g. of representing, there is by contrast no such thing acted upon, but mere action purely for itself.

It can also easily be shown how inner intuition can contain just such an activity and nothing else. Isolated for itself it contains a mere succession in time. If this is now to be brought under objective synthetic unity in experience, this can happen only through the schema of a lawful time-sequence, i.e. through the category of cause and effect. What is alterable, given in inner intuition, is therefore determined immediately as effect, a determinable, for which the determining, the I, is there as object of pure self-consciousness. The I is therefore cognized through inner intuition only as the thinking one, by means of thinking as its activity; the object of inner intuition must immediately be a wholly pure activity, whose existence is determined only as dependence on another, but not as inherence in another.

Just as the most general determination of matter as object of outer nature is: matter is the movable

[p. 12]

in space, so the most general determination of the I, as object of inner nature, is: I am the inwardly active in time.

But being in motion is only a relative determination, which belongs to one matter in relation to another, whereas inner activity, thinking, belongs to the mind not in relation to anything else, but absolutely for itself as its action. Thinking is not, like every external activity, cognized only from alterations as their cause, but immediately as alterable activity itself. The relative consists here in this, that the I is cognized only through the relation to its thinking, as the cause of it, but not in external relations of its activity to something else.

The original activity of the I is therefore an action absolutely, without any outcome of it other than that action has taken place, without anything acted upon; (just like the mere being-in-motion of matter, except that here there is talk of an immediate activity; whereas motion consists only in a relative state.) To be sure, there also occur in the mind efficacies that have an outcome, e.g. in desiring and willing, but this outcome can inwardly be only an aroused, altered activity; it must itself be activity, and ultimately such an original one, which itself has no further outcome, but subsists only in and through itself. To thinking there belongs an existence which is determined merely according to the relation of ground and consequence, as dependence, and not according to the relation of subject and predicate, as inherence.

[p. 13]

This activity held within itself we must observe closely for two reasons. First, it is the characteristic of life. The expulsion of all death from nature, so celebrated of late, has succeeded only through an indeterminate concept of life. One confuses either the organism with the living, which after all consists only in motions, or one calls every expression of power whatever life, which should not be. Both for the organism and for the expression of power of matter we use the word life only figuratively; life is only in inner activity, i.e., in thinking. In the material world all happening and becoming is only being-in-motion or arousal of motion. Being in motion is something dead, for it is a mere suffering without doing; the arousal of motion through attraction or repulsion of matter, however, is likewise only dead expression of power, in which one mass always shows its power only on another; life, by contrast, is only where a being is active in itself.

Second, the very fact that the concept of living activity does not occur at all in external experience causes the greatest misunderstandings here with regard to the inner, and for this reason we shall soon have to appeal again in detail to this exposition, since all previous theories of representing and cognizing have overlooked this law of living activity, and have always brought an object acted upon to it.

#### §. 5.

#### d) The Faculties of the Mind.

It has already been discussed here that in inner experience I do not intuit myself, but cognize myself only as subject

[p. 14]

of my inner activity. I cognize myself as cause of my inner activity, and therefore ascribe to myself faculties or powers of this activity.

Here again, in the dispute with metaphysical pretensions concerning inner experience, an exact distinction between faculty and power has been established, which indeed has its ground. We wish here, however, to content ourselves with remarking once and for all that, even where we speak of powers, we nonetheless make no further pretensions than those made for faculties of the mind. The distinction is this: power is the predicate of the substance, through which it is thought absolutely as cause; faculty the predicate of any subject whatever, through which it is thought as cause, irrespective of whether the effect belongs to it absolutely or only under certain conditions, whether it is substance, or exists as accident of another.

By the fact, then, that I attribute a power to a being, I at the same time place the whole cause of the effect unrestrictedly in it; by the fact that I attribute to it merely a faculty, it remains undetermined whether something else is not further required, as acting upon the subject, in order to bring the effect about. A faculty for an effect I can therefore at once attribute to a thing, when I cognize it as acting, whether it be restricted therein or not. Original attraction and repulsion I ascribe to material substance absolutely as power, but to the ripening fruit, e.g., I shall, according to this usage of words, attribute only the faculty of coloring itself. So we are certainly entitled to ascribe to the mind faculties of its inner activity, but whether the powers for it belong to it wholly, that demands proofs, in so far as it as substance

[p. 15]

exists, and how far it acts independently of anything else or not.

In what follows, then, we speak in general only of the faculties of the I for its inner activity, as these are grasped immediately from inner experience.

#### §. 6.

Now the little-heeded most general laws of these faculties constitute the first foundation of all our following investigations for the theory of inner nature; we must therefore draw them here as sharply as possible. The laws of inner activity are the following:

1) All causal relations of inner experience must be ascribed to the faculty of the mind as the cause, and not to the activity as its expression, since the existence of the latter is determined only as dependence.

That whose existence is determined only as dependence is also thought only as predicate of another; any action upon the dependent is here therefore action upon the subject of it, to which the causality belongs. E.g., to the sun as substance belongs the power to attract the earth at a certain distance with determinate velocity. Here the first cause is the moving power of the sun, the effect motion of the earth; but this effect is determined not only as dependence with respect to the sun, but at the same time as inherence with respect to the earth, and so it can be annulled or altered by some other moving power, without the attracting power of the sun being acted upon. But the first effect of the moving power of the

[p. 16]

sun, which is determined only as dependence, is a certain degree of attraction at a determinate distance; this attraction exists only as dependence, and therefore also cannot be altered without altering the power of the sun itself. In the latter relation, however, stand the inner activities of the I to its faculty; they are only dependences, and therefore one can act upon them only through the faculties.

2) In regard to the states of mind, therefore, states of the expressing activity of a faculty and states of the faculties themselves must be distinguished. The former are the first grounds of cognition in inner experience, the latter the grounds of explanation to which the former must be traced back.

3) If a faculty or a power consists, according to the law of its efficacy, merely in altering the state of a thing according to a rule (as is the case with all external effects, hence with all powers of matter, but also with many inner activities of the mind), then its essence consists in a relation; if this relation now occurs, it is efficacious, if it vanishes, its efficacy also ceases, the power becomes latent, as it were, without being annulled by an opposed activity, merely because the case in which it can act is not present. E.g., the power of a magnet when no iron is nearby. The case now occurs also with faculties of the mind, e.g. with the will, which as disposition can always remain the same, but yet comes to expression only on individual occasions.

But because inwardly only activity is given, such a faculty can consist only in this, that it modifies other faculties with respect to their expression,

[p. 17]

as e.g. sense acts upon the faculty of intuition, the will upon attention. Such faculties of the mind we can therefore *call mediate*, since they have their subsistence only through others; on the other hand there must also be *immediate* faculties of inner activity underlying them, which can show their expression for themselves, and are active absolutely according to a law of their own efficacy. So e.g. thinking and cognizing. These are indeed also, in their expressions, subject to the occasional stimulations of sense, but their *expressing themselves* does not consist in altering something else, but in mere inner activity absolutely.

4) Through these immediate faculties the mind properly shows its life, and for that reason its first activity must rest on an inner cause.

5) A faculty of the mind, in the state of its activity, so far as this were an enduring one, presupposes no other acting cause of it. But every alteration of its activity, in degree or in kind, presupposes another cause for it. This follows from wholly general laws of nature. In nature every thing persists in its once-given state if no cause of alteration of it is there, or comes to be added. Every faculty of the mind therefore persists in its once-given state of activity if there is no cause of alteration; every transition from one state to another, however, requires such a cause. If a faculty of the mind is once set into activity, it will act persistently, with a determinate degree of activity, in constant outflow.

[p. 18]

Often this simple law has been overlooked, and then a great fuss has been made about explanations where there was nothing to explain, while at other times one has quickly contented oneself where nothing was yet explained. The former, e.g., in the theory of memory, the latter in the theory of reflection.

6) Since there are alterable states of inner activity, causes must obtain for the manner of expression of faculties of the mind. In the case of lifeless matter these can only be *outer* ones, but in the mind *inner* ones obtain as well. Besides the action upon it from without, and its effect outward, inner faculties of it too can act on one another; indeed there can be mediate inner faculties whose activity consists only in determining the expression of other faculties.

7) No law of equality of inner effect and counter-effect can be specified, because the concept of inner activity is not to be constructed *a priori*.

The object of outer experience is represented wholly *a priori* as the movable in space; motion, whose concept is constructed, is the only effect in outer experience, but is at the same time also thought as inherence of the moved matter, and since it can belong only to different matters in relation to one another, it can be determined that between two bodies it can be effected only by means of equal motion and counter-motion. In inner experience, by contrast, the concepts of inner activity are determined only empirically, and are not constructible any further than that to every activity, and thus also to its faculty, there belongs a determinate degree, with which it fills time, which into

[p. 19]

the infinite can be thought larger or smaller with continuity. But as to its kind this activity cannot be brought under any constructible concept; it must simply be assumed as experience shows it. We must therefore also draw all causal laws here only from inner experience itself, without being able to determine them more closely according to an underlying law *a priori*.

8) The object of inner experience is a *system of faculties of the mind*.

Several faculties, which are thought as united in the same subject in interaction with one another, are called a system of faculties. The manifold appearances of inner experience can never, in the strictest sense, be explained from a single faculty of the mind, because then (according to 5) the state of the mind would have to be a persisting one without alteration. But all faculties are united in the I as a single subject, and so combined into one living whole; they belong together in one life.

#### §. 7.

9) The only mathematical law of nature which admits of an application to inner experience is the law of continuity in the flow of all alterations.

As a general law of nature the law of continuity must hold also for the flow of inner activities. All alterable states of my inner activity follow one another in time as states belonging to one subject; consequently all their alterations occur according to the law of continuity. All arising can take place only little by little, through gradual increase, all vanishing only little by little, through gradual decrease. A transition of the mind from one state to another can

[p. 20]

be very rapid, e.g. in the case of affects, but it is never a sudden leap; it always occurs continuously through all lower degrees.

Hence one also need not presuppose any complete annihilation of any inner activity that has once been there, since its degree, its intensive magnitude, can only be assumed as ever more and more diminished.

With this law the whole influence of mathematics on inner experience is also exhausted. For all inner magnitude is intensive magnitude of the activity or of the faculty. For this, however, no determinate measure obtains here, since no extensive magnitude can be brought into comparison with it, nor any indeterminate measurement either, since we have no fixed point from which we could start. The degree of every activity, the degree of every faculty, the degree of the whole power of the I, is alterable. The only measure, e.g. of the degree of strength of our representations, which we could still apply, is their greater or lesser clarity and distinctness. But even this yields no fixed determination; we here measure an activity by the force which it exerts upon inner sense in perception, but this effect will itself turn out differently with an equal degree of activity, according as the sense is affected from several sides or not, and according as the sense is at the moment more or less excitable.

10) The law of continuity in the flow of all inner alterations contains the rule for the sequence of the states of my inner activity, and thus for their whole determination of time, in so far as I perceive them immediately, for inwardly the manifold is given to me first of all only

[p. 21]

as successive in intuition. But the manifold expressing faculties of the I and their activities themselves are *at the same time*, and each stands under the law of the continuous flow of its activity. This simultaneity of several inner activities, of intuiting through all the senses, of thinking and cognizing, feeling, desiring and willing, is the most difficult thing for inner experience, since we cannot here, as externally in space, construct side by side, according to mathematical laws, what is apprehended successively, but can only unite it dynamically, as the effect of one and the same I.

From this arises the concept of the *composition* of an inner activity from several, which is constantly used in inner natural science, and whose relations one must make oneself exactly acquainted with in order afterwards to understand the applications, in almost every case, but especially in the theory of imagination. The difficulty lies precisely in the indeterminacy of those relations, for lack of mathematics.

The whole fact of such a composition, that I intuit, think and will at the same time, can be denied by crude empiricism or a speculation that misunderstands itself, because it does not lie immediately in the single inner perception. But it results with necessity from all the general laws underlying it here, especially from the continuous flow of the activity of each single faculty; without it not the smallest part of our inner history takes place, as we can show mediately from many experiences. Comparison, e.g., would not be possible if I were not *at the same time* conscious of the manifold to be compared,

[p. 22]

resolve and choice would not be possible if the different cases of choice were not simultaneously present to me, etc.

What we perceive immediately is the activity of the I, and only relatively through this does its faculty become determinable for us. The faculty contains the real ground of that, but the activity is the only ground of cognition of faculties.

Hence, as regards composition in my cognition, it is all one whether I assume that an activity is composed of different effects of several faculties, or whether I regard it as the effect of one faculty; further, whether I regard various simultaneously present activities as divided effects of the same faculty, or as effects of several faculties. The difference is then only a difference of expression.

But because to every activity and every power, in each single state, there belongs a determinate degree of strength, composition and division stand under the law that the sum of the degrees of the parts is equal to the degree of the whole. But of this proposition we can make no further application at all, because in the single case we cannot measure any degree. Yet we can derive from it some general corollaries. Many simultaneous expressions of one faculty must weaken one another, since they divide among themselves the degree of the whole; yet this law often hides itself very much when the activity is stimulated from without, the stimulation acts as a stimulus, and so raises the degree of the faculty itself. Further, a continuing activity can be weakened in two ways: first, when the same faculty is determined to several more expressions

[p. 23]

and then by the faculty itself becoming weaker.

In this merely relative determinability of faculty and power of the mind lies the warrant for systematizing reason to abstract, according to general marks which belong to several activities, general concepts of faculties, and through these to determine basic faculties, which serve the inner explanations as principle.

#### §. 8.

11) This derivation of the individual phenomena of inner activity from the basic faculties of the mind, and the unification of these basic faculties into a system, which presents the organization of our inner life in a determinate way, are the proper ends of inner natural science, for which much remains to be done, and for which we hope to give something new here.

The general fault of one-sided theorists, that they begin to explain before they yet know what is to be explained, and whether there is anything there at all that can be explained, or whether they are not just trying to derive the ground from the consequence, e.g. sense from imagination, shows itself nowhere more strongly and more often than here. The worst of it, however, is that all of them in fact lack the courage to venture even an attempt at a real theory of the inner life. One explains, to be sure, hither and thither around the outworks, but the first principle always remains: it is settled that the proper laws of our spiritual life elude all explanation and must remain a riddle, an opinion in which one is then, especially through the fear of lawless inner freedom

[p. 24]

(which one takes reflection to be), strengthened. For this reason our better anthropologists, when it comes to explaining, e.g., memory and fantasy, are at once occupied with the relation of the inner to the nerves and the brain, and console themselves there with arbitrary fictions, in which they themselves think nothing, since we understand far more of the inner functions of thinking than of those of the nerves and the brain. As to what concerns the inner, however, one distinguishes the faculties of cognition and of desire, reproductive and productive faculties, senses, imagination, understanding, power of judgment, reason, etc., as powers set outside and beside one another, which indeed work together into one life, but whose unification one finds most enigmatic. Against this it is now in all seriousness our intention to confine ourselves solely to the inner life, and to deliver here a true physical theory, in which it is shown, from the given basic properties of the human mind and its inner life, how everything derived had to take shape just as we find it, quite similarly to the procedure of mathematical physics, which traces individual facts back to general laws of motion, and from these explains them again.

But in order to show at the same time that we have been on our guard against the one-sidedness of those who, after the manner of present-day natural-philosophical constructions from elements which hold for the whole universe, claim to be in a position to explain this or that individual organism of the earth, a brief survey of our view of human life may follow here at once. The different moments of the organization of our mind, which cannot be derived from one another, are the following:

[p. 25]

a) Man is a *cognizing* being.

b) His cognition is *rational*.

c) His reason is bound to *outer* as well as to *inner* sense.

d) He possesses a *faculty of reflection*.

e) He cognizes not only the existence of things, but also has a faculty of *taking an interest*.

f) Finally, he has a faculty of *acting* in accordance with his interest.

All these determinations are basic determinations of our essence, of which none is wholly contained in another. For it does not lie in the concept of cognition that it must be rational, it does not lie in the concept of reason that it must be bound to senses, and not in the concept of finite reason that it must have precisely these outer and inner senses. Beings can be thought whose power of cognition would be organized in this respect wholly differently from ours. Further, it does not lie at all in the concept of a cognizing being that it must also have a faculty of taking an interest and of representing a worth of things, and finally we can think of feeling beings taking an interest which would nevertheless have no faculty at all of acting with will.

All the faculties named subsist, then, alongside one another in our mind in such a way that none is a mere consequence of another. We maintain, however, that once this organization of a sensible-rational being, taking an interest and acting, is given, the whole history of our life, down to the smallest articulations of the mind, is then explicable from the moments named. Not only memory and imagination, understanding, power of judgment and reason with their categories must, but also

[p. 26]

the whole human faculty of feelings of pleasure, desires and choice be explained from them, with just the determinateness with which we explain a solar eclipse and its time from the course of the moon. The means for arriving at such a theory are now nothing other than comparison, juxtaposition and classification of the individual inner activities, and if one has not long since arrived at significant results by this, the sole reason was that one did not go far enough with observation, and did not distinguish finely enough. The most important laws for the theory, which have hitherto been overlooked by the psychologists (e.g. that the faculty of pleasure and displeasure is no basic faculty, but only power of judgment, judging according to the rule of end and worth, or that the faculty of reflection is the faculty of voluntary re-observation of my inner activity) simply want to be seen; their truth gives itself only through observation.

For the method of theoretical treatment of these observations we must here still establish the following concepts.

12) According to the law of continuity in the flow of the activity of a cause, every cause is necessarily thought through a determinate law of its efficacy. This holds, then, also for faculties and powers; through them a being is thought not only as the cause in a single fact, in a single event, but absolutely as efficacious according to a certain law. The latter concept is presupposed every time when in a single event I call something cause, e.g. when in the single case I say: the powder is the cause that the cartridge

[p. 27]

ignited, I already presuppose a law according to which powder in general ignites.

So we come also to inner faculties of the mind, but the determination of these faculties always proceeds from single events, from singly perceived inner activities. Through this I am now indeed entitled to attribute to it indeterminately a faculty of acting in the manner occurring here, but the single inner perceptions lead only to the determination of very manifold, isolated faculties, which at first must be thought according to very restricted laws of efficacy, until abstraction separates out of them more general ones.

13) We must distinguish *basic powers and derived* powers, of which the former belong to a being absolutely immediately, while the others are only consequences of underlying basic powers. This distinction can also be transferred to faculties, whereby the concept of a derived faculty presents no difficulty, that of a basic faculty, however, can hold only relatively, since the subject of the faculty itself has only a relatively determinate existence, and it is not settled whether any basic powers belong to it, or whether its power is not grounded in another.

But since the mind is nevertheless the last immediate object of our inner experience, since it occurs there as ultimate subject, the concept of a basic faculty acquires for inner natural science a determinate meaning after all; it becomes the immediate predicate of its subject, and no further explanation can be demanded of its possibility.

The task of a theory of inner nature is therefore to explain the

[p. 28]

derived faculties of the mind from its basic faculties.

We can aim at this only by uniting many inner activities and the faculties corresponding to them under a general concept. In this way, however, there arise at first only *generic concepts of faculties of the mind*, e.g. faculty of representation, imagination, which must not be confused with basic faculties. The subordination of particular faculties under generic ones must be well distinguished from the subordination of derived faculties under basic faculties, in that the former belongs only to the classification of concepts, the latter to a natural system of grounds and consequences. A generic faculty designates only a general determination of a kind of faculty in general, or among the various faculties of one subject; one can indeed subordinate various faculties to it, as the particular to the general, but cannot derive them from it according to their essence and their actuality. The basic faculty, on the contrary, is a determinate, particular property of a being; thus in matter the original powers of extension and attraction are basic powers, whereas the concept of a moving power in general is only such a generic determination. Inwardly, the concept of imagination as an intuition without the presence of its object is a merely generic concept, in that two faculties wholly heterogeneous in their origin, the productive and the reproductive imagination, are grasped under one concept. Likewise representation is a more general concept than cognition: all cognitions are representations, but there are many representations, concepts and imaginings which in themselves are not yet cognitions. Notwithstanding this, the

[p. 29]

faculty of cognition is the basic faculty of all theoretical faculties of representation, from which every kind of theoretical representing is only derived, and representing is here a mere generic determination.

Such generic determinations are therefore important only in passing, before one arrives at the theory, and for language; the theory rests only on the basic faculties. These emerge of themselves as soon as self-observation attains a certain completeness; but the surest guidance for approaching them lies in the principles *a priori*, or the principles of the necessity of our cognition. The faculties of these principles Kant has already separated from the others, fairly completely, as *transcendental faculties of the mind*; they are of the greatest importance for our theory, because, on a correct view of cognition *a priori*, this belongs to the self-activity of our mind, and therefore to every such principle there corresponds a basic property of our mind.

Besides this relation of basic faculties and generic faculties there are, through the coordination of the faculties in inner interaction, still other relations, which are easily confused with it. Thus reason as the power of cognition is not properly a basic faculty from which sense or desire could be comprehended, but it is nevertheless a *principal faculty*, in contrast to which sense or desire are only subsidiary faculties; for without the power of cognition neither sense nor will would be possible, yet these are by no means given through the former, but come to it only in addition. Finally, a faculty sometimes stands so under the condition of the

[p. 30]

other that it can express itself only by means of the other, without depending on it as on a basic faculty. Thus sense is the first *causa motrix* [moving cause], through which all inner life is stimulated and without which even reason could not show itself.

[scan 93]

## First Book.

Investigation of Cognizing in General, of Sensibility, and of the Memory-Bound Course of Thought.

[scan 95]

### First Section.

### On Cognizing in General.

#### §. 9.

#### a) Cognizing and Representing in General.

Nothing would be easier than to fix a beginning for this investigation of the human mind, since we have to do here with mere description of nature, where every fact rests on itself, were it not that everywhere we are confronted by the prejudice which would string all our knowledge together into a chain of explanations according to a misunderstood logical method. This is how the absurd division of the investigation into empirical psychology, logic and metaphysics has arisen here, so that nowhere can a whole be obtained. In psychology it is said: this is a pure law of thought and therefore belongs in logic; in logic: this is empirical and belongs in empirical psychology; and as soon as cause and effect come up for discussion, the matter is referred to metaphysics, without asking whether the life of our mind actually troubles itself about these separations or not. So it comes about that logic remains unintelligible with its

[p. 34]

sucked-dry forms, psychology meaningless with its fragmented experiences, and metaphysics unable to solve its problem, because one does not know how to tie the knot after first tearing the thread itself. We hope that what has been said so far has sufficiently protected us against these common prejudices, and in what follows we shall therefore not justify ourselves specially, case by case, regarding the alleged confusion of logic, metaphysics and anthropology.

The usual division of the inner description of nature is that into cognitions, feelings of pleasure, and desires, of which the cognitions underlie all the rest and make up a system of inner activity of their own. We shall therefore also begin with their investigation.

The essential mark by which one decides whether an affection or an action of the mind belongs to cognition in inner experience is the relation to object and existence. That which is cognized is in general always object, representation. Representation and object are required for all cognizing. But not every doing or suffering of the mind that belongs to cognition can itself already be called cognition; cognizing is a composite fact of inner experience and not an activity of the mind that would be immediately perceived as a complete cognition. According to differing usage, cognition means now the objective representation, the representation through which an object is represented as such, now also the consciousness of an object as such. The most determinate expression is: cognition is consciousness of the existence of an object, or of a law under which the

[p. 35]

existence of things stands. Thus it is cognition, e.g., when I see or hear objects, or when I judge: All bodies are heavy; for in saying so I do not indeed say that there are bodies, nor that anything heavy is there, but I cognize that the existence of bodies in general stands under the law of gravity. Many activities of the mind that belong to cognizing are therefore not yet cognitions; if I merely think, in an indeterminate way, something red, or man, leaf, these are not yet cognitions but only activities of the mind that can be applied to cognizing. All such affections or activities of the mind are called, in general, representations. All doing or suffering of the mind, then, in which that relation to existence and object occurs, is consciousness or representing, and this constitutes the most general concept that can be at issue here. Examples of representations which in themselves are not yet cognitions, in contrast to these, will make the stated relation most clear. To my cognition of a determinate single tree it belongs that it is given to me in intuition, then that I recognize it as a tree, as this determinate species of tree; for this I need concepts of what a tree is in general, what this particular species of tree is, etc. Further, I see it perhaps only as leafy, but to my cognition of it there belongs also knowledge of the constitution of its blossoms, fruits, etc. Here the single intuitions and concepts are mere representations; the whole taken together constitutes the cognition of the tree. The clearest case of mere representations that are not cognitions is mere images of fantasy, mythological figures, fictions.

[p. 36]

Yet all this is not meant to contain a definition of the words “cognition,” “representation,” etc.; we wish thereby only to give occasion for orienting oneself with regard to them. Here follows a general remark which relates to defining in philosophical anthropology generally. Logic makes a distinction between the definition and the mere exposition of a concept. The definition combines some general marks with one another and designates this composition with a word of its own; it makes its concept for itself. The exposition, on the other hand, does not let a concept first arise, but presupposes that one already has it, and merely sets together facts from which one can orient oneself with regard to it, in order to use a word at least in a more determinate meaning than perhaps usually happens. Definitions belong in the system of the science, where one starts from the higher, general, and proceeds from there to the particular; but in most sciences the general is the less intelligible, so one must start from particular facts in order to become intelligible, and so arrive only gradually at the general. In such cases we must therefore not at once ask for definitions of the words, but make use of mere expositions, so as not to become unintelligible or one-sided. This is now the case in all natural science. Ask the chemist, for instance: What is common salt? and he will answer, if he wants to define: muriate of soda; and we understand the definition less than the thing itself; but the chemist does not proceed so either. Rather he shows us the salt, describes how it is obtained from sea water and from brine, and then shows how it acts in

[p. 37]

mixture with this or that thing. The relation in anthropology is quite similar. But there we cannot lay before another's eyes the objects of which we speak; each must seek them out in his own inner intuition. The only means by which we can make ourselves intelligible here are words. If we are therefore asked: What is cognition? we shall first answer that we understand by it what is so called in common German usage; but because this is perhaps indeterminate, we give in an exposition particular facts by which cognition can be provisionally distinguished from many other things; the closer determination is found only in the course of the investigation. Thus all our communication about inner nature, and, because we are accustomed to think only in speaking, all our knowledge of it, must always first pass through the medium of language, as well as through ordinary linguistic usage. Hence arises the power of the word and of language in all philosophy, so that almost everyone, however determinately in the wrong, retreats for self-justification merely behind his language.

#### §. 10.

The most general determination of all the inner activities that belong to representing and cognizing is thus the relation to object and existence.

Our aim now is to obtain, through self-observation, a whole history of our cognizing and representing: how it begins with sensible intuition, develops further through imagination, and receives its completion through the understanding. From the inner relations

[p. 38]

of this course of events we must then derive the basic determinations of the cognizing mind, and by means of them sketch a theory of our faculty of cognition. What matters most here, and has hitherto been very much neglected, is, first, precisely this completion of a merely descriptive presentation before one attempts the theory itself, and then that we be strictly on our guard not to repeat here the common errors in self-observation made by others.

To the latter we must pay regard here at once. Every word that designates general relations belonging here is ambiguous, and has thereby occasioned error.

To every representation there belongs a *representing subject* (the I, mind), a *representing* (consciousness), and a *represented* (object). A representation is cognition if in it an existing object is represented as existing.

With these verbal determinations we must compare the words: consciousness, representation, and *objective representation*.

First, *to be conscious* has three meanings. According to the first, consciousness means just as much as representing; it designates the activity of the mind in contrast to the represented, as its object, e.g. in the question: how does the object, as its object, come to the mere consciousness of my mind? Commonly, however, the other meanings are more usual. Here consciousness means as much as self-consciousness, and indeed either the mere *representation that I am*, pure self-consciousness, is so called, or the faculty of being conscious is in general the faculty of self-cognition, to which the inner

[p. 39]

sense is the ground. The last meaning is the one properly in force, e.g. in the expressions: to be in full consciousness, to lose consciousness, to be conscious of a thing. Here what is understood by it is the faculty of inner perception of my activities, the knowing of my knowing.

This ambiguity has had great influence on the disputed question: are there representations without consciousness, or are all representations accompanied by consciousness? According to the first meaning it goes without saying that this must be denied, since there representing and being conscious are one and the same; according to the last meaning, however, we distinguish obscure and clear representations precisely by this, that the former we do indeed have, but do not perceive again, whereas the latter we have not merely in us, but we are also conscious of them.

Second, *Vorstellung* [representation] and all similar words in *-ung*, Empfindung [sensation], Anschauung [intuition], Dichtung [fiction], are ambiguous in that by representation one understands just as well the representing, the activity of the mind, as the represented, the object of representing. This usually has no influence at all on the use of the word, since we have no need of the distinction between the two; in the investigation of the grounds of our representing, however, much depends on it. The student of philosophy must be made carefully attentive to it. Thus, for instance, he usually thinks of idealism as the assertion that our representations are only in us, but that no objects outside us correspond to them. Kant's doctrine of the ideality of space and time then easily appears as the absurd assertion that space and time would be only in us, but nowhere

[p. 40]

present outside us. Space and time, as the represented and intuited, are either outside us or not at all; the representing of them, however, is at all times an activity of the mind and to that extent in us, and idealism can only assert that to the represented, to the object of my cognition, no existence belongs in a certain respect. We must therefore always distinguish carefully the represented, the objective of the representation, from the representing, as the activity of the mind. This objectivity of representations is one of the greatest riddles in speculation generally.

#### §. 11.

#### b) The Relation of Cognition to the Object.

The relation of a cognition to its object, which in the newest Fichtean-Schellingian philosophy, under the names relation of the I and not-I, of the subjective and objective, of the real and ideal, following the example of the Platonists was confused now with the difference of the finite and the eternal, now with that of matter and mind, now with that of the I and the things outside us, usually with all of these together, has been the chief difficulty in almost every attempt at speculation. In all Leibnizian philosophy, and especially in the Fichtean-Schellingian presentation, this relation is the properly world-generating principle; the self-cognition of the Absolute, of the universe, of the deity, casts the duality into pure identity, or compels the irradiations of the one divine being into an infinite temporality. Here there lies, as the first inexplicable basic hypothesis beneath all, and

[p. 41]

bears the whole system, the presupposition: that the one eternal being is irresistibly compelled by an eternal, supreme fate to cognize itself. Here, then, the very incomprehensibility of this relation is supposed to serve as the ground of all comprehending, which then itself already announces itself as a mere makeshift of a failed attempt at a system.

But in every other earlier attempt at speculation too the same difficulty showed itself, as soon as one asked for the ultimate grounds of the validity of a cognition, since here the first answer is always: truth is the agreement of a representation with its object, and one then still cannot apply the concept, because there is wholly lacking a rule according to which this agreement or non-agreement could be judged.

Whence, then, these difficulties? Only from two errors in the treatment of inner experience. It is already erroneous that one wants to subject the concept of representing and cognizing to any further definition at all, since it is something immediate and first in inner experience; moreover, one attempted such a definition quite one-sidedly, before one had completely observed the whole history of our cognizing. One hoped to reach the goal either by reasoning merely from the bare concept of truth, as this offered itself immediately, or by wanting to explain everything already from the first sensible intuition in sensation.

Naturally one then confused inner relations of cognizing with its external grounds, and tried, one part of the phenomenon through the other, to

[p. 42]

explain, supposing that one was giving an explanation of the whole phenomenon. Thus Hume and others explain the objective significance of our representations by our thinking in addition, to the sensation in us, a ground of the affection, as if the objective relation were not just as much already contained in the representation of a ground, which would then need explanation just as much as sense intuition does. Fichte wants to explain the objectivity in the consciousness of things outside us from self-consciousness, but how then does objectivity come to this? The fundamental error lies properly in the following.

When I cognize or represent an object, this cognition or representation is my activity; I am active in relation to an object, for I represent it. Now the active relation of one thing to another is otherwise always that of cause and effect, the causal relation. E.g., the sun attracts the earth, or a man rolls a stone away: here there is an active relation between sun and earth, between the man and the stone; the sun and the man are causes, which act on the earth and the stone. All other active relations between things in nature are constituted in this way, and for that reason one has also always sought in the relation of the representing subject to the represented object a relation of cause and effect. One calls the cognizing mind the subject, the cognized object the object of the representation, and has in one way or another always wanted to regard this object as cause. But this is quite incorrect, and does not lie in our inner self-observation at all. Already in the investigation of inner activity in general we noticed that it alone contains an activity absolutely,

[p. 43]

which shows no third thing, as acted upon, on which it expresses itself. Such an activity absolutely is precisely representing and cognizing; in it there is immediately only action and nothing acted upon, but one sought to add the latter to it, and put the object in its place. Locke, Hume, and who not before them and with them, presuppose that the objective significance of our sensations is determined only thereby, that the object is that which affects with respect to sensation, i.e. that it is the cause of the sensation; and even Kant, who began his Critique with the remark that the law for our representation in metaphysical things is no longer to be sought in the object, falls nonetheless indeterminately back, in his judgment of the possibility of cognitions *a priori*, into the error of presupposing a causal relation here.

If we pay attention to ourselves, we can easily notice that to represent an object, e.g. a house, means neither that we make it, nor that we produce it, nor that we alter it; nor yet that we are made or altered by it, or that it acts upon us in any way; we say only: I represent it to myself, and this means something quite different from every causal relation; but what it says, *to represent something or to cognize something*, everyone can learn only from his inner consciousness; one can explain it as little as one can explain to a blind man what red or green is. So we appeal only to this inner self-observation, and in accordance with it we want to put together the facts about our cognizing and representing. This relation will be weighed still more exactly in the theory of sensation; but whoever

[p. 44]

will not let himself be turned away by our assertion, and yet demands an explanation of these concepts, to him we answer that he does not yet understand at all what explaining means. Only derived quantitative differences can be explained, not immediate qualities; the concept of cognizing in general, however, is a quality from inner experience.

#### §. 12.

#### c) Self-Activity and Receptivity.

Of our mind we cognize its own inner activity, and our self-cognition is limited to this alone. We thus cognize immediately only the doing of our mind; all its suffering, so far as we become conscious of it, is therefore only being determined to activity. Consequently there lies at the ground of all faculties of the mind *self-activity* or *spontaneity*; its *receptivity* or *receptiveness*, on the other hand, consists only in a receptivity for being determined to the expression of its activity; everything passive in the mind consists in this, that through some other influence it is compelled to express its activity in a determinate way.

By a usage of language recently developed more closely in the physiology of organized bodies we can make these relations clearer, in saying that our mind is in general an *excitability*, an excitable power.

Excitability we must oppose to spontaneity pure and simple; it is a self-activity which is not sufficient to itself in order to express itself, but always only under the condition of some other stimulation of its

[p. 45]

activity. The original moving powers of matter in their attracting and repelling we think of as spontaneity pure and simple: every mass acts immediately upon every other according to their spatial relations. To life, on the other hand, e.g. of the human organism, there corresponds only such an excitable self-activity, which must constantly be kindled anew with regard to nutrition and breathing if it is to express itself continuously. Just so now is the inner life of our mind constituted too: it is not the simple expression of a self-activity, but this requires a continued external stimulation in order to remain in activity.

Every excitable self-activity has a *form of its excitability*, through which its essence shows itself immediately, but to which there must still be added a matter of excitation, through which it first expresses itself, and which is precisely that which is determined by affection from without. Thus the essence of the mind as a faculty of cognizing, of taking an interest, of willing, is determined by the form of its excitability; but in order to arrive at actual expression of life in this cognizing, taking an interest, or willing, it must first be stimulated through a receptivity. Through this form the mind is determined not as a faculty of moving, of shining, of sounding, but, e.g., of cognizing; its stimulated activity must always be cognition; but if it is actually to come to cognition, an external influence stimulating the mind through affection is first required.

The excitable self-activity of the faculty of cognition we shall now call *reason*, its receptivity, on the other hand, *sense*. *Sensibility*, however, shall be the name of reason in so far as in the matter of its

[p. 46]

excitations it stands under the law of sense, but *understanding*, in the most indeterminate meaning, in so far as the form of its excitability belongs to it independently of sense.

A common error in the treatment of these concepts is that one regards sensibility and understanding as two separate faculties of our activity, whereas both are one and the same reason, only under different conditions of the expression of its activity. Sensibility is reason itself, only with the limitation that it is bound to sense and must first be affected in sensation in order that it may express its activity.

This error has often already prevented arriving at a correct view of the theory of cognizing, but far more harmful still is a misunderstanding with regard to spontaneity itself, in that one confuses the *self-activity* of the faculty of cognition with the *voluntary activity* of reflection.

In the activities of our mind we set *sensing* through *affection*, and *thinking* and *inventing* through *reflection*, in opposition to one another. In hearing and seeing immediately, and in all that sensation gives, we are simply compelled to represent exactly as we represent; in thinking and inventing, on the other hand, we give ourselves voluntarily the very representations with which we occupy ourselves; we direct our pondering voluntarily to this or that object, play voluntarily before the fantasy with this or that image. The faculty of voluntariness of reflection is now, according to the most proper meaning of the German language, that which we call understanding. This use of the word

[p. 47]

must, however, be carefully distinguished from the previous one: self-activity of cognition and voluntary activity in representing are two quite different things. It is this voluntariness in thinking which, under the name of the freedom of reflection, has produced the greatest confusions in inner natural science. Here we wish only provisionally to draw attention to the difference. The original spontaneity of the power of cognition is to be the source of truth in us; it can therefore by no means depend on the will, but must follow an unalterable, necessary inner law; it will show itself only in the persistent consciousness of necessary truths, and not in the changeable play of voluntary perceptions.

Sensibility and reflective understanding are both the same self-activity of reason, only under other conditions of its expression; affection and reflection, on the other hand, are the two receptivities of the power of cognition. In affection, that which affects in sensation is what determines the activity; in reflection, on the other hand, the will of the mind itself is what determines the activity; this, however, is just as foreign to the power of cognition in itself as that which affects in sensation.

#### §. 13.

The history of our cognition always begins, in time, with the affection of sensation, precisely because reason is bound to sense. Through this its activity is stimulated; but once it is set in play, the expressions of imagination and of understanding then show themselves also, according to inner laws, along with those. We observe in ourselves, then, first our state of sensation,

[p. 48]

and then a *course of thought* that supervenes upon it, from which we must learn to know all the remaining laws of cognition. This course of thought arises partly from involuntary laws of the inner play of representations, and is called in this respect the *memory-bound course of thought of the imagination*, partly from voluntary reflection, and is called: *logical course of thought of the understanding*. The sensible faculties and those of the memory-bound course of thought are usually called the *lower*, those of the logical the *higher faculties of cognition*.

In accordance with these distinctions we must observe the history of our cognitions step by step, beginning with sensation.

The first representations given in sensation are always *sense intuitions*. Here, then, we must at once draw attention to the difference between *intuitive and discursive cognition*. Simple and important as this distinction is, it has seldom been rightly grasped. We cognize either intuitively through *intuition* or discursively through *concept and judgment*. Intuition is the representation of an object in which the object is represented as given; it is immediate cognition of the object. Discursive cognition, on the other hand, is always a mediate representation through general rules and laws. It always belongs to thinking, whereas all cognition from sensation is intuitive.

But among intuitive representations too there are still many that we can have voluntarily.

What I have once heard or seen I can afterwards often recall voluntarily, or if I

[p. 49]

have seen a thing, I can, on the basis of a mere discursive description, myself sketch the intuitive representation of a similar one; I have seen, e.g., a common bear, and can now represent to myself a polar bear on the basis of a mere description. Thus intuitions of the imagination and sense intuitions are distinguished. The former, however, always presuppose certain previously given sense intuitions, from which they first develop, and the essential difference between the two is this: intuition in imagination does indeed also represent its object as immediately given, but without its presence; sense intuition, on the other hand, cognizes *immediately the presence of a given object*.

[p. 50]

### Second Section.

### Investigation of Sense Intuitions.

#### a) The Theory of Sensation.

#### §. 14.

Every cognition begins for us in time with sense intuitions, which are given to us in sensation; through these we cognize immediately the presence of present objects in space and time, and so a cognition of the material world outside us is initiated for us immediately through *outer sense*, through *inner sense* the cognition of an inner world of the mind's own activity.

The general relation of all these sense intuitions is a state of the wholly passive mind, called *sensation*, in which it is driven to intuiting. Since all our inner life begins herewith, this is the point to which every empirical philosophy has been pressed in order to fathom the theory of cognizing. One wanted to compose all our cognition out of sheer sensation, to explain all thinking only as a modification of sensing. Above all it also seemed as if here cognition properly comes into contact with its object; the phenomena of sensing therefore received for all speculation the highest

[p. 51]

value; one hoped to discover here the law of truth, and skepticism attached itself to the same investigation in order to show the impossibility of that discovery.

But all these hopes, with their skeptical annihilations, proceeded only from false self-observations, from erroneous presentations of the history of sensing itself. We wish to correct this presentation, and we shall see that the matter is extremely simple, but that speculation has, from this sense intuition, nothing at all either to hope or to fear.

Sensation is the passive state of the mind in which it is compelled to intuit. Every sensation contains perception within itself, and intuition of an object as present. In sensation the intuition of a present objective manifold is given to me, of a sound, of something colored, of something warm or cold, etc. This is sense intuition. Without this consciousness, through which in sensation something is intuited, sensation is a mere impression on sense, indeterminable for us, through which, however, cognition, namely sense intuition, is aroused in me. As everywhere where the mind is passively determined, so too in sensing its suffering is a mere being determined to activity. This activity is here sensible intuiting. From this, however, the mere determination of sense, the sensible impression through that which affects, through which that intuiting is brought forth, is to be distinguished. About this sensible impression we can say nothing further at all, for it contains the external relation to that which affects, but our observation is only an inner one, and that external

[p. 52]

is not perceived there at all. It is this sensible impression, however, which first of all, in so far as it is a hindrance or a furtherance to the expression of life at the time, is accompanied by immediate sensible pleasure or displeasure.

We must therefore not confuse sensation itself either with the sensible intuiting in it or with the feeling of pleasure which is aroused through it; it is a wholly passive state of the mind, which we, as bound to the interior of self-cognition, do not know more closely, but through which both sensible intuiting and feeling of pleasure are aroused in us.

#### §. 15.

With this we wish to compare the usual presentation. One starts here from the question: Sensation is after all a mere modification in me; how, then, does the objective relation come to be added to it? and while seeking the answer one confuses sensation with the sense intuition in it, or even with the object of this intuition, the sweet, warm, red, etc. Let us take the example: I see a green tree before me, and arrive through sensation at cognition of it. If I now ask how this comes about, I receive, according to the usual account, the answer: The tree affects my eye, thereby I receive the sensation of green, and because this must have a cause, I infer the tree as that which affects and as the cause of that sensation of green. Some, with Fichte, add further: and if I call the tree green, or the sugar sweet, this is expressed quite falsely; we ourselves are properly the green and the sweet. I think, however: God preserve us from a sweet mind,

[p. 53]

and I maintain that this whole story is altogether false. The tree is green and the sugar sweet, or else nobody; and when I intuit the tree, I see in sensation immediately something green outside me, without asking at all for a cause of my sensation. One says readily enough, the tree affects my eye and therefore I see it; but with that we have begun precisely with the difficult part. It is not the tree that affects my eye, but the light through it; and how does it come about that this affection of my eye becomes for me the intuition of the green? About this I can say nothing more, for that would be a matter of experience, but this experience is not in my power. Were I to intuit the thing outside me merely as that which affects with respect to sensation, as the cause of my sensation, I would in that case have to infer not the tree, but either light or a mere motion in my eye, etc. The matter is far simpler if we only remain with the observation itself. The main thing here is namely to notice that in sensation there is contained from the outset an intuiting of something outside me, or of an activity in me (according as it concerns outer or inner sense intuition), and that the representation of an object or of the objective is not first brought in afterwards through reflection or otherwise, but is already there completely from the very beginning.

The intuition in sensation has by itself immediate evidence, in that it represents the object as present. The object is not represented in it in so far as it is that which affects the mind in sensation, not as acting upon the mind, but according to its immediate characteristics, and simply

[p. 54]

as given in intuition; e.g. in a sensation of hearing I am immediately conscious of a sound, as something outside me, and not of the sounding body, which I cognize only through reflection in the connection of experiences; often I hear a sound without knowing the sounding thing from which it comes. Just so I see the green tree immediately as something green outside me, and not as the cause of my sensation of green. Only an extensive connection of my experiences first teaches me that my eye belongs among the causes of this sensation, and that the tree itself acts on it mediately. In the completed cognition of a thing outside me there do indeed drop away for the most part the characteristics which belong to it in the first perception, sound, warmth, taste, smell and color, since in the connection of experiences we cognize objects not precisely according to their relation to me, but preferably according to their relations to one another; yet so long as the representation is to remain intuitive, we can never abstract wholly from all these determinations, e.g. the seeing one never wholly from color, and the first predicates in perception determine for me the object itself according to figure, mass, position and motion, not in so far as they are regarded as its effects, but in so far as they are regarded as characteristics of it. Most clearly of all, finally, it appears in inner sensation that its object cannot be represented as its cause; for if there did not first come to pure self-consciousness through sensation another intuition of my activity, I could not even become conscious of the sensation itself, and still much less, through it, of its cause.

[p. 55]

What commonly misleads here is the following: what we take for a sense intuition can either really be one, or it is only a deception of the organ, a patch of color before the dazzled eye, a ringing in the ear, or finally it is even a mere imagination, dream or morbid fantasy. Among these representations the real sense intuition is distinguished by this, that a present object really corresponds to it, and one then commonly supposes that we in fact verify that intuition by comparison with the object. But this cannot happen at all. We always find the object only through the intuition, and we always verify representations only reciprocally through one another, one intuition through the other in the whole connection of our experiences. Only this connection of intuitions and experiences with one another shows us in the particular case whether we have had to do with sense or with mere imagination.

This error, in which one supposes the object to be intuited only as the affecting thing in sensation, lies at the ground of all the speculations in which the truth of cognition is derived from a causal relation to its object, or in which one wants skeptically to exhibit from this the uncertainty of our knowledge, namely that one must not trust this causal relation. Neither the Fichtean grounding nor the Humean objection has anything to say here, since the fact from which both proceed does not exist at all. Even taken quite metaphysically, the explanation that we add the object to our representation by seeking a ground of it does not hold water. For what is a ground other than

[p. 56]

an object through which another is; ground is therefore only a kind of object, and if we did not already presuppose the concept of an object, we could think neither ground nor consequence; this concept can therefore by no means arise through the latter.

#### §. 16.

Another common error in the doctrine of sensation consists in this, that one holds self-consciousness, inner intuition, self-cognition to be quite explicable, but takes the intuition of things outside us to be the difficult point in the matter. This faulty view lies, e.g., at the ground of the whole Fichtean *Doctrine of Science*, where the self-positing of the I is always regarded as the easily intelligible thing, and one troubles oneself only about how the I gets out of itself to the not-I, as the thing outside it. Here the following ambiguity lies at the ground: when I sense, this is accompanied in two ways by perception and thus by consciousness. First, when I sense, I am often again conscious of this sensation, I am conscious that I sense; but second, I am conscious in the sensation, through sense intuition, of an object. There is thus here a consciousness *of the sensation* and a consciousness *in the sensation*. Now it is indeed said quite rightly: sensations are mere modifications of the state of mind, for this is the particular fact, *that I sense*, at all times; but one then confuses with the sensation what is intuited in it. Here it is supposed to be comprehensible, indeed, how I can become conscious of the modification of my state of mind (of my representation, as one says), but difficult how

[p. 57]

from this consciousness a cognition of the wholly different object is supposed to arise. According to our explanation, by contrast, it will be easy to show how cognition becomes possible through the *given* sense intuition; but how this sense intuition itself is possible, both inwardly in the perception of a sensation or of any representation of mine, and in the perception of an object in the sensation, that is equally inexplicable on both sides. It is an analogue of an optical illusion that produces the opinion that consciousness of a representation in me is more explicable than that of an object outside me. The intuited state of mind is just as different from that in which it is intuited as the intuited outer object is from the state of mind in which it is intuited. That in the first case both belong to the same subject can make no difference; the difficulty is in general, how can an intuition be given to the mind in sensation? Whether I myself, my activity, or something else is its object, that does not matter—but how the mind can in general be conscious, represent and cognize, that is no task for a further explanation, that can only be accepted immediately as a fact on the testimony of experience, for it is an immediate inner quality and not something quantitatively composite that could be explained from simpler concepts.

Through this constitution of sensation indicated by us, according to which it contains *immediately* the intuition of present objects in itself, a firm foundation for the theory of cognition in general is obtained, in that we proceed from sense intuition,

[p. 58]

and then to show step by step how, in the inner history of our cognizing, we arrive from it, through imagination and reflection, at our complete cognition. To explain, from states of mind that contain no cognition as yet, how the object comes in and so cognition arises, is an insoluble and purposeless task, for cognizing is an immediate inner quality. A sound observation of sensation shows us in it already the beginning of our representation of things outside us, and of inner activities of the mind, which gradually develop in us into complete cognitions. By pursuing this observation we thus learn at least *how we cognize the objects*, even if there can be no question for the moment of *how they are*. We explain only representation from representation, and cognition from cognition, because this origination and alteration becomes a fact of inner experience; the object is then always already with the cognition, but cognizing itself can be derived from nothing further. With this, to be sure, with regard to sensation we remain only subjectively at the state of mind, and do not discuss at all here the relation of sense intuition to its object. But that is just what a correct procedure necessarily demands here: not to sense intuition alone, but to our completed cognition does the world correspond as its object. Only after we have come to know this complete cognition subjectively as an activity of our mind, is it time to ask about the relation to its object.

[p. 59]

#### b) On the Outer Sense.

#### §. 17.

Through the outer sense we receive sense intuitions of things outside us, whereby our cognition of the material world in space and time is introduced. The sensations of this sense stand for us in such determinate relations to the history of our body and to the affection of its nerves that we cannot easily describe them without reference to the latter. Our cognition arises here through the fact that, by the particular formation of individual nerve organs, sense intuition frees itself more and more from the merely subjective state of sensation. To the stimulation of the nerves in general corresponds an indeterminate *vital sensation*; in particularly formed individual organs, however, this is raised for cognition to an individual *organ sensation*.

Vital sensation is in general every indeterminate sensation that is commonly reckoned to the sense of feeling. To it belong the sensation of warmth and cold, hunger and thirst, pleasant and unpleasant tickling, shuddering and the like. Through every conflict of the inner and the outer in the vital movements of our body this vital sense is addressed. Thus, for example, the sensation of warmth and cold comes to us not only from without, but arises just so from within outward, for example in certain feelings and desires, in suddenly tensed expectation, hope and fear.

The momentary state of almost all the nerves in the whole body is always accompanied by a more or less determinate vital sensation, to which, however, we are accustomed to attend only

[p. 60]

when one of them becomes particularly strong or enters into a particular relation to the feeling of pleasure and displeasure; so long as it arouses in us only an indifferent feeling, on the other hand, it does not easily excite our attention. The cooperation of all these vital sensations at each moment produces a *general sensible life-feeling*, by which we actually always estimate our immediate well-being, and through this the well-being or health of our body.

This general life-feeling is at all times intimately bound up with our self-consciousness, and of great influence on the whole human being. Our momentary mood, the particular readiness at any time for cheerfulness or melancholy, and whatever else of the sort there may be, all this depends chiefly on this result of the whole of our vital sensation at the time. Indeed, in its further course this life-feeling contributes much, according as it runs on evenly, is more or less inhibited, is tuned up or tuned down, to the determination of a man's natural disposition and even of his temperament. What makes one man cheerful, open, confiding, good-natured, another melancholy or irritable, is often nothing but his livelier or more suppressed life-feeling. But this general life-feeling itself depends not only on my bodily well-being at the time, but just as much, by reaction, on inner activities and moods of the mind. The mood of cheerfulness, for example, sustains and nourishes itself. For the state of my excited and lively vital sensation in general produces a feeling of well-being, which attunes to cheerfulness, this cheerfulness

[p. 61]

acts further, however, on a greater inner animation, and thereby back upon the maintenance of the heightened vital sensation. Conversely, a mood once inclined to melancholy will likewise go on increasing itself more and more, and this can go as far as self-destruction, if, with a merely bodily disposition to melancholy, reason does not in good time become master over the sensation and turn attention away from it as far as possible.

#### §. 18.

In this way vital sensation is most effective through the passive state of sensation itself and its effect on agreeableness and disagreeableness. Nevertheless, in every such sensation there is already, to some degree, representation as sense intuition, in which I find myself touched by something outer. This sense intuition, however, becomes ever freer and steps more into the foreground, as the general vital sense shapes itself into the particular organ sense. For certain stimuli, like sound and light, act in the healthy state only on certain organs in a perceptible way, and through these the outer sensation is more and more purified into a representation of cognition. Thus vital sensation develops into touch, and sense intuition shows itself in taste, smell, hearing, until in sight it finally attains for us its greatest freedom.

Of the last four senses, hearing and sight contribute most to cognition, but in very different ways. In sight the consciousness of the state of sensation is, for a healthy, not overstimulated eye, wholly pushed back by the sense intuition; here we perceive immediately the colored object outside

[p. 62]

us, and the ease of obtaining the intuition from a distance, and of arranging many colors side by side before the eye, means that the seeing person holds fast almost his whole cognition of the outer world before the eye. Hearing, on the other hand, lets sound and noise appear to us immediately outside us, which we ascribe to the object, the sounding, resounding thing, only as its effect, whose own existence, however, takes place more determinately only in relation to me. This indeterminacy of mere tones, their floating, detached nature, becomes for inner self-cognition the great aid of the sign of language in the word. That is the most peculiar function of this sense in our mind, that it unites with the faculty of speech, thus makes our own inner life more distinct to us, and even leads to knowledge of the inner life of another mind. Tones are the most excellent signs of language, through which we communicate thoughts and have them communicated to us; they are the outer bond of the spiritual world, precisely because in themselves they signify nothing. In hearing, the sense stands just at that degree of development at which the subjective of the state of sensation and the objective of the sense intuition strike consciousness with equal strength. Hence we obtain music as the peculiar fine art of hearing. Sense intuition has here already freedom enough, which is not the case with taste and smell, to make a beautiful play of tones possible, and sensation is still strong enough, which drops out in the eye, to address the vital sense in general vividly. These are the two conditions of the possibility of music. The interest of this play of sensation rests on this, that the stimulus strikes not only hearing as an organ sense, but only by means of

[p. 63]

it the vital sense in general; it seizes the whole life-feeling intimately and strongly, the waves of harmony and the streams of melody move and sweep this whole life-feeling along with them, now strengthening and enlivening, now inhibiting and damping it. We are wholly in the power of music, and as every inner sensation and every feeling thus resounds in answer to it, it becomes for us a mere language of feelings without any concept, yet at the same time the play of its tones retains freedom enough to be able to take on beautiful forms.

The eye, on the other hand, with its freest intuition, is distinguished by this: that, whereas for the ear we can think a complete silence, and for every other sense an analogous state with consciousness, in that we sense nothing through it, the seeing person can represent to himself no state in which he does not see with consciousness, for here the positive representation of black enters in place of the lack.

#### §. 19.

Touch we should, anthropologically, actually not distinguish from the vital sense in general as a sense of its own, but only as a mechanism of its own for using vital sensation for cognition. Touch is distinguished from the vital sense in general not by a peculiar kind of sensation, but by the determinate formation of certain organs, through whose organization their vital sensations lead to further knowledge of things.
