The peculiarity of the representations that we receive through the sense of touch consists not in this, that something can be felt as warm or cold, soft or harsh, etc., but in the representation obtained through

[p. 64]

feeling of the figure, magnitude and distance of bodies, which we judge by the resistance they offer to the movement of our organs. To this belong, for example, the representations of the rough and the smooth, of the round and the flat, of the wet and the dry, of the hard and the soft. In every sensible cognition we must distinguish that which is contained immediately in the sensation as intuition, and that which is added to this intuition in the sensation only through reflection. The peculiarity of the sense of touch consists in this, that we possess organs which are especially suited to perform the reflection upon a part of our vital sensations. The organ of the sense of touch is therefore chiefly the hands, but quite especially the tips of the fingers, made more sensitive by nerve papillae of their own: five feeling-tips, which obtain the greatest mobility through all the joints of the fingers, the hand and the arm. These then serve reflection, in order to determine, in accordance with the sensation in the contact, our representation of the things touched. Every altered pressure, and every altered position of the muscles, can be noticed through feeling; thus we are conscious, for example, without seeing, whether we hold the arm stretched or bent, and this knowledge of the position and movement of our arm, hand, fingers, in relation to the sensations which a body touching them produces, guides our reflection to the determination of the figure, position and magnitude of things outside us.

Touch seems to us, in comparison with hearing and sight, to furnish the coarsest knowledge of the outer world, in that it demands immediate contact for the perception,

[p. 65]

but it is nevertheless the most necessary and immediate, for its representations already underlie our cognition through hearing or sight. We relate our representations through hearing and sight only to the immediate intuitions through touch, in order to determine the object. But since touch in this lays claim more to reflection than to sensibility, it must in its completeness remain a special possession of the human being.

#### §. 20.

This relation, to which we have been made attentive here through touch, we must still take more determinately into view. Through the kinds of sensation enumerated we receive immediately our sensible representation of the world outside us; but we must distinguish exactly, in this, what lies immediately in the sense intuition, and what is added to it only inwardly, and is determined and noticed only by means of reflection. What is added first of all over and above sense intuition is its relation to space and to time, which determines the form of our outer world. The complete intuition of things outside us does not actually contain the things as they are intuited in sensation, but only according to the *relations* which they have to one another in this intuition, in which, however, this intuition becomes quite different from what it is immediately in sensation.

Already in sensation we intuit something outside us as colored, as warm, as tone, as bitter; these determinations, however, we afterwards drop, and determine the things outside us further only according to their mutual

[p. 66]

relations in sensation. With the sense of touch, for example, we do not stop at the warm or cold, the pricking or blunt, the soft or harsh in the feeling, but these first determinations give me the representations of the relative resistance to the movement of my fingers, and so procure for me the cognition of the figure of my body. Thus sound is the immediate object of sensation for hearing, but this in the end drops out for me altogether in the cognition of things outside me, and in its place I find only vibrations in elastic media. Just so with the sensations of sight. These contain immediately colors, and since they are the finest and freest of all sensations, the seeing person cognizes the things outside himself, in relation to himself, indeed always as colored, and leaves this relation standing in all intuition, but yet in the complete cognition these determinations too drop out, and leave me only movements of light.

In the cognition of things outside us, as it is occasioned by outer sensation, we therefore in general always go beyond the object of sensation, and take as the further ground of reflection only the relations of the objects to one another in space and time, whereby we finally cognize them as movable and as matter. But this further cognition is no longer given by the sense itself, but by productive imagination, as we shall have to pursue this history further later. Here we want only to make the law itself still more distinct.

For our whole cognition of the outer world, this or that kind of sensation is always only the occasioning,

[p. 67]

but we should obtain in it neither unity nor coherence, only scattered individual images, if there did not lie at the ground of every sense a *uniting intuition common to all the senses*. The table, the tree, or any individual object is for us a thing under a determinate figure in space; this representation is the uniting one, whereby we cognize the one and same thing, whether it falls into intuition for us through touch, hearing, sight, or whatever other sense. Hence it comes about that in our representation of the outer world the qualities from sensation in the end matter far less than it at first seems. That we have precisely these senses, or that one lacks hearing, another sight, does not make so much difference here, for the most important thing is the uniting intuition of the material world, the same for everyone. We can express this through the law already mentioned earlier: there are for us two ways of intuiting the outer world; the one, in sensation, shows us the things only according to the *relation of what they are for the mind, for the inner living being*; the other, derived from it, on the contrary, lets us cognize one in relation to another, *matter in relation to matter*. Sweet or bitter, warm or cold, sounding, fragrant, red or green, a body is not for another body, but only for me, the living mind. Tone, fragrance and color express only the essence of a thing in its relation to me; a body in relation to another, on the contrary, is only attracting and repelling, the movable. It is therefore quite two different things whether I cognize the material world according to its relation to my inner life, or according to the relation of matter to matter. This

[p. 68]

easy, simple remark has nevertheless long been overlooked in natural science. Whoever attends to it will notice that in our physical theories of sound everything belonging to the phenomenon is indeed explained through the vibrations, only sound itself is not, and that likewise the Newtonian theory, or whatever other theory of light may explain everything, explains only color itself not, for sound and color are here, according to their relation to my inner life, qualities that can be subjected to no explanation at all. Schelling noticed this deficiency of the hitherto prevailing philosophy, atomistic as he thought it, and now attempted, in order to save the unity of the system, to place what was lacking, as the second, more ideal potency of light, between matter and mind; but it will never succeed in giving any tenable theory about these relations of the outer to the inner, for as mere quality they are precisely what is opposed to all theory.

Had our remark become clear earlier, no philosopher could ever have been deceived by the doctrine of materialism, since he would at once have seen the limits within which all materialistic explanations necessarily remain confined: relation of one thing in space to another, without ever touching a quality from sensation, how much less, then, thinking.

#### c) On the Inner Sense.

#### §. 21.

Self-cognition is the first and foremost of all faculties of the mind, for we live our own life only in that we also know again what we do. At the ground of this faculty lies first of all the inner sense, which gives it the content of its representations.

[p. 69]

The neglected investigation of this faculty is in the end to blame for all misunderstandings in philosophy. A further inquiry into the constitution of the inner intuitions of my activity, and especially into the relation that I must first be conscious of my representations myself again in order to be able to speak of them, is so subtle that it will easily seem hair-splitting, and one refuses to occupy oneself with it further. Nevertheless the insight into the theory of imagination and the whole constitution of logical thinking depends solely on this relation. Without knowledge of the nature of logical thinking, and thus of the proper significance of logic itself, however, no survey of metaphysics and no firm conviction of what philosophy in general is supposed to be is possible. We must therefore necessarily occupy ourselves more closely with this subject, and some relations which we here first come to know will accompany us through the whole theory of the faculty of cognition.

It is not enough that we *know*; we must also first know that and what we know, in order to be able to speak of it; we must first become conscious of our cognitions again. This, however, does not always come about so immediately, but requires an inner sense and reflection in common life, and all the refinements of inner self-observation for speculation. We proceed here from individual inner perceptions, and raise these only mediately to inner experience, through which we then first properly cognize our cognitions. Just as in outer experience we proceed only from individual perceptions of color, tone, warmth, etc., but out of these form for ourselves a whole cognition of the world in space and

[p. 70]

time, so inwardly too our cognition of what we cognize proceeds only from individual perceptions, and must first be raised to a whole of inner experience. These first perceptions are furnished to us by the inner sense; the further elevation to experience, on the other hand, takes place through reflection. All our cognition is contained either in intuitions or in judgments; intuitions are those cognitions of which we are immediately conscious again; we see and hear, for example, and know at the same time that and what we see and hear. Judgments, on the other hand, serve reflection, in order to raise these individual perceptions to the whole of an experience of our cognitions; in them we become *mediately* conscious of what we cognize and know, *without perceiving it immediately in ourselves*. Thus every human being knows and cognizes many mathematical and philosophical laws, he judges and acts in accordance with them, without being conscious that he knows them; only in learning mathematics and philosophy scientifically do we find these laws themselves again in ourselves. Thus, for example, everyone seeks a cause for it wherever he finds a change, but only through philosophizing do we become conscious of the law of causality itself.

This relation of the inner sense, and of the knowing of our knowledge, in its full application, is the fundamental correction which we have to make in inner natural science; the rest is only a consequence of it. However many individual remarks on it may already occur, no philosopher known to me has yet penetrated to the interior of this investigation. Almost all speculative heads, notably Fichte and Schelling, presuppose that if the mind knows something, it also knows

[p. 71]

immediately that it knows, and decline any further investigation of this relation. The obscure representations considered in every logic, however, might have made everyone attentive to the fact that this relation is not as simple as it is commonly taken to be. Locke and Leibniz disputed at length enough over the nature of these obscure representations, but the remaining relations were not yet distinct enough to them for determinate consequences to be drawn from them. Kant, too, disposes of the inner sense with only the single remark that it shows us what the mind suffers, reflection, on the other hand, what it does. Had the proper constitution of the inner sense only been known earlier, an end would thereby have been put to every philosophical mysticism and every higher dogmatism. That faculty of inner consciousness on which Reinhold's theory of the faculty of representation foundered was nothing but the misunderstood inner sense; the secret source of the Fichtean philosophy is again an inner intuition, whose sensible nature he mistakes, in that he passes it off as intellectual, and Schelling too could not have regarded the formal basic consciousness of all reflection as intuition and treated it so, if he had attended more closely to this inner constitution of the mind.

But to show the importance of a closer knowledge of the inner sense, we need not stop at the abstractions of the philosophers; it shows itself also more closely in life. On ignorance of this inner self-cognition rests almost all the delusion of superstition, which maintains itself even in the more educated classes, where one has indeed bidden farewell to belief in apparitions of spirits and in witches, but reserves for oneself intimations through some secret

[p. 72]

influence or even visions, in that mere imaginings are confused with inner intuitions, and so an accidental coincidence of similar circumstances is taken for proof of a secret, inscrutable fate. This confusion of imagination and inner intuition is the source of all higher inspirations, of all higher communion with spirits and fanatical kinship with God; this is the mine of spiritual treasures, says Kant, from which the sweet Bourignon, the gloomy Pascal and so many another knew so well how to draw.

But for this very reason we must carefully distinguish the scientific self-observation in general, which we demand for the purposes of anthropology, as also the firm, self-truthful look into the moral interior, from the moral self-observation of our inner disposition, which only too easily turns into mystical self-contemplation. Attending to oneself in intercourse is indeed necessary, yet it must become neither laborious nor noticeable, otherwise it is opposed to what is unconstrained and natural, it makes one embarrassed and affected. Moral self-observation in life, however, becomes the rack of all initiates of religious fanatics, and at the same time that which tears these fanatics away from life, shuts them up only in themselves, and bars to the pupil once won the way back into the free world. To examine oneself unceasingly in all one's actions and wishes, whether one means it honestly, to take exact care that one does not stand still in the good or even go back, but advance daily to a purer inner disposition, this is the anxious maxim of religious fanatics, and the good intention

[p. 73]

therein blinds easily the unprepared person who falls into the hands of such men, and, given the impossibility of discovering all the motives even of a single inner action, forces him, according as his temperament is, either into an anxiousness which wholly spoils him for life, or it gives him a certain morbid inner cheerfulness which can bear no light from without. The countless determining grounds which act on our will in every single action make it possible for him who engages in this would-be religious self-observation to represent himself in every action as good or as evil as his dreams just require. Observe, for example, two fanatical religious parties of opposed sanguine temper: the one will confess with the same joy that human beings must remain poor sinners throughout their whole life, with which the others pretend to lead, from the first day of their conversion, a holy life in God. This disposition has very many degrees of self-observation in life, of which the first only make one embarrassed or ill at ease, but the last border fairly close on madness.

Inwardly we perceive nothing but a flux of changes; the scene shifts every moment, and at no point can we stay. Whoever therefore wants to investigate the inner disposition in any single action, or to explain a single play of fantasy in dream or fiction, will never come to an end with it, but will soon hold mere imagination for inner perception and experience, and so, instead of observation, supply himself only with dreams. In this, then, false self-observation is distinguished from the correct, scientific kind: the latter keeps only to the general

[p. 74]

laws of inner activity, since it clearly sees that it is not worth the trouble, and is mostly in vain, to trace further the entanglements of their reciprocal effects for individual cases.

#### §. 22.

The scientific investigation of the inner sense is subject to many obscurities and confusions already for this reason, that one person thinks this, another that, with the word. To the inner sense belongs, for us, only the *inner self-intuition* of the mind in its changeable activities and affections. In contrast to the things outside us in space, we perceive inwardly representations, feelings and desires, which contain nothing spatial, but are inner activities of the mind; these make up the object of inner intuition. Inner intuitions are therefore to be distinguished exactly from imaginings, and inner sense from imagination. The sensible imaginings in dream and fiction are indeed also inwardly produced intuitive representations, which are even often voluntarily determined, but they contain for the most part only the intuition of objects from recollection, which are not present to us, but no intuitions of ourselves, no sense intuitions of our activity. Of the latter we are now speaking. How far imagination is akin to this inner sense will only be shown later; here we must separate the two and keep them wholly apart.

Besides, the inner sense is easily confused with reflection in general, and especially with feeling. Of both, however, we do not yet speak here. The

[p. 75]

reflection is a voluntary way of representing; now the will, to be sure, has mediately also much influence on the inner intuition of ourselves, which we shall learn about later, but the proper inner sense intuitions must be involuntary, they must be such representations as we are compelled to have, which therefore rest on sensation, for otherwise we should not cognize ourselves in them as we are, but at most as we want to make ourselves at will. With reflection we therefore have nothing to do here.

But just as little with feeling. The word feeling has in common usage manifold meanings. Of the outer sense of feeling there is here no question at all, but only of what can be called inner feeling. This is now often confused with sensation, because most sensations are accompanied by a feeling of pleasure or displeasure. This pleasure or displeasure, however, does not belong to cognition and therefore not to our inner sense.

Further, one also often speaks of feeling for truth, of aesthetic and moral feeling, where it concerns neither sensation nor pleasure and displeasure, and this feeling is then often reckoned in with the inner sense. But this too is a confusion, and indeed a confusion which in the recent English investigations of practical reason and of taste by Hutcheson, Smith and others has frustrated the whole effort, in that their language does not distinguish sense and feeling at all. The feelings last named, however, are not sense at all, but power of judgment; they belong not to sensation but to reflection. Feeling stands there opposed to inferring, as the immediate production of a judgment

[p. 76]

opposed to the mediate one, and so belongs with reflection. Here it is enough to see that feeling is no properly sensible representation at all; the closer treatment of it in its place.

According to this more exactly determined concept, the inner intuitions then contain perception of my changeable inner activities, determined voluntarily or involuntarily, in time; I represent myself to myself therein according to my individual representations, feelings of pleasure or desires. Inner sensibility is therefore that which we commonly call consciousness or empirical consciousness. Over and above the relation that I have a representation or other inner activity, there comes the further one, that I also become conscious of really having it.

#### §. 23.

In order to make this constitution of the inner sense wholly distinct to ourselves, we must consider the difference of the obscure and the clear in our representations, and attend especially to the presence in the mind of such representations as we have without being immediately conscious of them. I follow Kant's description in the *Anthropology* for the most part in this.

In the assertion that we have representations and other inner activities of which we are not conscious, there seems at first to lie a contradiction, for how can we know that we have them if we are not conscious of them? Locke raised this objection, and denied on that account the existence of such representations. But we can nevertheless become *mediately* conscious of having certain representations, although we are not

[p. 77]

immediately conscious of them. Such representations are then called obscure, in contrast to the clear, of which we are immediately conscious.

Moreover, in the expression “representation of which I am not conscious” there lies a further ambiguity, with which Reinhold could not come to terms. One can ask: do we have representations without consciousness? and then answer this question with Yes or No, according to the different meanings of the word consciousness. In the indeterminate meaning, being conscious means just as much as representing; then there is consciousness with every representation; in the most determinate meaning, however, consciousness is inner perception, and then there are representations without consciousness, namely the obscure ones.

Indeed this obscure field of our representations is even by far greater than the bright one of which we are conscious. Among the whole multitude of our representations at any time, the clear ones make only individual points of light in an immeasurable region of the obscure. How few of the sense intuitions that flow in on us continually do we notice in particular; here the unusual must in every case first awaken our attention, in order that we become conscious of them. Whoever, for example, listens to a lecture or to music hears all the words or tones in quite the same way, whether he attends to them or not; but if he is not attentive, he does not become conscious of the individual representations here at all; they remain obscure to him always. A scholar would see half a world lie open before his eyes all at once, if the whole multitude of the obscure representations of his memory suddenly became clear to him. Or what a multitude of representations must be awakened in a few moments in the mind of a

[p. 78]

musician who improvises on the organ and perhaps at the same time speaks with someone; where, besides, each of these representations needs a judgment of its own about propriety, since he would notice every dissonance, and yet the fantasy often turns out so beautiful that afterwards he regrets not having it written down. How few of all these representations, however, is he conscious of during the playing. The same shows itself in all pondering, where we are seldom conscious of all the individual representations that guide us and determine our judgment. The talent of the poet is called his genius, as if it were a higher spirit that whispers the ideas to him and guides his activity, precisely because the poet is here wholly in the power of his obscure representations, and can himself give an account of only a few things as to how he is able to create it. Out of this same secret interior Socrates heard the sayings of his daimon.

Thus the field of obscure representations is by far the greatest in the human being. Often we play with them, and the imagination takes pains, according as we are in a gloomy or cheerful mood, to obscure pleasant or unpleasant representations; but still more often we ourselves are the plaything of our obscure representations, feelings and desires. Often our judgment is determined solely by them, very frequently our whole mood.

This difference of the obscure and the clear in our inner activities now makes wholly intuitive what place the inner sense occupies in our mind; it is the receptivity of the mind to become conscious again of a certain activity of it. It creates for self-consciousness, which is wholly developed through reflection, its first content. The important law of the

[p. 79]

inner sense, through which light is brought all at once into the whole inner natural science, is this: *beyond the mere presence of an activity in the mind, a particular receptivity is further required, if we are to be able to become conscious of it*, for we have just exhibited obscure representations of which we are not conscious, although we have them; it is only through inner sense that we arrive at this consciousness, through which they become clear.

#### §. 24.

By what rules, then, do we obtain this consciousness?

It must first be remarked that inner sense, too, just like outer sense, is very dependent on the states of the body. This often comes about because its stage is animated chiefly through outer intuition, and this depends wholly on the body. But even apart from this, in sleep and in fainting fits at least all recollection of self-consciousness vanishes. In magnetic sleep and similar states a quite new self-consciousness is even generated, which often has no connection of recollection at all with the natural one that follows. The receptivity for inner intuition thus depends also on the organization of the body. This follows too from the fact that in illnesses our consciousness often loses so much in liveliness that we are unable to perceive in ourselves representations which in the healthy state we afterwards recall again with ease. Mediately, then, reflection too is thereby weakened, and thinking-over made difficult. On the contrary, in the first degrees of

[p. 80]

intoxication inner sense is far more receptive; representations which were previously obscure now become more distinct, and we can deal with them as otherwise only with far livelier ones. Afterwards, however, only a very indeterminate recollection of this state takes place, because the cause of their distinctness was not the representations' own liveliness but only the greater excitability of inner sense. Inner sense therefore does indeed depend on the organization of the body, and as a part of the organism necessarily corresponds to every inner function, so too such a correlate for inner sense would have to admit of being exhibited; but this reciprocal relation is still far too incompletely known to us for us to enter into particulars, and an explanation of the inner by the outer is in general not possible. For our theory we have therefore to observe only the inner relations for themselves.

Concerning the inner organization of self-consciousness we must now first remark that the inner intuitions do not make up the whole self-consciousness of the mind, but are only its individual, changeable, empirical determinations. For if we look at these intuitions more closely, we find that in each there is contained the representation: *I am* as inwardly active, which, however, is determined in each individual inner intuition as this determinate individual activity, as representation, desire, feeling of pleasure, in that I say: I see this, I hear this, I think about the existence of God; I rejoice, etc. In every inner sense intuition, therefore, the I is the universal object. They all have as their object the mind as the identical subject of the activities intuited inwardly, which

[p. 81]

is a mere correlate of them, but is itself represented as a singular without plurality.

#### §. 25.

This pure self-consciousness underlying all inner intuition, the mere utterance: I think, or more determinately, *I am*, we must first examine more closely. To designate what is peculiar to this representation we must first set up the law: *The representation: I am, cannot be given to the mind together with the individual inner intuitions, but takes place independently of each individual one, lies at the ground of them all already in reason, but comes to our consciousness only through the accompaniment of some individual inner intuition.*

The proof of this lies in the following. First, the representation, I am, relates to one inner intuition just as to another; the expression for every individual inner intuition is always: I sense, I think, I will, etc. Pure self-consciousness is thus already contained in or with every inner intuition. Secondly, the representation, I am, relates not merely to each individual inner intuition, but even to the whole of all these intuitions, in that it determines the object of the one at the same time as object of the others, laying the I at the ground as the identical, simple, one and the same subject of all inner activity.

The faculty of this pure self-consciousness is therefore not inner sensibility itself, but a faculty independent of it, which is called *pure apperception*, and which lies at the ground of inner sense

[p. 82]

lies. Pure apperception is a peculiar spontaneity of the mind, whose receptivity is inner sense; it is a form of inner sensibility, which is determined empirically in each inner intuition.

The second proposition for the knowledge of pure self-consciousness is as follows: *Pure self-consciousness is an immediate feeling of my existence, which, however, we perceive only as it is determined in each individual intuition as an empirical feeling, and is stirred up through it. This pure self-consciousness is itself no intuition, but only an indeterminate feeling.*

The last point is here the most important, and must be made more distinct. Intuition is a cognition in which an object is represented as immediately given; I see this determinate house, hear this determinate sound, look at this determinate mathematical figure; here I always cognize immediately *that* and *what* an object is, and the essential thing in intuition consists in this, that what the object is, is given. Now it may easily seem as if, in pure self-consciousness, if I say to myself: I am, this condition were given; but that is not the case. When I say: I am, then in this consciousness *my existence* is indeed given to me immediately, but I myself am not intuited therein, but only thought *relatively*. The object of this consciousness is the I, but if I think: *I*, then I represent thereby only a thing in general *in relation* to itself, without cognizing *what* sort of thing this is. Not *what* I am, but only *that* I am, is in pure self-consciousness stated

[p. 83]

it is thus not intuition, but representation of reflection. That is precisely the characteristic of a reflected cognition as opposed to an intuitive one, that its object is not itself immediately given, but is only thought in addition through a relation. If I see, e.g., only the shadow of a man, but do not see him, I can gather from it incidentally who he is and where he is, but not intuitively, only relatively, through reflection, in that I perceive not him himself, but only his effect, the shadow. In just this way, in: I am, the object *I* is given only relatively and not immediately, so that we cognize therein not at all what we are. What is deceptive, however, is that the thing is here represented in relation to itself. The mind says here: I, the representing thing, exist; thus every thing that represents, it might otherwise be what it will, a stone, an organized body, a spirit or the Deity, could just as well say: I am. This consciousness by itself distinguishes me from none, I am given to myself therein not as something determinate and individual, but only through a relation.

When I say: I am, I determine the object of this representing only as the same thing which is also the representing subject therein; in order, then, to learn of whom the talk is, I must first become conscious of this self-consciousness, in order to cognize its subject; but here it again means only: I am it, I the representing one am in the consciousness of self-consciousness subject and object of self-consciousness. And if I now go further, to the knowing of the knowing of my knowing, I experience always only the same: I, the same thing which

[p. 84]

represents, is here also represented; but what sort of thing this is does not occur in self-consciousness alone.

Pure self-consciousness thus determines its object only through reflection, and through it the object comes to determinate cognition no sooner than when it is empirically determined in some individual intuition of my activity. This proposition is metaphysically very important, as Kant first showed in the *Critique of Pure Reason*, in his appraisal of psychology. For if pure self-consciousness, independently of the individual inner sense intuition, were already to give a self-cognition, then this would be an intellectually determined immediate cognition, independent of individual determination of time. Now one can of course refute this presupposition immediately by experiment, for in self-consciousness I say to myself evidently only: I am *at this moment*, and not: I was at every time, and shall be in all the future, as this would have to be if its pronouncement had this meaning even without sense intuition. But in the case of undeveloped representations this presupposition lay at the ground of the usual attempts to prove the immortality of the soul, and in Fichte it plays the greatest part. It is only the obscurely thought presupposition of such a self-cognition which actually brought him to the assumption of an intellectual intuition, and is the reason why he wanted to make the self-positing of the I, as a representing of wholly different kind, the generating principle of all cognition, and to derive from it all positing of things outside us.

[p. 85]

#### §. 26.

My self-cognition thus shows me only my inner activity as it flows away in time. Here I obtain the content of the inner activities of cognizing, feeling and willing, and the determination of their time through inner intuition; the universal subject of them, however, is determined through pure self-consciousness, as the form of this inner self-cognition, by the mere: I am. Through this the given manifold in inner sensation becomes an inner activity of the mind. The individual inner intuition gives only a manifold of representations, desires, feelings, as existing one after another, which can therefore be cognized only as effect. This manifold is now always given in relation to pure self-consciousness, which contains the I as the active one in the relation of cause to that effect.

This relation of pure apperception, as form of inner sense, to inner intuition makes the great difference between inner and outer intuition. In it, to be sure, as in the outer, a continuous manifold is given in intuition, of something present in time, as outwardly of something in time and space. But the relation of each individual inner intuition to the pure self-consciousness already present makes it the case that the object here does not, so to speak, first flow together out of the manifold of the intuitions, as matter does in outer intuition, but that the individual intuition already has an activity of the mind as its object, in that I am therein

[p. 86]

immediately conscious of what I think, will and feel.

The organization of our faculty of being conscious of ourselves thus consists in the following: *At its ground lies pure apperception, as a faculty of the mind or of reason to be conscious of itself; this consciousness, however, is determined only through inner sense as individual inner intuition, and only through these empirical determinations do I arrive at self-cognition.* According to what laws, now, does pure self-consciousness obtain these individual intuitive determinations? How is the mind determined to individual self-intuition? E.g. I look at a rose in outer intuition. Here I have, first, a consciousness of the existence of the rose as a thing outside me; then, however, I am at the same time also conscious of myself in pure self-consciousness. How do I come, thirdly, to the consciousness that my activity is determined precisely as intuition of a rose? Since I am conscious first of the rose and then of myself in general, how does there come in besides a consciousness of myself as the one intuiting the rose? Or: I will; therewith I know that I am; how, then, do I know besides that I will?

I answer: through an immediate affection of the mind to an inner sensation, in which I intuit myself. In so doing I maintain that this is all we can say about it in general. For I intuit here my activity, e.g. my willing, not as that which affects me to sensation, but, as in all sensation, my activity, here my

[p. 87]

willing, is given to me in intuition *immediately as present, as something actually existing*. In original self-consciousness I am conscious of myself only as the determining one; in inner intuition, however, through the given determinable my activity is intuited. This intuition is a genuine sense intuition. Here only an activity of the mind, namely the inner intuiting, is perceived, to which inner sensibility is passively determined; we are compelled to intuit our inner states precisely as we actually intuit them, without the necessitating thing, what affects us, appearing along with it. The relation here, then, as in every sensation, is pure fact, whose cause does not fall within observation; through the connection of inner experience, however, we are afterwards led to presuppose the intuited activity itself as the affecting one.

#### §. 27.

Thus there result the two chief laws of inner intuition. *First, a determinate degree of strength is required of an inner activity, in order that it may affect inner sense sufficiently to be perceived. Secondly, only the activities of the mind sensibly stirred up fall immediately into inner intuition.*

As to the first, every inner intuition requires a receptivity of the sense for an affection of it, and then an activity which affects this receptivity, so that I become conscious of it. Both, however, the receptivity of the sense and

[p. 88]

the activity, have at all times a certain degree of strength. A certain strength of each of my inner activities, a representation, a feeling, a desire, is therefore always required, in order that it can affect inner sense sufficiently for me to become conscious of it. This requisite strength or liveliness of an inner activity, however, will be different in different states of mind, according as the degree of receptivity of inner sense itself is each time greater or smaller. Hereby the relation of obscure and clear representations or other inner activities becomes wholly distinct. A representation must remain obscure, I do not become immediately conscious of it, until it obtains sufficient strength to affect inner sense properly. Only of the liveliest among my activities, then, am I at any time conscious; these, however, make up only the very smallest part of my inner being.

As to the second law, what is given in inner intuition is in constant change, in flux through time; those activities which are to let themselves be perceived immediately must therefore occur in a continuous flux of changes; they must be bound up with sensible determinations. I perceive my activities in inner sensation only on the occasion of affections; enduring inner activity, on the other hand, everything abiding in inner experience, can be cognized only mediately, through the reflection that is added to intuition. This is again very important for philosophy. The enigmatic relation of necessary cognitions, or of cognition *a priori*, will be made distinct thereby alone. Of such general representations,

[p. 89]

like those of space and time, which occur in all my intuitions, I become conscious only on the occasion of an individual sense intuition. Every universal law according to which a mathematical relation, or the concept of cause and effect, or the ideas of the world and of God, are in my cognition, shows itself to me only through sensible representations before consciousness in individual applications, and can be brought out and exhibited for itself only through artificial reflection. Just so with regard to other inner activities. In the individual case I am indeed conscious that I wish, desire or will something, but according to what universal maxim of the will this happens, whether I do so from self-interest or disinterestedly, whether I wished, desired or willed thus from self-seeking or from benevolence toward others, that I can determine only afterwards through reflection.

#### §. 28.

On this rests a difference in my inner being, whether activities and states of mind belong to the *momentary empirical state of mind* or not, that is, whether I am just now conscious of them or not, whether they belong to the clear or only to the obscure representation. The series of the sensibly stirred up liveliest activities, which fall immediately into consciousness, makes up the whole empirical state of mind, and this is the sole source from which I can draw my self-cognition.

From this, reflection alone can borrow the materials, to the end that a knowledge of the far greater domain of my activities immediately unconscious to me

[p. 90]

may be obtained; only through its mediation do we then find the enduring laws and the fundamental determinations of our inner being, which lie at the ground of that constant change. As little, then, as what we see around us at the moment makes up, for this moment, the whole world outside us, just as little is our momentary inner being what we perceive of it inwardly at each moment. The raising of our self-cognition from the first inner perception up to a complete knowledge of our inner world is now the real task for reflection, and this is often subject to great difficulties, in which the source of all philosophical misunderstandings lies hidden.

The first further application of these propositions we shall have to make with regard to representations, in that we consider more closely the way in which representations are inwardly perceived. A clear representation, as opposed to an obscure one, is called a *perception*; this *percipiren* [perceiving], or the inner perception of representations, is properly the first thing in all our cognition, for only to the extent that I perceive a state of mind in me is it there for my reflection. We thus come at once back to this object, and shall then show its importance for inner natural science still more clearly.

[p. 91]

### Third Section.

### Investigation of the Memory-Bound Course of Thought.

#### a) Memory-Bound and Logical Course of Thought.

#### §. 29.

Complete cognition, or the whole of it, as we ascribe it to reason, comes about through the cooperation of two faculties of the mind, sensibility and understanding. These we have provisionally distinguished: sensibility as the faculty of the mind to arrive, through a receptivity called sense, at representations which consist in sense intuitions that we obtain in sensation; understanding, on the other hand, as the faculty of self-activity in cognizing, in so far as its representations are voluntarily determinable and belong to reflection. We have seen how sense supplies us with manifold intuitions of things outside us, but that our cognition of things outside us in space begins not through these qualities of sense intuition, but properly through the relations of things to one another. It is further shown that only through inner sensation can we attain to inner intuition

[p. 92]

of our own activity, in that the original pure self-consciousness is determined in the individual case through sensation to the inner intuition of my activity. Herein consists the contribution to cognition which sense, as the receptivity for sensation, supplies us. To this there now comes understanding, as the second chief faculty, with self-activity, and completes our whole cognition. The business of sensibility is to supply the manifold material to the cognition of individual things; the business of understanding, on the other hand, is to bring unity and combination into this manifold. For it is chiefly the universal concepts that serve this purpose, in which the activities of understanding come to our consciousness. Thus sense and understanding make up the two chief elements through which our cognition becomes complete. But besides this, from which cognition properly springs in the mind, there are still other inner states and changes of the representations in the mind, which concern the existence, the alternation and the reciprocal play of representations in our inner being. These belong in themselves neither to sense nor to understanding, but make up only a mechanism of inner changes, where the representations already present in the mind work further upon one another.

The consideration of inner sense has properly first shown us the standpoint from which our anthropological investigations must proceed; it has shown us the point from which alone we can consider ourselves. This was, namely, the empirical state of mind, which alone falls immediately into intuition. In this we have now first considered, of the activities belonging to

[p. 93]

cognition, the sense intuitions, to which we are involuntarily compelled in sensation. What now belongs besides these, of representations, to the empirical state of mind, we call in general the *course of thought*; this, then, is that from which all our further observations must be taken. Alongside the sense intuitions there lie in the course of thought the voluntary representations of reflection, which belong to the understanding. But between the two there lies yet a wide field of inner activity, which depends in part on voluntary determinations and in part not, but which even in its involuntary representations does not belong to sense in the proper meaning. For here quite inward changes and alternations of the representations show themselves, which are not given in immediate sensations of sense, but where an inner play of our representations maintains itself. This is the domain of the imagination.

Thus we have already spoken earlier of intuitions in which we do not cognize the object as present, as in sense intuition, but only intuit it in imagination. Of such not properly sensible representations of the imagination there are many kinds, which all contain an inner play of the representations among one another or presuppose it, and not an affection of the same to sensation. E.g. if something falls into my eye, then to the mere sensations of color there at once come in addition inwardly determined representations of the distance, magnitude, figure of the colored thing into my representation, which are occasioned only through sensation, and which moreover are not

[p. 94]

voluntary; just so the name of a place reminds us of its whole situation, etc. Such occasions of representations belong to the imagination. They all belong to an inner mechanism of representations among one another, where one works upon another, and thus the whole law of their operation must occur in experience; consequently the laws of the imagination, as a self-activity of the mind, must admit of being explained completely, and this determines our next task.

According to the aforementioned distinction between understanding and imagination I divide the course of thought, with Platner, into the *logical* and the *memory-bound*. To the latter belong memory, the inner perception of representations, recollection and the peculiar laws of the imagination. What distinguishes the former is the voluntary determination of representations, the understanding acting upon them through the will. Through this there comes properly life and free self-determination into the play of our representations. It spreads its activity over the whole course of our thoughts, and mediately determines also the laws of the memory-bound course of thought according to its ends, in thinking as well as in poetic invention. But this voluntariness is not the only thing that is added to our representations in the logical course of thought; with it there shows itself in particular also the logical manner of representation, that is, the mediate manner of cognition through concepts in judgments, after which this course of thought is properly named, and on which the whole re-consciousness of the cognitions of the higher faculty of cognition rests.

It must therefore not mislead us here if in the representations of the memory-bound course of thought there already depends much

[p. 95]

on our voluntary determination. We must always keep in view only the law according to which the inner changes each time follow; then only such laws belong to the memory-bound course of thought and to the imagination, according to which representations are inwardly, involuntarily, brought about or modified; everything else, on the other hand, belongs to the logical course of thought.

The laws of the imagination must properly be the last that are set in activity, or come into application, among those belonging to cognition, for they concern an inner play of other representations among one another. These representations must first be supplied by sense and reason, before they begin to act upon one another according to the peculiar laws of the memory-bound course of thought. We must seek these laws first, however, because through them the representations are mediated in which the activities of the understanding come to consciousness.

#### b) Memory and Inner Perception of Representations.

#### §. 30.

The first thing we have to consider in the memory-bound course of thought is the presence and persistence of representations in the mind, i.e., memory. Memory, namely, in the most determinate meaning, is the faculty of retaining representations once had. We must here still distinguish memory from the power of recollection, which is commonly included under it. We always have many representations

[p. 96]

in memory which are so weak that perhaps today I cannot recollect them with the utmost effort, whereas at another time they occur to me unbidden. To the power of recollection there belongs in addition that I become conscious again of certain representations (we shall find its theory later); memory, of which we are now speaking, consists on the other hand only in the faculty of retaining such representations as we have once had; it relates to the persistence of representations in the mind.

Since experience shows in such manifold and often seemingly wonderful ways the dependence of this faculty on the states of health of the body, there are here especially many attempts to explain it from material ideas, and according to all sorts of arbitrary hypotheses from the constitution of the brain and the nerves. For a correct inner self-observation, in which it is at the same time borne in mind that the inner appearances must be considered for themselves in their own connection, and that we must not confuse the material with the representing, the theory of memory is subject to no difficulties at all. It goes without saying that the mind must have memory, that representations once excited must persist in it. In nature every power, once it has been set in activity, goes on working with a determinate degree of power until other influences come in and occasion changes. Just this will therefore be the case also with regard to the faculties of representation and the representations flowing from them. Not memory and the retention of representations once had, but precisely the forgetting of them, needs a special explanation.

[p. 97]

But to make this relation wholly distinct, we must still attend to the difference of the clear and the obscure in our representations, or to the relation of their inner perception to memory. Only the liveliest changes affect inner sense sufficiently; we therefore perceive only a series of changes in our representations, whereas those which persist quietly are for the most part obscure. We therefore notice our memory always only in its influence on the inner perception of representations, and commonly think little of the fact that the chief possession of our mind consists in its obscure representations. All representations which we once have or have had remain present to us; the whole mass of all our representations remains lying in memory; but as new ones keep forcing their way in alongside the earlier ones and these coincide in the same representing power of the I, this power divides itself ever more, the preceding representations are thereby pushed back and very soon made obscure. If earlier representations are therefore not strengthened again from time to time, they become gradually ever weaker. In this way we must represent to ourselves that our whole knowledge is at all times present in the mind, but that at each moment only very few representations have the requisite distinctness to attain by themselves to consciousness, i.e., to be perceived.

Forgetting we can therefore think only as an ever greater obscuring of our representations, without our needing to assume that representations are ever wholly lost to us. The degree of their liveliness can, without end, be thought

[p. 98]

ever smaller; we need therefore never assume that they have wholly vanished.

Insight into this persisting presence of our knowing, cognizing, representing and of all other inner activities in the mind gives us first an intelligible concept of this mind. Without this persistence of the inner activities the inner being of the mind would be only a senseless play of outer impressions, without any independence. There must surely be something independent of the outer impression, on which this outer impression is first made; otherwise we obtain the contradictory concept of an inner being which would be no inner being. Such a representation of empiricism (as it is found at bottom in Locke's and Hume's theory), which would let all that is inner flow together only through momentary outer impression, thus contradicts itself.

But if we now observe ourselves inwardly, we see there nothing but constant change, constant alternation of our activity, a momentary appearing and vanishing of representations, desires, etc. This commonly misleading objection is refuted by considering the relation of inner activity to the perception of it before inner sense, and the direction of the latter through attention. Then we see that that appearance of constant alternation, of appearing and vanishing of the representations, is only a rising and sinking of their liveliness, that we indeed always become aware only of broken-off individual series of representations, that this, however, comes only from the fact that a series that has become obscurer withdraws from our view, and as it were into the interior of the

[p. 99]

mind, or because we have directed our attention to something else.

The difficulty in this investigation lies ultimately in this, that the form of inner sense, pure self-consciousness, gives no law of intuitive coordination of that which is *present together in the inner being*, as space does this outwardly. Many therefore assert, as Fichte does, that there is no manifold simultaneity at all in inner perception, without considering that then, e.g., no comparison at all would be possible. In general, however, there arises from this the objection: *Where* then is the obscure supposed to be in me, of which I am not conscious? One seeks, as it were, *a place* for it, and finds none anywhere. With an incomplete insight into the relation of the spiritual to the material organization of the body, one therefore commonly enters into no inner theory at all, but seeks to explain everything abiding and enduring in memory only through the body. But whoever knows pure inner observation, and does not spoil it with reasoning from false presuppositions, will easily find (e.g. if he reflects on the possibility of comparison, where I must necessarily be conscious of the one and of the other *at the same time*, in order to notice similarity or difference, or even only if he reflects on how I can at the same time see, hear, think and will so many different things)—he will easily find, I say, that such a coordination certainly does take place before consciousness, only *without an intuitive form of it*. The case is about the same as with the hearing of several tones at the same time. How with the same eye we perceive several colors at once is clear to us, since there we arrange the colors immediately

[p. 100]

in space side by side. But how with one ear we can grasp side by side the many tones of a concert falling at the same time seems strange to us as soon as we begin to reason about it, since here we coordinate not the sound itself, but only the sounding thing in space—that the simultaneous apprehension actually takes place, however, admits of no doubt. So too in the inner being.

#### §. 31.

At the ground of the memory-bound course of thought lies the persistence of representations in memory, whose most general law is a law of the mutual weakening of representations in the same state of mind, when with the entry of new representations the degree of our representing power is not raised at the same time. To this fundamental determination there is then added, through inner sense, the *perception* or inner perception of representations, whose laws are determined on one side by the receptivity of sense, on the other by the liveliness of the representations. The livelier a representation is, the more easily I perceive it, and the more receptive sense is, the less liveliness of representations it needs in order still to be able to become conscious of them. This receptivity of sense, and even the liveliness of the representations by themselves, depend on very fine nuances of mood and health, and make us, e.g., now more, now less disposed to thinking.

The states and differences of the mind with respect to inner perception are chiefly those of the

[p. 101]

*horizon of inner perception and attention.*

The greater or smaller horizon of inner perception, the greater or smaller field of vision, as it were, of the inner eye, which it commands at a glance, is a significant difference in a human being's disposition to thinking. One is able to hold fast before the inner eye a multitude of representations side by side at once; the other must let each follow the other one by one, in order to become conscious of them. The size of this horizon gives, e.g., in speaking and for recollection a great advantage, in that I can attach my recollection more many-sidedly to what I am just thinking of, and in reasoning or in a narration keep the whole before my eyes, without letting myself be disturbed in the exposition of the individual part, and without losing the thread of the story while I dwell on individual parts. But just as with a telescope one must reduce the field of vision more and more the more precisely one wants to see, the more magnification one wants to use, so here too the size of the inner field of vision of perception stands in inverse relation to acuity. Whoever surveys much at once will easily distinguish less sharply and judge more superficially, but on the other hand will more easily grasp similarities of things.

A narrow horizon of inner perception, on the contrary, favors sharp distinction and calm observation. The former makes one more readily witty, the other acute.

The most important thing in the inner perception of representations is attention and the distraction opposed to it. The apprehension of a representation is the

[p. 102]

act of the mind in the perception of it. Attention is the preferential dwelling of the mind on the apprehension of a determinate representation; it is a preferential direction of inner sense upon it. To this belong heeding, contemplating, observing, and the like. Opposed to it is distraction, as a state of mind in which either too many representations crowd together into inner perception, or in which we otherwise attend to none of them preferentially, the latter being made possible by the influence of the will on attending.

The steering, direction and tension of attention depend very much on the will, and through them it properly gains its dominion in thinking; but since here not only its inner, immediate influence comes into consideration, but incidentally also its influence on speaking, on thinking through speaking, and on much else bodily, we must make the closer investigation of attention only where voluntary representing will be observed.

#### c) Of Imagination in General.

#### §. 32.

Memory and inner perception of representations underlie the memory-bound course of thought, but the play of its representations is properly enlivened by the laws of imagination. Imagination is its principal faculty, for it first really sets its representations into play. Memory contains only the ground of their existence, attention the ground that they are perceived, but

[p. 103]

imagination adds the laws according to which that constant rising and falling of their liveliness is brought about which keeps our self-consciousness alive. It is in general the faculty of the involuntary inner play of our representations; to it belong the laws according to which representations in the mind act upon one another reciprocally.

The inner phenomena which we usually ascribe to imagination—in cognizing as mathematical imagination, in thinking as schematizing imagination, in dreaming and poetic invention according to their most peculiar functions—belong, under the guidance of the understanding, to the union of two faculties of wholly different origin in our mind. Both we must first investigate separately here, in order to obtain a theory of inner life. They are distinguished as *productive* and *reproductive* imagination. The reproductive gives us back only representations which we have already had; according to its laws various representations become dimmer or clearer, one that has just occurred calls another with it before consciousness, e.g. when I hear a word of a language known to me, the thought designated by it at once occurs to me as well; to it belong the laws commonly so called of the association of ideas. The productive imagination, on the other hand, goes to wholly new representations, which are first determined by others already present in the mind; it is the faculty of intuitive combination, of mathematical intuition or of formal intuition. To it belong, e.g., the representations of the magnitude, position and figure of things in space. We know, e.g., very well that the moon is a heavenly body, and that when it

[p. 104]

rises, low on the horizon, it is no larger than when it stands high in the sky; also the colored image which we receive of it is just as large below as above, as we can find if we measure it: nevertheless we imagine that we see it much larger below, when it has only just risen above the horizon, than when it stands high in the sky. Here the representation of the magnitude of the moon in the intuition of it is a representation of the productive imagination.

What we first and usually understand by imaginings are the intuitions of objects without their presence, the intuition of objects in the mere recollection of them, or even the intuitive representation of objects which we merely invent, e.g. in reading a narrative. These imaginings are nothing but the sense intuitions of the objects themselves, of which we afterwards become conscious only with a much diminished degree of liveliness. According to their material they all belong to the reproductive imagination; they are mere after-images of sense intuitions. However rich and inexhaustible imagination may be, especially in the faculty of poetic invention, everything new that it is able to bring forth consists only in the composition and combination of representations, it consists in a new form of the objects—but creative it never becomes. Of a pain that I have never felt, or of a color that I have never seen, I can create no imagining either. Indeed, even one to whom, e.g., yellow and blue were known would still not be able to project the representation of green as the middle color between the two by mere imagination without a preceding intuition.

[p. 105]

For a rational creature we can think of absolutely no fitting shape but the human, because experience shows us no other. Gods and genii imagination can fashion only after the model of man; as soon as it departs from him in more than incidentals, mere caricature remains. At most it adds a pair of wings to him, or gives its Krishna four arms and colors him blue, like the flower of the lotus or the sky. The productive imagination is therefore, in its material, always dependent on the reproductive; it is a mere faculty of form in intuition, whereas the reproductive does not confine its influence merely to the intuitive.

The intuitive representations of objects without their presence belong, at least in their material, always to reproductive imagination, but they by no means make up the whole store of its representations. Commonly, to be sure, this imagination is given only as a sensible faculty, and not, say, on the ground that it is nevertheless distinct from the understanding, but as if it had to do only with sense intuitions and not with the representations of the understanding. This, however, is incorrect, for the very persons who make this restriction (e.g. Jakob in his *Empirical Psychology*) afterwards nevertheless reckon the association of representations in general to the reproductive imagination, but this extends to all our representations: I remember just as well what I have thought as what I have seen, and the sound of which the word consists associates itself with the thought which the word designates. The laws of reproductive imagination, or of the strengthening and weakening

[p. 106]

of consciousness in different representations through one another, hold for all kinds of representations in general. Hence others divide its faculty into a *sensible* and an *intellectual* one, according as it shows itself in representations of sense or of the understanding; thus, e.g., a sensible and an intellectual memory, attention, etc. are distinguished. But this division of the faculties of the memory-bound course of thought has no value for theory, for at the bottom of it all there lies always only one and the same law.

#### d) Theory of the Re-Strengthening of Representations through Association.

#### §. 33.

The laws of reproductive imagination can be grouped according to two kinds of phenomena: the first are the phenomena of the re-strengthening of representations through association, the others concern the influence of habit on the inner play of our representations. First, of the reproduction of representations.

What we want to explain here is the reawakening of representations, that is, we are to state how it comes about that we become conscious again of such representations as had previously occurred in consciousness but had since vanished again. That this phenomenon constantly shows itself in the change of inner activity is obvious. (The laws belonging here are usually called laws of the association of ideas, after French or English usage, where the word idea means representation in general; recent German philosophy since Kant has with good reason

[p. 107]

departed from this indeterminate usage; we therefore do not use the expression association of ideas.) Here we must remark that by this reawakening is not understood that I, e.g., see again today what I saw yesterday, nor in general that a representation is awakened anew through external occasion, but rather only the phenomenon that a representation recurs through mere inner occasion, that, e.g., something comes back to me which I had long forgotten, in general that I recollect something. This reawakening now always takes place in such a way that one representation first recurs, and this is then so combined with another that it brings this too back to consciousness; that is, there are found associations of representations for mutual reawakening. According to what laws do these now arise in the mind?

On no object of inner natural science, surely, are there more investigations than on this one, and yet no one has brought it to a general, satisfactory theory. This for two reasons. Some, namely, instead of going to general laws of theory, remain standing at the explanation of individual phenomena; others, who sought theory, committed errors against the fundamental laws of inner natural science.

The former reckon these phenomena among the mysterious depths of our mind, the explanation of which will presumably never fully succeed; we maintain, on the contrary, that few simpler and more satisfying theories can be given than precisely for this imagination. An image will make this clear. One who cannot make lace certainly does not know how the pins are set and the bobbins

[p. 108]

thrown so that the pattern arises, but he will not on that account say that lace-making is a mystery to him, for he well understands its theory, he grasps well how by setting the pins and properly plaiting the threads a pattern must arise, even if he cannot give the rule for the particular. We are in the same case with one who demands of us the explanation of a particular poem, of a dream, of a folly; we do not know how the pins were set and how the bobbins were thrown to bring about just this pattern, i.e., we do not know the particular history of the representations of any human being down to the smallest detail, and this can be of interest to no one either; but we cannot on that account call the phenomenon itself either enigmatic or mysterious, for the theory according to which some determinate pattern or other had to fall out here we understand very well; only the mutual positions and relations of the particulars could we not observe.

Whoever, secondly, sought theory here and did not find it, always overlooked the important law of inner sense, according to which we must distinguish the rule of the presence of the inner activities from the rule according to which they are inwardly perceived. Immediately for self-observation the reproduction of representations, this coming forth again of what had already vanished, is a mere phenomenon before inner perception, which belongs to inner sense. Here it is now the one-sidedness of all theories hitherto attempted that one stopped only at this phenomenon before inner sense. One observed only the alternation of this re-consciousness, this alternation of forgetting and recollecting, and

[p. 109]

when one wanted to specify a cause of it, one therefore at once looked about again for the body and its nerves, and invented there material ideas which were to bring the connection into the inner events.

If, on the other hand, we attend to the multitude of all our representations that always remains lying dark in memory, and to how these must act upon one another, then everything is at once clear. One wrongly calls these phenomena a reproduction or regeneration of the representations, since it is merely a reappearing of them before inner sense, and presupposes no new generation of them at all. We know, rather, that the vanishing of representations from consciousness is occasioned only by their obscuration, and we know in general heightened receptivity of inner sense and heightened liveliness of the representations as the two causes through which obscure representations become clear again.

The phenomenon of the association of representations therefore consists in this, that when a obscure representation becomes clear again, it is so combined according to some law with other obscure representations that these too become clear again with it; and the explanation can be sought either only in this, that the receptivity of inner sense is heightened, or in an actual play of the representations themselves becoming darker and livelier, which communicates itself according to those laws. Were it only the former, the whole phenomenon would belong merely to inner sense, and there would be no imagination here at all, as a faculty distinct from it. But with a heightening of the receptivity of sense nothing can be explained here, for if the single representation acted on

[p. 110]

this, it would not call forth a determinate other one, but would only spread more light in general over my inner being. If, on the other hand, in association, e.g., the first verse of a stanza reminds me of the second, or the word of its thought, then this determinate representation acts just in favor of that determinate one; the effect must therefore arise from a relation of the representations themselves to one another, and the law of this relation is a peculiar law of imagination.

We therefore already know what we have to seek here: we must seek, from the phenomena of reawakening through association, a law according to which the enlivening of one representation communicates itself at the same time to others.

If we now compare the experiences on this point, there show themselves at first very many different relations according to which representations are associated. The cause reminds us of the effect, the means of the end and conversely, the most remote similarity leads over from one representation to another, or mere simultaneity of things however diverse, or uninterrupted temporal succession among similar representations, determines the association. All these relations can, however, in the end be traced back to two, that of simultaneity and that of affinity. Representations associate themselves by coinciding in one course of my life-expression, and all the more, the nearer they flowed from the same faculty of representation, i.e., the more akin they are; sensible representations, e.g., associate more easily with sensible ones than with representations of the understanding; intellectual ones more easily with intellectual ones. From these two fundamental relations all the others can be derived, if we will only take due account of

[p. 111]

the whole of our life, and not judge merely by individual moments torn out of it. This gives the following formula: The occasional strengthening of one representation acts on the strengthening of another, 1) in proportion to the strength with which representations were together and in relation to one another in earlier states of mind; 2) in proportion to the greater or lesser affinity of the representations with one another; 3) in proportion to the relation in which those states of mind in general act on the present one. The fundamental relation always remains affinity and simultaneity, but the effect is very much modified by the mutual position of the states of mind in general. The more lively, e.g., two representations once were together in the mind, or with the greater liveliness they followed one another, the more strongly they are associated. Yet with regard to the later effect it still depends on whether it is long since they so coincided, whether their association has been favored since, or whether the one or the other later occurred in other combinations. A child has through a slight association acquired a predilection for a certain occupation or station; if this is gradually favored, perhaps, by equally slight circumstances, it can become decisive for its whole life; if, however, it is soon interrupted, it has no further consequence.

This would be the general law for the association of representations. But further we find that the phenomena of association are not at all restricted to mere representations, but that they hold, entirely according to the same laws, for all inner activities. Feelings of pleasure and desires associate with one another, and again

[p. 112]

with representations, according to the same rules of affinity and simultaneity. Enjoyment attunes to cheerfulness, love makes the lover more tender even in intercourse with friends, pity awakens love; or how often does the most remote agreeable relation make an object forever interesting to us; what worth do rings and ribbons not often acquire, because their mere sight is associated with feelings. To this belong homesickness and countless other phenomena. In short, the laws of association govern our whole inner life with equal power.

To be sure, it might also be maintained that all reawakening of desires and feelings of pleasure is effected only mediately through imagination, because desires and feelings of pleasure are after all contained in representations in manifold ways and dependent on them. But even if we disregard that this explanation would have to turn out very artificial where only feelings of pleasure and desires act on one another, and that the appeal to imagination is after all only an unprovable hypothesis, observation itself shows immediately, when in the simplest cases we follow the course of our recollection, that it is properly an entire former state of mind that comes back to us, only that of course the image is mostly blurred, in that we recollect several states at once.

This leads us to a quite general significance of the above law, if in the law of reproductive imagination we put every inner activity in place of representation: In proportion to the relative strength with which inner activities of the mind were together in earlier states of it, in proportion to the relation in which these states of mind act on the present one

[p. 113]

and in proportion to the relation of their mutual affinity: the strengthening of a single inner activity acts at the same time on the strengthening of another.

With this law we have satisfied the demands of classification, in that we trace everything back to one fundamental rule. But this fundamental rule we have obtained through an induction which presupposes the indeterminate comparison of countless, often very complicated facts, and it also has the uncertain and wavering character of all such inductions. We cannot yet hope that everyone without exception will approve of our arrangement; some may at least think that it is a matter of indifference whether one chooses to arrange it thus or thus. Or if our arrangement is also correct: how then does this law come into our mind? Are we, with Malebranche, merely to accept it gratefully from the ordering hand of the Creator as a peculiar beneficent mechanism in our inner being? Or can a ground of it be exhibited from the laws of the organization of our life, and its necessity thus shown?

Only if the latter succeeds can we really lay claim to a theory of imagination. The law of the strengthening of one representation by another, with which we have to do here, is the opposite of the law of the weakening of them that occurred in memory. Both rest on the coincidence of the representations in one state of mind and on the relation of their affinity with regard to their origin.
