When one representation is added to another, it now weakens the latter, because both must share in the same degree of the faculty; but if they have once been together, and the one is strengthened again, then

[p. 114]

this communicates itself to the other as well. Hence we may conjecture that both laws may rest on a similar ground. It then further appears: the former is only a single case of a general law, and in the case of the second, experience likewise leads us to determine it more generally; the first holds for all activities of the mind insofar as they are parts of a single one, perhaps it will be the same with the second in a similar way; finally, the former follows immediately from the fundamental laws of all inner activity in general, should not the second also be capable of being grounded there? If we now compare, it is found: the mere being-together of inner activities is to be, in proportion to their more or less akin origin from the faculties of the mind, the cause why afterwards the one strengthens the other again. Thereby the following theory results. The individual, apparently different activities which the mind expresses at the same time nevertheless belong together in *one* action of it; the strengthening of a part of this activity is therefore at the same time a proportionate strengthening of this whole activity; that is, inner activities act on one another more or less according to the stated law, according as they belong together in one action of the mind. Simultaneous expressions of a faculty of the mind may seem very different, yet they belong together in one life-expression, in a unity of action. Hearing, seeing and feeling, as activities of the same outer sensibility, are very different, but they nevertheless coincide in one activity of my intuiting, and unite in the mathematical intuition of the same object in space. The desire to ride, and the

[p. 115]

desire to read a book are very different, but if they coincide at the same time, they unite as determining grounds of the same resolution, in which the one will overcome the other. Such a unity of action takes place for the whole life-expression of the mind at every moment. The mind, the I, is the same one subject of all its activity, and for every time unites its whole inner activity in one center. (The representation of this inner combination of everything manifold into *one* activity is, however, again difficult because we cannot make it intuitive, since inner sense has no purely intuitive form of the given of its objects.) In this unity of action in all my activity at any given time there now lies the ground of all laws of association. All my simultaneous or uninterruptedly successive representations, feelings and desires coincide in one action of the I, and indeed all the more closely, the more closely they are akin with regard to the faculty from which they flow. If now some part of this action is strengthened again and newly enlivened, this strengthening spreads proportionately over the whole unity of this action, and now exhibits before inner perception the phenomena of association. It is obvious that if we now go conversely from theory to experience, the very fundamental determinations found by experience are also the first consequences of the theory. Coinciding in a state of mind, as simultaneous or in uninterrupted succession, determines first that certain activities belong together in one action of the mind; but this unity of action must still exist now, if it is now to produce a proportionate re-strengthening

[p. 116]

hence the second rule, of the proportionate influence of that earlier state of mind on the present one; finally, more akin activities associate more easily than less akin ones, because they belong together in a closer unity of my action. The laws of the strengthening of the inner activities through association are therefore properly laws of the play of my life-activities among one another; they are the laws of the enlivening of our whole inner being through the heightened activity of some single part. Every smallest impulse spreads its vibrations proportionately over my whole inner life. Thus association becomes one of the most momentous laws of the whole of inner experience; through it, with the enlivening of one representation, the whole activity of the mind is at the same time stirred up. The effect of the law extends in this not only to inner perception, but many obscure representations are also stimulated along with it through it, without this being sufficient to reach perceptibility. Our associations develop with the history of our inner life, and are formed further daily along with it; in them lies almost the whole inner cultivation of our mind, and on them depend for the most part skill, talent and genius, prudence, stupidity and folly.

#### §. 34.

From these fundamental laws a multitude of individual rules can now easily be derived. I name here only the most general and momentous.

For association through mere simultaneity the combination of the word in language with the thought is the best example, in that the most heterogeneous representations,

[p. 117]

the mere sensation of a sound and general concepts of the understanding, never come to recollection without one another, as soon as they have been combined a couple of times. For the effect of uninterrupted temporal succession, learning by heart is the nearest evidence. These two lie immediately in the fundamental law. Of the influence of habit we shall speak separately. Then there is still to be mentioned the law that similar representations reawaken one another, and recollection.

*The association of similar representations* follows partly already from the law of affinity, but in general also from that of simultaneity. Representations are similar when they have identical partial representations; e.g., virtue and right are similar, in that both express a relation of my action to the moral law. Here, then, the identical partial representations will act according to the fundamental law, and therefore strengthen those with which they were formerly there at the same time. To these belong then also the other secondary representations which together with it made up the similar representation. Similar representations can therefore reawaken one another, if the strengthening effected is sufficient. I think, e.g., of Plato as philosopher, thereby of philosophy in general, and so Spinoza too occurs to me. Through this mode of association alone is it possible to be witty, in that, e.g., in a pun one meaning of a word leads quickly to all the others, or in general, when a relation presents itself, many similar relations occur to us.

[p. 118]

#### §. 35.

The most general phenomenon of the re-strengthening of representations is, finally, *recollection*. Recollection is properly one and the same with the general phenomenon of the reawakening of representations, for it is the consciousness of a representation as one that has already been there, the repeated perception of it. What makes the difference between the representations of the power of recollection and those of reproductive imagination in general is only this, that I am not always conscious again of just one determinate past representation, but the recollection of former states of mind is, more or less indeterminately, as it were blurred by the multitude of images. Every single feature in dream and poetic invention, or when I think, e.g., merely human being or red in general, is properly always recollection, but we usually call only the simplest cases so. In these, something more is added in recollection beyond the mere re-consciousness, namely the consciousness that and how an inner activity has already been there. This already requires the combination in time of the manifold of the inner activities of which I am conscious, through productive imagination. This perception of the manifold in time, the consciousness of the temporal determination of our activities, comes about only in recollection. Otherwise we should, as it were, live with our whole consciousness always only in one moment of the present. In recollection I become conscious, namely, that something is and yet also is not, that is, that something has been. E.g., I am conscious of my reading in Homer, and yet also that I

[p. 119]

am not reading in him; this I can represent only through the “I was reading him,” through the relation of a past time, or of the temporal sequence of my states in general, of which I here become conscious through recollection.

But let no one think that from the concept that something is and yet also is not, the representation of what is found one after another can be derived analytically, and just as little, from an analogous representation for space, that something and yet something else exists, the representation of what is found side by side. For this lies rather already immediately at the ground of the conditions of our intuition, and first shows us the possibility of those combinations of productive imagination which without it we could never obtain from mere concepts. What is explained here is not the origin of this form of intuition, but only its application, the way in which it comes to consciousness, namely to inner perception. (The confusion censured here lies at the ground of all peculiar explanations of the theory of the faculty of representation, of all deductions of the *Doctrine of Science*, and of all constructions of the philosophy of identity. The generating principle of nature is here only the embarrassment of the constructor in representing nature to himself. This embarrassment is the ground which entitles him, e.g., to postulate, in addition to his identity, duplicity, self-cognition of the absolute, potencies, etc.)

The power of recollection is that which is commonly called memory. Hence we earlier called the series of our determinate or indeterminate recollection, i.e., the series of the representations of reproductive imagination in their involuntary development, precisely

[p. 120]

the memory-bound course of thought. In general there stand opposed here in our inner being the memory-bound course of thought through association and the logical course of thought through voluntary reflection. Hence the conflict between understanding and memory, which is so often noticed in experience. Our consciousness at any given time must divide itself between the one and the other; both therefore do each other reciprocal damage. Hence, e.g., the understanding can do little to help recollection. However much one exerts oneself to call to mind something that just will not occur to one, one rarely attains one's end; one must rather look away from such a representation, and return to it only fleetingly from time to time, for the voluntary representations of the understanding only disturb the quiet course of the representations of memory. People who have little understanding but are otherwise not exactly weak usually possess a strong, though often useless memory, in that the memory-bound course of thought of the associations is little interrupted by the logical course of reflection, and so the whole degree of their consciousness falls to the former. Witty heads, on the other hand, mostly have a weak memory for the same reason, while the more serious thinking head must unite both in an eminent degree. The power of recollection demands three different capacities of the mind: to grasp something into memory, to retain it in memory, and to call something to mind. All three united in an eminent degree first make up a strong memory properly speaking. Usually they are not all found together in an eminent degree, since they belong to very different dispositions of mind. The power of grasping depends for the most part on attention and thereby

[p. 121]

mediately on reflection and the understanding. But to grasp well and to grasp quickly are two different things. To grasp easily and quickly is a property of a lively, mobile mind, but shows more agility than strength of mind; on the other hand, to grasp slowly and retain faithfully is rather combined with strength. The retentive faculty is what we called memory in the narrower sense; to retain well is an excellent disposition of mind, in that it bears witness to the inner health of the mind, but unfortunately it helps little without the faculty of calling to mind. In the faculty of calling easily to mind, memory shows itself most immediately in life; this gives the appearance of learning and diligence, and is the most useful of all the capacities needed for recollection; but for genius, intellect and understanding it is easily also the most dangerous, in that it precisely proves the dominion of association over reflection. One who calls to mind far too easily and abundantly what he has heard and learned cannot, for sheer citations and reminiscences, come to thinking for himself; he knows something fine to say about everything, but always only by repeating the thoughts of others, never or seldom from his own resources. For one who has so exceedingly compliant a faculty of calling to mind it is therefore exceedingly hard to cultivate his taste and his judgment, for it always spares him the trouble of thinking by the foreign thoughts, already lying ready, which it slips to him. The power of calling to mind rests wholly on the association of representations; to it, therefore, the art of memory properly addresses itself, which wishes to form a good memory. It works through habit toward a purposive direction of association, in that in the particular it seeks to bring about a *purposive accompaniment*, but in the whole

[p. 122]

above all toward an inner arrangement of the representations, toward *inner love of order*.

#### §. 36.

*Habit* is the name for the influence which the repetition of the same active or passive states of any being has on the future recurrence of this state, and this influence consists in the greater ease with which the same alterations afterwards occur again. This habit is so general a law that its domain is not only the whole inner life but also a great part of external nature. The power of habit extends through the whole of nature, as far as life or an analogue of life, as far as organization, is spread. Plants and animals grow accustomed, the human body is subject to the effect of habit, and the mind is for the most part ruled by it, in the life of the individual just as in the great social relations. The most general ground of this influence of habit is easy to state. The repeated falling of drops of water wears away the hardest stone, for however slight the effect of the single drop, it nevertheless remains impressed on the stone, and each new one adds itself to it for a greater result. So in general: where a cause leaves behind a lasting effect, and the cause frequently recurs, there the magnitude of the effect necessarily grows more and more, and thereby the influence of habit shows itself.

Of all these effects of habit we want here to investigate more closely only its influence on representing. Two laws hold there everywhere, wherever habit

[p. 123]

acts on an organization. Namely, first, passive alterations are always made weaker by habit; the external impression, both as stimulus on the body and as stimulation for sense, loses its force through habit, for the moment of health gives every organism a power of self-preservation with which it reacts to the external impression, and this will always grow through habit. Second, active alterations will always occur more easily through habituation, often also gain in strength thereby, in that through repetition the obstacles initially opposing are gradually annihilated. Thus it must be with the bodily habituations of man, passively in the influence of climate, or in food and drink, actively in bodily exercises, in dancing, fencing, vaulting. So it is also inwardly, passively, in that pain and pleasure and every sensible impression become weaker through habit, actively, in that inner activities are made ever easier through habit, such as thinking, poetic invention, abstracting or whatever else.

For this inner effect of habit and of practice we can, however, set up a still more determinate and more significant law, to which I here wish especially to call attention. *The inner effect of habit always bears upon the relation of reflection to association, upon the relation of the logical course of thought to the memory-bound*, which we have already noticed before. *Habit here always works toward the pushing back of the voluntarily active understanding in favor of association*, and all practice, all learning, consists here in a guidance of association

[p. 124]

through habit according to the ends of the understanding, whereby its immediate activity is gradually abolished.

The weaker impression which sensible affections gradually make in the mind rests, insofar as it is determined by the inner activities, on this, that they then no longer stimulate at all our attention, which contributes so much to the enlivening of our inner activity, are thus less heeded, and so set imagination into play through no voluntary impulse. On the other hand, something unexpected which interrupts a habit works far more strongly on us than otherwise, in that here attention is suddenly stimulated, and understanding and imagination are thereby set into activity.

Further, the inner effect of habit on our activities rests quite evidently on this, that an activity becomes *mechanical* to us, that with regard to it we need no external impulse, and need not first reflect on its particulars, but that everything results, as it were, of itself. This can easily be noticed in learning by heart or in learning some skill. What matters here always is to determine oneself, with regard to an action, only in general, but in the particulars to put out of activity the understanding that expresses itself with constant consciousness of its activity, and then to let the action follow only through the association of representations, where it is then driven forward by a necessary mechanism, and does not remain exposed to the interruptions and blunders of the voluntarily active understanding. So long as I, e.g., in reading, writing, vaulting, still have, at every single movement,

[p. 125]

to remind myself how I am to do it, so long I do not have an art or a trick in my power. Here the same relation obtains according to which a sleepwalker in sleep displays greater skills than he is able to when awake, according to which simple natural instinct often lets animals work more diligently than artificial understanding lets human beings, in that the simple mechanism of the association left to itself acts more regularly than the choice of the understanding that follows a foreign rule.

So it is, then, properly only a particular influence on association in which habit shows itself inwardly; it adds no peculiar positive principle to imagination, but the laws of association are the sole fundamental laws of its reproductive faculty. The law of habit in its particular application to representations is only a particular case of the association of representations. It runs, namely: The more often and with the greater liveliness representations have been together in a state of mind, the more easily do they reawaken one another anew. This formula follows immediately from the fundamental law and is of wide applicability. Not only the association of individual representations, but especially also certain modes of association in general become more familiar to us thereby. In itself it would be very difficult to fix a thought in memory by a word, but the habit of speaking makes this kind of combination for us one of the most familiar of all. Or, according to the fundamental law of the unity of action, the influence of the interest which we take in a representation would have to be very weak to strengthen this representation. But through practice from youth up we arrive at the point

[p. 126]

that for the most part the particular liveliness of a representation depends in part on our voluntary attention to it.

#### e) On the Productive Imagination.

#### §. 37.

For the history of our cognitions, the division of all our knowledge according to its origin into historical knowledge through experience, mathematical knowledge through pure intuition, and philosophical knowledge through concepts is very important. Here the first belongs by its origin to sense intuition, the second to the productive imagination, the third (if one does not misunderstand the words) to reflection. The productive imagination has a domain of its own with sharply drawn boundaries in our knowledge: it is the domain of pure mathematics in its whole extent, or the domain of intuitive combination. Its domain lies midway between sense and understanding; because of this, and because of the many misunderstandings of its producing activity in speculation, a more precise investigation of this faculty becomes especially necessary for us.

In considering the outer sense intuitions we found at once a certain unifying intuition, through which we first properly obtain the representation of things outside us, which is not contained in sensation but lies at the basis of all modes of sensation at once, and brings it about that through one and another we cognize the same object. Through this unifying intuition, namely, there comes to us the cognition of bodies as matter in space and in time. When we cognize the individual

[p. 127]

house, the individual tree, or whatever else, we always refer ourselves to this combining intuition, in which we hold fast the same object, whatever the sensation through which it appears to us, whether it belong to the ear, the eye, or touch. We saw further that the individual sensation lets me cognize the object only according to what it is for me, the intuiting mind; that unifying intuition, on the other hand, shows it to us as the objects outside us are in their relation to one another.

In considering the inner sense we found further that inner sensation determines only an underlying self-consciousness to the intuition of one’s own activities; the unifying intuition shows itself here only in the relation to time that is added to inner intuition.

All individual sense intuitions thus contain an immediately given manifold, which is intuited as combined in space and time. That unifying intuition which is added to sensation only afterward contains, by contrast, an intuitive combination, an intuitive synthetic unity of things in space and time. Thus it is the property of the productive imagination.

In the complete intuition, as sensible cognition, three conditions always come together: first, sensation; second, the reference of the intuition in sensation to the representations of space and time (to which, in inner sense, there is added the reference to self-consciousness); and third, combination or synthetic unity of the manifold given in the intuition by means of its reference to the representations of space and time. This construction of the

[p. 128]

objects into space and into time gives the intuitive representation of duration, magnitude, figure, position, distance, that is, the representation of the *figural synthetic unity* of the objects, or of the mathematical in our cognition.

What we therefore have to consider more closely here are, first, the representations of space and time themselves, and then the construction of objects into space and time, or the figural synthetic unity.

#### §. 38.

If we abstract from all individual differences of the manifold in intuition, there remains for us in the representations of space and time on their own, as the former underlies geometry, nothing but the representation of a homogeneous manifold in thoroughgoing combination. Intuitions are given individually in sensation, but the representation of space and time underlies each of them, and through it unity and combination first enter into it. These representations have been subjected to manifold investigations with much dispute; in describing them we must for the most part follow Kant in the *Critique of Pure Reason*.

1) Both representations, of space and of time, are involuntarily represented along with all our intuitions, so that, since we always find them along with our intuitive representations, we cannot even abstract from them. If we want to think a thing that is nowhere, thus an existence independent of the representation of space, there remains for us for it a mere idea; we cannot at all make the representation intuitive,

[p. 129]

any more than we can form for ourselves any intuitive representation of an existence that is independent of time. We can, in our representation, think all things away out of space and time, but to think space and time themselves away we are not in a position; our faculty of intuition is thoroughly bound to these representations.

2) The representations of space and time are themselves intuitions and not general concepts, for their object is an *individual* one and given immediately in the representation of it. There is only *one* space and only *one* time. Spaces and times are only parts of this one space and this one time. We do represent manifold representations in them, but never through them as marks. Space we intuit outwardly itself; time we cannot, to be sure, intuit immediately itself, since only in it do we become conscious of our representations at all, and it cannot be present, since it contains a continuous succession of the present itself; but we can intuit all its relations figuratively in space through the motion along a straight line.

3) We become conscious of the separated intuition of time and space only by abstraction from all the individual manifold in sense intuition. They remain then, however, not as general concepts but as original, necessary, intuitive determinations, which go far beyond what is given of the individual intuitions from which we abstract. For their representation *in abstracto* extends into the representation of an unbounded past or future and into the representation of an infinite breadth up to the representation

[p. 130]

of a *given infinite*. Space we represent to ourselves immediately as a given infinite magnitude; the representation of it can therefore not be given through the individual sense intuition, which is always finite. The infinity of time, to be sure, means only that every determinate magnitude in time is possible only by the limitation of one underlying time; yet even here the underlying time must be unbounded, so its representation is just as little given through the individual sense intuition, but both representations must lie in the mind originally at the basis of all sense intuition. Concerning these representations there are two conflicting views in our cognition, a mathematical one of immediate intuition and a philosophical one of reflection on their possibility. In the immediate mathematical representation these intuitions are the most evident of all our cognitions. Here, to their infinity there is added also the *continuity* of all their parts, according to which no part in them is the last, every duration and every length is divisible to infinity, and these properties lie, as it were, clearly before our eyes. But as soon as we begin to reflect on it, a contradiction seems to us to lie in this infinity, continuity and formal emptiness. Space and time *in abstracto* present, as it were, an individual object in intuition, without containing anything existing. This arises, however, from the fact that the existing itself is always given only in the individual sense intuition, so that space and time represented *in abstracto* can contain only an empty form of the combination of the existing given in intuition. That is, the representations of space and time are original and

[p. 131]

necessary forms of sensibility itself, which within our experience must be ascribed to reason as representations always accruing to it. Here, however, we have to do generally only with the evident mathematical view of these intuitions, with a mere description of them as they occur in our course of thought; the philosophical difficulties can be discussed only later.

4) The representations of space and time agree with one another in most determinations. Both contain the intuition of a homogeneous manifold in necessary combination. Their use in experience is therefore that through them the figural synthetic unity of every given manifold becomes possible. The kind of combination of the manifold is quite the same in both representations; they differ solely in the kind of the manifold. For this reason we can also represent to ourselves all relations of time in the image of a straight line.

In respect of what is here combined, however, time as form of sensibility in general contains an intuitive combination of the *existence* of things; it contains the possibility of change, or of being and not-being of the same thing, in that both can take place one after the other; but it does not contain immediately a combination of manifold *objects*; such a combination becomes intuitive to us only through the side-by-side in space. Both have a manifold *outside* one another in combination; this is in time the *one-after-another* of existence, in space the *side-by-side* of the objects outside us. In place of space, for inner sense pure self-consciousness is the form

[p. 132]

of the representation of its object, which however is no intuition. The customary designation, that time is the form of inner sense and space of outer sense, is not correct; time relates quite equally to sense in general, and to space there corresponds for the inner only self-consciousness with its union of all inner changes in the one I.

#### §. 39.

In this way the representations of space and time lie, as forms of an intuitive combination, at the basis of all our sense intuitions. Beyond them there must now come in addition a self-activity of the imagination of its own, in order to construct in them the individual sense intuitions through the figural synthesis of mathematical intuition. In order to learn to understand the organization of this faculty, we must first lift out once more from the description so far given of the representations of space and time the proposition: *The intuitions of space and time do not arise through sensation and its sense intuition in the mind, but from a basic determination of the mind, which is not first given through sensation, and the intuition of them distinguishes itself as pure intuition from all sense intuition.* Secondly, we must set beside this law the other: *The things are given to us in sense intuition, just as the relations come immediately to our consciousness, not as constructed in time and space, but only under the conditions of an always*

[p. 133]

*possible construction of them in time and space; the construction itself the imagination adds only in the representations of the figural combination, often even voluntarily.*

The first law is proved just as we have shown the originality of pure self-consciousness. The representations of space and time cannot be given to the mind simultaneously with sensation, although they come to consciousness only on the occasion of sensation, for they relate first to every intuition given in sensation and then to the whole of all these intuitions, so that they combine the scattered individual objects of them with one another as objects of one world. Besides, we can here add a further ground, that the representations of space and time in their infinity, continuity and necessity go far beyond what is given in all sense intuition; they must therefore arise from an original constitution of the mind, and take place quite independently of everything individual in sensation. Every sense intuition is restricted only to the moment of its presence; through it we cognize only fact and the immediately actual. By contrast, the intuition of space and time is a *pure intuition*, which goes much further. The sharpness of mathematical drawing, the point, line and surface of the geometer, the continuity and infinity of space and time are no objects at all of observation, of experience, of sense intuition; they can show themselves only before a quite other, the pure mode of intuition. The certainty with which we look backward into the past, forward into

[p. 134]

the coming future, the certainty with which we are convinced, beyond every boundary, of the extension of space beyond it, can by no means belong to sense intuition, for nothing of it lies in that; it belongs solely to the pure intuition of the productive imagination, which is not restricted merely to the individual actual, but in every doctrine of pure mathematics extends itself to the intuitiveness of universal laws. With precisely this pure intuition the imagination lays itself at the basis of mathematics, and thereby determines the peculiarity of mathematical knowledge, which we call the construction of its concepts. The showing in the individual example lets us here cognize the possibility of the concept in general, and the necessity of a universal law. By considering the individual numerical example I convince myself of the necessity of a universal law of calculation, by considering the individual figure on the board of the necessity of universal laws of drawing.

The second law was: Although space and time lie at the basis of every sense intuition as universal laws, yet before inner perception the construction of the objects of a sense intuition is not given simultaneously with sensation, but comes in only through imagination. Here, to be sure, it is evident that *in abstracto* we can deal quite voluntarily with the representations of figure and duration, as mathematics uses them, since we draw up geometrical drawings as we please, but in the actual application to the things outside us this representation seems ordinarily to belong to sense and not to an imagination of its own. In fact, however, all

[p. 135]

our representations of figure, magnitude and distance, in short all representations of figural combination, are nothing but a living geometry, which we, without heeding it, constantly apply in life with self-activity. (It is this faculty of mathematics constantly applied in life that, according to the so-called Pestalozzian method of education, is more regularly developed in pupils, and with good success, than was hitherto usual, whereby judgment by eye, every judgment about intuitive magnitude and figure, drawing and calculation, is so greatly sharpened and made secure.) This peculiar activity of the imagination will become clearer through the following.

If, with the manifold that is represented in intuition in sensation, the combinations of this manifold in space and time were at the same time given before consciousness, the objects in sense intuition would also at once already be contained as constructed in space and time, and would not merely stand under the condition of a possible construction or arrangement of them, which we must only afterward carry into them. In every perception of an object it would have to be determined in regard to the predicates belonging to figural combination in space and time. Figure, distance and all relations of position of a thing in space would have to be derivable already from every individual perception. Likewise for the determination of time. But this is not the case; rather we can obtain these determinations only from the comparison of several perceptions through reflection. There is a distinction between apprehension, as the first grasping of the intuition, and the recognizing of the object

[p. 136]

in it. This we can make clear to ourselves in such cases where the sense intuition does not suffice to make the mathematical intuition of the object complete, or where our voluntary judgment steps in between the sense intuition and the actual figural combination of the imagination.

In the determination of time it is in general evident that sense does not give it along, but that it first demands judgment, since we, without having a watch in hand or looking at the sun, can scarcely know it determinately to within a quarter of an hour. In the construction in space we ordinarily suppose that we see magnitude, position and distance approximately along with it, but in many cases the intuition cannot nevertheless be completed, or we are even mistaken, and can find from this that the representation depends after all on our self-activity and on our judgment. In space we can represent to ourselves the manifold relations of manifold objects according to two dimensions or on a surface; the third dimension is the dimension of distance from me; what I therefore view from one standpoint, and without intersecting movement, in contrast to which I am not in motion, is given to me only sufficiently for construction in two dimensions and not according to length, breadth and thickness. Hence, e.g., the possibility of a painting, which presents to me on a surface an entire landscape, just as I see it from one standpoint. So too our representation of the starry heaven: since we do not perceive our motion with regard to the stars, we posit only points of light scattered on the surface of a hollow hemisphere; if, on the other hand, the construction in space were here given along by sense, we would have to see the stars

[p. 137]

as world-bodies, and intuit all relations of the world-edifice at a single glance.

The matter becomes still clearer from the fact that we are subject to error in these representations, in that optical deception or, in general, so-called deception of the senses can take place. The two senses by means of which we arrive at mathematical intuition are chiefly touch and sight. Of both there are several known cases of deception. For touch the best known is when one grasps a small ball between two crossed fingers and rolls it back and forth on a hard surface. If one looks away, one believes one feels two balls, between which one reaches through, and this because each finger feels only half a ball, but we, through the imagination, because of the unusual position of the fingers, construct these not together but apart, and so from each half project a ball of its own, instead of uniting them into one. For the eye many cases are known. We often take an object from a distance for something other than what we afterwards find; we err with regard to its magnitude and distance. At another time we take a painting for a bas-relief; indeed, with a painting well shaded grey on grey we can take up with certainty a distance at which our judgment still remains undetermined whether we see something actually raised or something painted. Similar is the case with geometrical figures of bodies, which through habit we intuit at first glance not as flat drawing but at once, voluntarily, as bodies, and where we must do violence to ourselves to regard them as a mere plane. Still better known is the larger appearance of the moon

[p. 138]

at the horizon than high in the sky, and the larger appearing of objects in fog and twilight. Finally, the most striking thing of all is that we actually obtain a double, somewhat different intuition of things through the eyes, in that the one eye sees differently from the other; we usually unite this, however, on the spot into only one mathematical intuition. (In physiology, in considering the correlation of the eye with the sensation and sense intuition corresponding to it, the question is commonly asked: How does it come about that we see objects upright, since after all the image lies inverted on the retina? and how does it come about that with two eyes we see only one image? The correct answer to the former is: that inverted position holds only for the comparison of the image in the eye with the objects outside; but we do not see through this comparison, but only through the image by itself, in which all the mutual relations are correct; the said difficulty therefore does not arise at all. With regard to the second, however, the fact itself is now denied by many physiologists; they maintain that in the ordinary condition of the eyes we receive not two sensations but only one. Only when the healthy person squints, or the squinting person directs his axes in parallel, does he receive two sensations, and then he also sees double. The explanation is given thus. The sense intuition corresponds not immediately to the stimulation of the retina, but to the impression propagated into the brain upon the optic thalamus. To each optic thalamus, they hold, there corresponds the one half of the visual field, and in animals whose two eyes have a common part of the visual field, and thus especially in man, the commissure of the optic nerves serves to equalize this doubling

[p. 139]

in the optic thalami. As proof one adduces the observation that hemiopia (an illness in which the patient can see every object he looks at only by halves) arises from paralysis or induration of one optic thalamus. This observation, however, does not agree with the attempted explanation. According to the latter, it would have to seem to the patient in the said case as though he could use only one eye, and not as it actually happens. Not the visual field in general, but the half visual field of each individual eye by itself is darkened. There are also other experiments which decide precisely that the stimulations of both eyes for the common part of the visual field do not unite earlier than they correspond to sensation; e.g., otherwise one would have to see, if one covers the one eye wholly with a translucent blue, the other with a translucent yellow glass, yellow at one end, green in the middle, blue at the other end; but this does not happen, rather both discs, the blue and the yellow, lie sharply bounded beside one another. Likewise, if one turns toward the light and closes the eyes, covering one so that one sees black, but lets the other see the red of the translucent eyelid, then again both discs lie beside one another without mixing. Sense does, then, indeed give us a separate image for each eye, and the union is made only by the imagination.)

Our proposition would in general be far more evident if we did not learn, through habit, to bring about the construction of the given manifold far sooner than it is actually determined by what is immediately given in the individual case. Thus we draw for ourselves, e.g.,

[p. 140]

at first glance, out of the most indeterminate play of colors, houses, mountains, woods, rivers, an entire region—where, if the material were unknown to us, we would be unable to cognize anything at all from it.

This, then, is also the cause of all optical deception and of all deceptions through sense, in that in our intuition, in the first grasping, we put far more than is actually contained in that of which we are really conscious. E.g., the magnitude of the moon is not at all determined in the mere intuition of it at its rising; I see it only under a certain visual angle, through which its magnitude can first be determined when the distance is known. But I have accustomed myself, on seeing an object, to sketch for myself at once also a certain intuitive representation of its magnitude and distance according to an approximate estimate—and in this error then takes place.

#### §. 40.

From all this it will thus be clear that our representation of the figural synthetic unity depends for the most part on voluntary reflection and is not given along in sensation. Now, however, we must also turn the matter right around again, and show from the other side that these representations of the productive imagination nevertheless cannot possibly depend on voluntary reflection, for only thereby can the contradiction of a certain false idealistic representation be removed. If these representations were determined by our choice, they could not give us intuitions of a world outside us, but only representations of a self-made, fictitious order

[p. 141]

of things. The self-activity of the productive imagination just shown has driven many philosophers precisely to such an absurd idealism, which could no longer arrive at any truth.

These two expositions of ours must justify the theory of the productive imagination from opposite sides, against one-sided empiricism and against one-sided rationalism. Empirical philosophy found in these mathematical intuitions the first and most obvious contradiction of its principle, that all our representing is only a modification of sensing. One finds in it, especially in Condillac, many attempts to overcome these difficulties, and to explain the representations of space and time themselves only from the relations of the sensations; all these, however, will not prevail against a clear distinction of our pure mode of intuition, e.g., in geometrical constructions, from the empirical mode in sensation, for we cannot by habit form out of sensations the necessary convictions of things that are not perceived at all through sensation, as, e.g., the laws concerning *sharp* drawings of lines and angles *without any error*. On the other side, rationalism in turn misuses the independence of this kind of representation from sensation, and the voluntary activity of this imagination, for its one-sided views. Thus, e.g., Schelling wants to deny all truth of this mode of cognition, and presents it as a merely imagined play of our representations, from which the philosopher has to free himself. Against this we must again take the immediate necessity of mathematics under protection. How shall

[p. 142]

we, however, remove the contradiction of these two assertions, of the voluntariness and of the involuntariness of these representations?

One calls this faculty, because of its self-activity, even creative imagination, but it is not so mighty as that. No one can be so secure from error and fault as one who is able to create, for he gives his creatures the rule of existence himself—who will therefore charge him with fault? We, however, err often enough with our productive imagination, as optical deception shows, or at another time cognition is not determined sufficiently to complete the construction, and we had to make do with a half construction, e.g., in the drawing of the stars on the vault of heaven. This imagination is thus far from being a creative power; its true essence, however, can be made clear precisely from what was last noted. If the voluntary activity in the construction of figural combination can be charged with error and incompleteness, then what matters here are two different rules according to which our representations come about. According to the one rule our imagination attempts, with often voluntary activity, to form for itself a representation of the construction of things in space and time; in so doing, however, it acknowledges yet another law of truth, according to which this construction is properly to be made, which, however, it is at times unable to attain completely, and in respect of which it at times fails altogether.

To what do these two rules now belong? We shall understand their relation if we take into consideration the law of inner sense: The existence of the activities in the mind and the consciousness of them

[p. 143]

are not one and the same; there must first be added a relation of its own to the faculty of self-cognition, in order that we really find in ourselves what is otherwise only obscure in us. This faculty of self-cognition is, according to its basis, inner sense, but is developed through the influence of the will in reflection into complete self-observation. Just as, in the association of representations, from what showed itself immediately before inner sense we had to pass on to the more deeply lying law of the reproductive imagination, so we must now also here, in the productive imagination, distinguish what belongs to the inner faculty of re-observation and what to the underlying observed cognition. The difficulty here, however, is that we encounter self-observation precisely at its transition from inner sense to reflection. The expression productive imagination is accordingly ambiguous. By it we can understand the faculty *of having* mathematical intuitions of space and time and of the figural combination of things in them, or also merely the faculty, with regard to these mathematical intuitions as they lie in reason, *of only becoming conscious of them again*, of being able to perceive them in us. According to the first meaning, as immediate faculty of mathematical intuition, it is an original self-activity of the power of cognition, the faculty of intuitive unity and combination itself, through which we possess the pure intuitions of space and time, and in which the law of all figural combination is also contained. The theory of this faculty we can complete only later, in the theory of unity and combination. According to the other meaning, by contrast, alone does there belong to it the

[p. 144]

voluntary activity, through which we become conscious of the individual figural combinations, in that self-observation can partly still make use of inner sense, but often also requires reflection. The relation of these two faculties can become still clearer through the following. Scientific mathematical cognition is the art of observation of the productive imagination brought under rules; through it we can most easily orient ourselves in how we only find again and observe something immediately already given in reason. For the immediate faculty we can say here: He who has seen objects from only two standpoints has in his mind (up to the limit of the imperfection of his eyes) the whole construction of them according to magnitude, position and distance complete. This can be made clear to anyone who understands only a little geometry. For from one standpoint to the other I have had to come, I therefore know their distance, and it may be as small as it will, I have here a known base line, from whose two end points straight lines can be laid at a determinate angle to each object; I know therefore, for the position of each point that I have looked at from two standpoints, two angles and one side of a triangle whose apex is that point; its distance and position is thus given in my immediate mathematical intuition. We can say: it lies in our reason, through two glances at the starry heaven, to have the cognition of the magnitude, distance and relative position of all the world-bodies that I see; only the self-observation of reflection is here bounded, in that I can measure the differences only up to a determinate limit. Whoever

[p. 145]

had observed the heaven only a few times through the good instruments of a Herschel or Schröter would possess, in the immediate obscure representation of his mind, the same astronomical knowledge as they. The superiority of the latter, however, would lie only in the development of their inner self-observing reflection.

In this way the absurdity vanishes entirely that lies in most ordinary representations of the productive imagination. Its voluntary activity gives us no new cognitions, but lets us notice only those which already lie immediately in us. At its basis, however, lies an immediate faculty of mathematical intuition, which with an original self-activity gives the form to our intuition, in the intuitions of space and time and the law of figural combination.

#### f) The Imagination in the Union of Its Two Faculties.

#### §. 41.

The appearances of inner nature that we ordinarily ascribe to the imagination, in thinking as well as in invention, belong to it for the most part in the union of its two faculties. Reproductive and productive imagination are, however, of quite different origin. The former is properly the faculty of the memory-bound course of thought, for to it belongs the association of thoughts, and through this the whole involuntary play of representations is properly set in motion. The productive imagination, by contrast, adds a quite new share to cognition in mathematical intuition. How does

[p. 146]

it come about, then, that these two faculties, whose origin is so different, nevertheless come into such close union and almost always play with one another in our inner being? Through this: that the reproductive imagination becomes, through the play of its associations, the faculty of abstraction, or the schematizing imagination. Through the play of associations the representations are torn out of their first combinations; there arises *separation* in them; we represent again mere parts out of given cognitions; we obtain *mere representations* which are not already cognitions. Reason is immediately always *power of cognition*; it represents the existence of determinate objects or universal laws, under which this stands. Through the abstracting association, on the other hand, individual representations are separated from these cognitions, and thus come to consciousness by themselves. Thereby we obtain the free representations, which we can apply as images in poetry or as marks in thinking, without being bound to the strict rule of intuitive cognition. Thus we obtain in the intuitive imaginings of objects, without their presence, such detached representations, which, unlike the immediate sense intuitions, belong not only to these determinate cognitions of the individual object, but with which we can play more freely in thinking and invention. The productive imagination now lays the forms of its figural combination immediately on the objects of sense intuition themselves, but afterwards those images of the imagination too are supplied to it in the same way, and now it gives these also its forms, and unites itself therein with the reproductive imagination in all thinking and invention.

[p. 147]

The faculty of abstracting, or of having representations which are not already cognitions, belongs to the reproductive imagination, in that all these representations arise by association out of cognizing; its most determinate application, however, is made through the *schematism* of the imagination, in that it supplies us with the schemata for general concepts. There are certain intuitive representations in us which do not go to a determinate object but contain an indeterminate outline hovering among many images, which correspond to the determination of a general concept. Such a representation is, e.g., that of a horse, of a table, of speed, of the number 7 in general, by virtue of which I recognize in the individual case this determinate animal as a horse, this determinate thing as a table, this determinate number precisely as seven. This representation is called a schema of the imagination; through it the imagination subordinates itself chiefly to the voluntarily thinking understanding; we shall therefore become more closely acquainted with it only in the logical course of thought.

The union of both faculties of the imagination is therefore brought about by the productive imagination bringing its forms also to the images of the reproductive, as to sense intuitions, while its figural combinations, in turn, are also subject to the laws of association, like all representations. This united play borrows the material of its representations from sense, but also comes in our inner being into opposition with it, in that to sense belongs *intuiting*, to it *fantasizing*. On the other side this play is at once claimed by the voluntary activity of the understanding

[p. 148]

and variously modified, so that here the most intricate appearances of inner experience show themselves.

Here, in thinking as well as in invention, the *association* of the reproductive imagination always unites with the *combination* of the productive. The association of representations is one of the most important moments in our whole inner life. In degree, character, understanding, mind, imagination, etc. may be stronger in one human being than in another, but what really distinguishes in kind the system of thought of one from that of another is almost solely this association. It is formed through the whole history of our inner life, through the small down to the smallest just as through the great, in each mind in a different individual way, and thereby the individual trait of the wishes and desires, of the manner of judging and of the world-view of the individual is determined. Its determinateness and purity makes the great thinker, its purity, strength and liveliness the poet, and the predominance of individual associations over the voluntary activity of the understanding gives the fixed idea of the fool. Whoever thinks to raise, through the freedom of reflection, the genius of our thinkers and poets into a quite different, higher sphere errs greatly; it is the same play of associations that here lets systems of science and ideal beauty, there the commonest dream, come forth; here and there the same mechanism of inner laws of nature governs our course of thought; the freedom of the understanding nowhere tears itself loose from this mechanism; it can only steer and guide associations, but never produce thoughts or poetry independently of them. This guidance of association now takes place chiefly through the faculty of combination,

[p. 149]

that is, through the productive imagination subject to the voluntariness of the understanding. The faculty of combination is the most general faculty of the voluntarily determinable mathematical intuition; it makes its influence felt in all thinking and invention, and gives to mathematics itself still more general laws than general arithmetic. Its first laws are the most general laws of voluntary mathematical construction: we can represent what is once given to us in representation, before the imagination, repeated as many times as we wish; we can voluntarily represent what is given to us in one order, before the imagination, in altered order, and think a given magnitude in intuition before the imagination increased and diminished without end, i.e., voluntarily comply with the postulates of pure mathematics; for arithmetic demands that we increase any given magnitude in thought without end, geometry that we draw straight lines through infinite space and prolong them without end. From these simple elements, however, combination spreads its influence over all our thinking and invention; its relations nowhere forsake us, and have therefore in many another science, even in philosophy, at times aroused the hope of solving its riddles through mathematics. Here, however, combination remains bound to the general law of the productive imagination; only the form of figural combinations is in its power, every material must first be given to it in order that it may apply its form to it, and it can nowhere explain different qualities through one another. Hence in philosophy, to be sure, almost everything logical, all explanation, is its work, but it can never add the principle

[p. 150]

from which explanation is to proceed; it contains the rule of all involutions and evolutions, but first requires a *given index* for its application. The whole of all human cognition is the J for the index, which contains the series of all basic concepts, and whose evolutions present the systems of all the sciences.

#### §. 42.

In the whole composition of the inner activities for the imagination we obtain the distinction that we use it now for mediate cognizing in *thinking*, now in the mere *free play of representations* for *invention*. Thinking we must investigate more closely in what follows as the property of the understanding; here, therefore, we remain only with invention as the nearer property of the imagination. Invention is in turn involuntary or voluntary. The faculty of voluntary invention is called *inventive power*, the involuntary is called *dream*, and the faculty of dreaming *fantasy* in the most determinate meaning of the word.

The free play of representations, which is not at all directed to the cognition of things, is one of the most important among all inner phenomena, and spreads its influence over our whole life. Almost every human being lives in inventing or in fantasizing. Whoever is educated only so far that he becomes susceptible to boredom either plays himself with his freely inventing imagination, or becomes a plaything of his fantasy. To have boredom is, namely, already a sign of a cultivated imagination. The common man, when he has nothing to work at, can lie quietly for half days with pleasure, without thinking anything determinate. Every cultivated person, on the other hand, demands to have the

[p. 151]

free play of his representations always alive, he wants, in earnest or in play, to have *entertainment*, and boredom strikes him as soon as he comes into a situation where his imagination is unable to occupy itself.

In the free play of representations the mind, in that it seeks neither cognition nor truth, is occupied only inwardly with itself; it therefore comes into contact chiefly with pleasure and desire. Here the joy and sadness, the fortune and misfortune of a human being are properly determined. The narrow moment of the present is only the foreground of a wide landscape that lies sketched out by the imagination into the future, which is now brightly lit by hope, now darkened by fear. In this hoping or fearing consists the greatest part of the happiness of our life, and even in that which we hope or fear, fantasy often forces upon us its own law against the interest of sense.

Even with regard to cognition the imagination is in conflict with sense, in that it palms off its fantasies on us as intuitions in sleep, in fever-dreams, in enthusiasts and in philosophical dreamers, for most of our philosophy is only invented, because it is easier to play with representations than to think lawfully for oneself. But it makes still greater claims over sense in everything that concerns pleasure and desire and our judgment of the worth of things. Here almost all the happiness of human beings is fantasized. In that for which expectation was strained in advance we are mostly deceived, because fantasy at once soars too high, and it is too easy for it to paint everything more beautifully than reality can supply. Hence the pride of all enthusiasts

[p. 152]

in love or in religion, with which they despise and reject every other enjoyment; theirs rests solely on the imagination, they give it to themselves, and so have it most securely, and because they themselves determine its magnitude, it will easily seem to them far greater than all that sense is able to give. But even to him who is not an enthusiast, fantasy apportions good fortune and misfortune, as soon as he has freed himself from the first instinct and begins to compare good and evil for himself. Sense and fantasy then follow conflicting laws, and the latter promises the most. Sense demands only satisfaction of the need, and upon this follows indifference; fantasy, on the other hand, first makes us prize the need itself, its proper element is always a higher tension of hope or fear, where enjoyment sustains and heightens itself as long as increase is still possible. The enjoyment of fantasy aims at self-preservation, the satisfaction of sense at self-annihilation. The wedding is the end of the novel.

With regard to voluntary invention the imagination is organized very differently in different human beings, both in respect of vivacity and of the tone and mood of all its formations. Here it is quick and lively, there slow and cold; here fruitful and rich in images, there poor and empty; here directed to the gloomy, there to the cheerful and laughing. These differences in the vivacity, tone and mood of the free play of invention have an especially great influence on the way a human being shows himself in society. Taste and tastelessness depend for the most part on whether the imagination of a human being remains faithful in its formations to the pure forms, or

[p. 153]

loves the unshapely, whether it seeks the beautiful or, instead of the beautiful, only the strange. Vivacity and pure mood in this play of representations contribute most to amiability in society; vivacity makes one entertaining, the pure mood of the imagination makes one pleasing.

The proper domain of voluntary invention is, finally, fine art. On this soil all the flowers of beauty sprout and bloom, and that is just what gives this faculty its truest worth. As truth is the law for thinking, so beauty is the law for invention. Anyone can invent or compose, but to invent beautifully makes the artist. Every master of any fine art, even of music, painting or sculpture, can be called a poet, for invented composition is required for every work of fine art, and every artist must first grasp his presentation before the inventing imagination, before he can set it, as it were, outside himself. Beautiful invention, however, is that in which nature gives the rule to art, but conversely art also to nature. Every art demands rules according to which it proceeds. Every other art, as an art of the understanding, possesses rules that can be prescribed or drilled in, but fine art is mere art of the imagination, its rules can be neither taught nor learned, but only the nature of the artist gives him, through the indwelling talent of genius itself, the rule according to which he proceeds, he must always be original. On the other side, however, art in him does not seek in nature the form which he wishes to present, but generates it itself according to an inexpressible

[p. 154]

rule, and thus sets up its ideal, as it were, as the archetype for all formations of nature.

The talent that makes the artist is strength of imagination, in contrast to its mere vivacity; the latter often gives the name without the thing; a sustained power of imagination is required in order to draw sharply and to hold fast the drawn image, and not merely multicoloredness and light mobility, which make the poetaster. The strong imagination must, however, still be combined with idea, in order to complete the talent in the artist. In this talent two faculties are united, the faculty of creating beautiful compositions, which is called *genius*, and the faculty of expressing the created composition, of communicating it, of setting it outside oneself, which is called *spirit*. Genius is properly the inner essence of the artist, it is the higher genius that teaches him; but without spirit, as it were his own spirit in contrast to that higher one, he is nothing for others, because he cannot communicate his ideas. One may say that the genius is the same in every artist, the different arts differ only through the expressing spirit. But to designate the second essential moment of geniality, we still lack here the aesthetic idea and the investigation of our idea of purposiveness in the essence of things. Only where we can add this can the sketch begun here be completed.

Involuntary invention was the dream. Dreams and some phenomena related to them are explained very easily from the general laws of involuntary invention, i.e., from the laws of the association of representations. In the reawakened representations

[p. 155]

are namely the intuitions of objects without their presence, the sense intuitions themselves only with very diminished vivacity, just as they persist in memory, where they are ever more weakened by the constantly newly intruding sense intuitions, and also differ from these in that the latter are sustained by a continuously persisting affection, whereas the imaginings are only the consequence of these sensations, in which the mind is left wholly to itself. Hereby in the healthy, waking state we easily distinguish intuition from imagination. But if we find ourselves in states in which we receive no immediate intuitions, or in which by chance the imaginings are unusually strengthened, then the most lively fantasies must again take on the color of intuition, and deceive us with the presence of their objects. The former is the case in sleep, whence dreams arise, the latter occurs especially in illnesses, whereby fantasies, visions and phantasms arise.—To some people these phantasms appear even in the healthy state shortly before falling asleep, in half-slumber, and indeed sometimes not wholly involuntarily, namely when, upon falling asleep, the receptivity of the outer senses is already beginning to decline, this state lasts a while, and now lively fantasies equal the intuitions. For the same reason fantasy becomes especially active in twilight and in the dark.

We do not usually dream of that which has occupied us most during the day, but rather of that which once flitted through our mind vividly for a moment, because by day the logical course of thought has the greatest influence on our representations, which in sleep is almost entirely annihilated

[p. 156]

But we probably dream in all sleep; a sleep without dream might be death itself. A sound sleep in which we think we have not dreamed will probably be only one whose dreams we are unable to recall; hence we mostly think we dream only in the morning. A wholly dreamless sleep is improbable, since one does not see what should here become the cause of an inhibition of my fantasy.

[scan 219]

## Second Book.

#### Investigation of the Logical Course of Thought according to Its Form.

[scan 221]

### Investigation

### of the Logical Course of Thought

#### according to Its Form.

### Introduction.

#### §. 43.

The history of our cognizing comes to our consciousness through sense intuition in sensation, through the memory-bound and through the logical course of thought. Of these we have still to investigate the last. We distinguish it from the other, first, through the voluntary mode of representation of reflection, and then through the mediate logical mode of cognition, for which we use concepts, judgments, inferences and science. In investigating it we are really concerned with exact knowledge of reason as the self-activity of the power of cognition; but we wish to remind you once more at once that the voluntariness of reflection is by no means one and the same as this self-activity. A peculiar self-activity must belong to the mind originally; it is an activity of the mind which persistently continues to operate in each of its

[p. 160]

states, whereas voluntary inner activities always go only to what is changeable, they contain the living changes of my activity determined only from within, in contrast to those to which I do not determine myself immediately, which are the sensations.

Through these voluntary determinations of reflection we now possess the true property of the logical course of thought, the *logical mode of representation* or *cognizing through thinking*. We saw, namely, that the imagination led us, alongside invention, to thinking, precisely in that it freed mere representations from their relation to cognition; here the understanding now wants to lead this mere representing back again to cognizing, and seeks, precisely with the mediate cognizing thus obtained, to attain more than can be attained through the immediate.

The understanding therefore opposes here to immediate cognizing through intuition, as sense supplied it, a *mediate discursive cognizing* through thinking, through which it is really to show us more than sense and imagination are capable of. This discursive cognizing we must here become more closely acquainted with; it is characterized by this, that here we do not intuit, but cognize by thinking through word and language. For this we use concepts, judgments, inferences and scientific forms, but above all *two mediate modes of representation*, where representation is represented through representation, a mediate representation *through designation*, and one *through marks*;

[p. 161]

word and concept come into use here. We turn here first to the description of representation and cognition through marks, but give only a brief survey, since we shall justify what is peculiar to our presentation in a special work on logic.

[p. 162]

### First Section.

### Description of the Logical Mode of Cognition.

#### a) The Concept.

#### §. 44.

1) The fundamental relation of the representation of a concept is that of *sphere* and *content*, which is represented completely through *definition* and *division*. If I think the concept, e.g., of man or of the color red, it contains the same part in the representation in each individual man or red thing, on account of which I call this man or red. It is a universal identical part of all those representations, and is contained in them as a mark, hence every concept has a sphere of representations to which it belongs as a mark, and a determinate content, which belongs to it itself. For if the concept itself is to be thought in turn, I determine other concepts for it as marks, which make up its content, e.g., by saying, man is the rational animal of the earth. Thus a concept is thought completely according to its content if I define it, according to its sphere if I divide it.

[p. 163]

Through this relation of sphere and content there comes into our representations *subordination of genus and species, classification, subordination of the particular under the universal*.

2) The mediate mode of representation in the thinking of concepts according to sphere and content is not sufficient unto itself in two ways, in that its task remains incompletable unless it supports itself again on the immediate intuitive mode of representation.

First, there would be no thinking at all if we wanted only to think, for then every concept would have to be represented through the definition of its content. This definition composes its concept out of several others, each of which would in turn have to be defined, and so on without end. We therefore usually represent a concept to ourselves not at all through its definition, but only through a schema of the imagination.

It is an immediately intuitive schema of which the words man, horse, tree, four first remind me, and which I use in comparison in order to recognize an object as man or horse. It goes with us here always as, e.g., in geometry, where we explain hypotenuse by right-angled triangle, this by triangle, this by figure and side, this by surface and line, until we finally arrive at concepts like surface, line, point, direction, which we are no longer able to subject to any meaningful definition, which always remain schematic.

Second, through thinking there would come to be no cognizing at all if we did not first relate the concept to the existence of the *individual* object of intuition. Through definition and division we would attain

[p. 164]

never the individual, but would always remain only with the indeterminate universal. Even if we combine our marks in the definition ever so sharply and manifoldly, we still cannot overcome the merely numerical multiplicity into the infinite by mere thinking. However exactly I specify all the marks of a drop of water in the description, I can still always think infinitely many such drops that fit the description, so long as the single one is not determined as individual according to time and place for intuition.

3) Every concept is a universal problematic representation of an *analytic unity*, represented in separation, but always in relation to recombination, whereby nothing is cognized for itself, though something indeed is through the combination of concepts in judgment.

Concepts as universal representations arise for us through comparison and abstraction, in that we separate out single partial representations from a whole cognition; thereby they become mere problematic representations, through which nothing is yet cognized for itself, which we can use for cognition only through composition again, which happens with concepts in judgment.

To every concept there thus belongs an analytic unity, in that it is the same partial representation out of many single representations; the concept tree, e.g., is the identical element of consciousness that is contained in each single representation of oaks, beeches, firs, etc. With this analytic unity there always still attaches to it the form of recombinability, which we express in the principle of determinability: To every thing a concept either belongs or does not belong. Every concept

[p. 165]

can be determined, according to its mere form, either as *position* or as *negation*, as A or Non-A, where the negation is called the *opposite* of the concept. This opposition is the only difference between concepts according to their mere logical form, every other concerns their matter.

4) The representation of concepts is to be communicable, and cognition through concepts makes claims to universal validity.

Concepts are distinguished not as single representations of a thinking subject, but as comprehensions of a determinate material belonging to the representation of objects. They are to be arranged not as constituents in a single image of fantasy, but as partial representations in a universal cognition. Not subjective, a single consciousness of the mind, but objective, the consciousness of a certain determination of the object, is called a concept. It belongs, then, to a mode of representation which aims at objective validity, and in so doing makes claims to a universal validity that cannot be attained through intuiting. For the intuition of that which, e.g., I see before me just now, each individual has only for himself, and it exists even for me before my inner perception only as a passing state of mind, in which I just now cognize, without this cognizing for itself having a relation to my *cognizing in general*. By contrast, my cognizing through concepts, every universal concept of a man, of a tree, belongs not only to a single state of mind in which I just now cognize, but contains a certain determination of an object in general, which I can apply in cognition

[p. 166]

in general without regard to any single state of mind. The concept belongs not only to a single empirical consciousness, like intuition, and not only to a single subject, but is communicable, and can be the same in several minds. On the other hand, however, what is subjective, the single consciousness, the representation of a concept in the single case, is different: one thinks it distinctly, another only clearly, a third only obscurely. For in the single case I can represent a concept to myself according to the relation of sphere and content through definition and division, thus composed of other marks, and then the representation of it is *distinct*, or I represent it to myself only immediately as a whole by means of a schema, but yet separated for itself, and then the representation of it is only *clear*, or finally I do represent it, but not in determinate separation from other accessory representations, and then the representation of it is *obscure*. Thus we think the representations of cause, effect, substance, property obscurely along as partial representations in countless single objects, and only the philosopher makes them clear to himself. Or we commonly judge of virtue and right only according to clear concepts, the philosopher on the other hand seeks a distinct representation through definition and division.

#### b) The Judgment.

#### §. 45.

When we cognize, this happens either through intuition, or through word and language in thinking. Here the judgment is the cognition that is expressed through the grammatical
