[p. 167]

proposition. Whether we now describe this judgment as cognition through thinking, or as distinct cognition, it is always the cognition of objects through concepts, and this last determination already puts us in a position to state the general conditions of the form of every judgment.

Here an object is to be cognized through concepts. Now concepts relate to the cognition of objects only through the relation of these cognitions to their sphere. There is therefore required for every judgment:

1) A representation through which an object is cognized; this is called the *subject* of the judgment, and determines its form according to *quantity*.

2) A concept as *predicate*, in respect of whose sphere the subject is determined, which form constitutes the *quality* of the judgment.

3) In the *relation* of the judgment there is thought, through the subordination of the subject under the predicate, a combination of these two representations, which is properly that which is cognized in the judgment.

4) A *modality* of the judgment is determined according to the subjective degrees of representation in them, as it raises itself from mere thinking to universally valid cognizing.

1) The first, then, is the form of the subject; in the judgment not only a concept is to be thought, but an object cognized. This form is called the logical *designation* of the judgment. According to it the judgment is *singular*, *particular* or *universal*. Singular, namely, when an immediate cognition of an individual object stands in the subject, a particular

[p. 168]

or universal one, however, when the objects in the subject are represented not immediately but only through the sphere of a concept, in that the subject speaks either of only a part of the objects of this sphere or of the whole sphere.

The expressions: All bodies, and Some bodies, in the subject of the judgment thus signify not merely the concept body, but either the whole of all those objects, or only a part of the objects, to which the concept body belongs.

Designation is therefore an essential property of the judgment, if through it something is to be *cognized and not merely thought*. A mere combination of concepts without designation is, on the other hand, a mere comparison formula, through which nothing is yet cognized. In application the confusion of such comparison formulas with judgments leads to errors especially in that it substitutes a false meaning for the copula in the judgment. Only through designation does the copula acquire the meaning that it lets the combination of two concepts or its opposite be cognized, whereas in the comparison formula there is talk only of the sameness and difference of the marks. If I say merely in the comparison formula: Red is not round, this means only: the marks of the red and the round are different. If I say on the other hand, Some red is round and some not, I assert that in some objects of cognition both concepts are combined, and in others the mark red occurs without roundness. This combination of concepts is alone, however, what can be cognized through thinking.

[p. 169]

This confusion of the comparison formula with a judgment is the fundamental fault of the Fichtean philosophical language in the *Doctrine of Science*, and has also been inherited into the language of Schelling’s philosophy of nature. Mere equating and opposing, comparing and distinguishing, is confused with logical affirmation and negation, and thereby the right of the principle of contradiction is violated, in that one asserts side by side I equals I and I equals Not-I. The ease with which this philosophy of nature makes discoveries, and the importance with which it pronounces its laws, rests only on the art of this manner of speech, which in fact says nothing. One takes the formulas light = expansion, positive electricity = hydrogeneity, etc., for important laws of nature, and yet one has thereby cognized absolutely nothing determinate. Every thing is in some respect like another, for the other is indeed a thing; every thing is in some respect opposed to another, just because this is an *other*; in cognizing the only point is to state determinately *wherein* they are the same and *wherein* they are different; of this, however, there is no talk in those formulas. Light = expansion says, e.g., only that a certain likeness obtains between the two; how far it extends, and which it actually is, of this there is no talk, and that is just what we actually want to know. In all these natural-philosophical juxtapositions there is therefore nothing contained but provisional comparisons of concepts, through which we may be prompted to seek out the laws of nature themselves in accordance with them. According to its mere logical form every judgment is either a *universal* or a *particular* one. The subject of the singular judgment, as an individual representation, has no parts of its sphere, here it is therefore always

[p. 170]

a matter of the whole sphere, and so it also has the form of universality.

Second, with regard to the quality of judgments, there is contained in every judgment a *subsumption*; an object is cognized according to its subordination under the concept of the predicate. Here every simple judgment is contained either under the form: A is B, or under the form: A is. The word Is, however, does not mean the same thing in the two cases here, but A is means as much as A is existing. The concept of existence is thus here the B; i.e., according to the logical form all simple judgments are contained under the form: A is B (although otherwise the difference of the two forms is significant, in that A is states the *existence of a thing*, A is B, however, only the assertion of a universal *law*). Here the *is* means the belonging of a partial representation as a mark; e.g., the moon is a heavenly body means: the mark heavenly body is a partial representation in the cognition of the moon.

According to this subordination every judgment is either *affirmative* or *negative*; the subject is either placed in the sphere of the predicate, or excluded from it. The same difference of affirmation and negation already occurred, however, in the concept, with regard to its relation to combination in general. I determine an opposite for it through the very same act of understanding by which in the negative judgment I exclude the subject from the sphere of the predicate, yet this act of understanding works here in its highest degree, for instead of the mere exclusion of a subject, in the determination of the opposite the whole of my cognition

[p. 171]

is determined in respect of a concept, in that I divide *all my representations* into those that belong in the sphere of a concept, and those that do not belong in it. Besides the form of the judgment, then, the form of the predicate itself can also be determined negatively, and this gives the form of the *infinite* judgments, in which I place a subject in the sphere of an opposite. Negatively I say: A is not B, infinitely A is Non-B. This judgment is called infinite because the sphere of a single concept is only a determinate part of the whole of my cognition, and everything else, in proportion to it, infinitely many things, falls in the sphere of the opposite.

Third, as regards the relation of judgments, we have already remarked at the form of the subject that logical affirmation and negation must not be confused with mere comparison and distinction. If I say: Every A is B, every body is heavy, the meaning of the copula is not that both concepts, body and heavy, are one and the same, but they can be quite different; what is asserted here is that the one, the A, never occurs without the other, the B, that with the A in our cognition the B is always combined. If I say on the other hand: No A is B, every body is not simple, I assert thereby not a mere difference of these concepts, but a separation of them for my cognition, where the one occurs as partial representation, the other is missing; they are never combined. This combination is what is properly and peculiarly cognized in the judgment. According to it the relation of subject and predicate in the judgment is threefold. First, the *relation of subject and predicate in a more determinate meaning*

[p. 172]

or relation of the subordination of a representation into the sphere of a concept; second, *relation of ground and consequence*, or of the subordination of the assertion of one cognition under the assertion of another; third, *relation of a whole of cognition to the collected members of the division*; where predicate, ground and whole are the three forms of the superordinate universal. The first combination is represented in *categorical* judgments, the second in *hypothetical* ones, where one judgment is brought under the condition of the other. Finally, the third form is in turn twofold, one could call the judgment in general the *divisive*, but this is either *conjunctive* or *disjunctive*, in that the logical whole of cognition is either a composition under the form of the defined content or an opposition of the parts under the form of a divided sphere. Why we find precisely these *forms of combination* here, which in German are designated by In, Through and With, can become clear only later; here it suffices to describe what is found. Otherwise the named division is one of the most important in logic, one that is constantly repeated.

Fourth, with regard to modality we distinguish in the subjective mode of representation the merely thought judgment from the actually stated one, and with regard to the latter, further, the immediate assertion from intuition from apodicticity.

As we have so far considered the judgment, it is fully determined as the representation of a subsumption. To this there comes, however, still the relation of its truth in the

[p. 173]

*assertion* or *statement* of it. Every judgment is either a merely *posed* problematic one, or an actually passed one, a *proposition*. In judgment we want to cognize through thinking, we can therefore, e.g., as a question put together for ourselves the mere concept of a judgment, without actually asserting it, or as the task of an investigation whether it be true or not. Here we think the subsumption of the judgment without the assertion of it; through the latter, however, it properly becomes cognition.

The form of assertion is that of positing or cancelling, modal position or negation, holding true and holding false. This form is distinguished from qualitative affirmation and negation, for there it was a matter of an exclusion of the predicate from the subject, but here of a cancellation of the whole judgment.

The propositions are further either merely *assertoric* or *apodictic*, they are stated merely as contingent or with necessity. Cognizing through thinking has its advantage over mere intuiting in this, that thereby we can become conscious of what is objective and universally valid. This happens first in apodictic judgments; provisionally, however, we can also express to ourselves subjective and isolated relations of intuition in judgments of perception. Through the latter alone, however, no end would be attained with thinking, since it would be only an unnecessary repetition of precisely the same thing that can also be intuited. Hence it comes about that *in general we state every judgment under apodictic form*, and cannot distinguish merely assertoric propositions grammatically from the apodictic.

[p. 174]

#### c) The Inference.

#### §. 46.

In what precedes we have assembled all the general forms of judgments; but if we look to the end of judging itself, these forms contract much more narrowly for the completeness of judgment.

1) The understanding of the logical course of thought is to distinguish itself from sensibility through sensation in this, that it gives its cognitions universal validity. In modality, therefore, the end of judging is really attained only in apodictic judgments; these alone can lay claim to completeness.

2) In respect of quantity, nothing at all is really gained by singular judgments, since they do not go beyond the intuitiveness of cognition; particular judgments are only a contraction of several singular ones, they speak only indeterminately of a part of the sphere of a concept, without determining which part this is. The complete judgment is therefore, in respect of quantity, a universal one, which really cognizes the combination of two concepts. We call this the *rule*, and the singular in relation to it the case.

3) In respect of quality, all significant judgments are affirmative, for through negation nothing would be gained for cognition by itself; it serves only to keep off error. (Yet this and the preceding without prejudice to the ideal application of negation, which arises from this, that the representation of the whole is for the idea the complete one, since it embraces everything, but for sense and experience precisely the limitation, since there is to be nothing else beyond it. Thus through the proposition: the singular A

[p. 175]

is not B, something is indeed cognized, in so far as someone had held B to be the whole, namely: there is still something other than B; e.g. if someone held nature to be the whole, he would indeed gain by the negative insight: the acting human being does not stand under the law of natural necessity.)

4) The differences in respect of relation are the only ones that remain standing for the complete judgment, where it is either categorical or hypothetical or divisive, in that either only problematic representations or cognitions are subordinated to one another, or the completeness of such a subordination is represented in the whole and the collected members of its division.

Through the complete judgment, then, we always cognize necessary combinations of concepts, and the means of arriving at this cognition is the subordination of the particular under the universal. Intuitively we become conscious of many combinations through mere composition in space and time, by juxtaposition; judgment, however, seeks another kind of combination, which obtains between universal representations and thereby acquires the character of apodicticity. Such a necessary combination of concepts is what we usually call *law*. Laws of logic, laws of nature in physics, and laws of freedom in ethics are what is properly cognized through universal rules, hence through judgments generally. Such a law is now not the cognition of something actual that is there, but only of the necessary combination of several universal determinations, so that what stands under the one must also stand under the other.

[p. 176]

In this respect, then, every law and its rule is only a universal representation, a form under which cognitions can stand, but by itself not yet a complete cognition. If only the law is given to me: All bodies are heavy, I have thereby cognized nothing at all, unless bodies that stand under this law are actually given to me in the individual case. If I know only: Every free will ought to treat the other, in regard to its ends, as its equal, and there is not also a free will actually given to me under this law, then I know thereby as good as nothing. Were all the laws of astronomy and ethics known to me, but no world of individual heavenly bodies under the former, no human beings under the latter, this whole knowledge would nevertheless have no significance for me. We must therefore always first bring the law back, through subordination, to the individual of intuitive cognition, if something is really to be cognized thereby. This subordination of the particular under the universal of the rule now takes place in *inference*, which is consequently the second necessary stage of reflected cognition, as the determination of the case through the rule.

Inferring means deriving the truth or falsity of a judgment from others. In every inference, judgments are given, according to a logically hypothetical relation, as the ground from which another judgment follows. The given judgments are the *premises* of the inference, the one that follows is called the *conclusion*. The rule of the combination of ground and consequence is, however, in every inference the law which is usually called the *Dictum de omni et nullo*, and which is most determinately stated thus: *What holds of the universal holds also of the subordinate particular, and what of the*

[p. 177]

*particular holds also, conditionally, of the superordinate universal*, for the subordinate sphere lies in the superordinate.

Under this rule the inferences are now of two kinds: either only *immediate consequences*, where the premises consist in a single judgment, or *mediate inferences, syllogisms*, where several judgments are required for them.

In the immediate consequences, namely, it is only judgments themselves, according to their form, that are the universal to which subordination is here made. Hence all kinds of these consequences result if one compares in the table of the forms of judgment how far the one is dependent on the other. Thus the rules of subalternation, opposition and conversion result through the quantitative and qualitative forms, other individual ones through the forms of relation.

In syllogisms, on the other hand, the subordination is found in the matter of the premises, in the concepts contained in them. (Hence all consequences can also be stated as syllogisms, if one makes the relation of the forms of judgment from which they flow the content of a universal rule.) Every syllogism therefore requires, first, a *middle concept*, through which a *minor concept* is subordinated to a *major concept*. To state these relations, then, the relation of subordination between the middle and the major concept must be thought in a *major premise*, that between the middle and the minor concept in the *minor premise*, and in the *conclusion* the subordination of the minor concept to the major concept is cognized. If here, in the minor premise, the middle concept is superordinated to the minor concept, and inference is made from the universal

[p. 178]

to the particular: then the inference is in the *first figure*; but if the middle concept is subordinated to the minor concept, and inference is made from the particular to the universal: then the inference is in the *second figure*.

If an inference is now to follow from this according to the fundamental rule, then in the major premise a law of the combination of the middle and major concept must be cognized in a universal rule, in the minor premise a case of this rule is affirmatively subordinated, and in the conclusion the case is determined through the rule. To this lawful arrangement every inference can be brought back, if one frees it from interpolated consequences.

The combination under which subordination is made can be subordinated either according to the relation of subject and predicate, or of ground and consequence, or of the whole and the collected members of the division. If subordination is made according to the relation of the predicate, the inference is a *categorical* one; if according to that of the ground, it is a *hypothetical* one; if according to that of the whole, it is a *divisive* one. (The usual determination according to the major premises does not hold water, since at least from hypothetical and disjunctive rules one can also infer categorically.)

If we look in the categorical inference to the concepts, a middle concept combines its major concept with the minor concept

1) both affirmatively and negatively, in a graduated subordination of three concepts; all M are P, S is M, therefore S is P.

[p. 179]

2) When the superordination of two concepts over a third is cognized, where the same part of the sphere (M) belongs either to both (some S are P and conversely), or only to the one (some S are not P).

3) When two concepts are subordinated to a third, and indeed the one subordination turns out affirmative (all M are P), the other negative (M is not S), since here a part of the one sphere must lie outside the other (some S are not P).

Were we, on the other hand, to look more closely at the relation of the propositions, we should get all the prolixities of the usual scholastic presentation, yet could in the end reduce everything to the lawful arrangement of our first case, by altering the propositions through correct opposition or conversion.

For hypothetical inferences the particular rules are

1) In the first figure, for the *modus ponens*: If the ground is posited, the consequence too is posited.

2) In the second figure, for the *modus tollens*: If the consequence is cancelled, the ground too is cancelled.

This kind of inference belongs preeminently to pure mathematics.

The peculiarity of the divisive relation is that of a whole of cognition to the collected members of the division. Hence we obtain here only the following kinds of inference.

1) In the first figure, the inference according to *complete analogy*. Here in a conjunctive rule or definition a whole is composed, as the content of a concept, from more universal marks. This inference follows the rule: Of whatever all the marks of a concept hold

[p. 180]

or one does not, that belongs in the sphere of this concept or does not.

This inference is preeminently applicable in systems of classes, when we investigate, e.g., a flower or an animal, as to what place in the system it belongs to.

2) In the second figure, the inference according to *complete induction*. Here in a disjunctive rule a sphere of cognition is composed from subordinate parts. The inference then follows the rule: What holds of the parts of a sphere in particular or in general holds just so of the universal concept to which this sphere pertains.

Through the categorical inference we gain each time a wholly new judgment; in the hypothetical, only the assertion is the middle concept, which is added to a judgment already given in the premises; and through induction alone can inference be made with universality from the particular to the universal.

#### d) Science.

#### §. 47.

Through concept, judgment and inference the logical mode of representation has not yet attained its completeness. Through concept and judgment we represent only the logically categorical relation of subject and predicate, through inference the logical relation of ground and consequence; to these we must still add that of the *divided whole*, in order to arrive at completeness. The individual definitions and divisions of concepts relate to a whole of classification in our representations, in that every mark in a definition

[p. 181]

again be subjected to a higher definition, until we reach the highest universal, which cannot again be regarded as a particular. Just so, in the subordinations through inferences there still occur chains of inference or individual proofs, where we make a rule always again dependent on a higher one, and where we again do not arrive at completeness until we hold fast, in highest universal rules that cannot again be inferred, the supreme universal.

We demand here, then, for the completeness of logical cognition, in accordance with the first figure of inferences, a complete cognition of everything particular through its universal. The highest universal, however, is called a *principle*; the principle in concepts is called a *simple concept*; in judgments, a *basic principle*. Cognition from principles is *science*, and the highest logical form of the subordination of everything particular under its principle is *system*.

Let us now consider the forms of systems as they stand when the science has been completely formed, without regard to how the understanding in this or that science first comes to master this arrangement, i.e., let us consider them as, according to the first figure of inference, the particular is always cognized from its universal: then every science has a system of concepts and a system of judgments. The system of concepts proceeds from first given concepts, and subordinates to these the composite ones in definitions and divisions. The system of judgments subordinates every provable proposition to its basic principles.

The systems of concepts are here for different

[p. 182]

sciences different only in the manner in which they can be formed, in that we must sometimes proceed from given concepts, sometimes can begin at once with made ones. In the completed system, however, they all have one and the same logical form of classification in definitions and divisions.

The system of judgments, on the other hand, arises through proofs, and therefore through inferences, and as a completed system through inferences of the first figure. Here, then, the differences of those inferences again occur. At the foundation of the whole system of all sciences lie three simple systematic forms, of the categorical, hypothetical and conjunctive system. The difference of these three systems results in the following way.

By means of the relation of subject and predicate, in the first figure of categorical inferences a mark of a concept is transferred to a concept subordinated to it, whereby a new judgment arises, whose truth is represented as *wholly contained in the truth of the major premise*. Through categorical inferences only a case is drawn out of the one rule in the conclusion. E.g., if I infer, All bodies are heavy, therefore gold too, then gold was already contained among *all bodies*, and is now only named singly. Here, then, there takes place a real *inclusion* of the truth of the conclusion in that of the major premise, and this is the peculiarity of the categorical system.

Secondly, in the first figure of hypothetical inferences, the subordination of the consequence under the ground is already given in a hypothetical rule; to this the assertion of the ground is cognized, and now to the assertion of the consequence

[p. 183]

inferred. We obtain here, then, from the given judgments no new one; rather we merely give the assertion to a consequence previously thought only problematically, through the assertion of the ground. Here, then, the truth of the conclusion is not seen as contained in that of the ground, but is *only subordinated to it*. Thus, e.g., from the one hypothetical basic rule: If two points are given, only one straight line can always be drawn through them, the whole doctrine of the congruence of triangles in geometry is proved; we gain thereby in content at every step, in that we cognize the new truth not as contained in the preceding one, but only as standing under its condition. *Subordination* of certainty is therefore the peculiar law of the hypothetical system.

Thirdly, in the first figure of divisive inferences a conjunctive rule is used as major premise, which comprehends several universal determinations of the same whole. The minor premise subordinates a particular to the individual parts of the rule, and the conclusion then comprehends these subordinations as subordination under the whole. E.g., I have a sweet-smelling little blue flower; the flower droops on its stalk, the irregular corolla has five petals, the lowest of which is spurred, the anthers are grown together: it is therefore a sweet-smelling violet, for these determinations united together make up its concept. In this inference there is talk only of the comprehension of coordinated judgments into one. The conjunctive system has therefore to do only with the *coordination* of certainty in several judgments.

[p. 184]

According to these differences the three kinds of systems have very different relations to the logical mode of representation in general. Reflection has the most power over the categorical system; if the principles and the system of concepts are given, it can develop the whole system itself, but for this the whole content of truth is also already pronounced here in the principles. In the hypothetical system reflection already has far less power; it can only bring into subordination what is otherwise already given through intuition; truth is indeed made dependent on the principles, but science gains in content in its progress through intuition. Finally, in the conjunctive system the systematic unity rests only on the rule by which the arrangement of the judgments is determined; there are here properly no principles of science, but each judgment rests only on itself and is merely coordinated with the others.

[p. 185]

### Second Section.

### Theory of Reflection.

#### a) Results from the Preceding.

#### §. 48.

The result of this whole description of the activities of the faculty of reflection is that through all concepts, judgments, inferences and systems we want to express completely the *relation of the universal to the particular* in our representations. Concept and judgment form the foundation here; if this is given, then inference and system are determined as mere consequence. In this mode of representation there is given:

1) In the concept, the representation of the *universal* itself, but only as problematic representation.

2) This is led back again to cognition, in that in judgment we add again the reference to the object, which is the essential element of the representation of the *particular*, and which arises through the relation that the principle of determinability expresses: To every thing every universal concept belongs *either positively or negatively*.

[p. 186]

3) The cognition contained through concepts in judgments rests on two activities of reflection, subsumption or subordination, and assertion or statement. Assertion is that through which the judgment is determined as actual cognition, and not as merely problematic representation. A judgment, however, according to its form immediately contains only the assertion of a subordination. For even though there are propositions that state only the existence of a thing, yet here too, according to the form, this existence is attributed as a predicate to the thing as the subject. One can therefore say that just as intuition always represents the existence of a thing, so the judgment states *the presence of a subordination in our representations, and thereby at the same time a combination of universal concepts*, whose various gradations show themselves in the categorical, hypothetical and divisive relations.

4) The end of this mode of representation always aims at the *apodicticity* of cognition.

#### §. 49.

For the cognition of the particular through the universal we need the union of three logical faculties. Faculty of thinking the universal, *understanding*; faculty of subordinating the particular to the universal, *power of judgment*; faculty of determining the particular through the universal, *reason*. These repeat themselves at each gradation of the logical mode of representation according to the following table:

Understanding, Predicate, Rule, Principle; the Universal.

Power of judgment, Subject, Case, Theorem; Subordination.

Reason, Judgment, Inference, System; Determination.

[p. 187]

Finally, the gradations in thinking itself come about, in the difference of the categorical, hypothetical and divisive, almost according to the same law, only that each part is conditioned by the subordination of reflected cognition.

This accordingly presents itself in the following survey:

*Subordination. gives, in regard to the relation of representations in general.*

a) of problematic universal representations. Subject and Predicate.

b) of assertions. Ground and Consequence.

c) of the determination of the particular through the universal. Whole and the members of the division.

*gives, in regard to the particular logical relation:*

1) for the concept: 2) for the judgment:

Mark. Rule.

Statement of the mark of the concept. Inference.

Definition and Division. Science.

If the first table belongs here to the representation of the *universal*, the other belongs to the representation of *combination* through the universal.

#### §. 50.

If we wish to use this compilation for the further investigation, we must attend particularly to the following remark, which is the main result of all our investigations.

[p. 188]

*1) The end of the whole logical mode of representation aims at cognizing, with apodicticity, the necessary laws of unity and combination; apodicticity, analytic unity and combination are properly the new thing that appears in our representations through the logical course of thought.*

*2) Through the logical representations, through concept, judgment, inference and system, this necessity, unity and combination is not given to our mind, but only cognized mediately. These logical forms belong to the faculty of reflection, and their mediate cognition signifies only the re-observation of those laws in our interior. The faculty of reflection must be precisely distinguished from reason as the original self-activity of the power of cognition, because it corresponds only to inner sense, and supplements the inner perception of the latter into complete self-cognition, in that it extends this into a whole of inner experience.*

We must therefore distinguish *form and content of the logical course of thought*; its form belongs to reflection, its content, however, to reason. The *judgment* is namely not an original cognition of reason itself, but only a mediate cognition, *i.e. the mere formula of the re-consciousness of an original cognition*. Thus we must distinguish *rule and law*. The law

[p. 189]

is the immediate cognition which becomes the object of a rule, in that in the latter we become conscious of the law.

3) Concepts and judgments arise in our mind through comparison and abstraction; if we now, for the time being, presuppose that unity, combination and necessity merely as a fact in our cognition, we are then in a position to give completely a theory of the faculty of reflection, as the faculty of the re-observation of them.

#### b) Understanding and Reason.

#### §. 51.

First of all we must consider more precisely the difference between the faculty of reflection and reason. The first difficulty that meets us here is the ambiguity of the words understanding and reason, which conceals from us here, for ordinary language, the most important relations.

At the very outset we gave a verbal definition according to which we called the self-activity in cognizing reason, the receptivity in cognizing, sense. Since now in our interior everything is activity, our whole faculty of cognition is therefore reason, and sense is attached to it only as a limitation. Hence we called reason itself, in so far as in its individual manifestations it was determined by sense, sensibility, in so far as this was not the case, understanding. According to this verbal definition we could now investigate sensibility precisely, in that it was determined positively as the faculty of having sense intuitions through sensation.

[p. 190]

The definition of understanding given, however, immediately became indeterminate, in that it embraced only negatively what does not belong to sense. With this definition we can therefore do nothing further; rather we found, between sensibility and understanding, yet the whole domain of imagination, through which we obtained pure mathematical intuition, and the play of representations through association; beside this there then showed itself more determinately the proper domain of the understanding, as the domain of that in cognition of which we become conscious only through reflection.

Here, then, understanding properly signifies the faculty of reflection, and this is the most determinate concept that belongs to it in ordinary language. Within this we now distinguish once more, as parts of the faculty of reflection, logical understanding, logical power of judgment and logical reason, as was just stated. From these subordinate meanings of understanding and reason we shall, however, now abstract, and wish to consider only understanding as the faculty of reflection in general, reason as the immediate self-activity in cognizing.

Here, then, a correct determination of the faculty of reflection depends, first, on its relation to sensibility, and then on its relation to reason.

#### §. 52.

We distinguish the faculty of intuitive cognition, which is given to inner sense immediately in inner perception, from understanding as the faculty of reflection, the faculty of discursive cognition, to which belongs cognition through concept and judgment. This distinction of the faculty of intuition and of the faculty of reflection

[p. 191]

is the common distinction in language between sense and understanding. For first self-observation the intuitive and the discursive, the intuition determined by affection and the voluntary cognition determined by reflection, confront one another. According to these verbal meanings the dispute over the rights of sense or of understanding has also been conducted in philosophy for the most part. Thus *Kant* still says that he has not succeeded in deriving sense and understanding from one source in our mind, and hopes for much advantage from this union for philosophy, if it should succeed. On the other side the empiricists in philosophy sought really to establish this union, in that they derived understanding from sense, the rationalists on the contrary, in that they dissolved sense into understanding. Both, however, incorrectly, for the union does not come about by sense and understanding being reduced to one another, but by our bringing both together through a third, reason. All misunderstandings rest here only on this, that it was not noticed that the distinction between our faculty of intuition and reflection is only a distinction for the inner re-observation of our cognitions, and not for the immediate constitution of our cognitions themselves. The most exact determination of intuition is, namely: *Intuition is a cognition or representation which we perceive immediately in ourselves through inner sense;* reflection, on the other hand, serves to bring before inner self-observation also such cognitions and representations as we cannot perceive immediately in ourselves.

[p. 192]

Against those one-sided views we must exhibit that the intuition of sense and the judgment of understanding must subsist side by side as two different elements, and that we cannot reduce either to the other. Here, first, the proposal of the empiricists, to explain all thinking as a modification of sensing, does not stand up at all to a closer comparison with self-observation. In intuiting I am always bound to the moment of my consciousness; I can become conscious, as intuition, only of a cognition which at the moment of perception belongs to the states of my mind; I see and hear now this, now that. There lies in intuition, therefore, at most how a thing now is, but never how something must necessarily be at all times. Thus merely the fact that we have the concept of necessity in our representations, whether it be applicable or not, already shows something in our thinking mind that would not be possible through sensation, and designates for us a domain of judgment of its own beside intuition. The simplest mathematical cognition already goes beyond this domain of mere intuition, for if I see only four points beside one another, I am thereby at once conscious that 2 × 2 = 4 in all cases and at all times. The cognition of a universal law could not come to consciousness at all without concept and judgment.

On the other side the rationalists want to let only the rights of the understanding count, and most determinately *Leibniz* and the Wolffian school assert that only through the distinctness of the understanding can truth be obtained, that it is the aim of philosophy to reduce the obscure and confused mode of representation of sense wholly to distinct cognition

[p. 193]

mediately through concepts. Against this we exhibit that this cognition of reflection through concepts, that all distinct cognition, has a merely relative subsistence, that it cannot occur at all without immediate intuition, and that we are never able to resolve a great part of our cognitions into concepts.

The dependence of conceptual cognition on intuition we already noted in the description of concepts, for in individual thinking we must after all at some point set bounds to defining, and instead make use of an intuitive schema of the imagination, and also through all thinking can never reach the individual actual, if we do not go back to intuition. Pre-eminently, however, the whole of pure mathematics serves, as a science or in individual application, to show that there are many relations that can never be resolved into concepts. The first proofs of geometry for the equality and similarity of different figures are conducted only by my showing that the one can be laid wholly in the place of the other, or, as one says, that they cover one another, where I evidently make the congruence only intuitive. The same is the case with the whole science. But also in ordinary things the same shows itself, of which *Kant* has given the evident examples. There must be an inner difference in the essence of things, that the hop always winds with the sun, the beans, however, against the sun, or from right to left, about their pole; but this inner difference between the two kinds of plants can by no means be made intelligible through any concepts, but only through the external relation of intuition, here through the direction in the course of the sun around the earth, or through the relation of the right and left

[p. 194]

hand. Just so with right- and left-wound snails, or even the right and left hand of the same human being. However alike in all parts these hands may be, one could nevertheless, despite all inner correspondence, not put the smallest part of the one in the place of the other, in that in the one everything always lies reversed as compared with the other. This difference, however, can by no means become clear except through intuition, and never through concepts.

#### §. 53.

But these are only the more easily removable misunderstandings in the relation of reflection to intuition. Recently the remark has become more important here that the faculty of intuition and sensibility need not necessarily be one, that there could indeed also be an immediate intuition of reason, an *intellectual intuition*. Now even if we take the concept of intuition quite as strictly as it was just determined, there is certainly no contradiction in the concept of, as it were, an intuition of the understanding or an intellectual intuition. Intellectual intuition would be the original cognition of reason, independent of sense, of which reason would also again be immediately conscious without reflection.

Earlier, e.g. in *Kant*, it was presupposed as generally conceded, with regard to this concept, that in our reason there can be no talk of such an intuition, precisely because we are bound to sense and reflection. This intellectual intuition was regarded only as belonging to the idea of the divine understanding, in which the original model, the archetype of our cognition, lies, of which only an incomplete copy

[p. 195]

as ectype is possible for us. The peculiarity of the intellectually intuiting reason was found in this, that before its intuition the totality of the universe lies open synthetically, whereas we, guided by sense, can only ever grasp this and that single thing intuitively, and must always first make use of analytically abstracted forms of universal laws in order to arrive at cognition of a totality. Afterwards *Fichte*, by a confusion of concepts, began to speak of intellectual intuition as a property of our mind and the true eye of the philosopher, so that it has now become very hard to become quite clear about this. For first, the expression intuition has become ambiguous, and then various very different things are thought under intellectual intuition. In *Fichte* pure self-consciousness, or also inner intuition, was at first so called, but by and by the I purified itself to the pure I, to the idea of the deity, and *Schelling* then let only the Absolute, or the divine view of things, be grasped through this intuition. But in that he imagined he himself possessed this divine view (in a science of the All or Absolute), the fullness of the divine view of the world was transformed for him into the absolute void of the eternal unity of things that renders everything undifferentiated, out of whose abyss only the illusion of separate individualities arises before the finite view. For he here confuses the formal basic consciousness of unity in our reason, which we shall later come to know as original formal apperception, with intuition and at the same time with the perfected cognition of our reason, which we later call transcendental apperception.

[p. 196]

We can therefore clarify these misunderstandings fully only where we speak more closely of that basic consciousness of reason; for the present we must only censure the subordinate errors.

This much we can establish here at once. Were it possible for our reason to raise to intuition the original basic form of its cognition, independent of the affections of sense, did it therefore possess intellectual intuition, it would thereby at the same time, with regard to the re-consciousness of its interior, be freed from inner sense, and would possess no reflection at all. Into the same organization of a reason into which sense and reflection enter, no intellectual intuition can come. This would belong only to the idea of a reason wholly freed from sense, of which, however, we can form no positive representation at all, because our whole cognition would be annihilated as soon as we took sense away. The whole fiction of an intellectual intuition in our reason arises always only through the fantasy that we imagine ourselves freed now from this, now from that limitation of sense, while in fact we cancel the limitation only as an experiment, by negation. Thus *Fichte* believed he found in inner intuition an intellectual one, only because it is *not* given by outer sense, or in pure self-consciousness, because it is *not* sensible intuition, and just so *Schelling* in the basic consciousness of unity in reason, because it is *not* sensible. The latter we cannot yet make clear here, I therefore stay only with the other. About pure self-consciousness we have spoken earlier, and found there that the mere consciousness

[p. 197]

of my existence is indeed not determined in us by sense alone, but that it is no intuition at all, but only an indeterminate feeling, to which we can determine its object only through reflection. Inner intuition of our activity, however, could be held to be intellectual only through confusion with that pure self-consciousness. Whoever observes it himself finds its sensible properties unfailingly. For first, the inner intuitions are changeable, in that they present individual, changeable states of the mind, whose constitution has even for the most part been determined by outer sensation. They therefore presuppose for their possibility individual inner affections of the mind, which are determinations of inner sense. Indeed they stand even in such dependence on outer experience that they are not only periodically wholly interrupted by changes of the body, but even suffice only with the aid of outer experience to bring an inner experience about. They are therefore by no means original activities of the mind, but are contained only in individual sensations. Secondly, viewed from another side, this very thing follows from the analogy between outer and inner intuition, or the analogy between time and space. Although inner intuition through pure self-consciousness takes place independently of space, it yet stands under the sensible conditions of time. We can intuit all time-relations pictorially in spatial relations, indeed time itself is representable in the image of a straight line, and all inner states of the mind which are given to us in inner intuition are represented in time. We must therefore in this respect recognize inner intuition as of the same kind as the outer,

[p. 198]

it is just as sensible as that one, it rests like it on sensation, and is not intellectual.

Thus although the concept of an intellectual intuition contains no contradiction, our faculty of intuition is nonetheless bound to inner sense; we can raise to intuition before inner sense only sensible cognition in sensation and the first forms of combination that are added to it in the mathematical intuition of productive imagination; but in order to become conscious of something more and more universal in our interior, we need precisely mediating reflection.

#### §. 54.

So much for the relation of the faculty of reflection to sensibility; we must now compare it more precisely with reason, and this distinction is the most important for all our following investigations. The understanding as higher faculty of cognition is reason itself in its original manifestation, which belongs to it immediately as an excitable power of cognition; thus to it are ascribed the universal and necessary cognitions of philosophy and mathematics, which are an unalterable possession of every human mind. Of these persistent activities, however, we can become conscious only mediately, in the logical course of thought, through reflection. The faculty of reflection is therefore only a faculty of the inner self-observation of reason, and not its original spontaneity itself. With all reflecting we add nothing new to cognition, we only observe what lies in our reason, and must therefore distinguish this faculty of observation precisely from the

[p. 199]

first, what is to be observed here. To observing reflection belongs the voluntary and mediate logical representing in concept, judgment, inference and science. But this very voluntariness of reflection is usually not distinguished from the spontaneity of reason, and hence all the obscurities in this domain. By our will, after all, we plainly do not make truth and cognition, but only direct our inner self-observation. At the ground of the latter there lies first of all the spontaneity of reason, as the faculty of cognizing with necessity. The relation between the faculty of reflection and the spontaneity of reason is the same as that which we found in the case of inner sense and productive imagination.

The presence of the inner activities is still distinct from the consciousness of them; they must first be raised from obscurity to clarity in order that we may become conscious of them. Here now it is voluntary reflection, the faculty of re-consciousness, that completes inner sense into full self-cognition, whereas the spontaneity of reason, on the other hand, supplies those immediate cognitions of which reflection wants to become conscious again. In our reason there lies, as the law of its truth, exalted above all error, an immediate cognition, which however remains inexpressible in itself, which cannot be raised to intuition, of which we never become conscious as a whole, but only in scattered particulars or universal forms through reflection on the occasion of sensible intuitions. Through this immediate cognition, which properly belongs to reason as a self-active power of cognition, there comes first, over and above sensation, everything mathematical into our cognition,

[p. 200]

as the productive imagination supplies it, with space and time. But then also all universal laws, and above all the combinations that we think through the categories, whereby we think something as a magnitude, or according to qualities, whereby we represent to ourselves substances and the change of events as brought about by causes, whereby we are finally able to think the possible and the necessary alongside the actual.

Further, there lies in this immediate cognition the basic consciousness of all faith, from which our conviction of the highest reality proceeds, whereby we are convinced that in the eternal order of things the highest good and its ideal is the law of the existence of things, whereby finally the ideas of beauty, of virtue and of right obtain reality. This immediate cognition lies hidden in the inner essence of reason; reason cannot perceive it immediately in itself, but is bound to inner sense, through which reflection is introduced, which leads us gradually to an artificial re-consciousness, at first in positive concepts and judgments about experience, but finally only in negative forms of the ideas, and only thereby does our whole interior become mediately clear to us.

In this relation lies hidden the whole secret of philosophy; we have thereby anticipated all our following investigations, since it will be our sole concern to make this nature of reflection distinct, and above all to come to know that immediate cognition of reason in all its parts.

In all previous attempts at philosophy this relation of reflection to reason has been more or less

[p. 201]

wrongly judged. As soon as it comes to be generally understood correctly, we shall in fact have reached the end of the history of philosophy in its present significance, since science must then receive as firm and secure an organization as pure mathematics now has. The whole history of philosophy hitherto is nothing but the gradual separating-out of these concepts.

The first emergence of reflection showed itself in our history with the rise of Greek philosophy, in that this first grasped determinately the meaning of the speculative question: What is truth? All Indian and other pre-Greek philosophy known to us does not at all separate understanding and fantasy, truth and poetry, from one another in speculative matters. In Greek philosophy, however, the two elements part more and more. Already in the dialectic of the Eleatics and Sophists logic began to play its role, until the faculty of reflection was finally separated out wholly, as a distinct element, from our mind in the logic of Aristotle. With Aristotle there begins then properly the period of the now much-decried philosophy of reflection, against which one seeks to exalt as far as possible the older, chiefly Platonic attempts. But with the ancients it largely went only as it did in physics. Of the ocean and the course of the sun they had false representations, but not of the magnet and the course of Uranus, for these they did not know at all. So too here: they did not know the instrument with which the errors in philosophy are made, and so they could not err in this way either. We like, e.g., to overlook the clumsy logic in Plato’s dialogues, and delight only in the beauty of his ideas. Aristotle was the first to separate completely the forms of reflection from the

[p. 202]

remaining material cognizing, and so surrendered the faculty of reflection to itself, in order to make experiments with it. Immediately the error began to show itself, which seeks the law of truth only in the distinctness of the cognition of the understanding. Ever since, people have been constantly busy, with more or less self-activity, making philosophy with the faculty of reflection alone. The logical form of definitions, inferences and proofs, which serves only for the re-observation of our cognitions, was supposed to suffice for arriving through it at philosophy, a procedure exactly like that of someone who wanted to arrive at astronomy through the telescope without a heaven that he observes. If we except a few philosophers who until recently were decried as enthusiasts and fools, it is the general fault of all philosophers of this long period that with the aid of the mere logical form they tried to create the system of metaphysics out of logic, and thus in fact the whole period of Aristotelian, Scholastic and more recent philosophy up to Wolff is nothing but a preparation of Wolffianism, as the perfected logical metaphysics. Even the most famous more recent names, like Leibniz and Spinoza, stand in this series. For if one does not stop, in their case, at the presentation of their dogmas, which incline to Platonism, but observes in their writings themselves their manner of proceeding, we find everywhere the same hope of success from the strict application of the logical method, and from the regular superstructure of the theorems with definitions and axioms. Through this logical method, which was finally called the application of the mathematical method to philosophy, everyone here hoped to get by.

[p. 203]

Thus the philosophy of reflection formed itself ever closer to Wolffianism, until this was finally developed in the highest clarity, out of the principle of the omnipotence of logical power of proof and in subordination to the logical principle of contradiction, by Wolff and his pupils. Here the more correct relation finally became clear to Jacobi; he showed the insufficiency of merely proving speculation, stripped Spinoza of his logical form, and so pointed us immediately back to Platonism, which now, in opposition to reflection, had to transform itself into a philosophy of intellectual intuition, as soon as one wished, instead of regarding logical authority *only as insufficient on its own*, to reject it as *wholly unfit* for philosophizing.

At the same time as Jacobi, Kant made the same discovery in another way. Kant examined directly the procedure that had to be employed in philosophizing, and indeed especially in comparison with the then customary application of the so-called mathematical method. Here he soon found that the certainty and evidence of mathematics is not at all communicated by its method, but that it is precisely the essence of mathematical cognition that first makes it possible to apply this method immediately in it. He found that the security of mathematics rests on the construction of concepts in pure intuition, that the mathematical method is nothing but a logical method of teaching, a method of system in general, and achieves what it achieves only when favored by pure intuition. Now it showed itself to him that of this dogmatic method no use at all is to be made for philosophy, since in philosophy the most universal, in concepts and principles, with which that method as

[p. 204]

its principle begins, is precisely the difficult and unintelligible; that one may therefore apply here only an inverted, merely judging logical procedure. By the application of this critical method he was then in a position to exhibit, in his Critiques of Reason, what philosophy human reason in general possesses, and what the inner relations of this science are. As the chief result of his investigation he obtained: speculative reason can accomplish nothing at all by itself in speculation; all positive content of our knowledge of nature springs only from experiential intuition, and the reality of the ideas can be secured only through practical reason. In this he made, with regard to speculative reason, a distinction between an analytic use of the understanding in merely logical thinking, whereby no determinate objects would be cognized, and a synthetic use of the understanding in transcendental thinking, whereby objects were to be cognized, which, as he shows, came about through reason’s here only adding conditions of the possibility of experience to sense intuition. Here, however, he did not penetrate deeply enough into the nature of analytic and synthetic thinking, and therefore he could, as Maimon first remarked against him, exhibit in all philosophy only *quid facti* but not *quid juris*. He showed that nothing can be accomplished with merely speculative reason, but never came to the investigation why this faculty is so incapable by itself, and least of all did he state determinately why practical reason can accomplish more than that speculative reason. Here we can answer more satisfactorily: Kant’s speculative reason is nothing but the mere faculty of inference, the faculty of reflection; this can naturally

[p. 205]

by itself alone give nothing to cognition, precisely because it is a mere instrument of re-observation; all content comes to it only through another, namely through the immediate cognition of reason observed by it, which however with Kant was always only obscurely presupposed, never became distinct. For the same reason his practical reason too and its faith, which he likewise grasped only as a fact, remained something very obscure as soon as one asked how we came to it, for here too he saw immediately always only that which belonged to the faculty of reflection.

Thus through Jacobi and Kant the conviction became fairly generally current in German philosophy that by mere logical reflection nothing can be gained in philosophy. But it remained obscure why this is so, and what business must nevertheless remain necessary to this reflection, empty in itself. With this we came then to the proposal to attempt philosophizing independently of all reflection, i.e., to the philosophy of intellectual intuition. For once reflection is rejected, the proposal of an intellectual intuition lies very near to us through the following reasoning, thought more obscurely or more distinctly. One says: all our cognition is either intuition or concept. Now the concept is mere property of reflection, which cannot serve for philosophy; therefore true philosophical cognition must be intuition; but it is directed to the idea, and the idea and the eternal are therefore cognized through intuiting, through intellectual intuition. The fault in this is easily shown. The division: all our cognition is either intuition or concept, is correct only insofar as we consider it so,

[p. 206]

as it immediately becomes object of inner perception. We become conscious of our cognitions only as intuitions or through concepts. But if we look not at this mere relation of the re-consciousness of our cognitions in our interior, but at *their immediate presence in the mind*, then that division is incomplete; besides the clear representations of intuitions and concepts there are also obscure ones, and to these belongs above all the immediate, inexpressible cognition proper to reason.

If we therefore speak of the insufficiency of concepts and of reflection for philosophical cognition, this is to be understood thus: that both only help us to become conscious of our cognitions again through inference and proof, but that these cognitions do not consist in reflection, in judging itself, but lie at the ground of this in reason as the object that is to be observed only through judgment. We must therefore indeed go beyond reflection with our theory of reason to an immediate cognition of reason, from which alone philosophical cognition can be comprehended; but we may for that reason never renounce reflection, and hope to arrive at philosophy without it. For philosophical cognition can never come to consciousness for us otherwise than through reflection. It is an undertaking wholly contrary to the nature of our mind, to want to arrive, by passing past reflection, at a science of intellectual intuition or of the absolute. Whoever attempts this will only deceive himself by fantasizing, and before he knows it will himself, unnoticed, again be caught in the opposite error of a philosophy through mere logic.

[p. 207]

Our most recent history shows this clearly. It was Kant’s first judgment on Fichte’s I=I of the *Doctrine of Science* that philosophy was here supposed to arise from mere logic, and this was grounded far more deeply than Fichte and his pupils then saw; more distinctly still Schelling proceeds from the emptiest logical propositions and concepts, the A = A, absolute identity and indifference; the same holds of Bardili and of Reinhold’s thinking as thinking.

Our chief task will therefore be to exhibit the faculty of reflection as a necessary condition of our cognition in this, that only through it can we arrive at consciousness of our own immediate cognitions. What is observed through reflection is above all the combination and unity in our cognition, but the observing faculty is that of voluntary representing, which makes use of comparison, abstraction and analysis in order to form concepts and apply them in judgments. We shall therefore first subject our faculty of voluntary representation to investigation, and then show how by means of it we arrive at artificial self-observation.

#### c) On the Manner in Which We Represent Voluntarily.

#### §. 55.

Already several times I have called attention to the important distinction, hitherto always overlooked, between voluntary representing and self-activity in cognizing. To this self-activity belongs the persistent, ever self-same basic activity of reason, which

[p. 208]

comes to consciousness in us in the apodicticity of cognition and the necessity of its object, whereas to voluntary representing belongs only the changing play of that of which we are just thinking. The changeable activities in cognizing are sensation through affection, the involuntary play of thought through association, and the voluntary play through reflection; but common to all these there lies at the ground, as the abiding form, that basic activity of spontaneity.

Reason and the faculty of reflection are confused above all through the expression of the freedom of reflection, whereby the voluntariness of reflection is held to be an unrestricted self-activity. But first, this voluntariness is freedom only in a very improper sense; it means nothing but living inner self-determination, which appears in the mind as contingent so long as we consider the cognitions only for themselves, but in the whole is determined just as necessarily as every activity of inner nature. Second, the will is of course the highest spontaneity of the mind, but not as spontaneity of the power of cognition; for cognition, rather, it is a foreign faculty, which can determine only single changeable inner perceptions.

Every faculty works in nature with necessity according to a certain law, and can to that extent be ascribed to its substratum as self-activity. Properly, however, only that faculty is a self-activity whose effects are not given by any single external influences, but belong to their substratum absolutely, which are therefore not given through the single excitation, but lie at the ground of every excitation of this being as its form. Such a self-activity must

[p. 209]

indeed exist in our mind, and indeed as faculty of cognition, for we perceive inwardly and immediately only activities, and cognizing is that inner activity on which all the others first depend. But it is not this immediate self-activity that we are here seeking in the first instance. Choice is rather only a single self-activity of the first kind, namely a faculty of acting according to the selection of ends. It is therefore a faculty foreign to cognition, whose influences on our representations can be explained only through their dependence on desire and willing, and not from the nature of cognizing alone. With regard to the latter they are something contingent, out of which one has then made the freedom of reflection, of thinking, or even of consciousness in general.

Nothing is more common than, in the expositions of the metaphysical freedom of the will, to come back in the end to this voluntariness in thinking, and to want to explain the former through the latter. With metaphysical freedom, however, we have nothing at all to do here; all thinking lies in inner nature and follows its necessary laws. However much it may therefore be held against us by the enthusiasts that we want to touch the divinity of their genius in thinking and inventing with common physical explanations, we must nonetheless speak decidedly against all these supernatural liberations of thinking; whoever supposes that with thinking and its voluntariness, like *Fichte*, he grasps freedom, explains the infinity of our will only through a single finite expression of it.

We have therefore only to deal with the voluntary determinations of representing according to necessary laws of the inner

[p. 210]

nature. We seek out the laws according to which a representation becomes actual by my willing it. Here we find in inner experience very many kinds of representations that can be determined voluntarily. But it matters to us not merely to put together from experience any laws whatever according to which the will has influence on representation; rather the task is to find the fundamental laws from which its activity here properly proceeds. A single man governs a country, a general fights battles, but all this proceeds only from his voice and the movement of his body; just so there must be inwardly immediate influences, a first moving cause, through which the will acts on our representations, and these we must seek to determine.

In this connection, so much can already be derived in advance from the mere concept of a voluntary activity. Reason, insofar as I am to cognize truth through it, cannot depend on my will, for I am not to cognize as I want to have things, but as they are. It is evident that only reflection, through which I re-observe my immediate cognitions, can be determined by my will. In judging it indeed depends on my will whether I want to bring a truth to consciousness, but I do not make this truth; it already lies in my reason, and I only observe it again in it. If a representation is to become immediately actual because it is an end for me, I must already in a certain way represent it before I determine it voluntarily. The will can therefore determine only modifications of representations present in the mind, and indeed only of such as are themselves already thought as an end, mediately or immediately;

[p. 211]

a representation on which the will acts immediately must therefore already be a clear representation, which it only modifies. The whole influence of the will on representing thus relates to the inner perception of representations.

At first, for observation, the voluntary kinds of representation seem to be very manifold. First, attention and recollection stand under the influence of the will; second, the whole free play of representations follows the will in manifold ways; and third, with regard to the logical course of thought, language as well as deliberation, comparison and judgment are in its power, indeed even error in our cognitions exists only through its influence. Which now among all this is the immediate inner law of its activity? In most cases the will acts only mediately. For as soon as it discovers that some power suited to its ends is in its control, it soon applies this also to the effects standing in the remotest connection with its immediate manifestations; it makes for itself ends that it can reach only mediately through other effects; its activity becomes *artificial*. So there is then also an extensive art of representing and cognizing according to ends, of which every human being possesses some parts without really becoming distinctly conscious of it. To this artificial representing we owe all regulated science, regular observation of nature, philosophy and mathematics. What now lies at the ground of all this artificial activity, as the first lever of inner voluntary activity in representing?

To determine this more closely, we must first of all subtract all external aids whereby the will

[p. 212]

can act bodily and mediately on representing. We have in speaking, reading, writing and many another thing such strong means to guide our representations in thinking that the question might still arise whether all influence of the will here is not one mediated from outside. Thus I favor, e.g., a train of thoughts in a philosophical speculation by going somewhere where I am alone, by putting the single thoughts as they emerge into words, pronouncing them or even writing them down. But as soon as I cease these favoring aids, that train of thoughts is often instantly crowded out of inner perception. In general, all pondering is also, bodily, a speaking with oneself; it could therefore probably be found that all inner voluntary representations are effected only artificially through external changes.

But on the other side we again have so immediate a power to select among the imaginings the purposive ones and hold them fast, and to let others, which were but now vivid, suddenly drop, that we plainly recognize here an inner influence. Especially suited for individual experiment is the power of the will over many representations of productive imagination, e.g., in the contemplation of bodily geometrical figures, say the mere drawing of a cube, which of its sides I want to intuit as the upper one, whether a painted hemisphere is regarded as hollow or convex, a mere shading as painted or real, where we can subject the immediate inner influence of the will to observation.

We shall therefore now seek to determine the first immediate law of its inner influence by comparison of the different voluntary kinds of representation.

[p. 213]

First, attention is very much in the power of our will. Apart from the strength and liveliness of the representations, almost everything that enlivens attention—novelty, change, contrast and gradation in our representations—is determined by the interest that we take in the representations. We can not only give attention voluntarily a determinate direction, but also tense it more or less. It is, as it were, an inner eye, which we can direct voluntarily on this or that object, and just as the object on which I externally direct the axis of the eye is perceived more distinctly, so also here. We can voluntarily choose, among all the objects that offer themselves in inner perception, whichever we want, and attend to this one especially, but in doing so also increase and diminish the tension of attention. Against distraction, the firm and steady inner gaze needs to be practiced here, which contributes much to certainty in pondering. This tension of attention consists in its letting us perceive even obscurer representations, and dwell on this perception. Here the law holds that the tension of attention stands in inverse proportion to its duration. The more tensely we attend to something, the more easily we tire in doing so; on the other hand we can dwell longer on that which requires a less tensed attention. But the greater the tension has been, and the longer we have dwelt on a representation, with the more liveliness does such a representation afterward remain present in memory. The weakest series of representations remains vivid in memory if we have riveted our attention to it, whereas the most vivid

[p. 214]

representations are soon forgotten if we do not heed them. Thus in the midst of the noise of a lively company we can, if we wish, follow only the soft conversation of our neighbor, and for the rest we shall then often scarcely notice what is going on around us.

In this directing and tensing of attention the will indeed sometimes makes use of artificial aids, but for the most part its influence is an immediate one.

Second, the will often directs recollection voluntarily. Herein, however, the activity of the understanding is always artificial. The understanding is, with inner perception, near to a representation through related ones, and seeks thus to find it itself. In musing it must therefore seek to represent these related representations as far as possible alone, in order that they may work regularly and as strongly as possible according to the law of association. The laws of association, however, work of themselves involuntarily, and the understanding procures for itself artificial influence over them only by seeking, through attention, to hold fast individual representations that are led forth and to make them more distinct. So here too the immediate activity of the will touches only attention.

Third, nowhere does the power of the will over our representations show itself greater than in inventing. Here we have already seen that the productive faculty goes only to the form and not to the material in our representations; the latter is always supplied by reproductive imagination out of what we possess through sense and experience. But even with regard to form, inventing very often passes over into involuntary fantasizing. Whoever sketches to himself in imagination some situation, invents a narrative or a novel, directs in doing so through

[p. 215]

the understanding for the most part only his involuntary association of representations. That which we are able to do voluntarily with regard to productive imagination, and to which everything voluntary in its representations comes back, is the faculty of combining. But here too the voluntary repeating, transposing and line-drawing rests, as to its capacity, its possibility and its lawfulness, on the constitution of our productive imagination, whose laws hold of themselves involuntarily. This combination does not arise through the will, but is only artificially accomplished through it, and the instrument that it uses in doing so is again only the involuntary association of representations, in that the understanding, with the help of attention, recalls empirical line-drawing on paper, or the repetition and transposition of it, e.g., with counters, and now, on account of the unboundedness of productive imagination itself, discovers the possibility of an extension to infinity.

Fourth, the true domain of voluntary cognition shows itself finally in the logical kind of representation. Here the sign in language is exercised voluntarily, we deliberate, compare and judge at will.

Only through this influence of the will on judgment does error become possible in our cognitions. For error is a holding-to-be-true contrary to law. Now what were determined by the laws of our faculty of cognition alone would be determined with necessity as it is; there could here perhaps be conflict between two laws, but no violation of law, which afterward could moreover be recognized as such. On the other hand, in voluntary representing there come to the native

[p. 216]

laws of cognizing the foreign ones of an activity according to ends besides; we form for ourselves voluntarily, from the laws of cognizing, maxims according to which we then artificially pass judgments, and further produce other representations, which anticipate perception, but can also turn out contrary to it, that is, erroneous, in that we have either formed the maxims falsely, or erred in the application. All error therefore belongs to the voluntarily reflecting understanding, and neither to the senses nor to immediate reason, which proposition will become very important to us later. The so-called deception of the senses derives merely from the influence of the understanding on the re-consciousness of productive imagination, and other error always belongs to reflection through judgment.

Here too all influence of the will is only an artificial one through the guidance of attention. In language the choice of words for designating thoughts is wholly voluntary, but this voluntariness consists only in our making use of the involuntary law of association in order to arrive at inner perception or at the communication of representations. For the rest, even our freest pondering, in which we constantly let new comparisons and judgments follow one another, consists in nothing but a guidance of association by the attention constantly intervening.
