We can never, as it were freely, leap from one proposition or one matter to another without any connection, but can only seize and hold fast through attention, out of the material supplied by association, what is most purposive. All voluntariness in comparing and judging comes down to two faculties:

[p. 217]

voluntary *combining* of the given representations into judgment, which is only an application of the faculty of combination already considered, and voluntary *negating* in thinking, that is, the faculty, when any determination or a thing is given, of thinking also the thing that this is not. This latter is a peculiar kind of representation of the reflecting understanding, which however also follows the will only mediately, but of itself is an involuntary law of it, peculiar to cognizing. That we can think the negation of everything that we cognize follows from a peculiar constitution of our reason, but that we do think this negation when we wish depends on the direction of attention to this kind of representation.

There remain to us, then, of all voluntary representations, only the immediately voluntary inner perceptions, voluntary attention, and in this, consequently, the immediate ground of all other influences must be sought. The immediate influence of the will on our representations therefore always follows the law: *A representation becomes clearer in inner perception by my wanting to become conscious of it.*

If we now seek further a ground of this law, there arise the same two views that we have already noticed in the case of reproductive imagination. Does the law belong under inner sense, does the will act merely on the enlivening of inner sense, in order thereby to let representations be apprehended more clearly, or does it act immediately on the strengthening of the representations themselves, to which it directs attention? The movement of attention

[p. 218]

as it were like an inner eye from one object to another would make the first view more probable; but if we compare with it the effect of tensed attention on memory, and consider that the liveliness of representations in memory is precisely their peculiar strength, we must nonetheless assume that the will can act immediately also on this strengthening itself. For whether it acts through external means or immediately on inner sense, it can thereby only make the latter more excitable in general, but can neither, as in the direction of attention, select precisely the single determinate representation, nor, as in its tension, thereby enliven this one also in memory, unless it were at the same time able to act immediately in favor of the single representations.

We must therefore state the fundamental law of voluntary representing: *A clear representation becomes stronger by its becoming an end for me to represent it.* We need only compare this law with the theory of reproductive imagination, and we shall easily see how it enters into the organization of our mind. For it is only a particular case of the general law of association, whose influence has been heightened by habit. By virtue of the unity of action in all my inner activity, willing too becomes associated with representing, and the degree of strength of a representation rises as soon as the will directs itself on it and makes it an end for me. This relation between willing and representing, immediately according to the law of association in its whole universality, would be only very remote, and have little effect, if from youth on, by practice and habit, it were not

[p. 219]

strengthened. Only through the habit, in the waking state, of letting the will act constantly on our representations, and in doing so through the favoring external relations of organization, through voluntary movement, and above all through the faculty of speech, does the will gradually acquire in the human mind this superior power over attention, so that in the end almost all liveliness of representations in memory depends in part on it.

This result will make quite clear that all voluntary reflection can be used for cognition only for an artificial re-observation of our interior, in that the understanding directs to this end the perception of inner sense and the representations of reproductive imagination according to its ends. How we now come, through the mere voluntariness of attention, to actual self-observation, and through this gain more than what inner sense gives, this an investigation of comparison and abstraction must show. But before I pass on to this, I wish still to draw attention to the importance of this faculty in human reason. Only through this artificial self-observation, and so through the voluntary thinking of reflection, does human reason distinguish itself from a merely animal power of representation.

If we ask what distinguishes human representation from animal, we are commonly told that man stands, as a being of an entirely different, higher kind, above all animals, and that the difference is, in cognizing, reason, in willing, the elevation above natural instinct. But what now characterizes this human reason and this animal instinct? On this the statements are mostly

[p. 220]

very indeterminate. That the animals lack the higher faculty of cognition, or that which in strict philosophical language is called reason, i.e., the faculty of unity and combination, that would be hard to prove. A representing through sheer sense has no sense at all; representing is life; life is activity; there must therefore always be activity at the ground of sense, and that already touches our reason. To the animal there belongs not only apprehension of intuition but also recognition of the object, thus an analogue of our productive imagination. Many animals understand language, dream, err, so there must belong to them an analogue of inner sense and of inner perception of representations; finally, the faculty of recognizing what is similar, e.g., of being able to distinguish human beings, often goes so far that we must necessarily ascribe to them also an analogue of abstraction in some degree, which is in general already required for dream and error. What then properly makes the difference? In the outcome it is easy to say: the perfectibility of human reason; for man alone there is an education, and so a cultivation of the species, for animals only education of the individual. But through what in the end? Man alone can think and invent, man alone can think of whatever he *wills*, he alone can *voluntarily occupy himself with his interior*, that is, he alone has reflection. To the animal everything is possible that can be obtained through the mere memory-bound course of thought, but it scarcely approaches the logical even from afar; through the peculiarity of his organization, and largely also through the favoring of his sense of touch and speech, man alone rises to it.

[p. 221]

Whence, then, the infinite importance of this artificial self-observation? We may call the animal a sleeping intelligence; man is the only waking one on earth. Only by repeating our own life through reflection do we come by the representation I, and with it we live our own life, whereas in the animal given over to instinct it is only nature in general that lives; man, however, governs his life himself, he thus annihilates instinct within him, and this self-government leads him to the idea of freedom above nature.

So this self-cognition of our life, reflection, is properly the active principle in life, without which reason, merely in sleep or in dream, would remain unknown to itself. Let no one, then, hold in contempt this reflection and the understanding; it does not constitute the innermost essence of our mind, but it is the inner moving principle within it, without which reason could not show itself.

#### d) Theory of Comparison and Abstraction.

#### §. 56.

The instrument of reflection in self-observation is the logical forms: concept, judgment, inference, and science, that is, conceiving and judging, for through these the rest is already given. How, then, does reflection bring concept and judgment into its power? The means are twofold. Concepts and judgments are generated in our mind by *deliberation*, that is, by comparing, distinguishing, abstracting, analyzing, and subsuming; but they are brought to our consciousness chiefly by *designation* and language.

[p. 222]

Of designation we wish to speak first. Mediate representation through marks rises from pictorial representation, by similar relations, gradually to the wholly meaningless characters of language, and thereby gains the true freedom of designation, where in the inner play of thought we can use the word precisely as if it were the thought itself. For this reason empirical philosophers even maintain (by the strictest nominalism) that in abstract representations we think nothing but the word, since the thought accompanying the word is so hard to perceive inwardly by itself. What I represent to myself with the word “red” is easy to perceive, for the schematic representation of the red color has much clarity; but what I think alongside the word “cause” is hard to notice by itself, and becomes distinct only through expositions and examples, since the schematic representation of such metaphysical concepts has very little clarity. However important, now, this relation of reflection to designation, and the transition of symbolic representation to language, may become for application, we have nevertheless no need to dwell on it here, since the theory is altogether simple. The whole theory of this kind of representation is a simple application of the association of representations, which we use at will in order to grasp and communicate our thoughts more easily by means of the sign.

#### §. 57.

In the second place, we must still distinguish the thinking of concepts and the passing of judgments from the activities that are only preparations for them and belong to pondering, to deliberation. Thinking in concepts and judgments

[p. 223]

contains, even if not the existence of any object, still some condition of its existence. Even the mere representation of any general concept always contains a condition of the existence of any possible objects. To this kind of activity in thinking there stands opposed deliberation, not as consciousness of the object, but as consciousness of the representations in their relation to the mind, or to one another. Here we first generate the concepts for ourselves in self-observation; we seek out the subjective conditions under which we first arrive at concepts, or can apply those we have obtained. In comparison we investigate what different representations have in common or wherein they differ; we single out what is common, for itself, in abstraction, and recognize it again as a constituent of the composition in analysis. Or we deliberate in which powers of cognition certain representations belong together, whether they pertain to sense or to understanding, whether to the understanding, the power of judgment, or reason; we investigate, e.g., what influence habit and inclination have on our judgment, what errors and deceptions can occur in it, etc. These activities, belonging merely subjectively to self-observation and only preparatory for thinking, are therefore properly the first and most immediate thing of reflection. We ask here: how does reflection arrive through them at concept and judgment? And this is answered by a theory of comparison and abstraction.

The theory of comparison and distinction is easily made. Comparison and distinction are the consciousness of the relation of several representations toward

[p. 224]

one another. When several representations come together in *one* inner perception, I become conscious not only of each one singly but also of their relation to one another. Now the influence of choice on representing consisted precisely in this, that among all the representations lying before inner perception we can select individual ones to which we pay particular heed; so it is precisely comparison and distinction that first offer themselves to the understanding.

Here we can, as occasion arises, bring every representation into comparison with every other; hence it is here first that the Yes and No, the difference of the positive and the negative, come to consciousness in our understanding; the most general form of reflection becomes that of comparison, whether given representations *stand* in a given relation *or not*. Thus artificial re-observation begins with the logical opposition of the positive and the negative, the origin of which, however, can be discovered only later. And since in this way we wish to observe precisely the unity and combination of our cognitions, there results the following table of the most general *concepts of comparison*, which is at the same time the table of *logical oppositions*.

1) Do representations stand in the relation of unity, or not? *Sameness and Difference.*

2) Do representations stand in the relation of combination, or not? *Concord and Conflict.*

3) Is the unity of an object, or its combination with others, cognized through given representations? *Inner and Outer.*

[p. 225]

4) Do given representations belong, in a cognition, to unity and combination, or to the combined manifold? *Determination, Form*; and *the Determinable, Material, Content, Matter*.

With this we have all at once arrived at supposedly very metaphysical concepts, which have already played great roles in philosophy. One believes, e.g., first of all, that one has penetrated deep into the essence of things with the proposition: Everything is in some respects the same, in some respects different, since by this one means to indicate the highest union of everything in One, the combination of antithesis and synthesis in every cognition. But the law is very empty, and does not approach the essence of things at all. Of course everything must be the same in some respects, for under this *Everything* I count only that which I can possibly think or represent; it is therefore certainly the same in everything that it is a thinkable or a thing. Secondly, the relation of concord and conflict dominates the whole of logic; one wished to ground this on the principle of contradiction, and to develop all philosophy out of it, but we have already found that this is a one-sided philosophy of reflection. Thirdly, the inner and outer made great difficulties in metaphysics, in that in the end we find nothing absolutely inner in our cognition, everything dissolves into outer relations, and so being is lost to us under our hands, the more we exert ourselves to seek it. The most inward is still the I in the mind, the substrate of inner life; yet even this is only through its activity, and that must be kindled from without.

Fourthly and finally, the concepts of matter and form were the most difficult of all. Since through these we bring the

[p. 226]

difference of unity and manifoldness properly to consciousness, they have always figured in the highest dispute of speculation, but again undeservedly, for they do not belong to the essence of unity and combination, still less do they underlie it, but are the mere property of reflection.

*Kant* shows very clearly in his *Critique of Pure Reason* how *Leibniz* was bound to arrive at the principles of his intellectual philosophy through the mere misunderstanding of these concepts. We can easily determine here what can be accomplished with them at all. They are the forms of comparison, but this serves merely for the observation of unity and combination in our cognitions. They can therefore be used only to make us conscious of the unity, as it already lies in our cognitions, but in no way to obtain through them an insight into the essence of this unity itself. In this respect they are altogether empty forms; they belong merely as means to re-observation, but have no metaphysical worth at all, by which they could enter into principles as grounds of explanation.

#### §. 58.

Not quite so simple as the theory of comparison is that of *abstraction*. Abstraction is the second and most excellent means by which reflection advances in the inner self-observation of cognitions, for through it analysis and subsumption, concept and judgment, and thus the complete logical way of representing, immediately become possible. We must therefore here first raise the question: wherein does abstraction consist, and how does it come into our representations?

[p. 227]

Not every separation in our representations can already be called abstraction. Distinction of manifold representations within one, a simple severing in our representations, e.g., when in the intuition of a tree I distinguish in it trunk, branches, leaves, and blossoms, or in a hat that it is black and round—such a distinction is already possible immediately by the relation of comparison considered above, but it is not yet abstraction. What is peculiar to the latter is that, with regard to it, the representations are combined not by a mere putting together of what is different, but by a fitting of the parts into one another, e.g., when in the tree I distinguish not merely trunk and branches, but a thing that has a trunk, a thing that has branches, just as these determinations are united in the unity of the representation tree. The representation arising through abstraction is a *detached representation*; it contains a detached *partial representation*, which as the same representation belongs to many. The single arm of this determinate man, which I distinguish in him by turning attention away from the whole representation and directing it only to this part, is no representation *in abstracto*, but arm in general certainly is, as a mark of the arm, which can belong to many things. Likewise the geometrical representation of the figure of a man is for itself a representation *in abstracto*, inasmuch as it belongs, as what combines, as the same, to the representation of all the limbs of this man.

Representing *in abstracto*, namely, consists not merely in a withdrawing of attention from some representations, whereby I remain only with the consideration of certain partial representations, but it is a proper act of the faculty of cognition, a representation of which I

[p. 228]

am conscious, to hold off from combination with other representations in one consciousness. In this act the schematizing imagination still comes to the aid of voluntary reflection, which imagination is the proper faculty of abstraction. Abstracting is a separating out of certain partial representations from a given whole cognition, which becomes possible for us through the law of the schematizing imagination, through a particular relation of the association of representations to unity and manifoldness which we observe in our cognitions.

Through the association of representations, and through the will, representations are immediately strengthened; but for the reproduction of obscure representations it is still required that they be strengthened until they can be perceived inwardly. Representations are therefore often strengthened without being raised to perception. Now it is a law of reproductive imagination that the more often representations accompany one another, the more they strengthen one another and the more easily they awaken one another again. If, then, a partial representation often coincides with another representation, but in such a way that in different cases it has different accessory representations, or if we bring together in one inner perception several representations that contain the same partial representation, e.g., fir, oak, linden, beech, willow, in all of which tree is common: then this common partial representation is strengthened more than the accessory representations, and these accessory representations become, the more of them there are, darker and darker, so that finally they can no longer be perceived here at all; in place of the individual recollection, therefore, there comes about a separated consciousness of a partial representation, i.e., abstraction, which has as its ground the following law: *In similar*

[p. 229]

*representations that are strengthened simultaneously in the mind, what is common to them is strengthened more than the distinction, and can therefore be perceived separately.* Thus in the example given, when the representations of many species of trees, as similar representations, coincide in one inner perception, the partial representation tree remains over *in abstracto*.

This fundamental law of abstraction, and at the same time of the schematizing imagination, is connected in the following way with the general laws of imagination. In setting up the theory of imagination we found two laws, a law of mutual weakening occurring in memory, and the law of mutual strengthening of representations through association, to which there came, further, a strengthening of the same through the will. The result of the co-operation of these laws is the law of abstraction just found. Many similar representations strengthen what is the same in them, while the different accessory representations, on the other hand, extinguish one another, and so let a detached partial representation emerge as the same in many. Thus under certain conditions abstraction itself is introduced involuntarily into our representations, but its influence spreads far more widely through voluntary interventions of the understanding in reflection and through purposive determination of the same.

The involuntary fundamental law of abstraction is very important for its theory, because it determines the natural course of abstraction and the natural super- and subordination of representations. Through abstraction, general generic marks, as what is the same in many

[p. 230]

representations, but not the distinguishing marks, are separated out. Every distinguishing mark is therefore a specific concept contained under a generic concept, a part of the division subordinate to it, hence a particular that contains the general generic concept within itself, and not, say, a general mark that must be added to the generic concept in order to determine the species. The distinguishing marks always contain the general within themselves; we cannot detach them from it. Green, red, and yellow, e.g., are colors; there is therefore a mark that must be added over and above color in order to make the color red; this is a distinguishing mark, which is indeed contained in the red but not in the green and yellow. Here, now, the natural course of our abstraction makes it impossible to represent this mark separately; it occurs to us always only in the specific concept of the red color, and everything red is color. If, on the other hand, I represent to myself a red marble chair, I here compose my representation from three different determinations, none of which is a mere distinguishing mark: not all chairs are of marble, and there are more marble and red things than a chair; from this, however, it follows that my concepts of the marble and the red have not been formed in the same series of abstraction as chair, otherwise the general would have to remain lying along with it in the distinguishing particular. In a series of abstraction the general representation and the *differentia specifica* do not stand independently side by side, but the general reaches into the particular. Hence the logical rule: that every stem of subordinate generic concepts must have its own distinguishing marks, which would be in conflict in any other stem. Thus I can distinguish by oblique-angled and right-angled only in

[p. 231]

geometry, for both already involve the concept of the geometrical figure; or in ethics only by right and wrong, for both already involve the concept of the free action.

According, then, as individual partial representations occur in the whole of our cognition more often as the same in different representations, or as the distinguishing element in one of them, the former are thought separately *in abstracto*, the latter, on the other hand, only as *differentia specifica*. Here, now, there are many representations which, according to the nature of the human mind, occur only in the one relation or the other, and through this we obtain system and regular classification. Thus, e.g., general representations of combination such as magnitude, quality, substance, cause and effect are of the first kind, because they remain the same in all the manifold; the ultimate differences in sensation, on the other hand, are always of the other kind

#### e) Application of Abstraction to the Whole of Our Representing and Knowing.

#### §. 59.

Through what precedes, then, the origin of abstraction would be demonstrated as a property of the imagination, which the understanding takes possession of. The product of this abstraction is the *detached representation*, whose properties and relations in our mind we must still seek out more closely.

1) *The detached representation is at all times a problematic representation.*

[p. 232]

We distinguished at the very beginning representation in general from cognition, in that not every activity of the mind belonging to cognition is already cognition. Now we say more determinately: every representation is either *problematic* or *assertoric*, and assertoric representation is called cognition. A representation is called cognition as soon as a statement, an assertion, is contained in it. Either it states immediately the existence of a thing, like intuitive cognition, or only a law under which the existence of things stands, as in the general judgment. To this cognition there stands opposed a manner of representing in which nothing is stated, which we call the problematic, just as we called problematic the judgment in which nothing was stated. This problematic manner of representing shows itself in thinking when we represent schemata, or in fantasizing and inventing merely play with our representations.

Here we can now explain how we come at all to this manner of representing. For although representing is a more general concept than cognizing, and cognizing signifies only a kind of it, yet reason is immediately only a power of cognition, its true activity is always cognition, and the problematic representations develop for it only out of cognitions through the play of association according to the law of the schematizing imagination. For as soon as, in the reawakening of representations, the recollection becomes so indeterminate that only individual parts torn out of cognitions reappear, we have lost in abstraction the relation of assertion, and now hold fast in the detached representation a merely problematic representation before inner perception.

[p. 233]

We see, consequently, that all representations that are not cognitions belong to the schematizing imagination and arise through abstraction. Of them we then make a twofold use, either merely according to the law of imagination in inventing, or according to the law of the understanding in thinking. For thinking means to apply problematic representations again to cognition, or to cognize mediately through problematic representations. This happens through concept and judgment, and so here again intuiting, as immediate cognition, and judging stand opposed to one another.

#### §. 60.

2) *The detached representation becomes for us a means of becoming conscious of the unity in our representations.*

Every abstract representation contains the form of a unity in the manifold of our representations. Here two kinds of abstraction show themselves, and through them we first perceive in ourselves the difference of *analytic* and *synthetic unity*. We must set this up here at first only as a fact of inner perception. Every representation that we obtain through abstraction is either a form of combination, that is, of synthetic unity, that is to say, it is a representation *in* which manifold representations are united, or it is the representation of the form of an analytic unity, a partial representation that is contained as the same in manifold representations in such a way that these are thought as united not in it but only *under* it.

The first kind of abstraction we can call the quantitative; it consists in this, that in the representation

[p. 234]

of the whole we abstract from the parts, and so represent the mere form of combination into the whole. Most abstractions are synthetic and analytic at once, yet the peculiarities of the first kind are especially to be noted, e.g., in expressions such as the following: the French, Germany; the Apollo of the Belvedere, the group of the Laocoön, insofar as I thereby designate the mere figure of these works of art, which I can also possess in a plaster cast; in general all representations of determinate figures, and above all the representations of space and time *in abstracto*, as these become the object of pure mathematics.

The other kind of abstraction we can, by contrast, call the qualitative; it shows its peculiarity in the representation of every general mark, in that here an individual partial representation is lifted out, which occurs as the same in several combinations.

All combination (be it intuitive, like that of time and space, or first perceived through judgments, like that of general laws) we become conscious of as such only through abstraction, and likewise also of all analytic unity. Combination is properly that which we wish to observe in ourselves through reflection, but it is analytic unity that first becomes for us the means to this.

The representation of an analytic unity is the representation of *the general*, for it is a detached partial representation that can occur in several others, which then stand under it and are, in relation to it, *the particular*. Through this analytic abstraction the representations receive the relation of a *sphere* and a *content*; it becomes, then, properly what introduces

[p. 235]

the most determinate forms of the logical manner of representing, in that it gives us the concepts.

#### §. 61.

3) *By abstraction and comparison in their union there arises analysis (Analysis) and subsumption.*

Through comparison we saw the one form of the logical manner of representing arise for reflection in the opposition of the positive and the negative. Here abstraction adds, in the second place, the relation of the particular and the general. The detached representation was in general what is the same, which occurred combined with all sorts of accessory representations, and separated from these comes alone to consciousness. If we now compare this representation again with others, we obtain the formula: Was it contained in those as a partial representation, or not; does it belong to them as a mark, or not? and this is the relation of *dissection* or analysis, recognition of the detached representation as a part in that from which it was detached.

If the detached representation is here a representation of analytic unity, thus a general representation, then the consciousness of dissection becomes at the same time that of *subordination*, in that I place the whole representation, as the particular, in the sphere of the detached representation.

Abstraction passes through several stages up to this complete consciousness of subordination and classification. The first is that of the schematizing imagination. This supplies us with an immediate clear consciousness of representations *in abstracto*. Here the first degree is the intuitive imagining of an individual object

[p. 236]

without its presence, thus the complete intuition of a thing represented only without its existence. This is called the *image*. The image is an individual intuitive representation with determinate outline of an individual object in imagination, e.g., the representation of the figure of determinate persons and landscapes, of the Apollo of the Belvedere or the Medici Venus, likewise of individual events in history or poetry. My representation of space and time *in abstracto* too is a pictorial representation, and all demonstration of geometry proceeds from pictorial presentations of the constructions in space and time, in that here in the individual, perfectly drawn figure we cognize the general law.

This image is the lowest degree of abstraction; from it we rise to the *schema*, as the immediately clear consciousness of a detached partial representation. The schema relates to the general representation of a concept, in that it contains a representation in hovering indeterminacy of outline, as it were formed from what agrees in the individual images that belong under the concept, but indeterminate with respect to their differences; so that, if I wish to bring them closer to myself, I represent to myself alternately now this, now that image belonging under a concept. Thus I can, e.g., represent to myself the number four by 4 points or marks in an individual image and yet generally. But besides this I have also a general representation, in which I represent to myself neither points nor marks nor anything else determinate and individual, but only that the same is posited 4 times, without yet drafting a general concept of the number four out of marks subordinate to one another; it is only a

[p. 237]

clear representation of the general intuitive condition that underlies this concept. This is the schema. The same manner of representing occurs also with every other concept, that of a man, of a tree, of virtue, as it were as a monogram of the imagination, as *Kant* very fittingly calls this representation, whereby that which pertains to all objects of a concept comes to consciousness, in an indeterminate outline, of an immediately clear representation.

According to such a schema the imagination can present many individual images by marking out what is held indeterminate in it, often also without experience, e.g., in the drawing of imagined flowers or animals. Among these images there is one that is remarkable, to the formation of which imagination is often naturally led, namely that which contains the mean form of all the species and images belonging under a concept; it is an individual image which, however, makes as it were the rule for all other images belonging under the same schema. This is called the *Normal-Idea*. Such a normal-idea exists for every general representation, especially for every one that is more closely intuitive, but it becomes most determinate only in concepts that in their universality already come very near to the image, in determinate animal forms, and finally in the representation of the human figure. This normal-idea has been particularly noticed with regard to the human figure because there it has influence on the judging of beauty. All beauty here, namely, is either beauty of correct outline, of regular figure, or beauty of expression; for the former the normal-idea gives the rule.

This schematism of the imagination underlies all abstracting reflection; it is the means by which

[p. 238]

it first comes to isolated consciousness of partial representations. This consciousness, however, it perfects ever more through comparison and designation, as it advances from the schema to the mark and to the concept. Schema, mark, and concept are all three general partial representations represented *in abstracto*; a general representation, such as the one I designate by the words: man, quadrangular, swift, or whatever else, can be a schema, a mark, and a concept alike. What, now, is the difference of these three words?

The schema is the subjective consciousness of a detached general representation, as I obtain it through abstraction; mark and concept, on the other hand, are the same partial representation as it lies in the cognition itself. The schema is different in every mind, the mark is the same for every reason; the concept also, though one person possesses the concept more distinctly than another. There is a certain partial representation in the thing which makes it a man or a tree, or which makes me able to call something duty or right; this partial representation lying in the cognition of the object itself, which is the same in every reason that has it, whereby the thing becomes man or tree, duty or right, is the mark. The consciousness of it, as it is clearly separated out by abstraction and commonly applied in thinking when one speaks of men, trees, duties, or rights, is the schema; the complete mediate representation of the mark, however, is the concept. The mark is in every reason, but not everyone can raise it with equal distinctness from the schema to the concept. Whoever judges only commonly about duty and right has an indeterminate

[p. 239]

schema of both marks, but cannot separate it from all accessory representations, and still less represent it itself in turn mediately through other marks; the latter only he can do who possesses scientific philosophical cognitions here. Likewise, who does not know roses and lilies so that he can distinguish them roughly from any other flower? In this we possess a clear schema of the mark that pertains essentially to these flowers; but the botanist will analyze this schema still further into several other marks according to some system, in that he can state the characteristics of class, order, genus, and species; he is in possession of the distinct concept of this flower. The mark thus underlies this manner of representing; schema and concept, however, are different ways in which marks come to our consciousness. The schema is the property of each individual; the concept, however, becomes communicable, because in it we think a composition of determinate marks, without regard to the clarity in the consciousness of the individual. From this there arises for our abstraction the important law: For the consciousness of the individual the concept is altogether dependent on the schema; the concept becomes his in inner perception only through the schema, *and we have nothing in the concept that we did not previously have immediately in the schema*; all positive content of our concepts is, through comparison, always borrowed from the schematizing imagination; reflection for itself can add to it nothing but the negative form, *it can only think the given content either as concept or as its opposite*.

[p. 240]

Once reflection has put itself in possession of concepts as the complete representation of the general, it can apply these also in comparison, and with this it arrives at consciousness of classification and subordination; this, however, becomes judgment as soon as the subordinated particular is determined not as a mere problematic representation, but, as the form of the subject required, as assertion, as cognition. Inference and system, however, are mere derivations from judging. We have thus completely shown how the logical manner of representing arises as reflection in our mind. Comparison and abstraction give us the concept, and with this subsumption, and as soon as we apply this to cognitions, we obtain judgment.

#### §. 62.

*4) The importance of abstraction for reflection rests properly on this, that through the detached representation of the general, as a problematic representation, we tear ourselves loose from the momentary element of inner perception and raise ourselves to a whole of inner experience. Judgment is a mere formula of the re-consciousness of our cognitions, whereby we arrive from the individual determinations of the assertoric in inner perception at the apodictic in complete self-observation.*

Cognitions, as we become immediately conscious of them, are mere individual sensible intuitions with the addition of the mathematical in the representation through productive imagination. Therein our consciousness of our cognition, supplied through the

[p. 241]

inner sense, never goes beyond the moment of the present. I see, e.g., at this moment a man, a house, a landscape; but whether these are real objects or whether dreams deceive me with phantasms, that does not lie in the perception of this moment; I hear a sound, but whether that is a ringing in my ear or whether something outside corresponds to it, that again does not lie in the perception of the moment. Such an intuitive cognition for itself can never be expressed by: I know, but only by: I intuit; it holds only for the time in which it actually lasts, whereas a connected whole of cognition, a complete statement that something is, or that I know something, I can develop out of this intuition only through reflection. How, then, is it possible for reflection to tear itself loose from the moment of the present and to arrive at a wider survey of my cognizing in general? How can it arrive, from the individual perceptions following one another, of what I cognize, at the whole of a unified inner experience of my cognizing?

Precisely through the problematic representation of abstraction. This is a clear representation, but in such a way that the recollection in the perception of it does not go to a determinate present representation or cognition, but to what is the same in many representations that have been. The problematic representation is the re-consciousness of a partial representation out of my cognitions through reflection; but not only as a constituent of an individual passing state of mind, but indeterminately out of cognitions in general. The detached representation of a quality, e.g., red, remains for me indeterminate

[p. 242]

as a constituent of any possible cognitions lying before reflection, and so I can express it on every occasion: Every thing is either red or not red; so that the form of the logical principle of determinability immediately attaches to it, and it thus, torn loose from the perception of a momentary state of cognition, becomes a means to more complete self-observation of my cognition in general. I use the detached representation as a general determination for my cognition in general, for it remains with me not as a constituent of an individual cognition, but as a possible constituent of any cognition in consciousness, always in relation to the original unity of all my cognition, so that I can use it at once in a voluntary comparison for cognition in general, in that in the form of the subject I think all objects of the sphere of a concept as determined through this, and by means of it subordinate them to another as predicate.

So in judgment we represent not only momentary combinations of intuitions, but combinations of problematic representations in general rules, in which the activity of my reason in general is observed in its enduring states, and not only in the constant efflux of the sensible.

So the detached representation procures for reflection the advantage that it can tear itself loose from the moment of the present, and raise self-observation to a *consciousness in general*, before which the truth of our cognition properly first appears, in that we here find the laws for the whole of the activity of our reason.

[p. 243]

#### §. 63.

By this we are put in a position to make clear, from one side, the difference of the assertoric, problematic, and apodictic in our cognitions according to its anthropological significance. Merely assertoric cognition is that which is immediately perceived through inner sense; problematic representation of the general becomes the means for raising reflection to a higher standpoint; apodictic cognition is that which is determined as object of completed self-observation. The whole difference has therefore at first only a subjective significance; it belongs to the faculty of re-observation, and designates only the stages by which this advances from inner sense to the completeness of reflection. Consequently there belong here at first also only the differences of the actual, possible, and necessary in objects. The object of an assertoric cognition is called actual; the object of a problematic representation, possible; the object of an apodictic cognition, necessary. Possibility here corresponds only to universality or to problematic representation, whereby nothing is cognized for itself; the general is everywhere only a means for reflection to become conscious of the apodictic; hence we are driven from concept to judgment, to inference, to system, and only there obtain proper cognition again through the general, where we determine the wholly individual case through the rule. Neither through concept, nor rule, nor major premise, nor principle is more than mere possibility given; cognition itself always depends on subordination. But on the

[p. 244]

other side all cognition must also pass through the general, in order to come to consciousness as apodictic, for only through detached representation do we free ourselves from the present moment of self-observation, which alone lies open to inner sense. We become conscious of complete cognition, therefore, always only with the help of the general, which itself, however, is never sufficient unto itself. Thus we learn to understand the fundamental law of reflected cognition. *In accordance with the form of the syllogism it always demands first a problematic representation of the general, in order to arrive at consciousness of the apodictic; to this an assertion of the individual must be subordinated, and this assertion must, thirdly, be determined through the general, if we are to observe cognition as it lies immediately in reason*, and not only according to the particulars, as it appears to inner sense. The logical relation of understanding, power of judgment, and reason is therefore the fundamental law of our completed self-observation.

In the first investigation of all philosophy, the investigation concerning the origin of our cognitions, there stood opposed: the assertion of empiricism according to Locke, that all our cognitions are brought about by sensible impression, by sensation, and the assertion of rationalism according to Leibniz, that the necessary and eternal truths of every reason are given by innate ideas. Kant sought to settle this dispute by drawing the distinction: our cognition begins, in time, to be sure, always with sensible perception

[p. 245]

and is consequently introduced by sensation; but it does not, for all that, all arise in our mind out of sensation; rather the necessary truths already lie at the ground of all sensation as conditions of the possibility of experience. These cognitions independent of experience he calls cognitions *a priori*, and finds their distinguishing mark in universality and necessity, since through sense intuition we can ever grasp only the single case, and indeed only for the moment of the present. Thereby he was put in a position to teach us quite determinately which cognitions *a priori* are in our reason, how indispensable their use becomes to us, and how they must be arranged. But if, with regard to these cognitions, one asks for a theory, goes beyond the bare fact, and asks, as befits an object of natural science, how does our reason come to these categories, ideas, and to this practical faith? then Kant gives only the answer: they lie independently of all experience in our mind—we may also add, they are not innate ideas, for in fact all our cognizing begins only with sense intuition and sensation. But what else are they then, and through what do we obtain them? To this he never replied, and neither have we since been able to agree on any answer; but the following can lead us closer to the decision.

Objective validity and subjective universal validity are *de facto* different in our cognition, since we cannot, as it were, step outside our cognition and compare it with the object. But in the end they must nevertheless be reciprocal concepts, for if truth

[p. 246]

is to be the agreement of the object with the cognition of it, then the object contains the rule for the cognition, and only objective validity can become the ground of universal validity. But when the point is to judge our cognitions, we must at first always stay with subjective validity, in order only to see first how our cognitions are constituted; the comparison of this validity with the objective is then the more difficult matter, which we must let follow only at the last.

With this subjective validity we must now notice still further distinctions. We can say, first: subjectively universally valid is what holds *for me* in all cases, in contrast to what holds only in single cases. This expression could refer to incomplete induction; e.g., I devise for myself a hypothetical theory of the Voltaic pile, test it by experiments, and all my experiments agree with it, so this theory has for me subjective universal validity; another makes other experiments, which do not agree with my theory, and so this universal validity would again be cancelled. But this concerns only the incomplete certainty of the probable, so we do not wish to take the concept in that sense here. We say: subjectively universally valid is that which holds for me *in every possible case*; then every case of another can possibly become mine too, and under this universal validity there would be understood at the same time a validity for everyone whose reason is organized as mine is. We thus distinguish in general only the subjective universal validity of what holds for every case, from the restricted validity of what holds only in single cases. In order that

[p. 247]

one may not, however, think thereby solely of the distinction between universal and particular judgments, we must choose the expressions differently still.

Subjectively universally valid, or *apodictic*, is the cognition of that which everyone knows, and which for the individual has always the same validity; opposed to this is a merely *assertoric* validity of that which only the individual knows, and whose cognition belongs only to certain particular states of mind. What I hear and see—every sense intuition has validity only for me; everyone else must see for himself, I cannot communicate the seeing to him, and for me it belongs always only to particular states of my cognizing. Universal mathematical and philosophical truths, on the other hand, do not belong to me in relation to this or that particular state of mind, but hold for my reason as such, and are in everyone's reason as in mine. With regard to merely assertoric cognition I can learn daily, by transferring new cognitions into my reason, by extending my experience and collecting historical knowledge. Everyone has here his own cognition; to know who Jajadeva was, where the Tiber flows, how many moons Saturn has, that I cannot expect of everyone, for it must first be learned. With regard to apodictic, philosophical and mathematical cognition, by contrast, the Platonic saying holds: μαθησις ἀναμνησις, all learning is only recollection. Learning in philosophy and pure mathematics brings nothing new into our mind at all, but is mere cultivation of self-cognition; we only point out to the pupil all that he bears in the interior of his reason, without giving him new experience.

[p. 248]

Apodictic cognition is thus to belong to every reason as to every other, and in the individual reason to be at all times the same. It is the enduring, persistent, self-same element in the activity of our reason; it must spring from the original essence of reason; it is the most peculiar expression of its self-activity. From this we can make the anthropological side of this relation quite clear. Human reason is an excitable power of cognition. There lies in it a certain form of excitability, which however must first be stimulated to the expression of its activity by sense in the individual case. Here, then, apodictic cognition is that which is determined by the mere form of excitability, which consequently must be the same in every reason, and belongs to the individual in such a way that it lies at the ground of every cognition. On the other hand, that which is first given to us through the individual excitation, through sensation as sense intuition, will constantly change and become always another, will be constituted one way in one person, another way in another; this therefore yields the assertoric, subjectively contingent validity of what one knows and another does not.

Let us now compare further how this stands in relation to the re-consciousness of self-observation, for inner sense and reflection: it at once strikes the eye that inner sense can immediately perceive only the momentary character of the actual inner activity, only the transient excitations themselves in sensation; everything else is attainable only by reflection. Hence the fundamental law of human cognition: *The source of all necessity in our cognition is apodictic cognition, but this is only formal and*

[p. 249]

*universal.* That which is given by the form of excitability as the same in all our cognition, and thus as the necessary in it, can nevertheless come to consciousness for us only on the occasion of the individual excitation, as form in it; and if we wish to become conscious of it for itself, this can happen only through abstraction, by holding fast before reflection the separated representation of that form of excitation for itself.

This distinction of the assertoric and the apodictic coincides entirely with the Kantian *a posteriori* and *a priori*. Every single object we cognize only through the intuition occasioned by sense, from sensation; we represent the existence of an object only by its being *given* to us in intuition. Now we call the cognition of an object cognition from experience, or cognition *a posteriori*, if I cognize it thereby only *after* it has been given to me in representation. Cognition *a priori*, by contrast, is that in which I cognize the object before it is given to me. All assertoric cognition is therefore cognition *a posteriori*, for it arises only from the individual excitation; apodictic cognition, on the other hand, is *a priori*, for it extends, with the necessary form of its law, also over all future perception; I can therefore through it cognize objects even before they are given to me in intuition. E.g., of a stone that I hold in my hand I know beforehand, before I have yet seen it happen, that it will fall down again if I throw it into the free air. Here, however, one could still say: I infer this only because I have often already perceived that what is thrown freely into the air falls down. Then the cognition here would still depend on

[p. 250]

sensation, and the determination of the object would at bottom be cognized *a posteriori*. But there are also such cognitions as are absolutely apodictic and hold *a priori* without any perception of the object; these are then called *pure* cognitions *a priori*. To these belongs the whole of pure mathematics and pure philosophy; e.g., that the sum of the angles of a triangle equals two right angles we assert of every triangle, not because the proposition has stood the test in many trials, but absolutely, apart from all test in experience. Indeed, we could not even make the test of it in the individual case, for that would only show that that sum comes out nearly or approximately right, because we are never able to measure with perfect exactness. In the same way we assert quite apodictically the truth of the conclusion in a regular inference, not because the forms of inference often hold up for us in experience; rather, even after I had discovered a multitude of fallacious inferences, I should still trust the inference, and put the error only on the erroneous application of its form. In this way the Kantian *a priori* and *a posteriori* is easy to apply, and convenient for drawing our attention to the assertoric or apodictic origin of a cognition. Frequently, however, this distinction has been misunderstood in that the *before* and *after* was referred not to the givenness of the object in intuition but to the cognition itself, so that cognition *a priori* would be one that belonged to our reason before all perception. That would then be an innate idea, which in fact we do not possess, since rather all actual cognition is given to us only through perception and with perception

[p. 251]

given. Every actual cognizing of our reason is sensibly stimulated, but in each single one the original apodictic form also lies at the ground, which itself has not arisen from sensation. We can now therefore state what this cognition *a priori*, not arisen from experience, properly is. It is the property of the original self-activity in cognizing, which is determined by the mere form of the excitability of our reason; it is thus the necessary fundamental law of all our cognition, under whose condition every single cognition must stand, but we find it in ourselves always only through its imprint on the individual sensibly given material, from which we can separate it only through abstraction, and then bring it to consciousness incompletely as a problematic universal representation.

On this last rests the distinction between perception and experience. In individual sensation I perceive. These perceptions for themselves, however, are scattered and single, and one is independent of the other. I receive now this taste, now that, hear now this sound, now that, see now this color, now that; each of these activities of the mind occurs for itself, and has the relation to the others not in itself. All unity and combination, all order and coherence is added only through apodictic cognition. The complete cognition resulting from this is then called experience. E.g., I see a mill by the water, I perceive that the water streams against the wheel and the wheel turns; but in these perceptions there does not yet lie the proposition of experience that the streaming water turns the wheel by its pressure; there must here in the judgment still other mathematical and philosophical representations

[p. 252]

come in addition, whereby I first think the pressure, in order here to unite the perceptions into experience and to raise them to it. In general, outwardly we have in perception only the isolated sense intuitions, and thereby we arrive at the whole cognition of the external world as object of experience; inwardly we have in perception only the consciousness of sensible affections, but through reflection we arrive at a whole of inner experience in mathematics and philosophy. Experience here arises through the union of perception with apodictic cognition; it is not apodictic cognition, but also not perception, but the apprehension of the latter under the condition of the former. *We come to the complete re-consciousness of our cognitions, as they lie immediately in reason, only by first, in the place of the major premise, apprehending through abstraction the universal and necessary mathematical and philosophical laws of apodictic cognition, subordinating to these, in the place of the minor premise, the individual perceptions and historical cognitions of sense, and, in the place of the conclusion, determining the latter by the law of the former as experience.*

We must therefore still distinguish the apodictic element of cognition from necessity. Every possible given cognition is determinable with necessity as experience, for every perception stands under the rule of the apodictic, but only the universal laws themselves are subjectively universally valid, i.e., apodictic; the individual case is cognized by one but not by another, it is

[p. 253]

subjectively contingent. Schelling's reasoning, whereby the distinction of cognitions into cognitions *a priori* and *a posteriori* is to be rejected, is consequently incorrect. *Schelling*, namely, appeals only to the equally necessary determination of all our cognitions as soon as they are apprehended in their completeness as experience; but he has thereby by no means hit the true meaning of that division, for it does not concern objective necessity or contingency, but only two different levels of subjective validity. With regard to the complete immediate cognition of our reason there is indeed no distinction of the actual, the possible and the necessary, but over all there rules the one and same law of necessity; in science, however, this immediate cognition is only the object which we first artificially observe in ourselves, and mediately express again to ourselves. This re-observation, however, is unavoidably bound to those subjective distinctions; we can cognize the apodictic law for itself *in abstracto* only with the help of reflection, and must then first mediately subordinate the individual case to it. *Schelling's* proposal, instead of this detour of reflection to form a science through absolute intuition, could gain an illusion of plausibility in its favor only through a self-deception which arose from ignorance of the inner organization of our scientifically active reason.

#### §. 64.

We, on the other hand, have learned to see that complete self-observation can be reached only through abstraction and reflection. We must therefore, as

[p. 254]

a Katarktikon for all philosophical attempts, set up and hold fast side by side the two rules:

1) We need throughout the highest abstraction and reflection in order to attain to philosophy, for without these we shall not achieve any completeness in the self-observation of our cognitions.

2) All representations *in abstracto*, with them all representations of the universal *in a dissection laid asunder*, are only *means of self-observation*, and belong to the immediate cognition of our mind not as such, but only *in their recombination into the whole*.

Misapprehension of the coordination of these two rules for the most part brings hatred of philosophy among the people. One notices that through far-driven abstractions all life is lost, and fantasy loses all its play, and one therefore hates the dryness and the sucked-dry forms of philosophy, in that one supposes that life itself was meant to be grasped and painted by it. A misunderstanding which on the one side makes a false demand for general intelligibility or popularity on all parts of science, but on the other side, in fantasized presentations, gives to the secretive, mysterious element of a philosophy for the initiated only its very pretext. The whole error rests on this, that one supposes the forms *in abstracto*, which are mere instruments of observation, are to count for the philosopher as the essence of truth itself. Thus it is, e.g., Herder's sole objection to philosophizing, and what spoiled him for it, that he wholly lacked the calm for an abstraction in the form; the dissecting and laying asunder, without which

[p. 255]

no artificial observation and no science is possible, seemed to him the annihilation of all life, in that he supposed that philosophy wished thereby to give life itself.

For apprehending every apodictic cognition, if we wish to determine sharply and go deep, we inevitably need dry artificial abstraction, such as has never yet been disputed to mathematics; every other treatment gives only more or less elegant superficial popularity, however one may disguise it. Every error easily carries its opposite along with it: so here too others have supposed that with the mere forms from abstraction by themselves much could be accomplished in higher speculation. But the concept and the universal are, just like the most general forms of comparison, nothing but instruments belonging to reflection, made only through and for reflection, for inner observation, which have significance by themselves only with regard to the subjective validity of cognition, but not for the objective validity of immediate cognition.

Not in the dissections laid asunder, but only in the living unification of the whole shall we seek the essence of truth itself, but precisely therein we soon enough learn the deficiency of our mode of cognition, that we are able to observe only through dissection; where it often enough becomes impossible for us to hold fast the living unification of the whole with a single glance—*Encheiresin naturae*, chemistry calls it, mocks itself and knows not how.

The monstrous attempt at philosophy which tries to breathe a living breath into these torn forms,

[p. 256]

lets them rest like spirits on clouds or move through the sky in great nebulous shapes, as the archetypes of the true essence, of which only confused concretions appear here—this attempt resembles perfectly the proposal of an anatomist who wished to say: In the mad confusion of fibres, veins, lymphatic vessels and nerves of the concrete body you surely will not want to seek the true essence and life of the human organization; only in the cabinets of anatomical preparations is it to be found; to the freed, well-injected artery, the quicksilver-gleaming lymphatic vessel and the beautifully bleached skeleton the true essence properly belongs, that concretion is only a confused appearance of it. And the case here is just as there: certainly I can observe and study the organization more precisely on the preparations laid asunder than in the living itself, but the dissection, too, is meant to serve only as a means to that end.

The error against which we speak shows itself for the most part precisely in such a philosophy as apparently seeks to free itself entirely from reflection, but precisely thereby, because this freeing is impossible to human reason, only arrives at taking the means to reflection for more than the whole of reflection itself. The confusion of the mere forms of comparison with the immediate cognition of reason yields the Leibnizian view of philosophy; it shows itself often also in Fichte and Schelling. But if there the opposition between the ideal view of things and the natural one is confused with the contrast between concept and intuition, then the forms of abstraction of the universal concepts are also easily taken for immediate cognition

[p. 257]

—a confusion which is especially favored still by the normal idea of the schemata and by physical images of the archetypal forms of organization corresponding to these. From this are explained the number doctrine of the Pythagoreans, the doctrine of divine ideas of many Platonists, and the whole dispute of the Nominalists and Realists. In all these matters one can by no means arrive at a sharp final judgment unless one first understands how to separate the merely instrumental element of our reflection from immediate cognition. However clearly we may otherwise develop the falseness of these philosophemes, the half-true allusion in them to the ideal view of things will nevertheless never cease to deceive.

[p. 258]

### Third Section.

### Logic as a Philosophical Science.

#### a) Analytic and Synthetic Judgments.

#### §. 65.

A judgment is called *analytic*, a judgment by dissection, when in its predicate only representations of its subject are repeated; *synthetic*, judgment by combination, on the other hand, when it contains in the predicate new representations which are added to the subject. If I say, e.g., every triangle has three sides, or every equilateral triangle is equilateral, then the judgment is analytic, in that the predicate repeats only a part of the subject. If I say, on the other hand: every equilateral triangle also has three equal angles, then in the predicate there is added anew, beyond the equilaterality of which the subject spoke, equiangularity, as necessarily combined with the former; the judgment is therefore synthetic.

We cognize in judgment always the combination of concepts through the union of subject and predicate; we therefore cognize properly only through synthetic judgments, since these assert such a combination of different concepts. Through the analytic judgment, on the other hand, there is given to me only an empty form of distinctness for my

[p. 259]

cognition, whereby I can indeed dissect a concept, but properly cognize nothing. If I say: every equilateral triangle is equiangular, then I cognize that in regard to triangles equilaterality and equiangularity are always combined; but if I say: every three-sided figure has three sides, then I merely repeat my problematic representation, and cognize nothing at all; I do not say here that three-sidedness and figure are combined, but only: if they are combined, then they are combined.

We can determine this distinction also logically in the following way. In the synthetic judgment the combination of subject and predicate is represented by placing the sphere of the subject within the sphere of the predicate; in the analytic, on the other hand, not only are the spheres of both concepts compared, but the predicate is at the same time also posited in the content of the subject. E.g., without the concept of three-sidedness I can think no triangle at all; it is a part of the content of this concept; but if I combine for the triangle equilaterality and equality of the angles, then I subordinate here only the individual equilateral triangle, but not the concept equilateral triangle, to the concept of the equiangular.

This distinction of analytic and synthetic judgments is of the greatest importance for the whole of philosophy, for only through self-standing synthetic judgments do we gain real substance in our cognitions, while the analytic ones occupy themselves only with empty forms of elucidation. At first glance it seems to be without any difficulty: A is B gives an analytic judgment if B is already contained in A, a synthetic one if the B comes to the A as something new.

[p. 260]

Nevertheless this distinction has been so often misunderstood in the Kantian school. Reinhold confused it with the distinction between judgments of perception and judgments of experience, Fichte with that of affirmative, negative and infinite, Heydenreich with that of categorical, hypothetical and disjunctive, and more recently Schelling seeks to represent the whole distinction as unfounded. Whence now so many misunderstandings about so simple a matter?

The ground lies in this, that one must have grasped exactly the distinction of discursive and intuitive cognition, the distinction between cognition, intuition and concept, in order to be able to apply our distinction with determinateness. What do we properly designate by the word in language? I say the schema or the concept, as a universal problematic representation, and not the object of cognition itself, for through words in language we communicate to one another not intuitions, but only concepts. If I say, e.g., Frederick II, King of Prussia, lived in the middle of the eighteenth century, I thereby communicate only his name and the time in which he lived. What and who he was, however, of his history I communicate nothing here; analytically I thus have in the subject a mere name, to which in a further narrative, step by step, I could first add synthetically his history. But Reinhold, e.g., did not take it so, but rather referred, little by little, as I cognize more of an object, all this too under the word that designated it, and had to say therefore: all judgments would in the end become analytic, once our knowledge had only first advanced far enough, i.e., as soon as the single perception has been transformed into firm experience. If I think under the word Frederick II. immediately

[p. 261]

the whole man, as he lived, with his whole history, then of course everything that I can tell of him already lies analytically in this expression. But this second manner of designation is wholly contrary to the nature of our understanding; the words would then serve me not as sign of my thoughts, but each word would designate an *x*, an unknown object, which I was never able to determine completely. Our reflection requires that we restrict the meaning of words to that which is immediately thought with them according to concepts, thus only the universal concept which it first awakens; every further or closer determination, which then comes in as an extension of my cognition, must on the contrary be regarded as a new synthesis. From this it follows, the determinate application of the distinction of analytic and synthetic judgments requires first *universal judgments*, for the representation of the subject must be a universal concept, and secondly the concepts must be thought as determined by their definition, according to a completed scientific mode of representation, for otherwise the relation remains uncertain. If I say, e.g., every body is extended, has mass and fills its space, then the first is certainly analytic, for according to the barest geometrical concept of body it is a completely bounded space, and so extension already lies through space in its concept. But whether the judgments: every body has mass, or every body fills its space, are analytic or synthetic, that depends on definition and determination of words, according as I take into my physical concept of body quantity of substance or filling of space, or not.

[p. 262]

The distinction of the analytic and the synthetic can therefore not so much be applied to the individual case in life as to the general logical view of judgments as such for completed science. There, however, it is also very significant, in that through it we can separate all the empty, merely logical forms of our philosophical cognition from the substantive ones of metaphysics. All properly philosophical cognition expresses itself in universal and necessary laws; here, then, the distinction is in its place; we can divide these laws into analytic and synthetic, and the significant question of philosophy is then Kant's basic question: how are synthetic, universal and necessary judgments possible? Logic as a philosophical science is only the system of analytic judgments, whereby we do not become richer in cognitions.

All substance of philosophy would then be to be sought only in those synthetic judgments of metaphysics; to what purpose then the analytic prolixities of logic, and whence the importance of this opposition of the analytic and the synthetic in our cognition?

To the first the nearest answer is: We need the analytic forms of concepts, judgments, inferences and systems for the development and the distinctness of our cognitions. The second question, however, is answered through the essence of this distinctness itself. The distinction of the obscure, the clear and the distinct in our representations belongs to the faculty of self-cognition, as it shows itself through inner sense and reflection. Obscure in our interior is what we do not become aware of at all, clear what inner sense perceives, distinct that of which we become conscious through reflection. And thus there is determined, then, the

[p. 263]

universal law of the analytic in our cognition. Analytic forms in our cognition are those which arise only from the faculty of reflection, and analytic judgments are those whose truth or falsity can be determined by mere reflection. Now the faculty of reflection is only a faculty of re-observation of given immediate cognitions; the analytic forms therefore arise merely through the repetition of our inner activities before inner self-observation, and through them we can consequently gain no substance in cognition. On the other hand every synthetic judgment expresses to us an immediate cognition itself, of which we become conscious again in it.

Analytic judgments and forms of cognition are only the instrument of reflection, whereby it observes the synthetic in us; for this reason both forms must in our mind always run parallel to one another.

#### b) The Principles of Logic and Their System.

#### §. 66.

The definition of logic as a science of the universal laws of thinking is ambiguous, for if we understand by these laws of thought only the rules according to which our understanding conceives, judges, infers and builds systems, then this is no theme for philosophy, but only for empirical anthropology; we can here answer only from inner experience. Logic, on the other hand, is to be formal philosophy, and philosophical cognitions are to contain universal and necessary laws concerning the essence of things in general, and not individual rules concerning the way our understanding thinks. Logic as philosophical science

[p. 264]

is therefore only analytics, system of analytic judgments; the laws of thought are here not only subjectively the laws according to which we think, but objectively *the laws of the thinkability of a thing*. The philosophical basic laws of logic are therefore only laws of the determinations of the existence of things in general, only insofar as these are to be thought; but thinking is only a mediate repetition of that which was already immediately given; they are therefore mere results of tautology, or of the faculty of being able to say the same thing twice.

It would lead too far here if we wished to show historically what consequences the confusion of this anthropological and philosophical view of logic has had; I remark only that it was really through this that *Kant* was led to his prejudice of the transcendental, in that he namely, in the transcendental clue to the categories, grounds the whole certainty of his critique upon this ambiguous logic. His basic prejudice consists namely in general in the confusion of the anthropological conception of philosophical cognitions with the philosophical ones themselves, and it is chiefly this case of logic that has led him into it.

Upon this very confusion is grounded Schelling's attempt to abolish the distinction of the analytic and the synthetic. He asserts that the principle of all tautology: Every A is A, is not only that empty logical formula for which it is commonly held, but that it contains in the “Is” the absolute identity, the pronouncement of the necessary unity, which is the riddle of all philosophy. The matter, however, stands in fact in the following way. He who says: A is A, has thereby said nothing but an empty tautology; but in order to be able to utter even this empty pronouncement

[p. 265]

he had to possess the faculty of pronouncing, i.e., the faculty of reflection. Although therefore objectively, according to the metaphysical meaning, nothing is said by the A is A, we can nevertheless anthropologically, for the speaker himself, show in this formula a peculiarity of reflecting reason, namely that it relates all its cognitions to a basic concept of necessary unity. But thereby the law of unity and necessity itself is not pronounced, and Schelling's inference does not hold.

Just like the view of logic itself, the view of its principles also differs. Anthropologically their principles are the most general rules according to which we reflect and cognize with reflection; philosophically, on the other hand, they must be the laws of the determination of the object through mere reflection. In both respects we shall be put in a position by our earlier investigation to exhibit these principles systematically from the essence of the faculty of reflection.

Our cognition through reflection forms itself through comparison, abstraction and judging. Abstraction supplies us with the universal as the means for voluntary reflection, whereby its self-observation reaches further than that of inner sense; comparison determines the particular through this universal, and judgment is the mediate cognition, in that the object represented in the subject is first determined through a predicate. This now yields the following basic relations in all voluntary self-observation.
