1) Basic relation of abstraction. The universal representation is a part of the particular one subordinated to it. It is consequently the same cognitive activity which

[p. 266]

I bring to consciousness by itself in the representation *in abstracto*, or of which I become conscious as part-representation in the particular cognition. Consequently whatever holds of the universal holds also of the particular subordinated to it, and what holds of the particular holds conditionally also of the superordinate universal. (*Nota notae est nota rei ipsius.* [A mark of a mark is a mark of the thing itself.])

2) Basic relation of comparison. I can compare every object with every concept, and every object is determinable through every concept, in that the concept either belongs to it as a mark, or not.

3) Basic relation of judgment. a) Judgment is mediate cognition; its assertion is only the repetition of a cognition already immediately given in reason. Judgment therefore holds only through another cognition, already given in reason, different from it; it must therefore have a further ground of its assertion.

b) In the subject I think an object, in that I determine the cognition of it against the sphere of a concept; through the predicate I determine an object, in that I determine the cognition of it against the sphere of a concept; it is therefore one and the same activity of understanding by which I determine an object in the subject and in the predicate. If I have consequently determined an object in the subject through a concept, I can also repeat this in the predicate; but if I have a contrary in the subject, the concept itself may not belong to the object in the predicate.

4) The relation of the universal and the particular is either categorical, or hypothetical, or disjunctive,

[p. 267]

according to these determinations, therefore, all the important divisions of logic are made.

From this there result now, as anthropological principles of reflecting, the familiar formulas of logic. From 1) the *Dictum de Omni et Nullo*, which is usually placed at the head of syllogistic; from 2) the principle of determinability; from 3) a) the logical principle of ground; from 3) b) the principles of identity and of contradiction.

Of these formulas, however, only the following can be pronounced objectively, thus philosophically, as empty laws of thinkability. 1) The principle of determinability: Every thing is either A or not A (where A signifies any concept). 2) The principle of identity: Every A is A. 3) The principle of contradiction: No A is *Non-A*. 4) If one wishes, also the *Dictum de Omni et Nullo*: To every thing belong the marks of its marks; every thing which stands under the subject of a rule also stands under the rule itself. On the other hand the principle of ground rests only on the anthropological relation of reflected cognition; I cannot pronounce it in such a way that every thing becomes its subject, for only for judgment as my activity is the ground demanded.

To this exposition I must still make some remarks.

First, besides these laws we shall have no more basic laws of logic; from them, then, all analytic judgments must be derivable. They themselves, however, subsist side by side, and will not be reducible to one another, because each rests on a peculiar relation of reflection. The supreme of all we must call the principle of determinability or of the excluded

[p. 268]

third, since its logical disjunction, either A or not A, is the only thing we can assert of a thing through mere reflection. Yet that does not mean that the others can be proved from it. Kant earlier maintained that the principles of identity and of contradiction, and later, in the *Crit. of Pure Reason*, that the principle of contradiction alone, is the supreme logical principle, but wrongly, for from both he will derive only categorical, but no truly hypothetical or disjunctive analytic proposition. The attempted proofs of the other principles from that of contradiction are always mere plays on words, which can be justified only through a confusion of the anthropological and the philosophical standpoint.

Second, if one wants to place these principles at once at the head of a treatise on logic, or if one tries to explain thinking without having already discussed the relation of subject and predicate in determinate fashion, one arrives unavoidably only at indeterminate, indeed easily even at false expressions. For all these laws arise only from the repetition in the mediate self-observation of reflection. We shall show this in the individual laws.

1) The principle of identity must not be called the principle of concord [*Einstimmung*], but only the principle of sameness. Representations are called concordant when they can be combined. E.g., equilaterality and equiangularity of a triangle are concordant representations, but this concord is cognized not through mere reflection but through intuition, and does not concern us here. Our law is limited only to the sameness of marks, e.g., to the three-sidedness of the triangle.

[p. 269]

Through intuition we can represent one and the same thing only as simply A; but before reflection there is the immediate apprehension of it in the place of the subject, and the mediate apprehension of the same in the place of the predicate, so that we can say not merely A, but tautologically A is A, by naming the same thing twice.

2) The principle of contradiction has to do not with all conflicting representations, but only with logical contradiction. Conflicting are representations that cannot be combined. E.g., an equilateral triangle whose angle at the apex were half as large as one at the base is impossible, since conflicting marks would here have to be united for the triangle. But this cannot be judged according to the principle of contradiction, but only from intuition. Contradictory are only a concept and its opposite, i.e., positing a concept in the content of a representation and cancelling it in its content, A and Non-A. Of this alone does our principle speak.

3) All attempts to prove even merely the logical principle of ground are said to have failed, even after it had been wholly separated from the metaphysical law of causality. Yet we can most readily give a derivation of it from the principle of identity. But admittedly we must then not state it thus: every cognition must have its sufficient ground; for so universally it is not only unprovable but also wholly inapplicable. Only the mediate cognition of reflection demands a further ground, and that lies already in the concept of its mediacy itself. The meaning of this principle is therefore only: since in every assertion of a judgment only

[p. 270]

mediately a cognition comes to consciousness, the immediate being-given of this cognition in the mind must always precede, as the ground of the truth of the assertion.

The sober formulas: Concordant representations can be combined, conflicting ones cannot be combined, and every ground has its consequence, are therefore empty tautologies, which must not be confused with the logical principles, but merely furnish examples for the principle of identity.

#### §. 67.

The application of these fundamental laws of thought is made in two ways. First, every judgment in general stands under the form of reflecting; they are therefore negative criteria of truth for all judgments in general, in that none may be contrary to them. Second, they are supposed to be the principles of all analytic judgments; these must therefore be derivable from them.

A) The use of these principles as negative criteria of all truth in judgments relates to the modal distinction of judgments, in that by these stages we complete our reflection.

1) The problematic thinking of representations stands under the principle of contradiction: contradictory representations cannot be combined.

2) The assertion of the judgment stands under the principle of ground: every judgment is a consequence, and must therefore be grounded still further. The discussion of this law will show itself later to be very important.

3) For the apodictic assertion of a judgment there is determined from the mere form of reflection, according to the

[p. 271]

principle of determinability: of two contradictory judgments one and only one is true.

B) For the derivation of analytic judgments from their principles we remark in advance that every analytic judgment can be expressed universally and apodictically; there remain, therefore, in their form only the distinctions of quality and relation. So we obtain the following relations of derivation.

1) *For analytic categorical judgments* as well as for conjunctions the principle, when they are affirmative, is the principle of identity, in that I may repeat every given subject wholly in the predicate. For negations, however, the principle of contradiction holds, in that I may put opposites of the marks of the subject into the predicate of the negating judgment.

2) *For analytic disjunctions* the principle of determinability is the principle; every analytic disjunction is made only through a concept and its opposite.

3) *For analytic hypothetical judgments* the principle is the basic principle of the universal and the particular, for the sole analytic relation of ground and consequence is that by which the determinations of the universal are transferred also to its particular, and conversely.

Every analytic hypothetical judgment is an *inference*; its premises are the antecedent, the conclusion is the consequent. (Every inference is thus a hypothetical judgment, but not every hypothetical judgment is an inference, but only that in which the consequent is understood of itself according to mere concepts, when the antecedent is given.)

[p. 272]

For the *systematic form* these three moments determine the *definition*, the *division* and the *proof*, and so we see how our whole analytic cognition, i.e., the whole logical form of our cognition, arises from these principles.

In the execution of a science, among these three, inference and proof play by far the greatest role, and that for this reason, that analytic categorical and disjunctive propositions always remain only at empty analytic forms; but in the analytic hypothetical judgment several synthetic judgments can be combined in the antecedent as premises, so that significant synthetic judgments too come into the conclusion.

[p. 273]

### Fourth Section.

### Of the Idea of the Formal Logical Perfection of Our Cognition.

#### a) Perfection of Cognition.

#### §. 68.

From our investigations so far we can take the following as settled. Our power of cognition is stirred by sense to its individual activities, but to these stirrings it adds a form of cognition that remains the same, so that all content of cognition does indeed come to us from sensibility, but every sensible content stands under the condition of a form which arises only from the original essence of our reason as self-activity. (§. 63.) Furthermore, the presence of the inner activities in the mind is not sufficient to bring them to our consciousness; we have, in addition, a faculty of our own, that of inner self-observation, which consists of inner sense and the faculty of reflection. What is usually called sensible in cognition, intuition, is that which we perceive in ourselves through inner sense; what is usually ascribed to the understanding is that which we find only through reflection in

[p. 274]

ourselves. Inner sense shows us our cognitions only on the occasion of individual sensible stirrings; reflection separates by abstraction the universal form, which belongs to the self-activity of reason, from this individual element, and so brings complete cognition to our consciousness through universal laws in the apodictic relations.

What this faculty of re-consciousness in general now adds to our cognition we call the *distinctness* of cognition in the wider sense. This divides into distinctness of inner sense, aesthetic distinctness, which consists in clarity, vivacity, evidence of cognition, and into logical distinctness of reflection, which demands the analysis of cognition into universal partial representations, and finds its completion in the systematic form.

But everything that we ourselves can do with our cognition is only either extension of experience or rendering distinct through reflection. To this correspond two concepts of its perfection. Material perfection concerns the extent of our cognition, in respect of which we must delimit the field of our cognition against our ignorance in general, since we have to hope for all possible extensions only from sense and its experience. Second, however, formal perfection concerns the completion of its logical distinctness. Thereby arises the logical idea of a completed state of our science, in which our whole cognition would be distributed into its systems strictly in scientific form by definition, division and proof.

[p. 275]

This latter ideal of logical perfection has to do only with the cognitions we actually possess; it goes only to the completeness of self-observation through reflection, in that which our mind immediately and actually cognizes. We can therefore show here completely under what forms our cognition would have to appear if it is to correspond wholly to this ideal, whereby we arrive at the idea of a *formal scientific architectonic*.

According to this idea, in the completed systematic presentation of our knowledge, first, the content of every concept would be given through its definition, down to the most universal concepts, which can no longer be composed; second, the sphere of each would be determined by a division against its nearest subspecies; third, the most universal concepts would be combined into principles, and every other proposition would enter the system only through its proof from the principles. The whole would be completed cognition from principles; Euclidean geometry would be a single example of it; this idea demands what in the days of Wolff was called the mathematical method; it is that which all dogmatism regards as immediately realizable.

The system of concepts with its definitions and divisions would here have the same form for every science; in the system of judgments, by contrast, the three forms of the categorical, hypothetical and disjunctive system (§. 47.) would have to be ordered side by side and one under another under the highest form of experience (§. 63.), so that the whole is finally that which we call *theory*.

Under the form of the inference the philosophical, categorical system enters into the major premise, the hypothetical,

[p. 276]

mathematical into the minor premise, and the conjunctive, historical into the conclusion. Each of these systems subsists by itself, follows laws of its own, and flows from principles of its own, but the subjective progress to the apodictic determination of the whole determines the subordination (according to §. 63.).

These relations shall be developed more closely here.

#### §. 69.

Already in the investigation of productive imagination we divided all our cognition into historical from sensation, mathematical from pure intuition, and philosophical from mere concepts. This division becomes clearer now in the following way. All our cognition is either intuitive or discursive. It is namely intuitive, demonstrable, i.e., it can be shown in intuition (for demonstration does not properly mean proof, but showing in intuition), if we become conscious of it through inner sense; discursive, on the other hand, if we become conscious of it through reflection. Different from this is the division of cognition into assertoric and apodictic. Assertoric is that which we possess only through individual sensible stirrings of our activity; apodictic, on the other hand, that which consists in enduring activities, in original manifestations of reason. From the combination of the two latter divisions we obtain the first.

Historical cognition is demonstrable, and at the same time the peculiarity of the merely assertoric; it rests on the individual stirring in sense intuition. Mathematical cognition, on the other hand, is demonstrable and apodictic at the same time. The law of intuition belongs here to the productive imagination as a self-activity of reason

[p. 277]

it is thus its own law; we observe this cognition through reflection, but can nevertheless cognize its universal law from intuition. Finally, philosophical cognition is that of which we become conscious only through reflection; it is thus thoroughly discursive and apodictic.

With this division of cognitions into historical, mathematical and philosophical, the three pure forms of systems coincide. In the purely historical property of experience there stand only facts, each of which is given for itself, *beside* one another; they are ordered together, in the chronicle or in the class-system of natural history, only as parts of a whole in the conjunctive system. In the mathematical of pure intuition we can apply every basic law of cognition, as the simplest, by combination in a composition without end, so that the compositions, as the derived, are already determined *through* the basic law, but not contained in it. Thus through the presupposed continuity and infinity of pure intuition I arrive in arithmetic from the simple basic requirements of addition and subtraction, by mere composition, at multiplication, division, powers and the extraction of roots as the derived; in geometry from the simplest requirements of the drawing of straight lines and of the circle up to the most composite, and to the calculation of all curved lines as the derived. We here order, according to hypothetical systems, everything composite as consequence under the simple as the ground.

Finally, that of which we become conscious only in judgments must be necessary combination of universal concepts (§. 48. 3.); we can therefore also only

[p. 278]

bring this into application through the concept, in that we determine objects from the sphere of the subject through the predicate, i.e., we here always order only in a categorical system under the universal predicate, in that we regard the determination of the sphere of the subject as already contained in the determination of the sphere of the predicate. Thus the whole content of a philosophical science is already given in its principles; all that is philosophical in the doctrine of virtue or of right lies, e.g., in the one idea of personal dignity, and we arrive at further science only by applying this to the individual cases subordinate to it in the history of mankind. Philosophical cognition has the peculiarity that it gives us only a universal principle, without being able itself to create also the case of application for it.

#### b) Proof, Demonstration and Deduction.

#### §. 70.

The end of science and of system is to bring order and distinctness into our cognitions; but whoever hopes to achieve more by it, whoever wants to gain positively through the system and thereby extend his knowledge, deceives himself. In the system of science we do nothing but prove other propositions from principles; this proving, however, consists in a mere connecting of chains of inference, by which we show that the truth of the conclusion already lies in the truth of the premises. Beyond the given system of concepts and principles we gain in the system of a science nothing at all in actual content of cognition, but

[p. 279]

only in distinctness; there lies no more truth in the system than the truth of the principles, which is repeated only in part in the theorems. In the historical sciences our cognition is extended with every step, precisely because every new proposition, like a principle, rests only on itself; in mathematics the extension becomes possible not through logical proof, but through the possibility of composition according to the rule of the principle, which the intuition of the demonstration shows; and in philosophy we in fact gain nothing beyond the principles. Hence, however, the power of logic in these sciences stands precisely in inverse proportion to the extension of cognition. In philosophy the system can be developed from the principles with mere logic; in mathematics logic alone is already no longer sufficient; and in historical science it leads us not one step further.

We must not, in general, form too great a conception of proofs. There is not much to lose in what can be proved, provided only that we remain in possession of that truth which cannot be proved, which rather stands firm only in principles. The proof we shall find again soon enough, if only we first have a fund of truth from which something can be proved. All philosophy, however, has for a long time been strongly dominated by the prejudice that one must be able to prove everything that is to be true. One wanted to prove an eternal reality of things, the immortality of the soul, the freedom of the will and the existence of God, and that always from something that was neither eternal nor free nor the deity, but which one believed already to have been proved. We shall easily notice that this task

[p. 280]

was posed wholly wrongly: what we want to prove, its truth must already lie *implicitly* in that from which I set out in the proof; I find nothing new through the proof, I only make it more distinct to myself. But where, pray, do we have the eternal, the free, and the deity anywhere in the finite premises from which we want to conduct the proof? Deity, freedom and eternity are supreme conditions in our cognition, from which much can be proved, but which themselves cannot be subject to any proof.

We must therefore take back the prejudice entirely that everything must be provable; but what do we put in its place, to protect ourselves against error, doubt and unbelief?

*Jacobi* was the first among the more recent philosophers who attacked this prejudice of the Wolffians decisively, and thereby fell into a dispute with *Mendelssohn*. *Mendelssohn* thought that *Jacobi* was thereby striking dead on the spot his soul and his God, which had to live only from proof, and he could not well bear that. *Jacobi* appealed against this to faith and revelation, without which not even the simplest conviction concerning a color and a sound comes to us; but his propositions remained too indistinct, and he was right only with the negative. What does it help us to appeal to faith against doubt and unbelief? Those who have faith are well protected; the art is only to keep the unbelievers away from us. Against these, however, the praising of faith is only violent party-making, in order not to stand alone, but to maintain oneself in esteem with one's friends, as the elect and the initiated.

[p. 281]

We therefore demand yet another answer to this question; we obtain it from logic, and it will become one of the most important propositions for the whole present philosophy. Nothing more is needed than to bring it distinctly among the people, in order to put an end to all the superior airs and the mystery-mongering of philosophical schools, and to introduce philosophy into education as plain a school subject as arithmetic and geometry now are. To many it may seem strange how logic is to do such things—but it will do so all the same!

The ground of the prejudice which demands proof for every truth is a misinterpretation of the logical principle of ground. This principle of ground, rightly understood, namely, runs: Every judgment is a mediate cognition, it is merely the formula in which I become conscious again, for reflection, of my immediate cognition; every judgment must therefore have, in another cognition, the ground why it is true or false. This principle is the Katarktikon of all truth in mediate cognitions: for every judgment that I assert I must be able to give a ground why I assert it.

This grounding of judgments, which is demanded quite properly for the beginnings of our synthetic cognition, has now been confused with proof, which is after all only an empty logical thing, and is put together analytically out of inferences. We must therefore, with regard to the grounding of judgments, establish the following important distinctions. We distinguish first mediate and immediate judgments. Only the mediate judgment, which itself still depends on other judgments, is a *provable* judgment; all truth of judgments rests, however, ultimately on such propositions as have the worth of principles, and

[p. 282]

do not ground themselves on other judgments. Proof thus serves only to derive a judgment from other judgments; through it we always arrive only at unprovable principles, but the task was to ground every judgment, hence the principles too, and for this no proof serves us.

How, then, do we ground, according to the demand of the logical principle of ground, these first principles? The first answer to this is easily found. The judgment merely repeats before our consciousness another immediate cognition; its truth rests therefore on its agreement with this cognition. The immediate cognition which is merely repeated in a principle is therefore properly the ground of its truth.

Here two cases now arise. Either we become immediately conscious, ourselves, of the immediate cognition that we express in a principle, or this cognition is precisely of such a kind that we need judgment and reflection in order merely to find it in us. In the first case the immediate cognition itself is given, it is *intuition*; here, consequently, intuition is the ground of my judgment, and its grounding is *demonstration*. In all the sciences of experience and in mathematics this is the way in which we ground our judgments; we assert something because it has been observed or experienced, or because we can show its truth itself in intuition. But for all such cases we should properly need no reflection at all and no judgment; the judgment here merely repeats to us what we already know in any case, and of which we are also already conscious that we know it. The proper end of reflection lies only in such cognitions whose basic judgments precisely cannot be demonstrated. These are the philosophical

[p. 283]

ones. Philosophical judgments, when they are principles, we assert absolutely and, what is more, apodictically, without being able to appeal to any intuition lying at their ground; we state propositions which can only be thought, and yet depend on no other judgment.

On what, then, is our judgment here to be grounded?

When I say, e.g.: Every substance persists, every alteration has a cause, all simultaneity is determined by the interaction of substances, or when I judge about right and wrong, virtue and vice, and say at the very top: every rational being is to be treated, in accordance with its personal dignity, as an end in itself; or finally, when I assert: there is a God and the will is free, on what then do I ground my judgment? I cognize in the first case laws of nature, in the second laws of freedom, in the last laws of the eternal order of things, without any appeal to intuition. But precisely these laws, of which I only become conscious again in the judgment, must still lie in my reason as immediate cognition, except that I need the judgment precisely in order to become conscious of them. We can therefore ground our judgment here only by exhibiting what original cognition of reason lies at its ground, without being able nevertheless to place this cognition immediately alongside the judgment and so protect it by it. This way of grounding a principle shall be called the *deduction* of it.

Such propositions we can neither demonstrate, i.e., show in intuition, nor prove, for they are principles, but only deduce. In what, however, does this deduction consist?

[p. 284]

It is to exhibit the law in our immediate cognition which lies at the ground of a principle and is expressed through it; but since we become conscious of this law here only through the principle, the deduction can consist solely in this, that we *derive from a theory of reason* what original cognition we must necessarily have, and what principles necessarily arise therefrom in our reason. This determines the importance of anthropology for philosophy. The principles of philosophy lie without any grounding in our convictions; no proposition, however, may be accepted without ground; we must therefore protect them through a deduction, in which we show how the propositions expressed in them arise from the essence of reason. This, however, is a mere business of anthropology, and thus of inner experience; philosophy therefore appeals ultimately, with regard to the truth of its propositions, always to inner experience, but not in order to prove them, for thereby they themselves would become mere propositions of experience, but only in order to *exhibit* them as unprovable principles in reason. I do not prove that every substance is persistent, but I only exhibit that this principle of the persistence of substance lies in every finite reason; I do not prove that there is a God, but I only exhibit that every finite reason has faith in a God.

Through this deduction we satisfy the demands of the system, to accept no proposition without ground, but free ourselves from the burdensome and false imputation of having to prove everything that we assert in judgments. We thereby gain in philosophy an idealistic standpoint, which makes it possible for us

[p. 285]

to pass a decisive judgment on all truth, without leaping over from the limits of our essence into the object; we do not say: the sun stands in the sky, but only: every finite reason knows that the sun stands in the sky; we do not say: the will is free, but only: every finite reason has faith in the freedom of its will; we do not say: there is a God, but only: every finite reason has an intimation, in the life and the beauty of the figures through nature, of the all-ruling eternal goodness.

All our judgments are therefore either *provable*, or *demonstrable*, or only *deducible*. Only the subordinate judgments in the system can be subjected to proof; every basic judgment, on the other hand, is to be grounded either through demonstration or through deduction. For every judgment arising from the original self-activity of reason, thus for every apodictic judgment, deduction is possible. Mathematics and philosophy therefore rest on deducible principles, but only for philosophy does deduction become a need, because mathematical principles can also be grounded through demonstration. The advantage of all logical manner of representation in the systematic form is only order and distinctness, whereby we are, however, ultimately put in a position to distinguish principles from provable judgments, and to determine where the need for deduction shows itself. It is in one way or another always outer and inner experience that extends our cognitions; the concept and reflection add nothing new, but give only the distinctness through which we learn to understand our inner experience itself, and in that consists the whole interest of the *scientific form*.

[p. 286]

#### c) Empirical and Transcendental Truth.

#### §. 71.

In order to give the doctrine of the grounding of judgments its full completeness, we must still compare the distinction between deduction and proof with a more general one, the distinction between the *objective and subjective grounding* of cognitions. Objective grounding presupposes the reality of the object as the ground of the truth of a cognition; subjective grounding, on the other hand, explains only from the history of my reason how it arrives at this or that cognition.

Here we meet with the usual logical distinction between the ground of explanation, *ratio essendi*, and the mere ground of cognition, *ratio cognoscendi*, with which our subjective and objective grounding can easily be confused. This usual distinction, however, goes only to the opposition of regressive and progressive proofs. If I cognize the ground through the consequence, this is only the ground of cognition of my judgment, but not the ground of explanation of the thing itself. Or, e.g., in physics the first grounds of cognition are the individual experiments and observations, say about electricity; through these, however, I seek first regressively to divine the universal laws according to which the individual follows, and finally in the theory of electricity I apply these laws, first derived for cognition, as supreme grounds of explanation of the individual. Here, then, only for the progressive course of theory do grounds of explanation stand at the head, but for the regressive course of investigation mere grounds of cognition. But of that we do not speak here; the regressive proof, which cognizes the universal through the particular, rather does not here concern us

[p. 287]

at all. According to the architectonic idea of the completed scientific form, namely, in every system one infers only from the universal to the particular; every proof is progressive; grounds of explanation and grounds of cognition coincide here. E.g., only the theory in physics is taken into the completed system, the investigation itself belongs to the preparation. Our distinction of subjective and objective grounding is nevertheless to remain standing for the logical ideal of completed systems.

It will become clear through what follows. Grounding of a cognition is one and the same as the exhibiting of its truth and validity. Here, now, truth of cognition stands with the reality of its object in such a reciprocal relation that neither can be without the other, but the reality of the object is evidently the ground, the truth of the cognition only the consequence. Hence the usual logical definition of truth: Truth is the agreement of a cognition with its object. Beside this another concept of truth then also makes itself felt, in that we say: a cognition is called true if I am conscious of having it in my reason, false if I am conscious of having its opposite.

I shall call the first truth, which asks for agreement with the object, *transcendental truth*, the other, however, which asks only for presence in the mind, *empirical truth*. Grounding of cognition according to the first rule I call the objective, because here the object is regarded as ground; that according to the second rule the subjective,

[p. 288]

because only the inner history of my cognizing is asked about.

Commonly we now think, when we are not made attentive by artificial speculation, that all our aim in grounding cognitions goes to agreement of the representation with the object, and follows the first rule. That, however, is by no means the case. We determine very often whether an activity of cognition is true or not, whether a judgment passed is true or false, an intuition we have had dream or actuality, and yet we never ask in this about the agreement of the representation with the object. Rather, this agreement can help us in this not at all, for we cannot step out, as it were, from our cognition of the object in order to compare it itself with this, but every object becomes for us only object of a cognition. Even in the assertion, I am, the identity of the one asserting with the object of the assertion helps us not at all to come closer to this comparison, for I too become object to myself only by means of this assertion, and cannot place assertion and object, as it were, side by side for comparison. Nevertheless it is in many cases easy for us to judge about truth or falsehood; we cannot therefore then find truth in the agreement of cognition with the object, we must find it in something else. What, now, is this other?

I say: it is the agreement of mediate cognition with immediate, and with regard to the immediate, its existence in the mind.

[p. 289]

When in common life we speak of error or deception, this always refers only to a mediate cognition which the voluntarily active understanding has not correctly referred to what is immediately certain. When we want here to prove or refute something, we seek something else generally known or conceded, and show that our assertion either coheres with it or is contrary to it. Even such deceptions as seem to concern intuition immediately lie in this relation of the mediacy of cognition. We see the moon larger at the horizon than when it stands high in the sky, but can soon notice that we do not see any magnitude at all immediately, but first carry it mediately into our intuition; we therefore determine this magnitude more exactly by measuring, find it equal in both cases, and now declare the first representation to be a deception. Or a dream frightens us like anxious actuality; only on waking do we see that its wavering images did not keep the firm course of actual intuition, and declare it a deception, as in the previous case, in that on both occasions we had erroneously judged a mediate representation of the imagination to be an immediate cognition of intuition.

But even if we go beyond these usual cases of common life, if we do not merely ask straight out after that mediate cognition in its relation to the immediate, but seek to make ourselves masters of the immediate cognition itself, the individual cases show here too that human reason, in what it calls truth, seeks not agreement with the object, but first of all only the existence of the cognition in the mind. All immediate cognition

[p. 290]

is either sense intuition, or that necessary and universal which comes to our consciousness in the deducible basic principles as the principles of apodictic cognition.

In the immediate intuitive cognition of a given object, the evidence and truth of it rest wholly only on this, that it is given immediately to the mind, i.e., on its existence in the mind. Its truth derives wholly from no causal relation to the object, not from this, that the object has produced it, but only from this, that the object is represented in it as given. Even if, in order to bring unity into the whole of our experiences, we afterwards place the object itself in the series of causes which produce the sensation in which we first intuited it, yet the evidence of this intuition itself, and our immediate holding-to-be-true from it, would not rest at all on this extended connection, but intuition is an immediate state passively determined in the mind, it carries its truth immediately with it, and has absolutely no need of derivation through inferences. (§. 15.)

But sense intuition by itself contains only a momentary, contingent cognizing; only in reflection upon the intuiting do we become conscious of the necessary and universally valid in our cognition. The immediate in this is that of which we become conscious only in deducible principles of apodictic cognition. This immediate *a priori*, this immediate necessary and universally valid, eternal and absolute, or however else one will call it, has always been the stumbling block of all philosophy, and yet at the same time the proper

[p. 291]

object of its investigations, whose possibility one has never yet been able to penetrate fully. This much, however, is at once clear, that nowhere less than here could we ground the truth of our cognition in common life on an agreement of it with the object, since here we reach the object only through the concept or the idea; we may therefore, here too, first of all understand nothing else by the truth of our assertion than the presence of its cognition in the mind. Freedom, deity, world, and all objects of this conviction are precisely what is objectively and immediately unattainable for us; here, then, we must certainly first of all stay only with the laws of our cognizing.

The determinate relation of these two laws of truth is therefore as follows. The rule of transcendental truth, or of the agreement of cognition with the object, determines the validity of immediate cognition as it is actually present in our mind. If, on the other hand, we first ask: which cognitions are actually present in our reason? then this task belongs to the mediate faculty of re-observation, and truth then consists only in the agreement of my self-observation with the cognitions actually given in my reason. This second rule of truth is therefore our empirical truth. Here we ask only whether we have apprehended our cognitions correctly before consciousness through inner sense or reflection. We ask, in order to distinguish dream and actuality, whether an intuitive representation given before inner sense is actually sense intuition or only a repetition of the imagination; in the case of judgments, however, we distinguish truth and error according as the repeated

[p. 292]

reflection agrees with what is actually given or not.

From what has just been said it follows, then, that when we commonly ask after truth we in fact presuppose only the concept of empirical truth for re-observation, and a rule of the subjective grounding of cognitions, without going more closely into the objective grounding of transcendental truth. But the usual claims of consciousness run directly counter to this result. On the whole we always demand objective grounding. If I merely show someone: we human beings once and for all must always represent it to ourselves thus and so, we cannot think it otherwise—the main thing still remains with him: but is it then also really as we think and represent it? We always set the task, then, for objective grounding, but every single attempt at its solution we then make nonetheless with merely subjective means of grounding, and then usually take the one for the other, and this is the fundamental error of all erroneous speculations. What is misleading here is the following.

Our cognition has transcendental truth, or it does not have it, without our being able to do anything for or against it ourselves—of this we shall speak later; the truth, on the other hand, which we can procure for ourselves is only the empirical truth of reflection; of it alone, therefore, will there properly be talk in the scientific grounding of our cognition.

The means for grounding our judgments in the system were proof, demonstration, and deduction. Here, now, the ground of the usual errors is, first, that proof could really serve, within its limits, for an objective grounding.

[p. 293]

Proof derives one judgment from others; the consequence here receives the same validity that the premises have, so if the premises are objectively grounded, this holds of them as well. But whence the validity of the premises? Here, second, the real fundamental prejudice of empiricism makes itself felt, with the answer: *from intuition*, in that one takes demonstration for an objective grounding, which it nonetheless is not.

The obscurely presupposed prejudice of intuition, that a cognition is objectively firmly grounded if one has only demonstrated it, i.e., traced it back to intuition, is the misleading principle of all speculation. Through it the false confidence in proof is properly maintained, and thereby the false hope of gaining something for the grounding of our cognition through intellectual intuition. But whoever has come to see clearly that all evidence of intuition, and all demonstration from it, is likewise grounded only as subjectively as deduction is, must learn to view the whole business of speculation differently. That which one usually regards as the first foundation of all conviction is wholly lost to him; he must see that one has to begin the matter in an altogether different way in order to reach the goal.

The main thing here is therefore to see: through all intuition of the object as present, and through all demonstration from intuition, nothing is ever gained with regard to the agreement of the representation with the object, but there is talk only of subjective relations of my cognizing and of subjective grounding in the history of my reason. To

[p. 294]

the evidence of this assertion we have already given heed in the earlier investigations; here we have only to recall it again. Our intuition is mathematical pure intuition or sense intuition.

All mathematical demonstration ultimately appeals to the given intuition of space and time. But does this borrow its validity from an agreement of cognition with the object? By no means! It is given in our mind, we cannot detach ourselves from it, and that gives it its subjective evidence and certainty. And sense intuition? Here we have already endeavored, in the theory of sensation, to show that there is talk here only of a subjective history of our cognizing. It is not *what affects for sensation that I intuit as cause* of the affection, but *the given object simply*. The green color of its foliage and the brown of the trunk is what the cognition of the tree begins with immediately; of affecting through light and eye only philosophers then speak, and this concerns the natural way of cognizing little. Thus the mathematical determinations, and gradually all the moments of our completed cognition of nature, are added to sense intuition, only according to a subjective course of the history of my cognizing, without any transition to the objective.

*Proof is the only objective means of grounding in our cognition.*

Through proofs, however, we ground only the mediate in our judgments; all grounding of the basic judgments is demonstration or deduction. *Even for the ideal of a completed scientific form of our*

[p. 295]

*cognition, every supreme grounding is therefore only a subjective one, which refers merely to the inner laws of the activity of our reason in cognizing.* There is always talk only of how human reason knows and cognizes, and not immediately of how things in themselves are. This is the characteristic of a correct idealistic turn of speculation; it is properly this that is the spirit of speculation which *Kant* as criticism wanted to assert against the dogmatism directed at the objective. But however determinately *Kant* describes this subjective standpoint of his critique in the Preface to the *Critique of Pure Reason*, he has nevertheless not wholly seen through its relation; otherwise he could never have attempted transcendental proofs, and least of all could he have said (*Crit. of Pure Reason*, p. 124): “There are only two cases possible in which synthetic representation and its objects can come together. Either when the object alone makes the representation possible, or the representation the object. If the former, then this relation is only empirical, etc.” Here one sees clearly that he wants to explain the objectivity of sense intuition through a causal relation of that which affects, and in general aims at that which we call objective grounding of our cognitions. We must free his critical procedure still of this defect, and precisely thereby we obtain only the purely anthropological task of a history of our cognizing and of a theory of our reason, as the last need of all speculation.

[p. 296]

#### d) Theory.

#### §. 72.

Thus only according to this subjective view have we to ground the principles of the three forms of system. The logical whole of our cognition is the union of these three forms, i.e., *theory*. The whole logical task for our cognition is: to trace everything and each thing in it back to its last grounds of explanation, and to derive it systematically from these in theory.

We are therefore put in a position here to state the highest laws of all theoretical science. The systems of historical, mathematical, and philosophical cognition unite into the whole of our science; this rests, then, on the principles of these three systems. The principles of historical cognition were the immediate statements of facts themselves, whereby we know of individual existence; these are grounded only on autopsy, i.e., on empirical demonstration of each single judgment for itself. The principles of mathematics were first principles which are grounded through pure demonstration, and can be developed through their principle of combination in consequences to infinity. Finally, philosophical cognition rests on first principles which can be secured only through deduction.

These three beginnings of our cognition stand independently beside one another, but unite into one whole under the form of a syllogism, in that (according to §. 63) the single case of the historical stands under the apodictic universal rules of the mathematical and philosophical. This union is theory. But should real explanation of the one from the other

[p. 297]

come about here, then in the first place historical cognition does nothing toward it by itself. Its conjunctive system unites, to be sure, all facts as parts in a whole of natural description or history, but the system does not of itself add the unity of the whole through its own principles. It gives itself only the manifoldness of the individual facts, each of which subsists as a particular part for itself, without relating itself to others beside it. Every single existence is individual, and none is through the other.

Second, through the philosophical principles alone, too, no theory would come about, for here we have only universal rules of unity, which, however, can never themselves supply the case under the rule. All application is something foreign to the philosophical system, which it first expects from the historical.

We arrive at theory and explanation, then, in general only through mathematics. All series of ground and consequence are introduced into our cognition through time and space, i.e., through mathematical combination; mathematical intuition brings the rule to the historical fact, and the single case to the philosophical rule. For every mathematical principle, as supreme ground, already carries with it the germ of evolutions into infinitely many consequences, through the possibility of compositions from it by means of combinatorial repetitions. All explanation in our mind is combinatorial composition, derivation of composite complexions from their simple elements.

The fundamental rule of all theory is, then: *in our cognition the historically given individual existence can never be comprehended from the philosophical*

[p. 298]

*unity, but both come into connection only through mathematics by a hypothetical system of ground and consequence. The ground of all explicability is the mathematical composition, which is already given with every principle, but we can speak of explanations only where mere differences of mathematical composition out of the homogeneous, mere differences of magnitude, show themselves.* E.g., for the former: the geometrical axiom, between two points one straight line, and only one straight line, is possible at any time, would lead to nothing further if the possibility of points to infinity through space did not lie before our eyes alongside it. Through this, however, repetition of its application to infinity, and derivation of the laws of rectilinear triangles and quadrilaterals up to the most composite rectilinear configurations from this simple ground and a few others, becomes possible for us at once. Or if the dynamical relations in motion are asked after, then however the appearances of pull and push may be composed, we exhibit as the first fundamental relation the relation of two points and the straight line between them, and now know with certainty that every other relation must let itself be explained as a *composite from this*. We take, then, approach and distancing of those two points as simple fundamental relations, accordingly give every mass an original force of attraction and repulsion, and now know that from this all causality of motions must be explicable.

[p. 299]

Second, the limiting rule of all explanation in our cognition is, then: only differences through the composition of the homogeneous, only quantitative differences of mathematics, let themselves be subjected to an explanation. Every composition of magnitudes we can derive from its simplest elements, but different qualities from historical or philosophical cognition cannot be traced back to one another. Hence the Kantian proposition: There is only as much theoretical natural science as there is application of mathematics to nature. All physical explanations restrict themselves to mathematical combinations, but no quality submits to them. The physical theory of light and sound reproduces with the greatest determinateness all the mathematical relations of the phenomena, but it never penetrates to color or tone itself. Least of all does it have any meaning to want to draw together the outer theory of motion and the inner theory of thinking and willing into one system of explanations; outer and inner physics are here wholly separated by the difference of their qualities. That there is nonetheless an inner science of nature as theory springs again only from the mathematics in it. Kant remarks very correctly: The pure application of mathematics to inner nature stands to that in the outer as the doctrine of the straight line to the whole of geometry, and yet it is precisely this little of mathematics that still makes theory possible internally. Every inner activity has a determinate degree, according to which it can be stronger or weaker; this gives the difference of the obscure, the clear, and the distinct in our inner life, and through it alone are all explanations made in a theory of reason. Hence the gradual re-observation through inner sense and reflection, and through this

[p. 300]

all explicable gradations in representing, cognizing, desiring, and willing.

This dependence of all explanation on mathematics, and the inexplicability of all qualities, would long since have been noted more determinately and applied without contradiction, if it were possible for us even to grasp pure fact by itself without at once mingling it with the philosophical and mathematical in cognition. For example, it is astronomical pure fact that our earth belongs precisely to the planetary system of this sun, where at a determinate time, at precisely this distance and position, precisely these planets are ranged alongside it; but here we can never hold the fact fast for itself, for every single thing stands at once under the mathematical condition of time, so that with each determination of it a whole history through all time is demanded at once; every single thing stands at once under the mathematical condition of space, so that with each determination of it an interaction through all space is demanded at once. Here the purely factual element of cognition seems to vanish for us, in that we explain each fact from an earlier one, and now overlook that we nonetheless move the properly historical back into the past just as unaltered and unexplained as we first grasped it in the present, so that one finally conceived the idea of letting the history of the world grow out of chaos, as the historical zero, through mere mathematics and philosophy.

In our cognition no whole is possible as purely historical through the mere composition of the parts, nor any part as purely philosophical only through the idea of the whole according to the rule: *Totum parte prius esse necesse est* [it is necessary that the whole be prior to the part]; but every whole subsists only under the mathematical

[p. 301]

form through the interaction of the parts, that is, through the reciprocal dependence of the one on the other.

#### §. 73.

Against these limitations of all theory and all explaining there stands now the universal rationalistic prejudice of unity, just as against the limitation of the grounding of our cognitions there stands the empirical prejudice of intuition. More or less distinctly we find everywhere, with regard to the whole task of speculation, the prejudice which expresses itself in some as: Either everything must let itself be explained, or nothing is explained; whereupon it is held to be a weakness of human reason if we stop anywhere at inexplicable beginnings, e.g., at fundamental powers of matter. In others, by contrast, it runs: the highest task of science is: to derive everything from *One* highest ground of explanation, or, if someone had anything to object to the word ground of explanation, at least: to derive everything from One highest principle.

The first of these formulas trusts reason too little, the other too much. The watchword of naturalism: everything must let itself be explained, is correct only as an analytic proposition saying nothing, namely: everything explicable must let itself be explained. In its intention, however, there lies at its basis the entirely correct assertion: we can answer all theoretical tasks put to our reason satisfactorily; and the opposite assertion, whoever does not explain everything has explained nothing, is in general unfair. The inexplicable is of three kinds. First, the inexplicable that requires no explanation, because it is itself the beginning of explanation. This is

[p. 302]

mostly misjudged. Only the consequence can be explained from its ground; but of that which is only ground and not consequence, there can be no talk of explaining at all. For the principles in science, therefore, there can be no talk of explanation, because they are sufficient unto themselves; it is not a defect in physics that we cannot explain the fundamental powers of matter, but it is a sign of completeness in science that we have penetrated to independent supreme grounds of explanation.

Second, the inexplicable whose explanation would indeed be possible for us, only not for the present state of science, e.g., explanation of the supreme physiological laws of the organism from the most universal laws of nature. Here the reproach strikes not theoretical reason in general, but only the deficient experience of the individual.

Third, the inexplicable in which explanation might indeed be thought of, but where explanation is altogether impossible for our reason. E.g., explanation of the relation of the deity to the world, or of the intelligible order of the world to the world of sense. But here too the theoretical interest of reason can be satisfied in this: that one at least ceases to ask, in that one sees how and why all positive answers become impossible for us here.

Further, the second formula: to derive everything from one highest principle, is the basic demand of all rationalistic philosophy, which finds approval with the unprepared easily because reason really demands unity for every cognition. In fact, however, it is the faulty theoretical task arising from the confusion

[p. 303]

of the categorical system of philosophical sciences with system in general, in which one demands of the philosophical law, against the nature of our mind, that it give itself the case of its application. The following exposition will make the judgment of this controversy easier.

We have already shown earlier (§. 63) that objective validity or necessity of cognition for us must still be distinguished from subjective universal validity, or apodicticity. Every truth demands necessity of objective validity, but in purely historical cognitions this is not given as subjective universal validity; rather it remains contingent for every reason whether it has the single historical cognition or not; but if it is there, then it receives its necessity through the original subordination under the apodictic forms.

Before reflection, then, the necessity of historical cognition is indeed determined through a relation to the philosophically or mathematically apodictic, but it does not on that account itself become apodictic; rather the historical cognitions are only ranged alongside one another, under the apodictic form, as parts in a whole. The apodictic in our cognition is by itself only empty universal form, and the manifold of the content is first added through the single historical cognition. Genuine historical cognition rests just as much on the independent beginnings of its own conjunctive system as apodictic cognition on its. The particular stands, to be sure, always under the condition of the universal, but can never be completely cognized from the universal.

[p. 304]

Here the necessity of historical cognition is often confounded with apodicticity, first because it is a consequence of the latter, and then also in that probability and historical certainty are confounded in science. But probability belongs in none of our three systems; it has nothing to do with the idea of a complete systematic form, for it belongs only to the attempt to find one's way from the single historically given, according to mere grounds of cognition (*rationibus cognoscendi*), to the supreme grounds of explanation of an apodictic cognition; the system presupposes the completion of this labor already, and merely subordinates [the given] to the latter.

The subordinate certainty of the probable belongs, then, not properly to historical cognition but precisely to an incomplete apodictic one. Sciences which borrow their knowledge from experience and nevertheless lay claim to universal laws, such as chemistry, experimental physics, or empirical psychology, are indeed not sciences in the full meaning of the word, because they must content themselves with probabilities from incomplete inductions, with subordinate degrees of certainty. But genuine historical sciences, which only set forth facts, like history and natural description, have just as full certainty in their domain as philosophy and mathematics. The knowledge in them, when it is attained, differs from those not by degrees of probability but by a subjective relation to the understanding.

Historical certainty of the individual facts has, then, the same independence as any other apodictic one,

[p. 305]

and the task of grounding it still further through philosophy contradicts entirely the organization of our mind.

(The error of this false presumption shows itself in propositions like this: the part can be only through the whole; to the individual belongs for itself no being and essence—which are in clear contradiction with the basic law of our historical cognition, in that for us precisely every whole subsists only through its parts. Propositions of this kind, however, are used quite unreservedly, e.g., recently in Fichte and Schelling, because their philosophical language constantly confounds formulas of comparison of universal concepts with judgments, and thus loses the form of the subject in judgment (§. 45), and with this precisely the true determination of the individual through the universal.)

Further, the principles of philosophy that require deduction determine chiefly the unity, combination, and necessity in our representations, as we shall soon see more closely. The demand for this deduction has therefore been confounded with a derivation of all our knowledge from *one* supreme logical beginning. Since Reinhold began to have something of his own in philosophy, the old prejudice of unity expressed itself more determinately thus: it is the chief task of all philosophy to trace all our knowledge back to one supreme principle, and to develop the whole content of our knowledge again from this supreme one point. As in Chinese fireworks many-colored baskets of fruit and bouquets of flowers develop from a single-colored shining star, and green tendrils run from basket to basket, so here too from the unity of an immediately certain thing the whole fullness of life in our experience was to unfold. But we easily see that this whole was an absurd demand. The higher a

[p. 306]

principle stands, the more universal it is, but the more universal it is, the emptier and more devoid of content. The highest principle will have almost no content any more; nothing can be developed from it; it is precisely the simple, incapable of all development; one can only subordinate to it the material given from elsewhere. Every principle is the educt of an abstraction, and the higher we ascend with our abstraction, the more content we lose, the emptier the forms we retain. Whoever, then, wants to unfold all wisdom from one supreme principle harbors the shell of a blown-out egg in the incubator of his speculation, and if a life should seem to stir in it, it could be nothing but the straw of his fantasy that had caught fire, with which he wanted to warm the dear shell carefully.

Only from confusion and ignorance of the logical forms could the idea form itself of developing a science from a supreme principle; we obtain the content and the manifold not in the unity and universality of the principle, but alongside this through experience; we cannot derive the content from the principle, but can only put it together and order it under the principle. With all systematizing we can come no higher than the coordination of all philosophical and mathematical principles and of all infinitely many single historical data.

What, then, determines the unity of a science? Its principle, to be sure! But principle is so ambiguous a word that, for the decision of all dispute over our question, we shall do best to enumerate side by side the different meanings of the word with their claims.

[p. 307]

1) Principle means more than basic principle: already every most universal thing in a science, the mere concept of the object of a science. The concept of the coat of arms is the principle of heraldry, the concept of nature the principle of physics. The worth and content of a science lies only in its immediately certain propositions, or in the intuition that underlies it; the fewer basic principles it has, the poorer it will be; with one basic principle alone it can begin nothing at all, for from this no proof is possible at all, because for every inference we need at least two premises. A supreme basic principle can therefore never suffice to develop a science from it.

2) According to the strictest logical meaning the principles of a science are the beginnings of the system, the supreme grounds of explanation of its theory, the most universal basic principles and concepts from which it proceeds, e.g., for physics the supreme philosophical and mathematical basic principles and basic concepts of the philosophy of nature.

3) But in most sciences we cannot properly begin with this most universal, since it is precisely the hardest and least known. In such sciences the beginnings of evidence too can then be called principles; thus experiments and observations are the principles of physics.

4) The methodical principle of a science is the rule for the understanding according to which it arrives at the science, e.g., for physics the rule of the observation of nature.

5) In all these logical meanings the principle is now always only that with which the science begins, not that from which it springs; it is the beginning

[p. 308]

but not the source of truth, and in itself a very empty logical thing. Every false demand arises here through confounding all these meanings with two others, which to be sure pose the more significant task, but do not give the rule for solving it.

The constitutive principle of a science is the immediate cognition of which we wish to become conscious again through the science. This is, e.g., for philosophy the first immediate cognition in reason, of which we become conscious again only mediately in its system. This principle is easiest to show in pure mathematics. The logical principle of geometry lies in its axioms, postulates, and definitions, the constitutive, however, in the intuition of infinite space, whose laws we here want only to utter again. According to this meaning we are indeed to develop the science from its principle, but this principle is not the *one* germ from which the system unfolds as a completed plant with branches, leaves, and flowers, but only the original drawing of which we are to take a copy, if we have perhaps already learned drawing elsewhere.

6) If we finally seek the principle which is to be the producer of knowledge itself, we shall also be able to name this easily. It is reason as faculty of cognition, for cognition is only its activity. To trace science back to its last and supreme principle, therefore, means at bottom nothing more than to derive it from the essence of reason and to explain anthropologically how it is precisely what it is.

That, then, is also what has always been wanted with all speculation, but one has, by directing the eye

[p. 309]

always only at the object, through a universal amphibology of concepts, confounded this subjective source of all cognition with the source of all reality, and has thus arrived at the demand for a principle as a supreme ground of explanation, in which all being of things is to lie, which itself would be the One and eternally resting, but would comprise and include in itself all motion and all becoming. Such an idea arises only by analogy with an optical illusion, in that the subjective unification of all my cognition in the unity of my reason is confounded in an inadmissible way with the objective unification of all reality in one world-whole, i.e., analytic and synthetic unity in our cognition.

[p. 310]

### Fifth Section.

### The Development of Reflection.

#### a) Organization of the Faculty of Reflection.

#### §. 74.

The common distinction of the lower and higher faculty of cognition separates only that which we find immediately in ourselves through inner sense from that which we first perceive in ourselves through reflection. The original self-activity of reason in cognizing is the riddle of the ordinary psychology, of which there is in fact never really any talk, because one always confounds only the voluntariness of reflection with it. In place of this distinction (§. 12) we have set the threefold division: all representations are either involuntary intuitions through affection and sensation, or voluntary; the voluntary, however, are again either fiction of the imagination, whose laws lie in the idea of beauty, or thinking of the understanding, whose law lies in the idea of truth.

The faculty of representation would consist, then, in general of sensible faculty of intuition, imagination, and understanding, the last words being taken here in a very composite meaning, but one of the most customary

[p. 311]

in common life. Theory will here say, more determinately, faculty of fiction of intuitive presentation, and faculty of thought of reasoning.

If we now ask, since these faculties are so very composite, for a theory of the faculties of cognition after their simplest elements, the first important remark is the following. By the faculty of thought we understand, first, the faculty of reflection, the faculty of artificial self-observation, the faculty of the representation of the particular through the universal, according to Kant the faculty of logical thinking; but then also the self-activity of reason, the faculty of unity, combination, and necessity. Both further consist of understanding, power of judgment, and reason. But if the question here is how one understanding or power of cognition differs from another, is nobler or less noble, duller or cleverer, all these differences lie only in the faculty of reflection, for the self-activity of reason is a basic form for which there are no degrees, which must be the same in every power of cognition. The development of the faculty of thought concerns, then, also only the cultivation of reflection, and for the organization of the higher faculty of cognition we ask here only either after poetic presentation or after reflection.

These two are the result of the composition of all the elements of cognizing which we have investigated so far. The required elements of cognizing were, however, 1) lively apprehension of intuition for sense in general, 2) firm retention in memory, 3) acuteness of inner sense, 4) liveliness and energy of the inner play of representations for association,

[p. 312]

abstraction, and combination, 5) mastery of the will over representations in general. If one of these is to be raised as the higher faculty above the lower, it is the last, the mastery of the will in our inner life, and with that our first division of the course of thought into the memory-bound and the logical is justified, although of the latter we investigate more closely only thinking and not fiction, because fiction contains no new elements for the theory of reason. It is the mastery of the will over representations that determines the differences of degree between animal representing and human reason; it is this that immediately distinguishes the most thoughtless Pescherais or Carib from the most cultivated, most spirited European, the most stupid understanding from genius. The other advantages come to its aid only mediately.

The formerly usual claim of the psychologists, that strength of the lower power of representation belongs to fiction, strength of the higher to thinking, is therefore wholly false. Both here call upon the highest power, that of the will, as soon as there is any talk, however remotely, of art and purposiveness in thinking or fiction; they apply this same highest power only in different directions. But in what are we now to find theoretically grounded the difference most important for the philosophical critique of taste, between intuitive presentation through fiction and reflected presentation in reasoning? This difference, which so decisively throws all products of the mind apart into two classes whose production and effect follow wholly opposite rules. I say: this difference lies in the *figurative* and *schematic* use of the abstracting imagination.

[p. 313]

We found (§. 59) that all thinking and fiction depends on the possibility of problematic representations, but that the latter arise in our mind only through abstraction. This abstraction had an immediate and a mediate use. The immediate use, however, had two gradations, that of the image and that of the schema. The image is intuition of the imagination without presence of the object, the schema, on the other hand, was that (according to §. 44 and §. 60) through which alone concepts can be thought. Images we combine into intuitive presentations, to whose form beauty lays claim; schemata, on the other hand, we combine into judgments, whose law is truth.

#### §. 75.

Commonly one divides the faculty of reflection into logical understanding as the faculty of concepts, logical power of judgment as the faculty of judgments, and logical reason as the faculty of inferences; more generally the same division runs: the understanding thinks the universal, the power of judgment subordinates the particular to the universal, reason determines the particular through the universal, it cognizes from principles. However emptily logical this division may seem, it nonetheless characterizes itself very well in life: the understanding makes learned, the power of judgment clever, reason cultivated.

The weakness of this logical understanding is ignorance, a fault that can be remedied, for the understanding as the faculty of rules is precisely that which learns; rules have to be learned wherever one is to find them; the power of judgment, on the other hand, which determines the case under the rule, cannot be taught but only exercised; its strength

[p. 314]

is experiencedness. Its natural weakness is not ignorance but stupidity, which cannot be removed through cultivation; natural strength of the power of judgment is rather given talent. Exercised strength of the power of judgment makes clever, unexercisedness narrow-minded, or that which one calls limited understanding.

To reason in the faculty of reflection, on the other hand, we assign the cultivation of the mind. For cultivation it is not enough to be learned and clever; we demand in it, moreover, the reference of all powers to the highest ends of life. The true property of reason here is only the higher disinterested interest in the free beauty of life, which we characterize through the word idea. Thus for it too development takes place; it is not much without cultivation, and that which we call cultivation in the more eminent sense is precisely this cultivation of reason. Its strength and weakness are distinguished by a noble and a common cast of thought. It may seem striking that we ascribe such important moments merely to the faculty of reflection, but we live our life ourselves only in that we apprehend and repeat it through reflection.

Why then this cultivation belongs precisely to *reason* in reflection will become clear thus. Reason is the faculty of principles; this shows itself in the ordinary mechanism of thinking not at all in peculiar activity, for if here the premises are given through understanding and power of judgment, the inference makes itself of its own accord. The peculiar postulate of reason is only the principle itself, which expresses itself first in scientificity, but finds the proper sphere of its application through the ideas, whether these be truth, beauty, or goodness. In all experience we find

[p. 315]

rule and universal only through the particular; the most peculiar domain of cognition from the universal is that where, beyond all the empirical, we hold fast the rule and the principle for themselves, where the rule becomes the first thing for us, and this is the case most clearly in the application of practical ideas, in the demands of the ought.

#### §. 76.

We must here direct our attention especially to the power of judgment, for this is for cognition what is properly active and enlivening, in that it brings the particular to the universal. The understanding possesses only the rules which the power of judgment has supplied to it, and reason gives the conclusion necessarily as soon as the power of judgment has posited the minor premise. It first brings the material of sensibility to the unity of the understanding, and determines both reciprocally against one another. In the activities of the power of judgment there stand opposite one another *subsumption* and *reflection*; *feeling* and *inferring*; *acumen* and *wit*.

The activities of reflection proceed from the power of judgment, which cognizes the particular under the universal. Here the universal is now either already given through the understanding, or it is first sought for the understanding. If the rule is given, the power of judgment needs only to subordinate to it in the inference, it is only subsuming faculty; if, however, the rule is first sought, it becomes the reflecting faculty, through which we properly first produce distinctness and science in our cognition. This difference becomes very important; subsumption is that which, as dead understanding

[p. 316]

often stands in such ill repute, for it is wholly subject to the understanding, without a life of its own; it is the dead tool of dogmatism, which always demands first a given principle under which it can make its subordinations. The reflecting power of judgment, on the other hand, one does the honor of confusing it now with reason, now with intuition; it is the faculty of free investigation, which properly brings science into our cognition.

Secondly, in inferring too the power of judgment is the properly active faculty, for what is decisive here is the subordination of the minor premise under the rule that belongs to it; yet it shows its activity in this only ever mediately, with the help of the understanding. Besides inference, however, there also belongs to it an immediate activity, which we call feeling.
