The fault that is commonly called pedantry is nothing but troubling oneself with the formalities of inference where feeling has already decided.

Finally, acumen is the fine faculty of distinguishing, wit the fine faculty of comparing. Jean Paul should have censured these or similar explanations not on account of their incorrectness but only on account of their emptiness, which, to be sure, they share with all merely logical definitions. The element of acumen is earnestness, that of wit is jest; acumen demands more strength of the power of judgment, wit only agility of it. Even in conversation acumen stands the test longer; here the *fine* belongs to it, as the *witty* does to wit. Whence now this difference? Comparison is a mere *play of association*, fine distinguishing on the other hand an *affair of the will* in representing.

[p. 317]

In science wit gives the mere combination, which without the rigor of acumen has little worth. The significant combinations are usually, when the material is known, e.g. in the natural sciences, so easy to make that little worth is placed on them; the brilliantly witty, by contrast, is mostly set up merely to dazzle, and does not hold, since it is indeed easy to make superficial similarities without principle seem so for a moment, but to discover and pursue more deeply reaching similarities demands too much effort and more expenditure of acumen than suits the witty and can serve mere entertainment. The application of this remark makes itself felt now strongly and easily, with regard to the treatment of the philosophy of nature.

#### §. 77.

If we wish to test the articulation given here of the so-called higher or voluntary faculty of representation on an example from experience, this can best be carried through on the various forms of genius, or of original, distinguished power, that occur. Here we distinguish the aesthetic genius of great poets from the logical genius of great thinkers. The thinkers, however, we divide into theoretical geniuses as scientific thinkers, who are in turn either great philosophers or mathematicians, and into practical geniuses of life, of application, who are technical artists or great men of affairs, political geniuses. The distinction of thinking and fiction was also the first in our theory; the power of judgment, however, as the activity of the faculty of reflection, is the voluntarily guided schematizing

[p. 318]

imagination. The first difference in its use is the formation of universal concepts and rules, and the application of the rule to the single case; thus stand philosophers and politicians, mathematicians and technicians. Further, the first elements of the schematizing imagination itself were association or abstraction of the reproductive, and combination of the productive imagination; this difference repeats itself here twice, in the relation of the philosopher and the mathematician, and then in the relation of the politician and the technician.

(Against this assertion of the one-sidedness and single-powered character of genius Jean Paul, for example, asserts the many-powered character of everything genial. What is true in this is at first only that, to be a genius at all, (if one sets aside so instinct-like a one-sidedness as Mozart's musical genius,) strength of all the powers of mind is indeed required; but the actual emergence of genius always requires, out of the strength of the whole, one determinately predominant single power. The Kantian theory: just as the mere regularity of all the features extinguishes every expression of character, so too the emergence of any genius requires a one-sided direction of power, since the uniform strength of all the powers neutralizes itself in apathy, is grounded in the fundamental laws of the arousal of our mental activity. It is a quite different thing when a poet or historian, after days of reflection, vividly portrays individual situations from the life of a statesman, than when the latter, in the rapid flight of history, himself lives this whole life. If Jean Paul will not separate the genius of the poet and of the philosopher, this is, against Kant, only a dispute over words. Plato became a philosopher because he was not fit for a poet, and

[p. 319]

poems by Aristotle or Kant we shall hardly be eager to read. The misunderstanding of those who speak with Jean Paul consists in this, that by genius they understand not the original self-activity of the power of mind but the ideal direction of this power. Then it is indeed true: there are very many kinds of genius, but only one idea. A philosophical investigation may be guided by the interest of truth or of the good, or a poem may pay homage to the law of ideal beauty; yet underlying all this is only the unity of the highest idea, which expresses itself philosophically or poetically only under different forms.)

#### b) Speculation and Induction.

#### §. 78.

The actual development of reflection, which is to bring complete logical distinctness to our cognitions, sets the scientific use of the understanding over against the common use of the understanding. In the preceding treatise we exhibited, in the formal perfection of cognition, the logical ideal toward which we aim in this business. Our whole cognition is to be ordered, in the systems of philosophical, mathematical and historical science, in subordination and coordination. This, however, is only an idea to which we can approach gradually. How do we actually give our cognition these forms? From what has gone before, the answer is determined: All our cognizing begins in time with single sensible perception; what we are supposed to find further in ourselves, of this reflection will become aware only with the help of the abstraction of universal apodictic

[p. 320]

forms (§. 63.). We seek here, then, always the universal to be added to the given particular, which, as we just found, is the business of the reflecting power of judgment. In doing so this power of judgment observes two kinds of procedure, the one is *speculation*, the other *induction*. For the universal is either already actually given in immediate cognition as underlying it, and the point is only to exhibit it out of this for reflection, this is the case of speculation; or only single cases of historical cognition are given, and one first seeks the universal to add to them, this is the case of induction.

Through speculation we find the universal laws of pure philosophy and pure mathematics in our mind; through induction we seek, from given single perceptions, first to divine the universal law under which they are to be ordered.

The logical ideal of the perfection of our cognition, where in theory everything is finally subordinated to its highest grounds of explanation, and all historical fact stands under the apodictic law of mathematics and philosophy, demands a progress throughout from the universal to the particular, the *progressive advance of the system*, or cognition from principles. This would be the firmly established result of all scientific investigations, which at most we may flatter ourselves to have attained in some parts of mathematics. In this we needed only the subsuming use of the power of judgment; but in order first to arrive at this result, an opposite *regressive course of investigation* is required, which belongs to the reflecting power of judgment, and whose universal

[p. 321]

character is progress from the particular to the universal, reduction of cognition to its principles. In this latter alone, without distinction, lies the life of science; the progressive advance is only a dead result, for all our knowledge always unfolds only through the single, sensibly aroused case. This regressive procedure for science then has again the two forms, speculation and induction. Speculation, which only *exhibits* the universal standing above the given particular through abstraction and analysis, and induction, which seeks to *prove* its universal from the particular through combination and comparison.

#### On Speculation.

#### §. 79.

Speculation, or the speculative use of the understanding, as the supreme demand of the logical distinctness of our cognition, is opposed to the common use of the understanding by the formula: the common use of the understanding applies concepts *in concreto*, speculation applies them *in abstracto*. Single arithmetical or geometrical laws concerning magnitude; philosophical concepts such as cause, alteration, right and wrong, occur to us daily in thinking, but always only in such a way that we at once bring them into application for the judging of the single case; speculative science, on the other hand, in mathematics and philosophy, combines these abstractions in general. However often we presuppose in life the continuity of single magnitudes, the law of continuity in general is nevertheless only an object of speculation. Just so, however often we infer from alterations to causes in the single case,

[p. 322]

speculation nevertheless investigates only the combination of both concepts in general.

This speculation is the hardest business in thinking, because it is furthest removed from the evidence of aesthetic distinctness, for here reflection is left wholly to itself, it has the least help from inner sense, it is the driest business in thinking, in that together with the ease it loses the liveliness of the aesthetically distinct. Hence it is little liked by dilettantes, and even the masters seek to avoid it as far as possible. Only in mathematics has it so far maintained its right with security; philosophers, on the other hand, often seek to circumvent it by poetic or at least pictorial presentation, by a lofty, affected language and other aids of merely aesthetic distinctness; but whoever does not wish to play hide-and-seek with his thoughts, for himself or for others, will need a strict speculation in philosophy just as much as in mathematics. This follows already from mere logic. The common use of the understanding never raises itself by itself to truly universal judgments, for these were those in which both the subject and the predicate were a complete abstraction, where we therefore combine concepts *in abstracto*. They are the property of speculation. Now we showed earlier that universal judgments are properly alone complete judgments, every cognition therefore needs speculation as soon as it depends on judgment. Hence the claims of speculation upon all philosophy, and of philosophy upon every science that is not pure mathematics or mere historical enumeration. The most important domain of speculation, however, is precisely that which in philosophy we commonly oppose to it, the domain of ideas or of the

[p. 323]

practical. For the idea is nothing other than the concept generated wholly out of reflection and valid only through it, which raises itself above the obscure feeling of common consciousness only through speculation. The center of our mind is an infinite faith and an eternal love. Through this pure faith and this pure love alone does everything living enter the world before our eyes. In it, in our innermost being, is the sole source of all life. From here there announces itself to the common understanding, in the obscure feeling of the appraisal of the worth of virtue, in the obscure feeling of delight in the beautiful and sublime, and finally in the obscure feeling of the loftiness of religion, the eternally abiding alone. The commonest faith and the most refined speculation are equal here, when it is a matter of grasping the ideal of the highest good in the union of the purest love and the purest respect in the feeling of adoration, and likewise with every other object of religion. But there is a point where the idea of the eternal, enlivened by that faith and that love, steps out of the mere circle of feeling into the comprehensible; where the eternal announces itself not only in the obscure form of intimation but as a law for action of the most determinate conviction. There where ethics and politics separate themselves from the feeling of religion and announce to us in more determinate forms the law of the eternal, or where the feeling for the beautiful and sublime submits in more determinate forms to the laws of taste, there are, beyond the obscure feeling of the common understanding, determinate concepts, which speculation alone governs. Only for the speculatively educated judgment does the obscure feeling of the moral worth of the action resolve itself into clear concepts of the holy law of eternal right

[p. 324]

and into determinate ideas of how pure love and pure respect shape themselves into the laws of virtue. Where the fairer figures of the higher life confront us in history or in the representations of art, they seize the feeling and sweep it along; but whoever, guided only by this feeling, plunges into the press of full life, his being, lost to unknown figures, will tastelessly deform itself. The sole dominion of feeling begets an energyless pride, which pleases only itself, repels others from itself through its pretensions, or disgusts them through its tastelessness. To the cultivated belongs the composed, calmer course of a firm conviction, which passes beyond feeling and expresses itself in determinate concepts; and these very determinate concepts can be obtained only through speculative cultivation. Speculation here separates itself from common consciousness, but not in order to open to reason new domains of the supersensible, but solely in order to come to an understanding with itself in the long-acquired field of experience.

#### §. 80.

The essence of speculation has seldom been rightly grasped, through confusion of the subsuming power of judgment with the reflecting. The latter alone counts here, and indeed it has nothing at all to do here with defining and proving. This essence of speculation consists in this, that ordinary cognition is led back by analysis to its first and most universal apodictic beginnings, of which one demonstrates that in every single application they are in fact already presupposed in general as true, whereby one prepares these most universal

[p. 325]

principles for deduction. We lift out of cognition the law in its universality, which we use daily in the single application. We learn nothing new through speculation, but only make clear to ourselves what we already know; we prove nothing through speculation, but only make clear to ourselves from what we properly are accustomed commonly to draw all our proofs. If, e.g., someone asserts without contradiction that a vessel, after the artist has cast it, must weigh just as much as the raw metal weighed before the artist gave it the form: then speculation shows that he unconsciously already presupposes the correctness of the metaphysical principle of the persistence of substance, and derives his single judgment only from this. For only because he regards the mass of the metal as substance, and the concepts of substance and persistence as necessarily connected, does he judge that the weight of this determinate mass is unchangeable. Likewise, if someone declares a single stone heavy because it falls, he thereby already presupposes the necessary connection of the concepts, alteration and effect, according to the law of causality.

Only when speculation is completed are we in a position to set up the system of science dogmatically, in the subordination of the particular under its principles through definition and proof, which is only the dead business of subsumption.

Like the apodictic laws, speculation too is either mathematical or philosophical. Mathematical speculation is mathematical invention, it belongs to the mathematical genius, and can be

[p. 326]

learned only in minor matters; the discovery of wholly new mathematical methods demands original self-activity, which is a matter of talent and not of the school. Ready-made, invented mathematics, however, can be taught and learned easily and systematically through the merely subsuming power of judgment, without the pupil himself taking part in the speculation, for the most universal beginnings here are always demonstrable, immediately evident propositions, which can be seen for themselves, and from which the taught subsumption can then help itself further.

Mathematical invention is an open field, whose boundaries will hardly be marked out soon; philosophical speculation too is originally invention. Here, however, invention on the large scale will probably soon be concluded, whereas for the individual learner it must repeat itself every time. The rules of philosophical speculation are the rules of the critical method. The most universal, which is here exhibited as principle, is the hardest, the least evident and yet indemonstrable. Every pupil here, therefore, who wishes to attain insight of his own, must first have made for himself the regressions of speculation from common consciousness to the higher abstractions before he can penetrate to the understanding of the system. The essence of philosophical speculation has mostly been misunderstood, partly because it was confused with induction, partly because it does not immediately show a completed system. Most philosophers hold it wrong to communicate their speculation publicly; they think it fitting only to submit the completed system to public examination. But thereby the correct standpoint of judging is wholly shifted. Evidence is lacking to the beginnings

[p. 327]

of a philosophical system unavoidably, because they are the highest abstractions; the public can therefore take as the standard of judgment only either the handicraft-like usefulness of the results for theology, politics or medicine, or the so-called consistency, by which one often hears the ridiculous praise handed out: the man asserts, to be sure, the greatest absurdities, but he nevertheless remains consistent with himself.

The dogmatic activity of subsumption under the universal principles has very little worth for philosophy; it is not only, as in mathematics, a mere result for the first invention of the science, but even for the re-invention by every self-thinking pupil. One cannot here make ready-made philosophy, but only philosophizing, the object of a thinking instruction; ready-made philosophy can be learned only historically with the memory but not philosophically with the self-active power of judgment.

(I find this distinction of speculation and induction adequately appreciated in no logic, though it is after all the most important in all scientific self-activity. Speculation leads to philosophical and mathematical inventions, induction is only an aid for the subordination of single perceptions under universal laws. The ground of this oversight lies in this, that speculation was confused with the subsuming activity of system-making.)

#### On Probability.

#### §. 81.

The less willing resolute thinkers often are to heed the half-true and the probable, the more easily they themselves fall

[p. 328]

into error. If we could indeed follow immediately the rule of transcendental truth, where only agreement with the object would give the law, then every pronouncement would have to be, by determinate disjunction, either true or false. But we are at first always bound only to empirical truth, the agreement of self-observation with the immediately given cognition, and there is probability through limits and graduation of observation, half-truth through ambiguity of words.

Holding-to-be-true and holding-to-be-false are the two modes of the assertion of a judgment. Assertion, or positing, is the consciousness that I have a cognition; it is the proper act of the inner faculty of re-observation; to it belongs empirical truth. We hold a cognition to be true when we are conscious of having it, to be false when we are conscious of having its opposite. The assertion is correct if it agrees with the immediate cognition, error if it contradicts this. *All these determinations have thus at first nothing to do with the object, they belong only to the re-observing reflection.* (It is one of the chief faults in Fichte's speculation that he wanted to make positing the fundamental activity of cognizing.)

Every assertion was assertoric or apodictic; but we arrive at the consciousness of the apodictic only through the problematic. Every judgment can be regarded only as something merely assigned, for which sufficient grounds must be found, (through proof, demonstration or deduction) if it is to count as true. Thereby a comparison of merely assigned judgments with their grounds of determination

[p. 329]

takes place, whereby holding-to-be-true acquires, in respect of them, different degrees of certainty. Holding-to-be-true from sufficient grounds is *certainty*, every other is *uncertainty*. Uncertainty through grounds and counter-grounds standing against one another is *doubt*. The lower degrees of certainty from more or less sufficient grounds are *probability*. This graduation of certainty cannot relate to immediate cognition itself, in which truth and falsity are strictly separated; it is only a matter of reflection. Probable, therefore, only judgments can be, and indeed provable judgments, for demonstration and deduction give complete certainty. Hence the important law: *every probability rests on an incomplete proof, i.e., on an inference.*

I find the theory of these inferences of probability again everywhere very deficient. Kant and many after him speak only of incomplete induction and analogy as kinds of inference of the power of judgment, in contrast to syllogisms. But with this only a part of the whole is considered, and this too not in the right relation. The right relation is as follows.

The complete syllogism requires the knowledge of a universal rule for the major premise, whereby the inference became possible as mere subsumption and obtained objective significance. But the universal we often know only incompletely; then reflection, according to merely subjective relations, applies the forms of syllogisms to incomplete rules, and thereby we obtain the inferences of probability.

[p. 330]

The rule was a universal judgment, e.g. All A are B; opposed to this stands the particular, Some A are B, in respect of which one represents the sphere of the subject as divided into two parts, and the judgment holds only in respect of the one. Here there now takes place a comparison of the one part of the sphere with the other according to its magnitude, and I infer according to probability, in that I use for the major premise the judgment holding of the greatest part of the sphere, Most A are B. E.g. Most A are B, C is A, therefore C will probably be B. Most Germans are close to 6 feet tall; if, therefore, I know nothing more definite of the height of a German, I shall represent him to myself as close to 6 feet tall. So we infer in all forms of syllogisms also according to probability.

This kind of inference, therefore, always presupposes a divided major premise. Two cases are then possible: in respect of the other part of the rule I either do not know at all determinately whether the remaining A are B or not, or I know determinately that the remaining A are not B. From the latter rules follow *mathematical inferences of probability*, from the former *philosophical* ones.

The mathematical determination of probability, as it is calculated in practical arithmetic, presupposes a survey of all the cases possible in respect of a judgment, and stands under the rule: *more probable is that which, in proportion to one case that it is otherwise, in many possible cases is so constituted as the judgment states.* If I am therefore called upon to judge here, I assume that which in the majority of cases would actually be. Calculation of probability is here an improper

[p. 331]

expression, not the uncertain but the certain is calculated, namely the division of the major premise. The uncertainty I add only in the single inference from this major premise, beyond the calculation, where for this reason the determination of the probable still always requires many cautions. If it is asked, e.g.: how probable is it that among my 9 cards at ombre I have both aces, the calculation says: in all 40 cards there lie 780 pairs, in 9 cards there lie 36 pairs; I ask, then, after one of 780 cases, of which I each time hold 36 in my hand. So far the matter is wholly certain, and so far goes the calculation. But if I wish to use this in the single case, e.g. for a wager, I shall still have many cautions to observe.

The calculation of the major premise can, however, itself also be more or less indeterminate; thereby mathematical probability acquires more resemblance to the philosophical. But both nevertheless remain wholly separate according to their mode of procedure. The mathematical presupposes as known that the rule does not hold, and guesses only at the majority of the cases; the philosophical, on the other hand, infers for the most part before all else from the multiplicity of cases to the unity and universality of the rule, and grounds its inference upon that.

In experience we often use both modes of inference mixed with one another, when we judge incompletely subordinated historical cognitions according to the rule of apodictic cognitions. So we infer, e.g., that something will happen because we find grounds upon which it often follows; we infer that something has happened because much agrees that would have to be a consequence of it. The purest case of philosophical probability

[p. 332]

is, however, that where we seek universal rules from perception. Instead of the complete inference from the allness of the cases to the unity of the rule, we infer here from the multiplicity of cases to the unity of the rule. Now we saw in logic that only the disjunctive inference through induction serves to make a complete inference from the particular to the universal. We make use here, therefore, chiefly of induction, in order to arrive through probability at universal rules and laws. Complete induction was precisely the inference from all cases under a universal to this universal, e.g. what I prove of right-angled, acute-angled and obtuse-angled triangles, I thereby prove of all triangles. Incomplete induction, on the other hand, appeals for its rule only to many cases under it, e.g. I prove that something holds of gold, silver and platinum as the best-known noble metals, and now presuppose that it holds of noble metals in general.

Beside this induction there stands then also incomplete analogy. Analogy we called the conjunctive syllogism, which infers: a thing stands under a universal rule because all the determinations of it belong to it, e.g., this animal is a bear, this plant a palm, because these and these characteristics belong to it. Incompletely we infer in just the same way: a thing stands under a universal rule because many determinations of it belong to it, e.g. the animal to which these fossil bones belonged was probably a kind of bear, because these bones are most similar to bears' bones; these fossil leaves probably belonged to a kind of palm, because they are similar to palm leaves.

[p. 333]

The inference, however, which is commonly called inference according to analogy is not quite so simple. It is in general the inference according to similar relations, and is compared with induction in the following way: induction infers from many cases to the unity of the rule, analogy infers from many cases to the remaining ones under the rule. I infer, e.g., according to induction: rotation on an axis has been observed in most planets, therefore they will probably all rotate on their axes; according to analogy, on the other hand: because this and that planet rotate on their axes, Pallas and Juno too will probably do so. If we look, however, to the ground of warrant, the latter mode of inference is composed of an induction and our first analogy, and *what properly infers in it is the induction, so that this becomes the dominant philosophical inference of probability.* For if I infer from many cases under a rule to the remaining ones, then only the unity of the rule itself combines the known cases with the unknown; I therefore always make first, e.g., the induction: this and that planet rotate on their axes, therefore rotation on an axis probably belongs to the law of planetary existence in general, and only then do I infer further according to our first analogy, consequently this determinate planet too will rotate on its axis.

#### On Knowledge, Opinion, and Faith.

#### §. 82.

Probabilities have in general only a small worth in science, although very often we cannot get beyond them. Properly we are warranted in judging only in respect

[p. 334]

of complete certainty, i.e., where we can *know*; for knowledge means holding-to-be-true with complete certainty. Every probable judgment ought to be only a provisional one, to guide us in the search for the certain. The holding-to-be-true of a provisional judgment is *opinion*. But in the case of most cognitions we can bring it only to opinions, so that even the surest holding-to-be-true of the individual, in comparison with the constitution of a cognition itself and with the holding-to-be-true of all others, can count only as the opinion of the individual.

In grounds that merely preponderate for or against an assertion there lies properly as yet no warrant at all for judgment; rather we ought then to postpone our judgment until we can bring it to complete certainty. In order, therefore, really to judge according to mere opinion, there must be added, besides the preponderance for or against, the requirement of an interest that I have in determining my judgment with regard to an object, because without it I would not judge at all from incomplete grounds. Such a holding-to-be-true through interest is that which is commonly called *faith*. We thus subordinate here to knowledge, as complete certainty, opinion and faith according to probability, according to a merely logical meaning of the words, which concerns only relations to *reflection*; but we must not confuse these verbal determinations with the distinction of knowledge, faith and intimation, which concerns the transcendental determination of *immediate cognition* itself, and for that reason can be developed only later. The difficulties of the Kantian and of many another theory of faith

[p. 335]

are easily resolved if one only dissolves the confusion of the two concepts, *assumption driven by an interest*, which belongs to reflection, and *conviction without intuition*, which constitutes the common concept of faith, and assigns to each its own proper place.

According to its logical meaning every holding-to-be-true from probability is more or less faith, according as the grounds which determine us to judgment in the single case are stronger or weaker. Therefore, when we are asked about an object on which we are conscious that we properly cannot judge at all, e.g. on changes of weather, if we are nevertheless called upon to judge, we give out our opinion as a faith, in that we judge *only for this reason*, because we had to answer the question.

This influence, belonging to faith, of the interest in a judgment upon judging itself is legitimate so long as the judgment is not taken for more than a matter of opinion, and is often indispensable. Here the interest drives me only to have an opinion about an object at all, without determining which opinion, e.g. in the case of a physician who in a doubtful case is compelled nevertheless to think a determinate illness for a patient; from this, however, another influence of interest must be wholly distinguished, where it mixes itself into the determining grounds for or against, and so often occasions the most obstinate errors, in that we believe many things more easily or with more difficulty only through inclination or fear. Such an influence of interest leads only to error, for in the fact that I wish a proposition might be true or false there can never lie a ground of determination

[p. 336]

which entitles to judgment. (Even the so-called moral faith of Kant rests only on a confusion of our logical concept discussed here with the pure faith of reason, a conviction without intuition.)

#### On Induction.

#### §. 83.

Nevertheless there is a case which seems to rest on this, namely in scientific holding-to-be-true from an interest of reason, where I assume that everything manifold in my experience, e.g. the multitude of different kinds of matter which present themselves in physics first to observation, nevertheless stands under a few universal laws, since reason always takes an interest in such a unification. The means of philosophical probability was induction from many cases to the validity of the rule in general. This requires, therefore, as it were a scientific faith, in order to come to application. If I infer from many cases to the unity of the rule, the inference does not hold immediately from the many cases to the remaining ones; for itself, without presupposing the rule, (e.g. in grammar, where I spell out a rule, say for word-endings, from single cases,) there is equal probability for or against their agreement with the rule. One could indeed say: since every new case is for or against the rule, it becomes ever more probable, the more cases I collect, that of the negative ones, however few they may be, one would surely be found.

[p. 337]

But even *one* case against the rule proves its untruth; it could therefore rather be asserted that, according to this way of reckoning, the probability for and against the rule is equal only when just one case still lies undecided. But in fact we do not apply induction at all in this way, e.g. in the natural sciences; rather, we guess at universal laws at once if only a few cases agree with them, a few experiments often suffice there to lead us further. For in the decision of the judgment something else is at work here—the speculative interest of reason in law and rule in general. It seems, then, as if an interest unlawfully determined our faith. But this is not the case. The voluntarily active reflection does indeed sketch out for itself, according to the interest of reason, in judging according to probability, maxims for the power of judgment, but the ground of the interest lies not in the will but in the relations of the cognitions themselves; it can therefore certainly serve as ground of determination of the judgment.

We make scientific use of induction where speculation is no longer in a position to state to us exactly the philosophical and mathematical laws as far as the subordination of the single experiences, in order to try whether we cannot conversely guess the superordinate rule from the subordinate cases. Here the true ground of warrant lies in this, that we already know in general: all historical cognition stands under apodictic laws and rules, which we are only not always in a position to state determinately enough for single cases. If we therefore order particular experiences according to the guidance

[p. 338]

of a scientific method under determinate *guiding maxims*, then from far more incomplete grounds we shall nevertheless infer with more probability than outside all systematic connection in a tumultuary procedure.

Very often, however, this maxim degenerates into an unlawful interest, through the craving to let nothing lie undecided and to want to explain everything, which does much harm both to sound judgment in life and to science. In matters of uncertain opinions the postponement of judgment is precisely one of the surest means of protecting oneself from error. Many, on the other hand, fall into the greatest embarrassment at the mere idea of having to postpone their judgment on an object; one often sees them, in common life, prefer to take refuge in the acceptance of the most groundless superstition, in order, as they think, to have some explanation at least, rather than calmly admit to themselves the uncertainty of the matter.

In science this snatching after explanation does the greatest harm; it draws away from observation, impatiently demands a premature survey of the whole, and entangles in arbitrary hypotheses, which soon lead so far that one no longer knows how to separate the certain from the uncertain, and substitutes the arbitrary explanation itself as fact. In natural science it succeeds only with few to free themselves from the infinite apparatus for explaining, so as before the explanation first to know at least what is to be explained.

[p. 339]

#### On Error.

#### §. 84.

Error is holding-to-be-true contrary to law. How, then, is contrariety to law possible in cognizing? In nature there may well be conflict of opposed powers, but no power can contradict its own law. We have therefore already remarked earlier that only through the influence of the will upon representing does error become possible, in that the will seeks to conform itself to the laws of cognition, which are alien to it. The senses do not err, nor does the immediate cognition of reason err, but only voluntary reflection. The will merely combines problematic representations in thinking, and seeks in judgment to hit upon the rule of cognition itself, as the law of truth; error is therefore possible for it in this, because it artificially prescribes to itself a law immediately alien to it.

For what follows we have no need here to go through all the heads of a logical doctrine of error; for speculation in general we need only the one important remark. *All difference between error and truth is only a matter of re-observing reflection, and not an immediate matter of cognition.* Neither the intuition that underlies demonstration, nor the immediate cognition that underlies deduction, can be erroneous; erroneous are only mediate judgments of the understanding. All error therefore rests on inferences, and consequently on inferences of probability. Entirely without ground

[p. 340]

the understanding cannot judge; the ground of an error is called *illusion*. Illusion consists, then, always in the incomplete premises of an inference of probability, which the power of judgment has unlawfully supplemented. (We can say: all error consists in this, that we falsely presuppose something as not present because we have not perceived it, namely the opposite of the supplementing of the divided major premise in the inference of probability.)

By restricting all error only to judging and to mediate imagination, we obtain a free field of the immediate cognition of our reason, in which we can let various kinds of conviction subsist side by side with equal validity, as knowledge, faith, and intimation. Error takes place only in mediate, reflected cognition; the whole dispute about truth and validity of cognition does not touch the inner essence of reason at all; in this there is nothing but truth under one form or another, of the finite or the eternal, of the ever-abiding of nature, or of the ever-changing of beauty.

The ground of all misunderstandings lies here again in this, that one confuses empirical and transcendental truth. Since one commonly believes one must demand objective grounding of judgments, one also refers the dispute between truth and error to this; in fact, however, it concerns only the empirical truth of reflection and its subjective grounding. This distinction is the sole means of extirpating skepticism

[p. 341]

from speculation. Skepticism always rests on the conceded premise that we are unable to cognize the essence of things as they are in themselves, and therefore condemns reason to an unavoidable doubt in speculative matters, in that it confuses the limitation of our reflection, and of empirical truth, *the possibility of error*, with the limitation of our immediate cognition and of our transcendental truth, i.e., with *the finite view of things*. Whoever sees that the disputing about truth belongs only to reflection will never hold his reason to be given up to uncertainty at all.

#### c) The Theory of Feeling.

#### §. 85.

Kant draws our attention to how important it is for speculation to separate properly the use of the words inner sensation and inner feeling, in order to part feeling from sense. He shows that if we want to sense the beautiful and the good just as we sense the agreeable, if we transform all feeling of pleasure and displeasure into sensation, we thereby already give up the principle of all practical philosophy and of philosophical aesthetics, since nothing but the empirical would remain as the foundation of the laws of the good and the beautiful. He has, however, touched thereby only one case; the domain of feeling extends further in our mind than to the judging of pleasure and displeasure; it is for speculation in general highly important to make its true essence clear.

[p. 342]

We often find something immediately true or false without fully having insight into it, without engaging in proof, without even being able to give exact account of why we find it so. This we ascribe to feeling. Accordingly we have a feeling for truth, which very often guides us in our judgments, but applies itself preeminently as feeling for beauty and moral feeling. When we judge the moral worth of an action or the beauty of an object, we appeal in this for the most part only to feeling; yet with the difference that, with regard to the worth of an action, we still concede that complete grounds for the justification of our judgment must be capable of being given, even if we should not now be in a position to develop them; whereas in judging beauty, e.g. of a work of art, we do concede that much can be said toward correcting the judgment, but in the end we demand the decisive pronouncement here only from feeling, since with all the concepts and proofs of the world we can force upon no one a judgment about beauty.

What, then, does this feeling consist in? What do we mean by it? The chief thing is to separate it properly from sense. It was the most harmful misunderstanding of English empiricism, especially of the opponents of Hume, who observed this aesthetic and moral feeling so closely that they always took it for a finer sense, for a modification of sensation, and the Germans, to whom translated wisdom is mostly more illuminating than their own, echoed them long afterwards, although we need almost only a development of our own linguistic usage in order to get the matter

[p. 343]

clear. Feeling we set over against inferring, if we make the comparison quite general. Inference contained the generation of a judgment mediately from others, and indeed in such a way that I am again conscious of the act of this mediate representation. Feeling, on the other hand, generates its judgments immediately. Feeling thus belongs to the very same faculty to which judging and inferring belong, only that here its activity expresses itself without mediation. Feeling we call the immediate self-activity of the faculty of reflection, i.e., as we have shown earlier, the immediate activity of the power of judgment. The faculty of feeling is therefore by no means sense and sensation, but voluntary reflection only in its immediate activity, opposed to mediated inference.

We can accordingly distinguish three kinds of feeling. The first kind rests only on the degree to which I am conscious, just now, of the grounds of a judgment, the second is the immediate activity of the subsuming, the third of the reflecting power of judgment.

When I am just now passing a judgment, I cannot always derive every judgment through distinctly thought chains of inference from higher judgments up to the principle, but there is some part of the chain of inference where I become immediately conscious now of certain premises and infer from these; often all the premises indeed coalesce in my mind, I do not become conscious of them singly, yet from the obscure representation of them we can nevertheless draw a correct conclusion, which is then called a pronouncement of feeling. To this belong,

[p. 344]

first, *moral feeling*, according to which conscience measures the worth of an action immediately, without engaging in a reckoning back through all the premises of its judgment. Belonging here, secondly, is what is called *practical tact*, which everyone needs so necessarily for his business; where someone who possesses sufficient strength of the power of judgment and joins practice with it knows how to judge, even in complicated cases, at first sight of the matter, and then readily decides more correctly than if he had, with much effort, reasoned around his theme, as e.g. a physician who after a few questions knows how to judge a patient’s condition exactly, a jurist who decides the most complicated legal case clearly after one survey, or a natural scientist who, in complicated experiments that he performs for the first time, already knows how to state the outcome in advance, in that he obscurely thinks of many analogies which he perhaps would not even be in a position to make clear to himself on the spot. Such a feeling must speak most determinately there, where in moral feeling all the determining grounds of the judgment belong to reason itself, so that they all co-operate in the determination of the judgment in feeling and its obscure representation; whereas if I wish to think the premises singly first in chains of inference, perhaps some can be forgotten, and an erroneous result thus emerges. But if feeling once deceives itself, then, since its activity does not fall within observation, the error is also far harder to find; thereby it becomes the secret workshop from which prejudices spread their consequences.

Secondly, even to the subsuming power of judgment must

[p. 345]

belong, for the subordination of the case under a given rule, an immediate activity. Only the understanding can be instructed, by being given universal rules. If a rule is now given, I may well give yet a new one that teaches how to proceed according to this, but in the end I must still proceed according to one immediately, i.e., apply the power of judgment without a mediating understanding. The power of judgment shows here an immediate activity, not properly in that it thinks the conclusion, but in that it places the minor premise under the rule, or in that it thinks simply the *Is* in the judgment.

Thirdly, the subsuming power of judgment nevertheless always presupposes a rule or concept that the understanding has given; the activity of the reflecting power, however, is wholly independent. This shows itself as feeling in every judgment that we take immediately from intuition, and in every basic philosophical judgment that we borrow from the cognizing spontaneity of reason, e.g. in the *I am* of self-consciousness. Preeminently, however, this feeling shows itself where the power of judgment judges according to a law that the understanding cannot at all express as a rule, where rather peculiar principles of the power of judgment are found. This is the case in our judgments about beauty, whose idea fits into no rule capable of being grasped according to concepts. *If, then, from the power of judgment by itself, independently of the understanding, cognitions of its own spring, their principle, though it cannot be given in intuition, can yet not be brought to rule and concept, but springs only from feeling without concept*

[p. 346]

*and yet with necessity.* This is the secret of the origin of beauty in our reason.

We say, then, that the faculty of feeling is the immediate self-activity of the power of judgment; with this, however, we come into conflict with the Kantian theory of the feelings accepted by many. We agree with him, to be sure, in that he separates feeling from sense and sensation, but we cannot, with him, restrict it merely to pleasure and displeasure. Had Kant noticed that in place of feeling of pleasure one can quite generally also say judging of purposiveness, this whole part of his anthropological theory would have turned out differently. His exposition of feeling in relation to sensation is quite one-sided. He says: Feeling is the wholly subjective in the representation, whereby the object is not cognized; sensation, on the other hand, is objective: the green color of the meadow belongs to sensation, its agreeableness to the eye to the feeling of pleasure. This exposition is properly correct only for pleasure in the agreeable; it cannot, however, be referred to feeling at all, but only to pleasure and displeasure, since feeling surely has very many another object besides pleasure. In Kiesewetter’s *Logic*, on the contrary, just conversely, following the Kantian theory, the feeling for truth itself is reduced to pleasure and displeasure, in that it is explained roughly thus: the pleasure in the harmonious agreement of our representations determines us to hold something to be true. This is, however,

[p. 347]

again one-sided; it hits neither the pronouncements of practical tact nor those of moral feeling. The most important thing here is the consequence for the theory of the feelings of pleasure in general. Kant assumes this feeling of pleasure as a peculiar original element, derivable from no other, in the organization of reason, and has found much approval in this; we, on the other hand, shall show that it is nothing but the power of judgment, which decides according to the rule of *worth*.

## Critique of Reason

by

#### Jacob Friedrich Fries.

#### Heidelberg,

#### Mohr and Zimmer,

1807.

[scan 413]

## Critique

of

## Cognizing Reason.

[scan 415]

## Third Book.

#### Investigation of the Logical Course of Thought according to Its Content.

[scan 417]

### Introduction.

#### 1) What Is Metaphysics?

#### §. 86.

The word metaphysics has gone somewhat out of fashion among many of our philosophers, with the assertion that there is no metaphysics. This assertion, however, rests only on a verbal dispute. If we determine the concept by the hopes of individual philosophers, e.g. of the Wolffian school, then there may indeed in many a way be no metaphysics; if, on the other hand, we look to the ultimate aim with its concept, then there is either no philosophy at all, or metaphysics too. We divide all philosophy, then, into logic, or formal philosophy, and metaphysics, or material philosophy. The forms of logic by themselves are altogether empty, for they belong only to the re-observing faculty, if there is not an object that is to be observed here; this is metaphysics. With this word, then, we designate the content of philosophical speculation in general. This coincides precisely with the theme of our present investigation

[p. 8]

We have observed hitherto our cognitions in sense intuitions, in their memory-bound course of thought, and finally in their logical course of thought, the course of thinking. In the logical course of thought we found that it shows immediately the phenomena of a faculty of reflection, through which, however, we sought to observe in ourselves only that which would otherwise remain hidden from inner sense. We determine further that the proper object of this observation, cognition, of which we can become conscious only in this artificial way, is *the philosophical in cognition*, which, if it were observed completely or grasped before reflection, would present *philosophy as science*. Of this philosophy we then came to know at once that empty, formal part, logic, because it sprang only from reflection itself, and contained the influence of the artificial re-observation on the cognitions, without giving observation an object. The content of the logical course of thought must therefore properly lie in what is newly observed in us through reflection; this we just now called metaphysics.

Sense intuition gives us the first content of the cognition of an outer and inner world; mathematical intuition brings into this material the first combination. The material combined by mathematical intuition in space and time is then raised through reflection to historical and mathematical science. Here, however, reflection and the logical course of thought add nothing to historical science except the co-ordination of the parts; all content lies in the sensible intuition of experience; likewise to mathematical science reflection adds nothing except coherence

[p. 9]

and arrangement, for the content lies always in intuition. But beyond these two systems there shows itself, for our consciousness, in reflection itself, still philosophical science; this has its content in certain principles and basic principles of which we would not be conscious at all without reflection. Whence, now, does reflection take this consciousness of the philosophical principles? How does it come to this peculiar content of the logical course of thought? The logical course of thought cannot give it to itself, for reflection is an empty faculty of re-observation; it must lie in original cognitions of reason, of which we cannot become conscious immediately, but only mediately through reflection. Our present task, then, is to come to know, through exact observation, the peculiar content of the logical course of thought, to see what philosophical principles are found in our inner experience, and how these spring in reason and its original immediate cognition.

The most important proposition for the more recent philosophy is that logical reason, as a faculty of reflection, is a mere faculty of repetition of cognitions which always already underlie it in reason, as the observed, as immediate cognition. We become conscious of our cognition with completeness only in propositions of reflection, but among these reflection can give itself only the empty logical analytic judgments, which for that very reason contain no extension of our cognitions, and the provable judgments which we derive through logical forms of inference from basic judgments otherwise already given.

[p. 10]

The synthetic basic judgments, on the other hand, contain properly the whole stock of our knowledge. Among them, those of historical and mathematical science rest on intuition through demonstration; in philosophical science they should be capable of being grounded only through deduction. Philosophical principles, which let themselves be neither proved nor demonstrated, are consequently the most difficult of all judgments; they are what is presupposed in all philosophical proofs, which never appears itself, but only in its consequent propositions, before common consciousness, since it cannot become intuition. We do indeed frequently use the consequent propositions of practical philosophy, in that we judge about duty and right, but the highest principles of faith in freedom and in the deity, from which these are proved, either do not occur at all in common consciousness, or are contested propositions. These only deducible principles are the final result of the most artificial abstractions; it already demands the most artificial reflection to become conscious of them even in isolation. We have here, then, two tasks for the critique of reason: first, from a survey of our cognition, to point out these principles of all philosophical assertions, and then, for those discovered, to carry out the deduction from a theory of reason.

What we seek here, then, is metaphysics, and we can state its concept thus: it is the science of the cognitions of which we become conscious 1) *only through reflection* 2) *in synthetic judgments*; it contains, then, *in a categorical system* provable judgments, which rest *on only deducible highest principles*. The first distinguishes it

[p. 11]

from historical and mathematical science, the second from logic; the remaining one is only a corollary of the first determination (according to §. 65. and 70.); the whole coincides exactly with Kant’s definition of a science of synthetic judgments *a priori* from mere concepts. Development from mere concepts means the same as apprehension only through reflection, and the *a priori*, or universality and necessity, will result from this as a consequence (§. 63.), because only sense intuition receives individual empirical determinations.

If one now asks: how can one find which metaphysics at all belongs to our reason, what the peculiar content of our logical course of thought is? we give the answer from Kant’s critique of reason: dogmatism is for the unprepared the more natural procedure in philosophizing, but we must exchange it for criticism.

All the disputing and wavering in the attempts to develop metaphysics has its ground in this, that in explaining and grounding our cognitions we are accustomed always to ask for objective grounds of transcendental truth, where in fact there is talk only of subjective grounds and rules of empirical truth.

The ordinary meaning of the question: how do you explain that, how do you prove that, how do you derive that? always goes to the demand to trace the essence of things back to its higher grounds, to its higher unity. In the philosophical, however, our cognitions of this highest unity, of the highest grounds of explanation, are precisely that which itself most needs grounding. All our physical explanations, e.g., run

[p. 12]

up in the end to highest philosophical premises of causality, or of some unity or other, but who guarantees us the validity of these? More obscure is the bond which makes all moral ideas dependent on the faith in freedom, immortality, and deity, and it is precisely this latter, in turn, that is properly first disputed. One thinks, then, that the aim of speculation is the objective securing of that which actually is; but when one undertakes to speculate, the investigation is driven of itself, though confusedly enough, toward another side, which one then calls idealism, and now seeks, now hates, without understanding it. The very expression: that the cognition of the highest grounds of explanation in the philosophical is to be grounded, shows that here no objective grounding can any longer be asked for, but that we have to do only subjectively with the history of our own cognizing. A proof by induction according to mere probabilities finds absolutely no place for genuine philosophical principles; we have to do, then, only with speculation. This occupies itself solely with inner self-observation, in that it seeks out what universal principle already underlies the individual applications of philosophy in our mind, and afterwards can only deduce how our mind comes to the pronouncement of those principles.

By induction I can indeed, e.g. for theoretical physics, as experiences widen, find new objective grounds of explanation for the appearances, e.g. electricity, oxygen and hydrogen, etc.; this procedure, however, finds no application at all for speculation and the investigation of the highest grounds of our metaphysical convictions. For the result of our

[p. 13]

logical investigations is this: with regard to philosophical cultivation the most cultivated philosopher differs from the crudest understanding not by an extension of his knowledge, but only by the logical distinctness of a form of cognition which in every reason is the same, by a clarification which belongs only to the faculty of reflection. Objective principles can be newly gained only in the empirical sciences, with the help of mathematics, through induction; metaphysical cultivation, on the other hand, develops for itself only the principles which lie once and for all at the basis of all judging in every human reason, and is directed, for their grounding, to a mere deduction.

The difference pointed out above (§. 71.) between subjective and objective grounding of our cognitions characterizes itself here thus: that every metaphysical investigation goes out only on mythological adventures as soon as it tries to take the second way, since it then confuses its own business with the heuristic maxims of an empirical natural science.

Our present task, then, rests on the following questions: 1) about what sort of objects do we judge, without grounding our judgment on intuition? 2) what principles do we presuppose in this way of judging? 3) how do these principles arise in our mind? In considering the forms of reflecting, we have always already presupposed, as fact, that which we are now investigating, the essence of immediate rational cognition in necessity, unity, and combination, as that which is observed through reflection. Now we must gather these facts of inner experience

[p. 14]

completely, and then ask above all: how does our reason come to this its immediate cognition.

#### 2) Survey of the Objects of Metaphysics.

#### §. 87.

Thinking, by itself, adds nothing to our representations whereby we might gain new cognitions; it serves only for self-observation in cognizing. But if it is not to be something purposeless in our mind, there must be cognitions of which we could not become conscious without its aid, which without reflection would have to remain always obscure to us. These are those which we express in judgments without grounding these judgments on intuition at all.

We judge, however, without laying intuition at the ground, everything that concerns the ideas of *truth*, of *goodness*, and of *beauty*. We presuppose here every time a universal legislation for the essence of things, which we do not learn from intuition, but according to which we nevertheless judge each and every thing that falls in intuition. The highest lawfulness in the *existence* of things, the highest lawfulness of the *worth* of things, and *beauty and sublimity* as law of nature in general correspond to those three ideas.

Of everything apodictic or universally valid, in general, we can become conscious completely only in judgments; every apodictic will therefore also claim its share in our

[p. 15]

present investigation. This then gives the following survey.

The first universally valid element that we found in our cognitions was pure mathematical intuition; to this came logic, whose principles, as principles of analytic cognition, sprang immediately from the form of conceiving and judging. The logical form itself was the form of the apprehension of an analytic and synthetic unity present in our cognitions, *under the presupposition of which* we have given the theory of the logical; how, however, we come at all to analytic and synthetic unity in our cognition we have not yet shown hitherto, so that even the theory of the logical still awaits its complete perfection in what follows. Likewise we have hitherto indeed exhibited mathematical intuition as a fact in our cognitions, but how we arrive here at drawing apodictic judgments from the mere immediate intuition of such a construction is not clear from what has gone before.

To these mathematical and logical apodictic principles there now come, besides, the metaphysical ones in synthetic judgments from mere concepts, the survey of which is what we are properly concerned with here.

Through the demonstrable judgments there arises in our cognition a knowledge of the world, or knowledge of the nature of things in space and time according to outer laws of the existence of matter and inner laws of the existence of reason. To this metaphysics adds, first, the most universal laws of necessity and combination, and is called in so far speculative philosophy.

[p. 16]

The first, merely assertoric, cognition through perception or sense intuition (§. 63.) we commonly call cognition of experience. Experience, however, consists not only in perceptions, but is mediate apodictic cognition, in that it raises the single empirical consciousness to a consciousness in general. Experience contains the necessary coherence of perceptions. In experience there is added to bare perception the mathematical form, and beyond this, further, a metaphysical apodictic determination in the complete judgment of experience. We have in every synthetic judgment of common life about that which we immediately see, hear, or otherwise perceive, still mathematical determinations of the spatial and temporal, but then also general concepts such as magnitude, reality, substance, cause, existence, and necessity, which, being of metaphysical origin, are a mere addition of the logical course of thought to perception, in order to make it into experience. Hereby coherence with the principles of necessary unity and combination is added to perception, and these principles are called principles of the possibility of experience, because only through them do we possess more in experience than in perception. The combination of all perceptions in one experience gives us then our completed cognition of nature under the laws of natural necessity. Thus metaphysics, with its first speculative part, lays claim to the completion of our first cognition from sense intuition, in that it adds to it pure concepts of the understanding; it forms thus the *metaphysical part of physics* as metaphysical science, which still attaches itself wholly to the material of experience.

[p. 17]

Every other cognition possible to us must enter into connection with this cognition of nature, with the metaphysical cognition of lawfulness in the existence of things; it can be of application only through relation to nature. For we possess no other intuition of given objects than the sensible in immediate perception; all cognition in judgments can therefore receive significance only through it. For this reason we call the completed cognition of nature exclusively *knowledge*.

All apodictic synthetic principles which there are in our reason besides these principles of the cognition of nature must belong quite immediately to reason itself, without a positive relation to sense. They will contain their certainty wholly in themselves, but in our cognitions, and in so far as they are to be expressed in judgments, they will find application only in relation to the intuition that underlies knowledge and the cognition of nature.

Now we call a concept that finds its object directly in intuition a concept in the narrower meaning, or concept of the understanding; a concept, on the other hand, that belongs to reason for itself, and cannot show its object positively in sense intuition, an *idea*. All metaphysical principles that go beyond physics will therefore rest on ideas. Call the holding-to-be-true in them *faith*, or as one will, it will always assert and maintain itself as an immediate conviction from mere reason in the common use of the understanding; for philosophers, however, the hardest task will be: in what

[p. 18]

as it were mysterious way these principles, independent of all intuition, come into our judgments.

We separate all these principles springing from the idea, as the property of *higher metaphysics*, from the *lower*, hitherto considered. The principles of the idea begin with the opposition of freedom to nature, with the opposition of the eternal of the idea to the finite of nature; they contain thus in the ideas of the soul, of the world, and of deity the ideal completion of those physical principles of synthetic unity. As such, however, they serve only as the foundation of two other systems of principles, which first give them their positive significance. The first of these systems is that of a universal legislation of worth, or for freely willing beings, a system of the principles of the final end in the existence of things. Reason adds of itself to the contingent prescriptions of willing a necessary Ought, which gives the rule for all willing; we lift ourselves through the idea out of nature, and determine our community with other reason according to the relation of the same to an intelligible world-order exalted above nature as object of our knowledge. The other principle of the application of the ideas is the principle of purposiveness in the existence of things for a universal judging of nature.

Metaphysics as a whole consists, then, of *speculative philosophy*, *practical philosophy* or *ethics*, and *teleology of nature*. To speculative philosophy belongs in part the metaphysical natural science, but then also the doctrine of the ideas; ethics grounds on it its doctrine of personal dignity and of the reality

[p. 19]

of the highest good; finally, teleology is the doctrine of purposiveness in the existence of things.

The beginning of all metaphysics is a metaphysical natural science, whereby it only supplements sense intuition with its mathematical form to apodictic cognition; this science rests on the laws of natural necessity, which are known preeminently under the names of the law of continuity, of the persistence of substance, of causality and interaction. The progress from there to the doctrine of the ideas takes place in our consciousness through the pure opposition of knowledge and faith, which announces itself in common consciousness through the conflict of natural necessity with freedom. We set against, in the idea, the finite being of nature, with the incompletability of the mathematical series in space and time, the eternal order of things according to the eternity of the world, of the soul, and of deity.

Only on this presupposition does ethics then ground the pronouncement of its faith in the highest good, which gives life to its doctrine of virtue and of right. Teleology of nature, finally, judges according to aesthetic ideas of purposiveness the free forms of intuition as beautiful and sublime, which judging becomes the theme of the critique of taste, connects with it the religious interest in the idea of the highest good, and shapes itself thus into the doctrine of religion of the intimation of eternal goodness in nature. It can only make the conclusion of all speculations, in that in its principles it presupposes ethics too.

The speculative part of science lies, then, at the ground of all the others, and demands the first investigation.

[p. 20]

In it, however, the relation of lower metaphysics to the higher, the relation of philosophy of nature to the doctrine of ideas is the chief matter, and the relation of the concept to the idea in general is the most important theme of all speculation.

Anthropologically we can see thus why we must begin precisely with this. The immediate cognition of reason underlies metaphysics according to the determinations which belong to it through the mere form of its spontaneity. Here, however, the speculative part belongs only to the *spontaneity of cognizing* taken by itself, whereas the other parts spring from the way in which the spontaneity of cognitions is first determined through the original practical faculties of reason.

[scan 431]

#### Form

## of Rational Cognition

or

#### Theory of Unity and Combination.

[scan 433]

### First Section.

#### Exposition of the Supreme Grounds of a Theory of Unity and Combination in Our Cognitions.

### First Chapter.

### On Unity and Necessity.

#### 1) On Necessity.

#### §. 88.

We have now to investigate the oft-mentioned immediate cognition which underlies reflection, as that which we wish to observe in ourselves through it. In this regard we already found: it is properly apodicticity and necessity of cognition of which we become conscious only through reflection, and then especially also unity and combination; these two objects therefore offer themselves first to our investigation.

As to necessity, the essence of reflection already showed us (§. 63.) that apodicticity consists

[p. 24]

in this, that a cognition is judged not only as belonging to a transitory state of my cognizing reason, but in its relation to the whole of my cognitive activity in general, for the survey of the whole history of my cognizing in one consciousness in general.

With regard to the use of the concepts of the actual, the possible and the necessary, it is now well enough known that their difference immediately concerns only subjectively the understanding, i.e., reflection; the sphere of the possible is, for the essence of things, neither greater nor smaller than that of the actual and the necessary; every thing is with necessity as it is, and when I say of something, that is quite possible, that may well be, this means only: I cannot judge whether it is or whether it is not, which therefore concerns only my reflection and not the essence of things themselves. Necessity is the sole law for our completed cognition; of the contingent there can be talk only with regard to subjective relations of apprehension by the individual reason. In so far as we become conscious of a cognition only through inner sense, as belonging to our momentary state of mind, we call it merely assertoric; reflection, on the other hand, raises through problematic universal representations this assertoric consciousness to an apodictic one, which holds for reason in the whole course of its cognizing in general, in that the individual inner perceptions about cognizing are raised to a whole of inner experience. There must, however, also lie in the immediate cognition of our reason itself a ground why reflection can complete its observation only in the threefold gradation of the actual, possible

[p. 25]

and necessary. We already know the decision on this too. The content of our immediate cognition is given to us only through the sensory stimulation, which in each of the changing states of mind is a different one, and only in this change can inner sense first become conscious of our cognizing. To the self-activity of reason, however, belongs a form of its excitability, which is the enduring, self-same element in its whole history; this is expressed also in its cognition, it is apodictic, can be grasped only by reflection, and indeed solely in that we take possession of its mere form by abstraction, and find the individual content standing only mediately under its condition. Thus all apodictic cognition becomes immediately formal and universal, but also a law for every content that may in any way be given. This form of spontaneity now adds the unity to our cognition, as we shall presently observe more closely.

We thus give here an anthropological theory of necessity, as the first application of our maxim of a merely subjective grounding in philosophy. Necessary cognition, and its origin in reason, is the whole riddle in philosophy; with all attempts to answer it one always fell into the dilemma of a one-sided empiricism or rationalism, in that one confused the subjective universal validity of empirical truth (§. 63. and 71.) with the objective validity of transcendental truth. Empiricism seeks its objective validity in intuition, through the delusion that demonstration is objective grounding of judgments; rationalism seeks its own in the

[p. 26]

necessity, in that it confuses the transition of assertoric cognition to apodictic cognition with the addition of the objective validity of cognition to a merely subjective play of representations. We, on the other hand, here too decline altogether the question as to objective validity, by showing that the difference of the actual and the necessary also belongs only to the subjective history of our cognizing, which proceeds from momentary self-observation to a survey of the whole history of our reason.

#### 2) On Unity.

#### §. 89.

In that we thus make through reflection this progress from the momentary to the whole life of our reason, there shows itself to us, as something new in our cognition, unity and combination, and to this extent the common explanation is justified that understanding or reason is the faculty of unity in our representations.

We found above (§. 60.) that abstraction becomes a means for observing the unity in our representations. There unity showed itself under two kinds of forms: as synthetic unity, whereby a manifold is united in one representation, as e.g. the representation of the figure of a man unites the representations of his individual members into a whole, or as in the representation of causality the union of the existence of the effect with that of the cause is thought; and as analytic unity of the universal, where manifold representations

[p. 27]

are thought as united, as the particular, *under* a universal.

In general, *combination* and *separation*, synthesis and analysis, are two opposed activities of the mind occurring in inner experience, for separation is the cancellation of combination. If we presuppose combination, we already found above how separations or abstractions must arise in our representations by means of an inner mechanism of the representations among one another. In this, however, analytic and synthetic unity showed themselves side by side. Of these, synthetic unity comes about immediately through combination, for combination is nothing other than the representation of a synthetic unity. Analytic unity, on the other hand, by no means arises only through analysis or abstraction, but is named after it only because we become conscious of it only through separation, whereas we are able to perceive many combinations also immediately.

Of every separated representation, e.g. of the red color, we become conscious with the form of the concept: every thing is either red or not red. Taken by itself, the analytic unity of the universal lies in the representation of a concept or of a rule, *under* which many representations belong together as the particular. It is an identical consciousness, which is the same in many representations; such a one lies, just as combination does, already in the mind before separation, but is first perceived through this. This analytic unity we already know as the means of raising inner perception to inner experience. Logic showed its various forms in concept, judgment, inference and system. The concept

[p. 28]

was the first perception of the universal; system contained the representation of it in its completeness, in a subordination of everything particular under its universal.

Among these forms, however, only that of the concept contains mere analytic unity; the others already help to observe synthetic unity in us. With judgment a synthetic unity always came in as well, namely in the combination of the subject with the predicate, and therein lay the end of judging in general. (§. 45.) Judgment thus contains a higher synthetic unity, of which we can become conscious only with the aid of the analytic, as combination of concepts. For no judgment is without a concept, i.e., without perception of an analytic unity. A peculiar kind of synthetic unity, which can come to consciousness only in judgments, therefore always requires a preceding analytic one, through which alone it can be comprehended. This is consequently a synthetic unity of which we can become conscious only in the raising of inner perception to inner experience.

I call it a higher synthetic unity, because earlier we already got to know another in the mathematical one, which still falls immediately into inner perception. In the immediately given material of sense intuition, in sensation, no combination occurs as yet; the first relation to it lies in the condition of the presentability of the manifold in space and time. The intuitions of space and time we found to be universal forms, which belong to the mind independently of the intuition of the individual manifold, but under whose condition every

[p. 29]

individual intuition stands.
