If we abstract, in the representation of these, from everything given and individual, then they contain (insofar as they are the object of mathematics) the synthetic unity of a homogeneous manifold, and this is the first synthetic unity in our cognition; we called it the figural synthetic unity, and ascribed it to the productive imagination; it is an intuitive combination, whose representations can still be perceived through inner sense. Besides this combination there is now another, of which we become conscious only in judgments. This is therefore called, by contrast, the representation of the *intellectual synthetic unity*. Whether a thing is red, warm or hard is contained immediately in the intuition of it; so too whether it is four-sided, round or angular, the former immediately in sensation, the other through the intuitive synthetic unity of the imagination. Whether, on the other hand, a thing is substance, or whether things stand in the relation of cause and effect, cannot be intuited. These concepts, however, likewise contain forms of a synthetic unity. We think the existence of the effect as combined with that of the cause, we think several inherences as combined in one substance. These representations therefore belong to intellectual synthetic unity.

The latter is just as much as analytic unity a property of the logical course of thought. It is that of which we become conscious in synthetic judgments precisely through judging. Synthetic judgments were those in which the concept of the predicate is not contained in the subject, but comes in addition beyond it and is combined with it. The analytic judgment, on the other hand, contains indeed also a synthetic unity of subject

[p. 30]

and predicate, but here the predicate is already thought in the subject, and thus the combination is already obscurely contained in the subject, no true property of the judgment. A new combination therefore comes about only through synthetic judgments. *We become conscious of the intellectual combination insofar as we, in synthetic judgments, with the aid of the analytic unity, reflecting upon inner perception, raise it to inner experience. The forms of analytic unity in judgment, inference and system appear here therefore at the same time as the means for becoming conscious of the intellectual synthetic unity.* They must be so constituted that in judgments we become conscious of that combination, through inference and system of its completeness.

There must therefore be an analogy between the forms of analytic unity and those of intellectual combination. Now we have become acquainted completely with the forms of analytic unity; we can therefore also, by an analogy with them, assemble a complete survey of the others from the manifold of inner experience. Separation by itself contains only relations of the perceiving of representations in comparison and abstraction, but at the basis of the forms of judgments, inferences and systems obtained through it there lies, besides the analytic unity first grasped in them, also combination. This idea is the guiding thread according to which Kant in the *Critique of Pure Reason* found the table of categories and the system of ideas of reason as the forms of intellectual combination.

[p. 31]

1) The forms of analytic unity were contained, first, with regard to judgment, in the logical table of the forms of judgment. To these correspond the synthetic forms of the categories. These categories determine the objects of perception according to the concepts of magnitude, quality, relation and modality as objects of experience, and can be assembled completely under the guidance of the table of judgments, since it is precisely the category that determines those forms; it is the concept of the determination of an object, insofar as the judgment is determined, with regard to it, according to one of the logical forms of judgments. With the form of synthetic judgments we become conscious, through the categories, of that first-named combination which is added to intuition and mathematics (§. 87.) in order to make our cognition of nature complete. We thereby obtain the forms of connection of perceptions in experience, that is, the forms of the unity of experience, which, just like the individual judgment, apply immediately to the manifold given in experience.

2) The transcendental ideas, on the other hand, aim at a highest synthetic unity of all our cognition, at an absolute whole of all possible experience, in analogy with the completeness of the subordination of everything particular under the universal in the forms of system, so that all those ideas can be exhibited in subordination under the highest ones of the soul, the world and the deity, according to the categorical, hypothetical and disjunctive relation. For these ideas again contain an activity of reason, which lies, as it were, imprinted in those logical forms. That the transcendental ideas, however,

[p. 32]

belong to forms of synthetic unity, is easily noticed. The idea of the soul aims at an absolute union of all the manifold of inner experience in one subject; the idea of the world is the concept of the synthesis of all objects of experience in a whole, and the idea of the deity contains the concept of the absolute unity in everything.

3) In analogy with the requirements of induction there arise heuristic maxims of an always possible application of the logical forms, in that reason not only pronounces for itself the forms of systematic unity, but at the same time demands their validity for our cognition in general. These heuristic maxims show themselves especially in the opposed claims of the theorists and the empiricists, which are critically reconciled through the limitation of all theoretical demands.

Through this analogy between the forms of analytic and synthetic unity we are therefore in a position to seek out all the different forms of combination, their laws and applicability in inner experience, by following the course of the Kantian investigation in the *Crit. of Pure Reason*. But our problem goes further; we demand not only the knowledge which forms of combination show themselves in our cognitions, we also want the explanation of how these forms arise in the mind, and how they come to consciousness for us, since only thereby do their principles obtain the deduction demanded. This is the ultimate end of a theory of combination.

Our problem is therefore: to show how necessary cognition, analytic and synthetic unity, arises in our reason.

[p. 33]

### Second Chapter.

#### Supreme Grounds of a Theory of Self-Activity in Cognizing.

#### a) Unity of the Rational Cognitive Power.

#### §. 90.

*Necessity in our cognition is possible only through an original, enduring, self-same activity of the one power of cognition in our reason.*

What constitution is presupposed in a power of cognition, so that it can possess necessary or apodictic cognitions, as our reason does? Immediately in the sensible element of intuition there lies no necessity; what sort of constitution of our reason is it, then, through which it possesses necessary cognitions, through which, however, these too do not immediately make up its whole cognizing, but stand only as a condition above everything contingent?

If we first have insight into this constitution of reason, through which it attains to the necessary, then we have secured ourselves completely against empiricism or skepticism, in that we have, wholly experiential and freed from all suspicion of speculative deceptions, a criterion

[p. 34]

by which we judge the necessity of our cognitions.

Necessity was the determination of the object for an apodictic cognition. Apodictic cognition was a cognition whose validity does not belong merely to a determinate state of mind, but holds for reason in general in the whole history of its cognizing. If, then, there are to be apodictic determinations in our cognitions, if there is to be even the mere concept of necessity in our representations, there must belong to reason in cognizing an original enduring activity, through which all its cognition is determined as the effect of *one* power, for otherwise one could not even speak of a whole of the history of its cognizing. Its immediately apodictic cognition must consist directly in such original activities; the rest can obtain its necessary worth only through dependence on these.

Merely sensible cognition by itself is an ever changing, daily new cognition, in which ever other and other intuitions follow one another, without any being in any relation to the other, and without its having a sequel beyond its duration; such a faculty of cognition would resemble the bright surface of a mirror, on which ever changed images pass by in constant change; they arise only through a foreign external power, which breaks on the surface, and none leaves a trace on it. The sensible cognition of our reason is not so constituted; it too changes, indeed, constantly, and is daily another, but all these changing images are held together by the bond of space and time; here every one flows

[p. 35]

into the other, and comes into relation to a whole of our cognitive activity, which concentrates itself in the *consciousness in general* of reflection. No single image once gained vanishes, but each obtains in time and space its lasting role, and a universally valid worth through its influence on the whole of my cognizing activity. And beside these changing intuitions there then show themselves also immediate apodictic cognitions of universal laws, which express an original and persistent activity of our reason itself.

The peculiar character of the *rational* in a power of cognition consists in this originality of its manifestations in cognizing, where its self-activity adds to cognition something unalterably self-same. Our power of cognition thus has such original manifestations, because it possesses the concept of necessity; but with these it is not sufficient to itself, rather this its original self-activity must first be stimulated by sense in order to manifest itself, and thereby it obtains in sensible cognitions only isolated, changing activities, which indeed stand under the condition of its original activity, but do not themselves belong to it.

That is to say, as we remarked at the very beginning, our reason is no independent spontaneity of its cognition, which would produce its cognition immediately, as matter its attractions and repulsions, but it stands under the condition of an external stimulation to cognize, like the organism in its vital manifestations. We therefore distinguish our reason as an

[p. 36]

excitable spontaneity, as finite reason, from an absolute reason, which would be thought as spontaneity of intuition pure and simple, of which, however, we can form no positive representation. Such a reason, which would possess its complete cognition immediately through itself (and not merely, as ours does, a form for it), would be a faculty of intellectual intuition, before whose gaze its whole universe would lie unfolded unalterably without motion, a reason which would not possess, as we do, free play in time and space or similar forms. In its cognition everything would be immediate, completed apodicticity and necessity; reflection would find as little place for it as sense. In our finite reason, on the other hand, there is found only a formal original determination of its activity, through which the law of necessity for our cognition arises; every individual manifestation of cognizing, however, must first be determined contingently through sense. Hence our cognition can come about only through a union of sensible intuitions under formal necessary laws, as we find them in our cognition of nature. Precisely for this reason our self-cognition too stands under the same condition of sense; inner sense becomes indispensable for us, and this must first be supplemented by reflection before necessary and apodictic determinations of our own nature come to our consciousness; consequently we cognize even the original formal and persistent activities of our reason in the end only through reflection, and not in intuition.

[p. 37]

#### b) The Transcendental Apperception.

#### §. 91.

*The occurrence of analytic and synthetic unity in our cognitions proves that to our reason there belongs a thoroughgoing unity of all its cognizing, whereby the whole of all its cognizing belongs together with necessity in one transcendental apperception.*

What constitution of our reason is presupposed, whereby it can be in possession of the analytic as well as the synthetic unity actually belonging to it?

The answer to this question will determine more closely wherein properly consists the necessary cognition of our reason that springs from the form of its excitability.

1) Through every representation of the analytic unity of a concept the whole sphere of my cognizing is recognized as determinable; this sphere must therefore be originally determined as *one whole*, all my cognitive activity falls together in *one*.

We have come to know as the supreme principle of logic the principle of determinability: Every thing is either A or it is not A. By this we are put in

[p. 38]

a position, as soon as we have, through abstraction, extracted from the individual intuition some problematic representation as an identical consciousness in several intuitions, to determine through this *one* representation the whole sphere of our cognizing. For every such representation of an analytic unity can be used as concept in the principle of determinability, and becomes thus, through the universal and necessary form of its logical disjunction, a ground of determination for *each and every one of my cognitions in general*. How can this thought of either A or not A now take place in my reason? What, for example, has the colored object which I cognize through the eye to do with the sounding object of the ear, that I can use the individual redness as a ground of determination, positively or negatively, also for the sounding, and thus for every thing in general? This presupposes first a unity pure and simple for my reflection; all my consciousness must unite in *an identical consciousness of self-cognition*, so that such a determination of everything through each thing may become possible for my reason. This unity of reflection, however, cannot itself take place without an underlying unity of immediate cognition. This makes the synthetic unity still clearer.

2) The occurrence of combination and of necessary objective synthetic unity in our cognitions proves that our reason possesses a transcendental apperception, i.e., that a thoroughgoing identity of the cognitive activity takes place in all its cognizing, a whole of all its immediate cognition.

[p. 39]

Necessary objective synthetic unity is the original union of manifold cognitions into *one* cognition itself; it is the identity of apperception in manifold representations. We must first develop this concept more closely. Different representations can be in accidental subjective combination, without thereby becoming *one* representation. There are very many such subjective combinations; a familiar example is the mere association of representations, say word and thought in language, which are indeed always combined for my consciousness, but without going together in *one* representation, without being united into an identical apperception. If, on the other hand, I consider one after another the various plots, the shrubberies, lawns, etc., of a garden, and now gather them together into the whole representation of the garden, this is objective combination. Through mere subjective combination objective synthetic unity never comes about; the latter, namely, is to contain not only a combination in my representations, but a representation of combined objects. This therefore demands not merely the coming-to of one cognition to another, but actual unity of cognizing, union into one cognition, so that every individual cognition falls into the whole cognition only as partial cognition. E.g., not through the fact alone that I perceive several windows at the same time does the synthetic unity of the house enter into the representation of it, but only through my gathering the partial intuitions of the windows, etc., in the whole intuition of the house, through my bringing the various representations of it together in the one representation of the house, or, more generally, in the representation of

[p. 40]

space, and thus represent them as objectively combined.

Objective synthetic unity does not arise through this alone, that manifold representations belong together in the same subject, in the same reason, for I could think my cognition also as a motley medley of individual perceptions without any combination; nor would it be obtained through this alone, that I am conscious in *one* inner perception that all these representations, as *my* representations, are representations of the same subject, for this too brings forth as yet no union of the manifold representations into *one* cognition, and only in the latter does objective synthetic unity consist. It demands, beyond the unity of the subject, to which, e.g., all these individual intuitions belong as its cognitive activities, and beyond the unity of reflection or self-observation, in which I am conscious of all these different intuitions side by side as my own, also *unity of cognizing itself*, so that each individual one is only a part of a whole cognitive activity, which is represented through combination. Thus synthetic as well as analytic unity rests on an identity of consciousness in different representations. Analytic unity demands an identical consciousness as partial representation, which as the same is contained in different representations of the particular standing under it, for therein consisted the representation of the universal; synthetic unity demands an identical consciousness in which manifold representations are contained.

So far, then, as different cognitions are in objective synthetic unity for our reason, so far there is

[p. 41]

in it identity of apperception, union of its cognitive activity into one cognizing. Now combination is found in our cognitions not only here and there or scattered in individual groups, but we lay claim to a necessary connection of all perceptions in *one* experience, to a law of a thoroughgoing, necessary, objective combination of all our cognizing, as we can show in many individual requirements. This lies in the claims of every universal law of mathematics, of every universal principle of physics, etc.; it lies in the requirement of a system of all the sciences of my reason, and above all in the idea of truth itself, in the requirement that there is to be truth at all, and only *one* truth for our mind. Every combination, however, demands that all combined cognitions be only parts of one and the same cognition; thoroughgoing, necessary, objective, synthetic unity therefore demands that all my cognition be only parts of one and the same cognitive activity of my reason.

With objective synthetic unity we arrive at the same result as with analytic unity. The latter is by itself only the identical consciousness in certain given different representations, which are subordinated to it as the universal. But in that I detach it as problematic representation from the individual, it remains for me in reflection as a determination with regard to the whole mind in general, and its application to cognition likewise relates to a determination of the originally identical element of all my cognition. The ground of reflection alone, the possibility of even applying the principle of identity or of contradiction

[p. 42]

to our cognition, already presupposes precisely this requirement. For I can assert that what is contradictory cannot be combined only if for my reason all the different spheres of individual concepts are contained in the end in *one* supreme sphere, if there is in my reason only *one* system of truth, for otherwise in the one the proposition, in the other the opposite proposition could hold, just as the events of today differ from those of yesterday, today happens what yesterday did *not* happen.

We say therefore: The cognizing of our reason is at every moment *one* whole of immediate cognition, which we call the transcendental apperception, and which is properly the object that is re-observed in us through inner sense and reflection. We prove this first in that only under this presupposition is even the thought of the emptiest logical law possible, but most clearly in that a thoroughgoing, necessary, objective combination takes place in our cognitions, which in fact expresses nothing other than that unity of transcendental apperception. That, however, such a thoroughgoing and necessary combination is actually in our cognitions, we must make still clearer. We presuppose this combination already in that we have at all the *idea of truth*, the idea of a subjective universal validity, for without such a thoroughgoing unity no claim of a universal pronouncement would take place; we presuppose it, further, through the idea of *one* system of all our cognitions; we presuppose it, finally, quite clearly through application of the *idea of the world*, in that by world we understand precisely a whole of all objects

[p. 43]

of cognition, and thus think objective synthetic unity of this whole. Yet here we can appeal only to the ordinary use of the concepts of truth and world, without being able to establish their applicability more closely; skepticism could therefore still contest this argument with us, in that it asserted that the idea of the world is a mere product of our fantasy, and the idea of truth expresses only the pious wish to possess a better organized reason than the one we actually have. We must therefore seek to document that thoroughgoing combination with simpler facts of inner experience. For this, pure self-consciousness offers itself of itself. In every moment of my consciousness I can become conscious of myself in pure self-consciousness, in that the “I am,” the consciousness of my existence, is present before reflection in every waking state. If, then, I cognize anything else, e.g., the existence of any thing, I can always express this: I am, and that is too; I connect the existence of each thing that I cognize with my existence as belonging to one and the same world. Every one of my cognitions by itself thus gives an objective synthetic unity with my existence; every one of my cognitions is thus united with my pure self-consciousness into one cognitive activity. There is thus here a unity of my cognitive activity, in which pure self-consciousness lies, and with which every other consciousness that we possess coincides.

The union of my whole cognition into one activity, which is only ever enlarged by the intuitions constantly streaming in anew, constitutes the inner truth and necessity for our reason.

[p. 44]

We see from this that we did very well to explain truth at first only as the presence of cognition in reason, as empirical truth (§. 71.), for everything that appears isolated and scattered in sensible intuition makes up after all only parts of the original unity of all my cognitive activity, and the nearest question about truth is only the question about the subjective relation of individual cognitions to this original unity of all my cognition. The originally single cognitive activity of reason contains cognition as a whole of its immediate cognition; we become conscious of it, however, only partially through inner sense and reflection. According to the sensible essence of our reason it is not possible that we ever become conscious of this whole of immediate cognition, but the difference of the obscure, the clear and the distinct in representation is unavoidable for us. Only individual parts does inner sense apprehend immediately as intuition; the form of the whole is observed only by abstracting reflection. Had we not this gradation in self-observation, there would be no difference between intuiting and thinking, and invention as free play with representations independent of the law of truth would not be possible at all.

#### c) The Original Formal Apperception.

#### §. 92.

*The relation of the material and formal consciousness in our cognition proves that in the immediate*

[p. 45]

*cognition of our reason there lies a basic consciousness of unity and necessity as original formal apperception, which is the pure result of the form of its excitability in cognition.*

Matter and form are two concepts that were already encountered earlier among the forms of comparison, by which we wished to observe the unity in our representations. Matter means the determinable in general, form the determination of it. Their use in philosophy, however, is ambiguous. By matter, or the determinable, one formerly understood what is universal and receptive of many determinations, whereas form was called the determination of the particular under the universal; matter here signifies, as it were, the indistinguishable substrate of being, which has no determinate figure but is receptive of many figures; matter is being simpliciter, form the kind of being. Thus, e.g., in the marble statue the mere marble by itself is the figureless material, which becomes a statue only through the determinate figure. Almost in contradiction with this, however, with us it is precisely the universal, the mere unity, that is called form, and matter, on the other hand, the individual, to which this form pertains as determination; the universal rule is the form, the particular that stands under it the matter; figure by itself is mere form, the particular figured thing the matter. The latter usage is more determinate; matter refers to the manifold to be combined, form to the unity in our representations.

[p. 46]

I call the matter of a consciousness the object of it, or, if one prefers, the objective in it, that which in it refers to the object. Thus in an intuition it is the object itself that determines the matter of the representation, whereas in the concept of the color red it is precisely the red color and not the individual red objects themselves. A consciousness is therefore called *material* insofar as it has an object, formal, on the other hand, insofar as it is considered only with regard to the fact that something else is contained in or under it. But because a consciousness without anything represented in it cannot be distinguished at all from another, every consciousness is materially determined in some respect, but not every one formally. Completely materially determined is the empirical intuition, which contains its determinate object as given; a universal concept, or the form of a combination, on the other hand, do indeed have material determinations in themselves, but are nevertheless not completely material consciousness, for they have no complete object. The single empirical intuition in sensation is only materially determined; the pure intuition of space and time, on the other hand, contains within itself everything manifold of intuition, it is a form of these intuitions; likewise the intuitive representations of determinate figures, e.g. of the Apollo Belvedere, of a pyramid, or the representation of a determinate duration, day, hour, are formal representations in which others are contained. Further, every representation of the universal, every concept, is a formal consciousness, in that it contains other representations beneath it as the particular of its sphere; likewise a universal rule is a form for all particular cases, for which it

[p. 47]

can be used as a ground of determination. Most concepts and all rules are here determined as formal in two respects, both with regard to the particular that they contain under them and with regard to the manifold that they comprehend in themselves. Thus all consciousness of the categories and ideas is formal also in this, that we use, e.g., magnitude, or the relation of substance and accident, or the idea of the world as forms of the connection of objects that are comprehended in them.

Formal consciousness is thus in general that through which I immediately represent to myself the unity in my cognition, be it analytic or synthetic. Every formal consciousness contains the possibility of an objective unity in our cognitions, and wherever we become conscious of the unity in our representations, this happens, analytically or synthetically, always only through a formal consciousness, as it were the bond through which representations that appear different are nevertheless recognized as the same. In analytic unity I find the same consciousness again in different representations; in synthetic unity, representations that appear as different are comprehended in one form. Without such formal consciousness single empirical intuitions would lie separated beside one another, none would concern the other, and the like in many of them would never make possible a rule under which these many would stand together.

In every whole of cognition we must make the threefold distinction between the whole itself, the unifying form of it, and the matter united in it. E.g. the intuition of a single tree is such a whole, its figure, the concept of the determinate

[p. 48]

species of tree to which it belongs, etc., makes the form of it, the aggregate of its trunk and its branches, just as they are actually found in this individual, makes the matter. Or let the whole of cognition be the revolution of the moon around the earth: then motion and a determinate interaction of moving forces make the form of this event, earth and moon the matter. Or let the cognition of the universal rule be given: All bodies are heavy; then this is an empty form if the intuition does not actually furnish individual bodies as matter for application, whereby the whole of cognition then becomes the system of all bodies under this rule. In all these cases formal consciousness is that through which the unity comes into the whole of cognition, and that through which we become conscious of its unity as a tree, as an event of an interaction, as a universal law.

This formal consciousness it was now, with regard to analytic as well as synthetic unity, that reflection observes in cognition; we became conscious of it through abstraction, and according to this universality and combination distinguished the two kinds of abstraction. In the whole of our cognition there always lies subjectively at the ground of the given matter, as the manifold of intuition, or the particular case under the rule, the form of its combination, or the universal of its determination, which is lifted out by abstraction and represented separately, but is immediately that which is added to cognition originally by reason itself. We thus have in this formal consciousness at once that which constitutes unity and combination in cognition, and the means

[p. 49]

whereby we observe unity and combination through reflection.

Now we saw above that there are not merely single unifications here and there in our cognition, but a thoroughgoing unity and identity of all my cognitive activity for reason in general. There is not merely here and there a single whole in cognition, but all my cognition as transcendental apperception makes up only one such whole. All unity in such a whole of cognition, however, was to arise in it only through a formal consciousness; the whole transcendental apperception itself therefore becomes possible only through such a universal and original formal apperception, which is the source of all unity in our reason. Necessary analytic unity, and thoroughgoing necessary objective synthetic unity, exist only through the unity of an original formal apperception in our cognition.

There is in our reason such a first basic consciousness of unity and necessity. Every single formal consciousness which reflection apprehends, and through which it determines any whole of cognition, is only a part of this one original formal basic activity of reason.

This formal consciousness of the unity and necessity of all my cognition is the result of the form of the excitability of our reason, which is the one and the same in all our cognition, but can come to consciousness for us only in the broken single forms of analytic and synthetic unity. It is that which characterizes reason as such,

[p. 50]

that which it by itself contributes to cognition, nothing but the law: every cognition of our reason can only be a modification of its one cognitive activity; this is the subjective principle of its unity and necessity, its original formal apperception.

The assumption of such an original formal apperception is the supreme point of a theory of the spontaneity of the power of cognition, and thus the highest principle of anthropology, from which the theory of reason must proceed. Let us survey once more how we arrive at this presupposition. Truth can take place in our cognitions in general only through the union of analytic with a thoroughgoing synthetic unity, since only so does the validity of each single cognition become determinable against every other. If there is therefore to be a universally valid worth in our cognitions at all, this rests on the presence of a thoroughgoing combination in our cognitions. Thoroughgoing combination, however, is found only in a thoroughgoing unity of all my cognizing, and this is possible only through an original formal apperception, which is the condition of every other cognition.

If therefore only some apodictic assertion (even if it were only a wholly empty logical formula, like the principle of identity A is A) is admitted, there lies in it already that there is a universal validity in my cognitions, that is, an original relation in reason against which truth in general is to be determined, and that is an original formal apperception of it. Whoever therefore admits anything at all universally valid arrives at the necessary

[p. 51]

assumption of such a formal apperception, and of all that then follows from it for reason. Indeed, whoever did not wish to go directly into this himself still cannot fail to notice in himself the coincidence of every single consciousness with pure self-consciousness, and arrives thereby at thoroughgoing necessary combination, and thus at original formal apperception.

This original formal apperception lies in reason as a basic consciousness of unity and necessity, but cannot be reached in its purity either by inner sense or by reflection, for it is precisely the persistent, undifferentiated self-sameness in everything, whose single material determinations alone are perceived by sense, and since reflection too must always attach itself to sense, it apprehends, in the universal and necessary and in every combination, indeed the consequences of this underlying unity, but always only singly and never as a whole. In the obscure representation of our mind, the fund of memory, there lies the whole immediate cognitive activity of my reason as its immediate cognition, as its transcendental apperception, whose form is the original formal apperception. Before re-consciousness, however, only single parts of it are repeated in clear and distinct representation, in intuiting, inventing and thinking.

[p. 52]

### Appendix.

#### §. 93.

1. The supreme relation of a theory of our reason is the one exhibited here, that of a formal, material and transcendental apperception. There lies in our reason a unity of transcendental apperception as its immediate cognition; this arises in such a way that its original formal cognition of unity and necessity is supplemented by single, added material consciousness. The basic consciousness of our reason would be wholly empty by itself if the single stimulations through sense did not come to it; as soon as these begin, however, they enliven it, and it then communicates to them its apodictic worth. These relations are the highest result of the subjective investigation of cognizing; through them we must unveil the secrets of all speculation; they are difficult to make intelligible, because the highest abstraction retains so little content, and the prejudice of objective grounding so readily draws the glance away again from our investigation. This compels us to be more detailed here.

It has often been remarked that the doctrine of pure apperception, or the section on the possibility of combination (p. 129 ff.), is the most difficult and unintelligible in Kant’s *Critique of Pure Reason*, and yet that on which everything depends for theory. One can also easily notice that the Kantian theory does not here achieve what should be demanded of it.

[p. 53]

The question of the possibility of combination in our cognitions is a problem of inner physics; the highest grounds of explanation of this possibility must be principles of a physical theory, so that the forms of combination actually occurring can be derived from them singly. The latter, however, the Kantian theory does not achieve at all; it gives only an empty analytic proposition as the supreme principle of the understanding, and leads to a peculiar view of the copula in judgment in general, which, however, remains very obscure. Kant was reproached with being unable to state why we possess precisely these forms of category and idea, and he answered only that this is no indispensable need of his Critique, which, as he had set the task, was not incorrect, but for the evidence of the whole system was nevertheless a considerable deficiency. Afterwards we have received various attempts at really theoretical derivations of the forms of the categories; but they have all soon been forgotten again, and I know of none that has pursued the matter through a deeper investigation of the doctrine of pure apperception, which is yet the only subjective way appropriate to a theory of reason.

Wherein, then, lies the incompleteness of the Kantian view? This we can show quite determinately. The fundamental error of the Kantian theory we have already censured: he confused the understanding as faculty of reflection with immediate reason; he did not know the merely repetitive nature of reflection. When he distinguishes sense and understanding, this touches only the distinction given above (§. 74.) between what we find in ourselves through inner sense and what we can observe in ourselves only through reflection. A consequence of this error shows itself

[p. 54]

also in his doctrine of the possibility of combination. That which we call transcendental apperception, or the whole of the immediate cognition of our reason, he did not notice at all, in that he confused it with the objective existence of things. Further, what he calls pure apperception and thoroughgoing identity of all apperception is a mixing of our original formal apperception with pure self-consciousness. (The apodicticity that lies in the Is as copula of every judgment has nothing to do with pure self-consciousness, but is only the imprint of the original formal apperception in the judgment of reflection.) His error here, namely, is that he confused the unity of reflection (designated under b) 1)), the comprehension of all my cognitions into a *unity of self-observation*, with the immediate unity of all my cognizing, and thought that with the former, which is yet only the property of reflection, he could already attempt a theory of combination.

We must here distinguish the following expressions.

First, *pure apperception* we call pure self-consciousness, which is expressed through reflection as: I am, or I think, which is the form of inner sense and determines for every inner intuition the I as the one and the same thinking object. This I am determines then also the unity of inner perception, and through this the unity of reflection or self-observation, in that the reflected self-consciousness gives the form here.

Second, *transcendental apperception* I call the immediate whole of the cognition of my reason in each moment of its manifestation of life, with regard

[p. 55]

to which the I of pure apperception is the only *immediate content* that sense has not given; *original formal apperception*, on the other hand, thirdly, is the *immediate form* of that whole; in it lies the law of apodicticity, in it the source of all single forms of unity that reflection apprehends. We must not designate it with Kant by the I am, for this is only a single material determination of it; it must rather be compared only with forms, as e.g. the intuition of infinite space *in abstracto*, as geometry retains it, or the forms world, world-order, which comprehend everything in one whole, or also the form: To every thing there belongs either a concept or its opposite, as form of the determinability of everything by each. All this, however, is as it were only single imprints of the one formal apperception before reflection; it cannot be better named than basic consciousness of unity and necessity. Kant’s error in this whole view of our reason can also be characterized by what we have censured in several places: self-activity of the power of cognition is for him always its *voluntariness*, i.e., reflection. (See e.g. *Crit. of Pure Reason*, p. 130.)

The Kantian synthesis, as he sets it out in its forms and develops it in the principles of the understanding, is nothing but an act of the faculty of reflection, a repetition whose original he does not know. His synthesis is the act of the understanding of adding one representation to another and uniting both in one consciousness (*Crit. of Pure Reason*, p. 133), which only reflection does. What in the immediate cognition of our reason is not already combined, that will not

[p. 56]

be represented through that synthesis as objective synthetic unity of cognition. Kant, however, attempts his theory of combination without taking account of this immediate cognition. The Kantian synthesis is that which, in the mathematical representations of productive imagination and in the formation of judgments, falls immediately into inner perception. We have already above (§. 40.) drawn attention to the distinction between the immediate unity and combination of productive imagination, and the repetition of it before inner perception. We showed that this distinction frees us from the contradictions in the usual theories of productive imagination, where this faculty appears as voluntarily creating, as it were inventing, and then nevertheless demands truth from its representations. E.g. I see the disc of the moon at the horizon larger than high in the sky, and call this deception not only because the moon is not larger the one time than the other, but because it is also not farther away the one time than the other, and especially because my immediate intuition, which I observe more precisely by measurement, really shows it no larger the one time than the other. The immediate synthesis is here observed through measurement, the faulty synthesis, on the other hand, belongs only to repeating reflection; it is the *judged* representation of the size of the moon’s disc. In every judgment we have this distinction still more clearly. In it we voluntarily put together concepts as subject and predicate, and combine them; only afterwards do we ask whether the judgment is true or false. Here holding-to-be-true contains the derived synthesis of reflection, which *lays claim* to apodicticity, the

[p. 57]

immediate unity and combination, on the other hand, contains the *law of truth*, according to which our holding-to-be-true is correct or error.

When Kant develops the form of a combination, e.g. proves the law: every succession in time takes place only through causation, he actually remains only with the relations of reflected synthesis, and appeals, instead of to the original unity of cognition, to the being of the object. He distinguishes the mere succession of perceptions in voluntary observation from the succession of the appearances themselves, and shows that we need necessary concepts of the understanding, here that of causality, in order to pass for cognition from the former to the latter. “I perceive the parts of a building one after another, but say they are simultaneous, because I can voluntarily observe the building from top to bottom, or from bottom to top. I perceive a ship one after another upstream and downstream on the river, and say this is an event in a temporal succession, since voluntary observation can proceed only from upstream to downstream, but not the reverse. In order to represent to myself completely the event of the simultaneous or of the successive, I need each time a concept of the understanding, but that I actually apply in the particular case, e.g. that of causality, lies in the impossibility of being able to reverse the series of perceptions.”

This Kantian exposition remains incomplete because it concerns itself only with the activities of reflection. It does not distinguish, first, the mathematical necessity of occurring one after another (Christ’s birth falls after the battle of Actium) from the intellectual necessity of the through-one-another (the lunar eclipse results

[p. 58]

from the shadow of the earth), in that he postulates the help of the understanding only by this, that an indeterminate representation of necessity in the objective synthetic unity of events is demanded. Second, it traces the objective validity of the temporal succession of appearances, as against the subjective validity of the succession of perceptions, back to the impossibility of an *voluntary alteration of observation*, whereby one actually regards the object affecting for sensation (e.g. the eye) as the ground of the objective significance. In fact, however, in this empirical experiment of reversing the series of observation, which belongs to reflection, it is not at all a matter of *objective* determination, but only of usability of the given material of perceptions for *judging* and for *subjectively universally valid* results in judgment. For in itself every series of perceptions has the same objective worth of time-determination; also in the observation of the building I perceive, if I begin at the top, a preceding state of the existence of the summit, and a following one of the existence of the ground.

The difficulty lies here too, then, once again in the unfamiliarity of our subjective view of cognition. When we put together a whole experience out of many perceptions by synthesis of reflection, the assertion corresponds entirely to the common prejudice that we here add to the merely subjective significance of single perceptions the objective significance of experience. This, however, really does not happen. Rather, as in our representations the sense intuitions fall to one another, the whole of experience forms itself in our *immediate cognition*, in that each

[p. 59]

sense intuition is only a modification of my *one* cognitive activity; but the single sense intuition is perceived immediately only by inner sense, the whole of experience can be observed only by reflection, and the gradations of validity are again only subjective ones, according to problematic attempts at judging and really warranted apodictic decisions.

Here the relation of the faculty of reflection to immediate reason can be determined still more closely. We must not make the difference of the two straightforwardly through analysis and synthesis, logical and transcendental thinking. Analysis as well as synthesis are functions of the reflecting understanding; but for analysis reflection is sufficient to itself, whereas synthesis it cannot give itself, and therefore the riddle of speculation can be put: how is synthesis *a priori* possible? On the other hand, both the presence of analytic and that of synthetic unity in our representations belongs to immediate reason, and not to reflection alone. Only that the forms of analytic unity can, as it were, be observed earlier by reflection, those of synthetic unity only with the help of the former. For the theory of reason, therefore, the question: how is analytic unity possible? is just as much a question as: how is objective synthetic unity in its cognitions possible? and both we must be able to answer through the theory of unity. The two basic acts of reflection are *abstraction and composition*, i.e., separation and recomposition of what is separated; but before both, first, the *original combination of immediate cognition* must

[p. 60]

be given to us, without which neither abstraction nor composition would be possible; *whose* laws we seek here.

#### §. 94.

II. For whoever has become so fluent with the concepts of our inner natural science that he is capable of a determinate dispute over individual presentations, it may easily be striking that we want to ground the theory of unity in our immediate cognition almost with the same formula to which we traced back the doctrine of association. We sought, namely, at that time to explain the phenomena of association by saying that all activities of the disposition of mind fell together in every moment in a unity of the act of our mind, whereby the liveliness of inner activities simultaneously excited would become so dependent on one another that the one afterwards communicated its enlivening to the other; thus we explained the combination of the sound in the word with the abstract thought designated. Now, on the other hand, we say: all forms of unity and combination in our representations we possess through an original formal apperception, and our cognition obtains necessity by this, that in every moment all my cognizing is united through this original formal apperception in one cognitive activity. Unity of the whole activity of the disposition of mind in every state of mind thus lies at the ground the one time as the other; both modes of combination, the subjective one of association and the objective synthetic unity of reason, are nevertheless of thoroughly different nature; however closely word and thought may be associated, the remote synthetic

[p. 61]

union of their objects will thereby be brought no closer. Words will give this relation no great clarity, because we have no intuitive form for the union of the simultaneously given in our inner activities; but whoever observes himself will find that the unity of our inner activity applies itself in the two cases in quite opposite ways. In the unity of the cognition of reason there is, *as it were*, talk of the whole of its extensive magnitude, how all parts must fall together in one form of the whole, whereby the degree of liveliness of the representations does not matter at all, but everything depends only on their lying beside one another in the whole. The play of associations, on the other hand, has precisely to do only with intensive magnitude and its unity, in that a whole of the degree of liveliness distributes itself in every moment among all inner activities; associations too have to do only with this alternation of vivacity and its distribution among the single simultaneously lively activities.

#### §. 95.

III. The theory of reason, which we here develop from anthropological principles, affords the advantage that in matters of the highest speculation it supplies decision, without our needing to engage in the greatest difficulties of speculating itself. It is physical theory, and rests therefore on experience and inner intuition, which, even if as inner intuition it is hard to communicate, nevertheless always admits of far firmer judgments than the highest abstractions

[p. 62]

of speculations themselves. If we venture, without anthropological assistance, to judge about quite general speculative things, about the essence and necessity in things in general, about freedom, or whether the deity is to be presupposed with Spinoza as the ultimate being, or with Leibniz as the ultimate thinking being, we shall have thereon immediately little firm judgment. Although on one side we are well aware that such things are not at all to be decided according to probability, we feel nevertheless on the other side that we confuse ourselves in words more than we judge, and can easily notice that the conflicting judgments of the one and the other come precisely from this, because more indeterminate associations than truth guide our judgment. This arises naturally from the fact that those high abstractions are so hard to schematize, and inner sense retains in them so little material which reflection could grasp securely, that our composition here easily becomes more play with words than judgment from concepts. The most uncertain here is the composition of the single abstractions, and precisely this is made uncommonly easier for us by the anthropological treatment; we obtain here in the theory of reason, which exhibits the origin of every single abstract form, precisely through this origin a firm place for it, and can now determine its relations to other abstractions in accordance with experience, so that the universal judgments themselves then become only an easy result. If, e.g., the question concerns the law of causality: every alteration is an effect, I do not compare both concepts in order to ascertain the truth of the law, but the theory shows me already in the large in what relation pure time-determinations and categories

[p. 63]

in our reason stand, and from this the validity and the case of application of the single laws then results of itself.

In general the treatment of the highest abstractions is so indeterminate and wavering that hardly any philosopher arrives at a determinate system otherwise than by presupposing (often unconsciously to himself) a psychological hypothesis about the theory of reason, by which he tests and judges truth in speculative matters in the highest instance. These hypotheses are in the end all of two kinds: one-sided empiricism and one-sided rationalism. In the dispute against these two we have then also actually been compelled to derive the highest principles of our theory of transcendental apperception through inductions from inner experience.

At the ground of all empiricism in philosophy there lies in the end the anthropological hypothesis that man possesses only a sensible power of cognition. This we first of all oppose. We exhibit from the occurrence of representations in our mind that this hypothesis, to let all our cognition flow together only through sensible impressions, does not at all explain what is actually there. Not only the claimed necessity in application, but even *the empty concept of necessity, the empty thought* of the Is, as the copula in judgment grasped only in A is A, would be impossible in such a merely sensible power of cognition. Otherwise empiricism defends itself for the most part only apagogically against the claims of reason, in which case both parties are often wrong in the common presupposition. Epicurus and Locke appeal to this, that every human cognition only awakens through sense,

[p. 64]

begins with sense, that no content can be exhibited in judgment which is not borrowed from sense, that every content was first in sense before it comes into the understanding. Their conclusions from this hold, however, only against the untenable rationalistic hypothesis of *innate ideas*, which presupposes a content of its own of the *merely rational*, whereas to reason independently of sense belongs *no content, but only the form*.

Or Hume contends chiefly by showing: all our application of universal laws is borrowed through induction only from experience, one could therefore explain all presupposition of necessity, as it occurs in our mind, just as well merely by habit (we presuppose that that will follow which we are accustomed to see follow). This objection, expressed psychologically, says: What you seek to explain with your theory of reason can be explained just as well by mere imagination, which, *as is well known, is only a sensible faculty*. Here lies the error to which I wish to call attention, in the last presupposition. Had Hume observed more correctly, he would have had to notice that his power of cognition enlivened by impressions must possess either not even imagination (intensive unity of its activity) or also reason at the same time as source of necessity (extensive unity of its activity). This, to be sure, could not become clear to him (so long as reason and reflection were not properly separated).

At the ground of all rationalism in philosophy there lies in the end the anthropological hypothesis that man possesses a cognition to be freed from sense through mere

[p. 65]

reason. In opposition to this view we can designate our theory by the assertion of the emptiness of the basic consciousness of reason. If one is not quarreling over words, every rationalistic philosophy contains the presupposition of innate ideas; we, on the other hand, assert: mere reason gives only the form to the sensibly stimulated consciousness. There are, to be sure, in our cognition cognitions from mere reason, namely the cognitions *a priori*, the sources of universality and necessity, but these by themselves are always only *formal apperceptions*, which neither in the small nor in the large ever make up *a whole of cognition*; they occur *by themselves* only through abstraction, but immediately in each case as forms in a whole of cognition whose material is borrowed from sense. We can make this clear best by comparison with the organic life of our body. What we ascribe to mere reason independently of sense corresponds to the form of its excitability. Cognition is in general the excitation or manifestation of life of reason; the form of this manifestation of life is now determined in general by the essence of reason itself, but it can never come to an actual manifestation itself, to a whole cognizing, without sense. Thus organization determines the form of its vital functions, circulation of the fluids, respiration, assimilation, nutrition, but if new material in the way of food and air is not continually supplied, then, even if the organization continued to exist (like, e.g., the dry germ of a plant, which lies for years without development), the *manifestation of life* must cease. Just so cognition. Organization and reason determine the forms of manifestation,

[p. 66]

the manifestation itself is also at all times its activity, but only under the condition of an external influence accidental to it, a stimulation through receptivity for stimulating potencies or sense. Every cognition *a priori* is in itself a universal law, which becomes a whole of cognition only by the fact that determinate objects of intuition are subsumed under it through the minor premise in the inference; even the ideas of the world and of the deity first demand application to this intuition, in order that something be cognized through them. Rationalism, on the other hand, wants a higher cognition of reason which is to be sufficient to itself, i.e., it demands the intellectual intuition of an absolute reason, which would be not merely excitable power, but spontaneity simpliciter, which would create for itself the content of its cognition; it demands innate ideas, which were precisely what made objections easy for empiricism. We refute it anthropologically by the simple exhibition of how all necessity in our cognition is really determined only through the forms.

Human power of cognition is limited through its sensibility in two ways, first in that the content of its cognition is given in sensation by an external influence merely accidental to its inner essence; second in that it possesses within itself obscure representations. Through the former it is bound to the condition that a law foreign to it supplies cognitions to it only in part, and it therefore can never arrive at a closed whole of its cognition. The rationalist, who presupposes an independent reason which determines for itself the law of its cognizing also with respect to content, demands, on the contrary, the law: the part should subsist only through the whole, and not the whole first come together through

[p. 67]

parts, whereas in our cognition, with the continuity and infinity of the forms of our intuition, every whole subsists immediately only ever through its parts; it demands a *forma substantialis*, a form to which essence belongs, after the image of organization, whereas in our cognition subsistence belongs only ever to matter, and form, although the necessary, attains to application only through matter. Our positive cognition knows no other law than the mathematical one of the side-by-side ordering of manifold parts into the whole, and only the ideal view of reflection, which proceeds from the original unity, can reverse this order, but only through negative forms.

Second, just like cognizing in general, our self-cognition too is limited. We cannot even survey the whole of our own cognition, our transcendental apperception, at one glance, but inner sense perceives only the liveliest alterations in our inner being, while the most remains obscure to us. We find this peculiarity of our reason especially in the relation of the understanding to the power of judgment in reflection. If we want a survey of the whole of our cognition, we cannot grasp the totality of our world in one glance of intuition, but are referred to the universality of separated forms in concepts and rules, where it still remains accidental whether and which objects the power of judgment finds in sensible intuition that stand under the universal. In opposition to this organization we can think a reason which would survey the whole fund of its truth, its transcendental apperception, without obscurity, for which

[p. 68]

the whole of its cognition would be an intuition, and which would not first need, as we do, to guess the law of necessity of its cognition through reflection. Such a reason would need no discursive understanding; it would be a purely intuitive faculty, its cognition would be intellectual intuition. The law of our truth, the unity of transcendental apperception, which we must first seek laboriously, would lie open to it at one glance; its cognition would be the archetype of truth, of which our understanding possesses only a copy. We can therefore best make clear to ourselves figuratively the relation of our transcendental apperception to the systematic cognition of reflection by the relation of this *intellectus archetypus* to our *intellectus ectypus*. But it is an error when rationalists in philosophy would impute to us ourselves this intellectual intuition and its absolute knowledge, for this would require the annihilation of obscure representing in general.

The principle of all theoretical explanations of our reflected cognizing is the relation of our original formal apperception to material consciousness, and the incompleteness of the previous theories lies in this, that one did not grasp the essence of this formal apperception. Whoever knows Fichte’s *Doctrine of Science* can easily find that with the opposition of his I = I and I = Not-I he sought precisely this relation of formal unity to material consciousness, but substantiated this unity subjectively, and afterwards wanted rationalistically to obtain everything through it alone. When Schelling objects against Kant’s separation of empirical and pure cognizing *a priori* that in the end the whole of our cognition nevertheless stands under a law of necessity, he has our

[p. 69]

transcendental apperception in view, but overlooks (because he postulates intellectual intuition) that this can be observed only through those separations and in them. Schelling has our formal apperception in view when in the copula of A is A he wants to exhibit his absolute identity, but he fails to recognize its original emptiness, in that he wants to see in it not only the form of unity and necessity, *systematically*, but also the essence of his absolute reason, or of the All-One, as it were *physically*.

[p. 70]

### Third Chapter.

### First Development of the Theory of Reason.

#### §. 96.

A theory of our cognizing is possible only if we first know all the immediate peculiarities of our human reason, which cannot be derived from any others but contain the elements of all experience. These we have so far put together. 1) The rationality of our cognition expresses itself through the original formal and transcendental apperception in it; 2) our rational cognition is, however, limited in that it receives all content of cognition only with the help of sense, as a modification of its basic activity; 3) to this there is added the particular relation of pure self-consciousness.

#### a) The Pure Self-Consciousness, Inner Sense, and Reflection.

#### §. 97.

Our highest presupposition consists in this, that to reason there belongs an original and unique self-activity of consciousness, which is the higher faculty of cognition in *immediate cognition* (just as voluntariness is in mediate, repeating reflection), and which our whole power of cognition

[p. 71]

itself is. In the *one* activity of this faculty all our consciousness, however manifold it may seem, must be comprehended and combined. This one activity underlies every empirical consciousness, but of itself adds only the form of unity and necessity, and expects from elsewhere all its material determinations, through which it comes to actual cognizing. These are then of three kinds: 1) original material determinations of formal apperception from the essence of reason, or *cognitions a priori*. 2) Empirical material determinations through sense in sensation, or *sense intuition*. 3) Immediate material determination of transcendental apperception, or *pure self-consciousness*.

The first material determination of my cognizing is pure self-consciousness. If I think away, from any state of my empirical consciousness, all the determinations by which it is distinguished from others, there then remains in every such state the pure feeling of my existence, as a consciousness that would accompany every other in me. Our power of cognition is therefore immediately determined as a faculty of being conscious of itself. We must assume that along with reason there originally belongs to us a faculty of being immediately conscious of ourselves; a faculty with regard to which there can no longer be any question of explanation, since inner experience shows no composition of its organization any more, its expression appears as wholly simple, and so it is given along with all reflection, for inner sense, as a formal basic consciousness.

[p. 72]

This consciousness of my existence is, however, also the only immediate material that we have in our cognition; every other is first given through sense. Were the whole material determination of cognition already given to us together with pure self-consciousness, we should have neither sense intuition nor formal apperception, but only a necessary intuition of reason. There would then be for our reason neither universality nor combination; the difference between analytic and synthetic unity would be abolished; everything would be one absolute unity, for which, however, we can think no content. This explains the course of thought of every one-sided rationalism, which wants to begin with the I or with intelligence. We come thereby once more to the idea of an intellectually intuiting reason, whose image we needed in order to think the whole of our transcendental apperception, which in this way does not come to consciousness in reflection. According to our organization, truth seems to us to lie, as it were, objectively outside our reason, in that it is something that we can never bring wholly into our power. This happens, however, only by analogy with an optical deception, in that, entangled in reflection, we take our faculty of reflection for our whole inner being, fail to recognize that immediate cognition of reason, and project its laws outward into the objects. Whoever knows the right relations sees, on the contrary, that truth is for us at first something wholly subjective, the immediate constitution of transcendental apperception.

We already know of pure self-consciousness (according to §. 25) that it is not cognition but only a

[p. 73]

pure feeling of my existence, as a quite particular kind of formal consciousness, such as belongs to reflection at every moment, but which nevertheless must always first be kindled through empirical material determinations of inner sense intuition in order to become cognition. Thereby our self-cognition, and with it all our cognition, became bound to inner sense. Yet pure self-consciousness is not mere form; rather it is an immediate material determination of our cognition that we are at all times conscious of our own existence as soon as any consciousness of ours is aroused. This matter of pure self-consciousness reflection grasps through the representation, comparable to no other, of the relation of a thing to itself, and so expresses *I am* as a judgment without determination of time, according to the mere category of cause of the activities that inner sense shows.

This consciousness can, to be sure, show itself only through the single intuition of inner sense, as form in it, from which it borrows its determination of time. But in that it falls into the original formal apperception, it prepares the *standpoint of reflection*, which can raise itself above the singularity of sense, because it thus determines the one and the same object of every inner perception, and with this the *unity of all reflection*, as the *thoroughgoing unity of all inner perception*.

[p. 74]

#### b) The Original Formal Apperception.

#### §. 98.

Our reason is limited to this, that it possesses only a formal basic consciousness, which is brought to cognition of the world only through an outer sense, and to self-cognition through an inner sense. The supreme law of our cognizing reason is the union of everything material in individual cognition in one formal consciousness, into immediate transcendental cognition of reason. From this we obtain the following first rules of the theory of reason.

1) *Necessity and unity are the first concepts and universal laws of our reason.* Both, namely, are nothing but the character of the rationality of a power of cognition, which expresses itself, precisely in the emptiness of our basic consciousness, through the original formal apperception.

2) *The original formal apperception we must become conscious of through analytic and synthetic unity.* Our actual cognition arises in this way, that individual material cognition is added to formal apperception; of the latter we cannot become conscious by itself, because it is nothing but the condition of any material to be given, but as soon as matter of cognition is actually given, formal apperception must cling to it and show itself in it. From this there follow the two supreme laws of its appearance before consciousness. The individual material cognition is necessarily added, in the unity of basic consciousness, to the other; so there arises *formal*

[p. 75]

*determination of material consciousness* as combination or synthetic unity. Every material cognition by itself lies, however, also in formal apperception; thereby there arises *material determination of formal apperception* as analytic unity or the universal.

3) *All apodictic relations in our cognition must consist in synthetic unity, and can be grasped by reflection only through analytic unity.* The only thing that is determined by the form of basic consciousness is necessary unity as formal determination of material cognition, that is, combination. Now the apodictic was that which must belong to every human reason in cognition immediately, as to the others; this therefore always has the form of a combination. Reflection, however, can grasp formal apperception itself, with its necessity, only through its material determinations; it can therefore become conscious of the apodictic character of cognition only by means of the representation of the universal. For if through separation some problematic partial representation remains lying in consciousness alone with its matter, it still always lies here together with the adhering formal apperception, and this gives it the form of analytic unity, or of the logical principle of determinability. This analytic unity by itself is, however, empty, because it adds to the individual content nothing but the relation to apodicticity. From this it follows, then:

4) *All re-consciousness of apodictic cognitions is possible only through combination of universal representations, through combination of*

[p. 76]

*concepts, but this was cognized in judgment.* (§. 48.)

5) *All cognition a priori is original and thoroughgoing material determination of formal apperception; it is necessary and universal.* (§. 63.) The apodictic, or the subjectively universally valid, in reason must belong to it along with its formal apperception; it must therefore always be formal, like this source of its unity and necessity itself. Apodicticity is therefore original material determination of formal apperception; the necessary determination of any cognition whatever (§. 63), on the other hand, is given through the place which belongs to it, by virtue of formal apperception, in the unity of the transcendental whole of cognition. Every individual cognition is a material determination of transcendental apperception, and gives a material determination of the formal; but not every one is an *original material determination*, for that requires that it be given through the essence of reason itself, and so belong to its unchangeable, persistent, but for that very reason also always merely formal activities, which can no more subsist by themselves than formal apperception itself, but show themselves only on the occasion of sensible stimulations. These are the cognitions *a priori*. These can therefore arise only in that, with the transcendental understanding as faculty of the original formal apperception, other original faculties of reason come together, which then, as soon as the activity of reason has once been aroused, give it thoroughgoing material determinations. Thus we shall find that all cognition *a priori* arises only either from the forms

[p. 77]

of the limitation of reason through sense, or from the original determination of reason as practical reason. With this we have, then, theoretically derived again all the relations of §. 59–63.

#### c) The Supreme Relation in Cognition.

#### §. 99.

The investigation of reflection already showed (§. 63) that the supreme relation of our cognition corresponds to the *forms of syllogism*. The necessity of the whole of experience could be cognized only at the place of the conclusion, in that we subordinated the merely assertoric content of perceptions to the apodictic worth of universal and necessary laws. We now see how this relation originates in reason; it is the consequence of the emptiness of its apodictic basic consciousness and of the contingency of every material consciousness for the individual reason.

There lies in the essence of our reason a difference of transcendental understanding, power of judgment, and reason, wholly analogous to the logical difference that we know, in that the latter repeats the first relations only for apprehension. To the transcendental understanding belongs the original formal apperception, to the power of judgment the falling of all material consciousness into this form, and to reason the whole of transcendental apperception.

Every cognition must have, in the completed consciousness of reason, a universally valid worth, by virtue

[p. 78]

of its transcendental apperception. But as we become conscious of cognition, there is contained, among the three upper faculties of cognition, first in the understanding a merely formal apperception, against which the particular, given, material consciousness is first determined by the power of judgment, and then can be grasped by reason only according to the relation of apodicticity. The understanding gives a *universal condition*, under which for the power of judgment every *conditioned* of sense stands, so that the *determination of the conditioned through the condition*, which belongs to reason, must always be possible. The material apperception, which first procures an object for cognition, is given only empirically, but always under the condition of the formal apperception of the understanding. Every *whole of cognition*, whose necessity we want to cognize, must therefore be grasped according to these three moments. Thus the differences of the problematic, assertoric and apodictic designate these three moments for the apprehension of analytic unity; the differences of the categorical, hypothetical and divisive the same moments for the apprehension of synthetic unity.

This agreement of the form of syllogism with the first and supreme organization of our reason is an important regulative for all speculation, in that all science from mere reason must attach itself to these forms, especially in that part of philosophy which arises from ideas and is exempt from the laws of mathematics, for here the idea is always given by itself as form, as the universal, as major premise, against which nature as object of experience first

[p. 79]

must enter into the minor premise, in order then, in the place of the conclusion, to determine the content of the science.

#### §. 100.

The cognition *a priori* and its principle can consist only in thoroughgoing material determinations of the formal basic consciousness, but in the manner in which this material determination forms itself in reason, the difference of the three upper faculties repeats itself again.

The understanding was the faculty of the original formal apperception itself; this, however, as basic consciousness of unity and necessity, was the condition under which every material cognition stands. There is, then, an independent cognition *a priori* of the understanding, in which this basic consciousness comes to consciousness as the formal condition of all material cognition given and to be given through sense. This independent cognition *a priori* of the understanding contains, accordingly, all principles of unity in our cognition; to it must belong all forms of the mathematical, intuitive unity, of the analytic, logical unity, and of the synthetic unity in category and idea; and it becomes the most extensive task of deduction to derive all those forms from the relation of sensible material to formal basic consciousness in the unity of transcendental apperception.

The peculiar constitution of the power of judgment was the contingency of material consciousness for the immediate cognition of reason. If, therefore, there are to be peculiar principles *a priori* which belong to the power of judgment,

[p. 80]

then this contingency, as an original limitation of formal apperception, must be the source of them.
