Every material cognition must necessarily accord with the unity and lawfulness of reason, because it is only a modification of its one basic activity; but the individual matter of sensible cognition does not fall to us according to the relations of this unity and lawfulness, but in contingent isolation into perception; the law of formal apperception of the understanding and the singularity of intuition stand separated before my inner view, and thereby the agreement of what is contingently given with the law of unity can be judged, as it were in subordination under an inexpressible major premise, in a free manner according to maxims of the power of judgment, which in their highest independence give the aesthetic ideas of the beautiful and the sublime.

Reason is the faculty of the whole of immediate cognition. A thoroughgoing original determination of our basic consciousness, which, besides the limitations of sense, takes place already from the essence of reason itself, will therefore belong to this immediate reason itself, and must lay claim to the highest reality in our essence, independently of the barriers of sense. Such a one is the determination of principles *a priori* through the idea of absolute worth, which arises from the essence of reason as a faculty of taking an interest.

We obtain hereby, then, retrospectively, for all deduction of principles *a priori* from the theory, the first guiding ideas. All cognition *a priori* must either

[p. 81]

under the idea of necessary lawfulness in the existence of things, or under the idea of beauty, or under the idea of the highest good.

#### §. 101.

In the logical doctrine of truth and error, assertion is found, with its two kinds, holding-to-be-true and holding-to-be-false, as the activity of the inner apprehension of a cognition before reflection. We further call this assertion *conviction* when we proceed lawfully according to the form in order to arrive at it, *persuasion* when this manner of procedure is false. (We can here often be only persuaded of truth, like the surveyor who has learned by rote the formulas according to which he computes, or the common man who learns his religion from the catechism, but convinced of what is false, like the mathematician who computes his formulas himself but errs in the calculation, or the philosopher who errs in his speculation, for calculation and speculation are here the only correct manners of procedure according to which we ought to seek truth.)

For conviction we now know three logical gradations belonging to reflection, which we designated as knowledge, opinion, and faith. (§. 82.) Knowledge led to complete certainty, opinion and faith only to subordinate kinds of a deficient certainty, in that for the observing reflection supplements were still lacking. Here we now have to do with immediate cognition itself; its character is thoroughgoing necessity, its relation to the individual

[p. 82]

faculties will nevertheless determine difference in apprehension, and thus different kinds of the immediate conviction of reason.

The most common manner of conviction in ordinary consciousness is that through *demonstration* or intuition, to which the peculiar manner of conviction of the understanding *through inference* attaches; both together constitute here *knowledge in the strictest sense*. Few of the principles *a priori* fall immediately into intuition; most belong only to deducible judgments and are a theme for reflection. However, the principles of the understanding are nothing but a form of unity and necessity which underlies sensible intuition and through which it is supplemented into experience; they are principles of necessity in experience; they only apply the material given in sensible intuition, in that they ascribe to it its necessary determination through formal apperception. Knowledge as the peculiar manner of conviction of the understanding therefore rests actually always on intuition. When it is asked whether we know something, that means nothing else than whether the truth of a cognition is grounded in the necessary connection of our sensible intuition; we then submit ourselves to the truth of this intuition and of the universal laws of its objects.

If, on the other hand, our reason has a conviction purely out of itself, then this can come to consciousness for us only in a law of the original formal apperception, which does not at all borrow its truth from those intuitions, and also is not grounded in their necessary connection, but it is to us only

[p. 83]

true for its own sake; it is the purest utterance of our innermost essence. Thus the source of pure respect and pure love lies in our innermost being, of which we can become conscious only in a wholly reflected holding-to-be-true without intuition. We call this peculiar manner of conviction of transcendental reason *pure faith of reason*.

Finally we have already found that independent power of judgment can become conscious of its complete peculiar certainty only through *feeling*, without a determinate concept. Such a holding-to-be-true, which is grounded neither on intuition nor on concept, could, according to the ordinary treatment of the matter, where one proceeds without anthropological deduction and asks the object alone about truth, be only a vacillation of conviction abandoned to superstition and without principle, which had to lie unrecognizably disguised in mystifications. I call the peculiar manner of conviction of transcendental power of judgment *intimation*.

These three manners of conviction have, then, in our mind the wholly equal degree of necessary certainty; the alleged sole validity of knowledge cannot deceive us; there are determinate objects of knowledge, one in which we only have faith, and a good deal that we are able only to intimate. The prejudice in favor of knowledge arises only from aesthetic distinctness, from the self-evidence and common intelligibility of sense intuition, which makes no difference in thoroughness. Far from pure faith of reason being a less certain holding-to-be-true than knowledge, it is precisely the firmest that we have, in that it springs purely from the essence

[p. 84]

of reason. We should actually have no knowledge at all if not already an element of the faith of reason, a conviction from mere reason without sense, were in it. Intimation also belongs to the same degree of certainty, of conviction, even though it must renounce completeness with regard to the determination of its object. It is only a relative holding-to-be-true of the relation of faith to knowledge, and cannot count as complete, in that it springs precisely from the consciousness of the barriers of our essence. We know, however, that no human reason will succeed in the *salto mortale* out of itself to dissolve the secrets of intimation. For that is the summit of human wisdom: to know what we do not know, and what we also cannot know without first having our own essence transformed.

#### d) Determination of the Object through Cognition a priori.

#### §. 102.

In his first proof that we do not cognize things through sense intuitions as they are in themselves (*Crit. of Pure Reason*, Aesthetic), Kant presupposes the impossibility of cognizing things in themselves through pure intuition, or in general through cognitions *a priori*, because we thereby lay claim to determining the object without its being given to us as present in cognition. We must rather say, however, if there are things whose existence in itself is subject to universal laws

[p. 85]

as we find it in nature, then there may very well also be a reason, like ours, which anticipates this law before it knows all cases of application. The error of the Kantian presupposition lies here again in his deficient representation of objective validity in our cognition. He found the concept of objective validity in the determination of the object in a necessary cognition, but placed its origin in the causal relation of the object, as that which affects, to sensation. To this there corresponds also quite his manner of deducing, e.g., the categories. He presupposes the objective validity, or empirical reality, of the objects of sense intuition as unquestioned, and believes that he now has only to prove the equal rights of what is given *a priori*. For the proof he then showed that without the categories we should be quite unable to cognize the objective validity of those intuitions, that we, e.g., cognize succession of things, and not mere sequence of our representations, only in this, that the one is *through* the other, according to the category of causality, that we can call things simultaneous only when they are *with* one another through interaction. However correct the latter may be, the intention of the whole exposition is nevertheless made faulty by the misunderstanding of what is objectively valid. Objective validity is not something that we first add to it mediately in the history of our representing, but it lies immediately in every cognitive activity. Those gradations of validity, to which the understanding first adds necessity, belong on the contrary only to subjective validity; they are stages of re-observation, which in the necessity of reflection is completed only so far as we are able to complete it.

[p. 86]

We can specify the determination of the object in our cognition still more closely here by comparison of its rational form. The object is cognized through the whole of our immediate cognition. If, then, objective validity is asked about, we may therewith compare neither individual sense intuitions nor individual forms of thought; these broken parts of observation through inner sense and reflection differ only according to subjective relations.—We must set over against the object solely the *complete whole of our cognition*, as it is immediately in reason. Objective validity belongs, then, neither to intuiting nor to thinking taken by itself, but to each only according to its relation to the whole of transcendental apperception. Through this latter alone does our reason properly cognize. We can subjectively dissect our cognition well enough, into that which is in it through its original formal apperception, as universal and necessary law, and that which is in it only through fulfilling intuition; we can also ask how the one or the other contributes to the determination of the object for my cognition, where one part determines it as actual, the other as possible, the third as necessary: but *their objective validity belongs altogether solely to the closed whole of transcendental apperception*.

This last is here the most important rule of all metaphysical assessments. There are indeed in our cognitions certain determinations of the object *a priori* through analytic unity, others through synthetic unity, but in these divisions we may

[p. 87]

not relate the *validity* of cognition to the object. A piece of reasoning in which objective validity is derived from a causal relation of the object to cognition always has the error that we reject the determination of the object *a priori*, and want, on the contrary, to ground the validity of sense intuition in its isolation from the whole of cognition on what affects in sensation. We found this causal relation inadmissible right from the start, and see now that the judging of the objective validity of cognition must absolutely be the last result of all speculation, for only after the whole artifice of inner re-observation through reflection has succeeded, i.e., after we have completed our speculation, does the whole of our transcendental apperception lie (as far as is possible) before our own inner view, and only to this does the object of cognition correspond. We must first have gone through all the fragments of sensing, fantasizing, inventing and thinking, in order to learn to understand the inner unity of our cognizing, but this alone makes our cognition properly, it alone has the object. This is, then, the riddle of transcendental truth, which seeks agreement with the object; only for the whole of transcendental apperception does this have meaning at all; everything else, the ordinary true or false in our representations, seeks only a rule of inner re-observation. All our speculation lets itself be reduced to the one question about the validity of our cognition and the reality of its objects, and we can say, this alone interests us in all philosophizing,

[p. 88]

but we may not begin with an answer to this question; we must first come to know very much, which at the beginning we did not at all demand to know, before we arrive at the one sought-for theme, because we must first know all rules of empirical truth before a judgment about transcendental truth can be obtained.

[p. 89]

### Second Section.

### Development of the Individual Forms of Unity in Our Cognitions.

#### General Survey.

#### §. 103.

The supreme relation in our cognizing reason was that of syllogism, or of the original formal, material, and transcendental apperception. We can also call this the relation of the *pure form*, of the *fulfillment* of the form and of the *fulfilled form*, in that the object in every whole of cognition is determined only as fulfilled form, to which formal apperception determines only the pure form, the material apperception its fulfillment (thus, e.g., the matter falls in space and time, or the case under the rule). That, however, which in this relation constitutes rationality was the original formal apperception, the basic consciousness of unity and necessity; and what constitutes the rationality of cognition in the particular organization of this reason (e.g., as finite or as

[p. 90]

practical reason) were the original and thoroughgoing material determinations of its formal apperception through what is particular to its inner organization, i.e., the cognition *a priori* peculiar to it.

A theory of our reason has, then, to show how its cognitions *a priori* spring from the subjective relations of its organization, i.e., it is the deduction of all principles *a priori* demanded above (§. 86). For this we now know already that it must develop itself according to the three systems of understanding, reason, and power of judgment, in that we see how formal apperception is determined materially through sense, the practical faculties, or the mere contingency of material consciousness.

Of the elements of this theory we have so far learned completely the first, that of sense to formal apperception; the systematic deduction of all principles *a priori* belonging to the understanding must therefore also be in our power.

I take as known from our logical investigations that the philosopher by his art does not want to produce, as a Mystagogue, secrets of new wisdom which would be wholly invisible to the unphilosophical view, that he cannot create his truths but can only exhibit those that are at all times present in human reason; he is no ποιητὴς τῆς ἀληθείας [maker of truth], but his business is only the ἀνάμνησις [recollection] of Plato. Our theory has therefore to do only with this: to show, by deduction, how the forms of cognition actually present in us spring in our mind. If the supreme elements of the theory are once given here, then the development is properly a combinatorial artifice, which follows, as it were as a check of the calculation of

[p. 91]

the preceding analysis. The derived forms arise only through composition of the first elements, and the test consists in this, that the combination gives no meaningless empty compartments, and yet also represents completely all the moments that show themselves in inner experience. Yet this combining is not so unconscious a mechanical play as the development of algebraic formulas, but one must always keep in mind the meaning of each individual sign, because the combination here contains no empty juxtaposition of the individual elements, but often also a determining of the one and the other in and through each other.

We call reason *speculative reason* in so far as its cognition is given merely through the reciprocal determination of formal and material apperception, i.e., through the reciprocal determination of sense and its basic consciousness of unity and necessity. For this, then, the highest elements for the combination are:

1) For immediate cognition.

a) material cognition,

b) original formal apperception.

2) For inner apprehension.

a) Apprehension through inner sense.

b) Apprehension by reflection.

The combination gives the following:

The cognition grasped through inner sense is *intuition*, which is *either* individual material cognition as *sense intuition*, which becomes *historical science*,

[p. 92]

*or* the first formal determination of material cognition, *pure intuition*, which becomes *mathematics*.

Reflection grasps the relation of material and formal cognition in transcendental apperception; the cognition grasped through reflection is *thought* cognition, which before consciousness must be

*either* materially determined formal apperception, *analytic unity, logical thinking*, which as a science becomes *logic*,

*or* formal determination in material apperception, *synthetic unity, transcendental thinking*, which as a science becomes *speculative metaphysics*.

Thus our mind arrives at these four ways of cognizing of speculative reason, which we shall call the *four moments of speculative cognition*. Self-observation, however, becomes complete only through reflection, that is, in thinking; consequently the moments of intuition too stand under the condition of thinking; the pure intuition of mathematics is only the transition from empirical apprehension to complete apodictic consciousness, and the systematic form of logical thinking makes its claims upon every way of cognizing, hence the historical, mathematical and philosophical form of the system.

Further, complete self-observation must bring to consciousness, step by step, the determination of all material consciousness through formal apperception in the transcendental whole of cognition; thus the first threefold division recurs here at the very top, always:

[p. 93]

empty form, fulfillment of the form, and fulfilled form. In the history of our life, material cognition, through contingent sensible stimulation, falls only little by little into formal apperception, so that the formal condition and the conditioned material are apprehended side by side. Hence for reflected cognition there must be three different standpoints, those of the understanding, of the power of judgment and of reason, from which we can grasp the relation of original formal apperception to material apperception. From the standpoint of the understanding, formal apperception is the condition of all given material cognition, by which the latter is determined with necessity; this yields the *principles a priori of the natural view of things*, of the possibility of experience.

Here reflection proceeds from the given material cognition and adds to it the law of unity; if, on the other hand, it grasps from the standpoint of reason the law of the whole of transcendental apperception, then unity and necessity are thought as the condition of all material of cognition that may ever be given, and we raise ourselves above ourselves in the *ideal view of things*, according to the highest principles of unity.

Thirdly, from the standpoint of the power of judgment the law of formal apperception as the condition for all material cognition is so applied that here material cognition, in the contingency of its being given, becomes the determining factor for the law. This yields the *regulative maxims of the power of judgment*, in which the law of unity and necessity is applied only methodically to induction.

[p. 94]

In all our speculative cognition, therefore, the *threefold division* of formal, material and transcendental apperception, and the *fourfold division* of apprehension, pure and empirical intuition, logical and transcendental thinking, must recur, whereby in the end thinking is always superior to intuiting, but a *mediate representation* always demands a repetition of consciousness, since inner sense shows immediately only the single material, in which reflection, through separation, first becomes aware of the original form.

[p. 95]

### First Division.

Deduction of the Principles for the Doctrine of Nature, or the Unity of the Understanding in the Essence of Things.

### First Chapter.

### The Forms of Cognizing.

#### 1) The Empirical Intuition.

#### §. 104.

The most essential feature of the standpoint of the understanding was the starting out from *given material cognition*, for which formal apperception is to be determined as the condition. Here, then, empirical intuition is the first.

The stumbling block of every system of nature undertaken without critique is the opposition of matter and mind. We see here the attempt constantly repeated to draw our whole cognition of nature together into one theory. Some try to subject the mind to matter, life to death, others want to subject matter

[p. 96]

to the mind, granting reality only to the living; still others seek to unite both in a third, true essence of things, in whose success our philosophers of nature still deceive themselves today. But none of these attempts can lay claim to real explanation, for the organization of our reason, in the manner in which it receives the material of its cognition, makes a double view of nature, a material and a spiritual view of the world side by side, unavoidable for it. We receive the material of our cognition through sense, but here we possess inner and outer sense as two quite differently organized faculties side by side. Outer sensation supplies a sense intuition which falls immediately into formal apperception, and thereby, alongside pure self-consciousness, modifies transcendental apperception. Inner sensation, on the other hand, supplies a sense intuition which falls first into pure self-consciousness, and only through this modifies transcendental apperception. Accordingly the formal determination of outer sense intuition, space, falls at once into the intuition, whereas the formal determination of inner sense intuition, self-consciousness, can be grasped only through reflection.

#### 2) The Pure Intuition.

#### §. 105.

The pure intuition of the spatial and the temporal belonged to productive imagination, and was characterized by containing an intuitive objective synthetic unity, whose rules we from the individual demonstration

[p. 97]

pronounce at once with universality and necessity. Here it becomes clear how we arrive at it. All material consciousness falls together in one basic consciousness; the formal determination of it must therefore begin to show itself already before inner sense, i.e., as intuition.

We begin with it to apprehend cognition according to relations of transcendental apperception; the relation of the empty form, of the fulfillment of the form, and of the fulfilled form must therefore already manifest itself here. So it does. Kant’s pure sensibility, the faculty of intuition of space and time *in abstracto* as empty forms of what is side by side and successive, corresponds to the understanding; in the voluntary synthesis of productive imagination, through which optical deception became possible (§. 40 and 93), the power of judgment shows itself, which constructs the individual intuitions into that form; and finally the underlying whole of mathematical intuition (§. 40.) belongs to the transcendental apperception of reason.

Accordingly we can compare most determinately how the mathematical intuition of productive imagination makes the transition from intuiting to the reflected self-observation of thinking. Particularly remarkable here is the relation of voluntary productive imagination to the logical power of judgment. According to the transcendental ground, in the immediate cognition of reason productive imagination and power of judgment are quite one and the same; only that the same moment of unity and combination in our representations can at first be grasped intuitively, but afterwards grasped again only in concepts. Hence the great kinship of both

[p. 98]

faculties in anthropology. Both unite in the schematism of concepts, and the judging of the beautiful is the property of the one as of the other; taste is the freest power of judgment, genius the strongest productive imagination.

#### 3) Logical Thinking.

#### §. 106.

Logical thinking comes (according to §. 103.) into our mind through this, that in the complete self-observation of reflection we can grasp the material of cognition only through material determinations of formal apperception. Hereby the supreme peculiar relation of logical thinking is determined as that of problematic, assertoric and apodictic representation, in that here the logical understanding, in the problematic representation of concept, rule and principle, grasps formal apperception in its material determinations as condition, the logical power of judgment, in assertions, subject, case and theorem, subordinates what is conditioned in material cognition, and finally logical reason, according to the law of transcendental apperception, in judgment, inference and system, determines the conditioned apodictically through the condition.

But since we need this progress from the assertoric, through the problematic, to the apodictic for all apprehension of the relations of transcendental apperception, all the other moments of perception, pure intuition and combination must at the same time be repeated along with it.

[p. 99]

The repetition of the moment of pure intuition for logical thinking yields the subordination of the *homogeneous* particular under a *universal* of the problematic representation, the subordination of the unity, plurality and totality of the subjects under a concept, of the cases under a rule, of the theorems under a principle, the relation of the infinite *sphere* of every concept.

The repetition of the moment of empirical intuition for logical thinking yields the mediate representation of material cognition through the material determinations of formal apperception in *affirmation, negation and logical disjunction*, in that some real element of material cognition is thought, through affirmation according to its relation to formal apperception, through negation or opposition according to its relation to some other material of cognition, and through logical disjunction with its opposite according to its relation to the whole of transcendental apperception in general.

Finally the repetition of the moment of thought synthetic unity makes itself felt in the logical distinction of the categorical, hypothetical and disjunctive, of logical ordering-in, subordination and co-ordination in judgment, inference and system.

We thus find again here progressively, for logical thinking, all the moments which offered themselves above (§. 48 and 49) regressively for theoretical derivation.

[p. 100]

#### 4) Transcendental Thinking.

#### §. 107.

Transcendental thinking, or the synthesis of reflection, is to come into our mind (according to §. 103.) through this, that complete self-observation can become aware of formal apperception only through formal determinations in material cognition; these formal determinations are, secondly, to be *thought* (and not merely intuited), so that the determination of transcendental apperception may be reached, and thirdly we want here to present the forms of synthesis for the *unity of the understanding* as they show themselves when we proceed from the *apprehension* of one material cognition to the *comprehension* of several in the same formal apperception.

Hereby the difference of combination in one another, through one another, and with one another, as categorical, hypothetical and divisive synthesis, is determined as the basic relation of transcendental thinking, in that the whole of cognition here contains the *necessary side-by-side ordering* of everything material in the original formal apperception, which however we can grasp only by thinking, first, the *ordering-in* of the individual material cognition into the basic consciousness, then the dependence of the one on the other, *the being-determined of the one by the other* in the original combination, and finally by determining this dependence of the parts on one another in a dynamic whole as reciprocal.

[p. 101]

The repetition of the moment of pure intuition for transcendental thinking yields the representation of magnitude through thinking (in contrast to intuition). Here intuitive combination as *composition*, in which the manifold comes together only contingently, stands over against the *merely thinkable* synthesis of *necessary connection*. The thinking of composition is the representation of *totality*, or of *measured* magnitude, to which, as a whole of cognition, we can attain only by proceeding from the apprehension of a single material cognition of a *named unity*, and, in the comprehension of several material cognitions of the *plurality* of the parts, determining these as the conditioned through the condition of unity as the measure.

For the repetition of the moment of empirical intuition, apprehension here gives the representation of a reality, but comprehension the representation of the *finitude* or limitedness of every given reality, which we must think through the relation of one reality to another by opposition, in that in the same all of reality each single one negates the other.

For the repetition of the moment of logical thinking, the apprehension of a single material here gives the representation of the *state* of a thing, the comprehension of several materials the *manifoldness of its states*, (or *alteration*) and the determination relative to transcendental apperception the representation of its necessary *essence*. (To understand the agreement

[p. 102]

of these kinds of representation with the modal determination of intellectual synthesis, one need only compare the definitions: the particularity of an object in regard to its state is its actuality; in regard to the manifoldness of its states in general, the sphere of its possibility; —in regard to its essence, its necessity.)

[p. 103]

### Second Chapter.

#### Determination of the Object through These Forms of Cognizing.

#### §. 108.

These forms of cognizing contain, in the transcendental whole of our cognition, our complete *cognition of nature*, which however we can grasp only in the separation of experience, mathematics and philosophy. Through knowledge of the individual forms we are in a position to show what each adds to the determination of the object; this then yields the deduction of the principles and immediately certain propositions of all natural science, according to the following survey.

1) Empirical intuition yields, *in immediately certain propositions the facts of experience* as material for the *description of nature*.

2) Pure intuition yields the *demonstrable axioms of pure mathematics*.

3) Analytic unity yields the *principles of logic*.

4) Synthetic unity yields the *merely deducible principles of metaphysical natural science*.

[p. 104]

We see at once also why, in the execution of these sciences, the system of the science of mere thinking, as philosophy, had to turn out categorical, that of pure intuition hypothetical, and that of empirical intuition conjunctive (§. 68.). For the science through mere thinking can come to consciousness in its principles only in original material determinations of formal apperception. These principles are therefore only deducible cognitions *a priori*, in which, with the material determination of formal apperception, thus with the moment of apprehension, we remain standing in the form, which is precisely the categorical relation of ordering-in (§. 107.) Secondly, mathematics cognizes intuitive formal determinations in given material of cognition; its moment is therefore constantly that of the comprehension of the one and the other in the form, so that a condition of comprehension *a priori* is given as the rule of many comprehensions, according to the hypothetical relation of subordination (§. 107.) Thirdly, empirical intuition supplies its content for the side-by-side ordering in transcendental apperception immediately; its system must therefore be the conjunctive one of side-by-side ordering, only that it cannot give itself the rule of combination, but must first expect it from philosophy and mathematics, to which in return it sets the problems of a theoretical natural science.

With regard to the actual deduction of the principles in the above table, we need not dwell here at greater length on the determination of the object through empirical intuition, since everything in it depends on the individual material of sensation, which concerning the difference of the

[p. 105]

outer and inner physics concerns the particular. For the other three moments, however, a deduction in detail is important, in order to be able to ward off one-sided claims, both empiricist and rationalist. Against the empiricists we thereby exhibit the ground of entitlement to apply certain cognitions *a priori*; against the rationalists, on the other hand, we show the unavoidable limits of all our theorizing and of all our reductions to unity.

The difficulties of our undertaking lie first in the entanglement of the individual moments in language, and then in the boundary of deduction and proof. The individual concepts, as they form themselves in language, usually contain entanglements of pure intuition, of analytic and synthetic determinations, and even the sharpest abstraction cannot present these separations quite completely. Kant believed he had accomplished more therein, with the isolation of his pure concepts of the understanding, than can really be achieved. Thus we must set up the concept of causality, with him, as a pure concept of the understanding, although we are unable to separate it from every purely sensible time-relation. The reason why I can think the community of two beings only as the interaction of both lies only in the time-relation of apprehension, in that, in order to represent the necessary connection of their existence, I can only start from the one, represent the state of the other as dependent on it, and then conversely go back from the other to the first. We thus look here always only to the predominantly determining moment. Secondly, the relation of deduction and proof, as different means of grounding judgments, has already been sufficiently discussed above (§. 70.); but here we must call attention to the fact that in

[p. 106]

metaphysical natural science the domain of deduction extends further than is often assumed. Much that one has here tried in vain to subject to a proof occurs precisely only as a principle in our reason, and can be protected only through deduction. To this belong the relation of inner and outer physics and, e.g., motion. Is motion a purely geometrical concept? At least the possibility of every Euclidean postulate presupposes a kind of it, the description of a path without regard to time and velocity. Kant calls it an empirical concept; but how, then, are *principles a priori* possible through this concept? Every alteration of the state of a matter has an external cause; now motion is alteration of position—why do we not here refer the law of causality to the continuation of the motion itself (of which we rather assume that it goes without saying, once the motion has begun) but only to the alteration of its direction and velocity? Precisely because being in motion is a state and not an alteration of the state of a matter. But why this latter? It is important to notice this wide sphere of deduction, in order to make quite clear to oneself the inadequacy of the usual demands made upon proof.

#### 1) Most General Concepts from the Determination of the Object through the Four Moments.

#### §. 109.

The most general metaphysical concepts in general must correspond to the moments of speculative cognitions

[p. 107]

in that they contain the determination of the object in them. This then yields the following table of primary concepts and their combinations.

The determination of the object through material cognition in general is the *What* of intuition, the *given of the object* (G). The determination of the object through the relation of material to formal apperception is the *How*, *being*, *existence* (S). Object with existence (SG) is *something*, without existence *nothing*. Existence with the given (GS) is *manner and mode*. The relation to formal apperception is represented through thinking; hence every material grasped by reflection in the concept becomes only a manner and mode of being.

The determination of the object through sensibility in general is *manifoldness* (M); the determination through formal apperception, *objective unity* (E). Manifoldness in unity (EM) gives the *particularity* of a thing, analytic unity; unity of the manifold gives (ME) *combination*, objective synthetic unity.

The combination of the given of the objects is (GE) *magnitude*; the particularity of a given in the unity of manifold objects is (GM) *quality*; the combination of the existence of things is *relation* (SE); the particularity of the existence of a thing in the unity of manifold objects is (SM) *modality*; which four concepts are called the *moments of the understanding*.

Quantity and quality are the moments of intuition, of the pure and the empirical; relation and modality

[p. 108]

the moments of thinking, of the transcendental and the logical.

Magnitude and relation are the moments of combination, as *composition* and *connection*; for both there holds a difference between the falling of a single material cognition into the formal and the falling-together of several in the form; the first gives *intensive magnitude* of the real for *coalition*, the other *extensive* magnitude of appearance for *aggregation*; the first gives *metaphysical connection* of the existence of things *a priori* in their subordination under laws, *nature of things*, the other *physical connection* of the existence of things with one another.

Quality and modality are the moments of the manifold and of analytic unity, hence their preeminent influence on logic.

#### 2) Determination of the Object *a priori* through Pure Intuition.

#### §. 110.

Pure intuition contains the intuitive formal determination of all material of cognition; the determination of the object in it therefore takes place in the following way.

a) Pure intuition must give us, for *combination* or quantitative composition, *series*, i.e., *a form of the order of things*, in which the things are given *with* one another but not *through* one another (as intuitive order of things, in contrast to the thought order through interaction).

[p. 109]

b) Let us see at once why these forms must be *continuous and infinite*. Infinity (the *indefinitum*) is the property of a magnitude that no whole is in it, continuity that no part in it is the last. Continuity is here a consequence of the thoroughgoing unity of the thoroughly manifold (MEG), hence a consequence of the first law of our cognition proceeding from the given material; infinity is (EMG) the consequence of the law according to which sense supplies us the material; it is a relation foreign to our reason, according to which it is affected to sensation, hence the subjective contingency of the single material cognition and the incompletability of its whole; whereas to every single given cognition there corresponds the *finite*, completely bounded and *discrete* part.

c) But why do we possess precisely the three series of the greater and smaller, of time and of space? Figuratively, for immediate intuition, we possess only the latter two; the series of the greater and smaller is a schematic abstraction for thinking, in which only what is common to the composition in both, conditioned by the successive apprehension in time, is brought out. This schematic series is therefore, quite in general, the object of combination or of the synthesis of composition; it becomes number-form through the problem of measuring, i.e., through the problem of *thinking* magnitudes.

The difference between time and space comes about according to the concepts existence and object. Time is the determination of the object through the relation of every material consciousness to formal apperception, a relation falling into intuition; from this it is clear why it becomes an

[p. 110]

*order of the existence* of things (§. 38. 4.), and why it belongs to sense in general, for this relation is the same for all sense intuition. Space, on the other hand, is the determination of the object through the falling-together of all the given manifold of outer sense intuition in formal apperception, so far as this formal determination still falls into intuition. Space therefore combines immediately the given of the objects, and belongs only to outer sense. For inner sense there can be no analogue to it, because there the manifold given does not fall together immediately in formal apperception, but first in pure self-consciousness.

But why has time only one, space three measurements? *Dimension* is, in a purely intuitive form, the law of the order of things in it, so that in the whole of the form the rule of a single possible and necessary arrangement must be contained, which however extends according to one or several dimensions, according as the law of arrangement is simple or composite.

What is peculiar to time is, first, that it has only one dimension, and then, that in it reality accrues only to the simple moment of the present; the past *is gone by*, the future *comes to be only* by being reached by the present; whereas in space the simple point is only the limit of all reality, and only the sum of all three dimensions, corporeal extension, comprises the real itself. This is derived as follows. Time has only one dimension because it corresponds to the relation, equal for every material cognition, to the unity of formal apperception, which

[p. 111]

makes a simple law of arrangement in it necessary, so that the progress from one moment to the other is possible only through *this determinate* intervening duration, and there is in time only one direction. But reality accrues solely to the simple moment of the present, because every other existence must first be combined with the “I am”, but this itself appears to me only in infinitely manifold states.

Space, on the other hand, recognizes no single correlate of the real, like the “I am” of existence, and the order of things is determined not through the simple relation to the form, but through the infinitely manifold relations of the sense intuitions among one another. Hence the three dimensions. Namely: 1) a dimension of infinitely manifold given objects; 2) a dimension of infinitely manifold relations of the single given. The first is the dimension of length, the other that of directions. The first by itself gives the continuous series of points in *one* direction, the straight line, whereas the second determines the possibility of the *curved* (manifoldness of the combination of two points), through the combination of a series of growing lengths with a series of changes of direction, which becomes possible through the continuous series of lines in the surface.

Through these two, however, no law of the necessary arrangement of things would yet be given, if there were not added 3) the dimension of the fixed relation to the standpoint of the observer himself present in space, whereby first the whole is closed. Hence it comes about, e.g., that as soon as in intuition the last relation, say the distance of the single objects

[p. 112]

from the eye, is not determined, only the conditions for the construction of objects according to two dimensions are found, for the picture plane of a painting or the surface of the vault of heaven. The distance of the plane and the rounding of the vault, however, are only arbitrary expedients of imagination, for strictly only the lines of direction, as legs of the angles of vision, are actually given, so that the place of each single star remains undetermined by a whole dimension, namely with regard to the choice of some point on the whole infinite straight line which indicates the direction from the eye to the star.

(This thoroughly subjective showing of how the intuitions of space and time arise in our mind convicts the treatment of these forms in Schelling’s philosophy of nature of many an error. Schelling wants, through the dynamic construction of matter, to develop the dimensions of space itself objectively (thus to subject them to a *proof*); this is false, for these forms altogether precede the possibility of matter, in that they are only filled by the latter, as the possibility of representing future time even now makes most evident. He also errs when, in the language and theory of his *Bruno*, in the derivation of the Keplerian laws, he equates the difference of the three dimensions with the supreme difference of the cognition of the finite, infinite and eternal; this we applied above (§. 105.) to mathematical intuition, whereas the dimensions rest on a particular relation which concerns only outer sense.)

d) Through the demonstrations from pure intuition pure mathematics develops as an apodictic science

[p. 113]

*a priori*. The division of this pure mathematics into arithmetic and geometry has been wrongly traced by Kästner and others to the difference of discrete and continuous magnitudes, by Schulze and others falsely to the difference of time and space. We must divide thus: The most general activity of productive imagination is combining, of which all other constructing activities are only species. The chief difference is here determined through *schematic* and *figurative* construction. Schematic construction is in general the *ordering* of the *theory of combinations*, of which the *summing of arithmetic* is only a particular species, namely the combining of *homogeneous* elements. Figurative construction concerns either space, for *geometry*, or time, for pure *chronometry*. That *reckoning* in arithmetic and *drawing* in geometry, however, then find preferentially the wider application, is because through the combining of equal parts in the *number-form* we bring magnitude in general to concepts, and hence by it alone can *measure*; on the other side, however, the pure form of time with its one dimension admits too little arbitrary construction. All figurative arbitrary construction therefore rests on *motion* in space, which as *transcendental motion*, where only the description of a space is regarded, underlies the postulates of geometry, as *phoronomic motion*, where the relation to time, i.e., its *velocity*, is also regarded, the principles of phoronomy, and finally as *dynamic motion*, where the moving force is also asked about, dynamics and mechanics. Geometry and pure phoro-

[p. 114]

nomy are still purely mathematical sciences; dynamics and mechanics contain an application of mathematics to the philosophy of nature.

From the anthropological elements indicated here we could furnish, for all these disciplines of pure mathematics, a deduction of their basic concepts and principles; but we prefer to leave this business here to a *philosophy of mathematics* of its own.

#### 3) Determination of the Object *a priori* through Analytic Unity.

#### §. 111.

The forms of analytic unity give us the logical principles and everything that depends on them. For this we have already had to supply the theory at length above, but saw at the same time that these analytic forms really contribute nothing to the extension of cognition, but are only in the service of reflection. They really lay claim to the determination of the object under the form of the concepts of reflection, in that they determine what is identical and different, agreeing or conflicting, what belongs to the inner or the outer of an object, to matter or form. But also with regard to these concepts we saw above (§. 57.) that they give no content of their own, but are only of instrumental use for self-observation in thinking. Here, finally, we have come to know two moments of speculative cognition, the thinking of qualities and modality, to which analytic unity lays special claims.

[p. 115]

1) The quality apprehended from intuition is repeated through the forms of affirmation and negation in thinking. The condition in the moment of quality is the manifoldness of the given. Here the particular is grasped immediately through *affirmation* as real; the synthetic determination of the one by the other in the falling-together in combination gives the *limitation of every given real*, as a part of the whole; the analytic determination of the one by the other in the manifold gives, from the form of the determinability of everything through each in the same formal apperception, *negation* and the opposite of a concept. If we therefore want to bring to concepts not only the *one* for itself, but the *one and the other*, the manifold, there offers itself to us the form of negation for the determination of the object; but this is a quite empty analytic form, with which nothing at all can be gained with regard to the determination of the object. This form of negation has nevertheless been applied very frequently in speculation with false hopes. The statement: A is not B, expresses to me only the analytic relation of the one to the other, when both are already given as manifold; instead of this, one seeks precisely to explain manifoldness theoretically through negation, and so to make oneself independent of sense with regard to the real and to get by through thinking alone, by defining the different through negations, helping oneself in synthetic sciences with logical disjunctions, and tracing manifoldness in general back to a dualism of nature, which is to be explained through the conflict of positive and negative principles. It is indeed

[p. 116]

in logic that the definition of a thing solely through its opposite is a mere nominal definition and not a real definition, yet one often thinks that in metaphysics one has brought a concept under one’s command by such a negative definition. One defines, e.g., alteration in time as a successive being and not-being of the states of a thing; with this correct nominal definition, however, nothing can be settled about the nature of the alterable; the alternation of being and not-being of the same state has no reality in itself and does not fall within observation, but alteration is positively the sequence of *this and other* states of the same thing, where the manifoldness is first awaited from sense. With regard to divisions we often find in logic the false assertion that only logical disjunction is complete division; it is rather just as much a mere nominal division, with which nothing is gained in itself; every real division can first be borrowed only from the synthetic conditions of the cognition to be divided, since only so is real difference of qualities cognized. The illusion for this supposedly positive use of negation lies in the confusion of the synthetic concept of the conflict of that which cannot be combined with the logical contradiction of a concept and its opposite, and in the confusion of the mathematical opposition of magnitudes both with the logical opposition of the positive and the negative, and also with the dynamical opposition of that which is comprehended in interaction. The latter has had a particularly harmful effect on the philosophy of nature. Every outer finite appearance is the product of conflicting powers, which reciprocally *limit* one another, (as positive parts

[p. 117]

in a dynamical whole,) of which, however, the one does not *merely negate* the other. Mathematically opposed magnitudes are then the magnitudes of these *products* of the one and the other power, each of which is measured by the *negative numbers* of the other, if the powers oppose one another only as cause of the increase and decrease of the homogeneous. But in order that such an opposition may become possible for us at all, we require a previously given purely sensible form of intuitions, in which a manifold of the *thoroughly homogeneous* becomes representable. This whole mode of representation can therefore find application only where all qualitative differences are reduced purely to quantitative diversities, i.e., in mathematical physics. Disciples of the philosophy of nature have, on the contrary, wished to apply this opposition, in its empty logical meaning, throughout the whole of nature, and Schelling himself errs in that he regards the one power of nature *only as the inhibiting one*, simply as the second, whereas both must first stand positively beside one another, each according to its own nature, before they can come into opposition by limiting one another.

His rule of the opposition of positive and negative principles is very serviceable when the point is to collect and order experiences with regard to determinate phenomena, e.g., those of organization. Here there is for the phenomenon a native positive power through which it itself subsists, e.g., the organizing principle of nature; this, however, is found on the whole always in conflict with other powers, foreign and external to this phenomenon, which with regard to it we can regard as the negative ones. But we must by no means forget how far the

[p. 118]

use of this language reaches, and that for theory nothing at all is said thereby. The history of nature appears to us through the interaction of physical powers, which limit one another and alter the states of the substances. Here it would, first, have no meaning at all to take the one power merely as the logical negation of the other, but, second, no phenomenon would come about either if the one were only mathematically opposed to the other; this happens only through the *dynamical opposition of the heterogeneous in interaction*. E.g., power of expansion and power of contraction are mathematically opposed to each other, but each has its positive essence for itself, for expansion is increase of volume and decrease of density, contraction is decrease of volume and increase of density. Through the conflict of the two, however, no phenomenon at all would come about, if, besides the homogeneity of the products of both, there did not take place a *heterogeneity of the law* according to which they act, if they did not act, e.g., according to different laws of spreading into the distance; for in the purely mathematical opposition the limitation yields only less of one of the two, a determinate expansion, which is just as much a determinate contraction, or even zero, if both powers are equal, but never a composition of both. Likewise there would be in general no history of the movable, if besides rectilinear approach or withdrawal there were not also oblique direction in space. For this reason Schelling’s exposition leads to the wholly unmathematical presupposition of regarding everything finite as a limited infinite; he has two infinite powers in conflict limit themselves together

[p. 119]

into the finite, which is self-contradictory. Least of all, however, can anything be gained in the inner nature of the mind by a merely mathematical opposition of indeterminate positive and negative powers, as is now so often attempted; for here the sway of mathematics is weaker, and all reaction takes place with qualitative differences of the heterogeneous in cognizing and willing.

Our principal proposition here is: manifoldness is in our cognition the first thing, which can never be merely thought, but is always borrowed from intuition; each *one and other* is given immediately for itself, and none can be reduced to the other, but can only be combined with the other in a *unity of the manifold*. Every quality has in our cognition its separate essence for itself, without being able to be made indifferent with another; negation, however, serves only reflection, in order, among manifold qualities already given, to think the one only in relation to the other.

2) The quantitative determination of analytic unity is the multiplicity of the homogeneous manifold in the sphere of every universal concept. There is therefore necessarily expressed in the sphere of every concept infinity and continuity as the universal law of magnitude. Infinitely many individual things are indefinitely possible as objects of every sphere, and the continuity of these spheres we express through the well-known logical laws of *homogeneity, specification and continuity of the logical forms*. Nothing can be so heterogeneous that it could not be coordinated in the sphere of some higher concept, and different things can never be thought so homogeneous that there could not

[p. 120]

still be thought something else between the two, with smaller differences from the one or the other. These laws are perfectly correct logical rules of the systematic formation of concepts, which under each law form a particular infinite sphere of real possibilities, but their claims also go only to the problematic representation of mere possibilities. The magnitude of the sphere of the possible under each law, e.g., of the plant and animal forms of our earth, is infinite and continuous, so that not only are there infinitely many species in general, but between any two determinate neighboring species infinitely many intermediate species are still possible, whereas the magnitude of the sphere of the actual under the same law is finite and discrete; there is only a determinate number of genera and species with regard to the actual objects under each concept or law. Here too the determination of the object through analytic unity is wholly empty, and belongs only to the thought-forms of reflection. For the problematic concept every given quality falls under the law of continuous intensive magnitude, and could also be thought greater or smaller, but for actual cognition it can occur in this or that case only under a determinate magnitude. We can therefore use those laws also only logically for the ordering of concepts, without making thereby claims upon nature itself that go beyond the worth of remote heuristic maxims, in that the diversity of things in nature fills not the continuous series of differences but only, by leaps, individual places of it, but also, because of the smaller differences possible to infinity, that which for us is not to be distinguished can be something different.

[p. 121]

3) *All our cognition is a relative one*, in which no object is cognized for itself as something simply inner, but always only one in relation to another, each thing only as it manifests itself. For all necessity arises for us from synthetic unity, (§. 98. 3.) and lies therefore only in the relation which combines the one with the other. Thus we cognize matter only through movement in the relation of the one toward the other, or in sensation in relation to the cognizing mind; the mind, however, we cognize only through its relation to the activities in which it at least manifests itself to itself, and God finally only in relation to the world, the world, however, through the relation of all things toward each. This relativity is the analytic expression of synthetic unity, but through its concepts of the inner and the outer we obtain as little a significant law for the essence of things as through negation and the continuity of the forms of concepts. The simply inner of a thing is its subsistence, its outer, on the other hand, is its state and the alternation of its states. Here our cognition always grasps only the alternation of states before intuition, the subsistence, on the other hand, is only the necessarily presupposed in the form of synthetic unity. We can grasp it immediately in no cognition, but can also dispense with it in none. Leibniz attempted the former in his monadology, in that he thought the utterance of the I in the thinking being showed something simply inner; we have shown, on the contrary, that this I also signifies only the *relation* of a thing to itself, where its subsistence is just as much presupposed elsewhere. Fichte and Schelling attempted conversely to hold fast the I as mere

[p. 122]

acting, nature only as productivity, in that they let the alternation of states be sufficient to itself, thus transformed the outer simply into an inner, or rather let it subsist without an inner, which, however, could conceal the contradiction of a relation without something that is related only through the obscurity of language. The illusion for this lies especially in our material view of the world, where the subsistence of the mass is the indistinguishable, the figureless, the infinitely divisible, but all figure and unity become possible only through outer combination in the forms of physical processes.

4) Modality is properly the moment of logical thinking; it compels us to reflection through the separation of the original form of excitability, as formal apperception, from the merely contingent excitation of the individual sensible-material cognition. This gave the peculiar distinction of logical thinking in the gradations of merely assertoric, problematic and apodictic representations, and this determines for us, for the determination of the object *a priori*, the conflict of form and matter. The complete subjective validity of our cognition we find only by ordering the individual content of existence under the universal and necessary form of law and determining it through this. Existence comes to us only from the individual assertion of sense, necessity only from the universal apodictic law of the understanding; each arises from its own subjective source of cognition, and the union of the two gives one of the most difficult views of the dispute between empiricism and rationalism. The modal determination of the object *a priori* through analytic unity

[p. 123]

gives the *metaphysical connection of the existence of things*, according to which all existence stands under *universal laws*, the universal becoming the form *in abstracto* as the complete ground of determination of the individual content alone actually given.

Where, then, does the principle of objective validity for our mind lie? In the matter or in the form? Universal laws, such as: All bodies are heavy, 2 + 2 = 4, Every alteration has a cause—are these true through the universal connection of their determinations, as we grasp them by speculation, or only through an induction in the essence of things, precisely because every individual case agrees with them? Is every individual body heavy because the rule holds: all bodies are heavy, or does the rule hold precisely because every individual body is heavy? The same thing is expressed less completely in the dispute of the Realists and Nominalists: whether reality belongs immediately to the universal concept for itself, or only to the individual object of its sphere, and to the concept only through the latter? The first is a rationalistic, the other an empirical presupposition. The proposition that all bodies are heavy has application and meaning, however, only if there really are bodies that stand under its condition; of these, however, each has its own existence; what, then, is the validity of the necessary law for itself, without the individual actual body, to signify; does not the law rather subsist only through those individual realities under it? That too is not well possible; were the individual cases first the ground of the validity of the rule, we could assert nothing with universality, for under no concept can we exhaust the totality of individual things; but we nevertheless

[p. 124]

have insight into many a truth in general; in this alone consists all our mathematical as well as philosophical speculation, only thereby can we speak of necessity at all. But what are those empty necessary forms, valid for themselves, to us then, the conditions of existence, which themselves do not exist? Just such an essence of things we call *nature*, in which the necessary lawfulness stands above all, and first imparts to each individual its determination under its form. The essence of things seems, therefore, here to depend on laws of nature, on an order of necessary but empty forms, which are the supreme grounds of determination of individual existence. Such a law is itself essenceless, but the immutably commanding, to which every being is subject—that is what we think under the name of *fate*, and so far as we cognize the essence of things as nature, in the validity of each individual universal rule, an immutable fate announces itself, according to the organization of our reason, to which every actual being, even the gods, is subject.

This conflict of form and matter is the nearest ground of the highest speculative dualism in older philosophy, which opposes to one another two independent primordial beings as principle of form and principle of matter, a figureless but all-figure-receptive original being and a figure-forming being, Ahriman and Ormuzd of Zoroaster, who then, according to this or that image, as matter and spirit, as death and life, as evil and good, as chaos and figure-forming νοῦς κοσμουργός, the Eros of Hesiod, as dark, figureless mass and forming light, as rest and motion, or however otherwise, enter into combat against one another. It would be the triumph

[p. 125]

of all rationalistic philosophy, if through its principle of form it could overcome all matter, and through form alone could ground all reality in the essence of things. Fichte ventured here a new step, in that he tried to degrade being, and to raise a validity of that to which no being belongs above all being, but he had to give up this absurd thought himself again; Schelling, on the contrary, still thinks to hold fast the form so long sought in vain as substance in his absolute identity, in that he gives reality only to the universal and to the forms of the organism; but as soon as the obscurities of language are removed, here too matter will again appear unovercome beside form.

How, then, are we to resolve this conflict of matter and form, of universality and necessity with individual existence? Through the above law of objective validity. (§. 102.) Every analytic understanding, which uses reflection, can arrive only at an analytic universality of its laws, and not at the synthetic totality of its intuition, but this separation concerns only moments of subjective validity and of re-observation. The objective validity of cognition belongs only to the undivided whole of transcendental apperception, neither to the empty form, nor to its fulfillment, but only to the whole of the fulfilled form. Neither the empty form of space and time, nor the mere fulfillment of them through sensation, but only the whole of the fulfilled form of the basic mathematical intuition stands in relation to objective validity; neither the rule, nor the case under the rule in its separation from it, has objective validity, but

[p. 126]

only the undivided union of the two in the immediate cognition of reason.

It is the last principal proposition that we have to establish about the subjective validity of cognition: *that all metaphysical connection of the existence of things, according to which the universal becomes the ground of explanation of the particular, appears only through abstraction, and designates only degrees of subjective validity, without being of objective significance*. The error, therefore, why the necessity of the law and the existence of the individual would not harmonize, lay again only in this, that we related our cognition to the object in the separation of its individual parts and not in its immediate whole. However plausible it is that with our explanatory physics we wish to make the individual objectively dependent on the universal law as ground of explanation, yet here too all classification of a physical theory belongs only to the subjective gradations of apprehension, and not to the objective significance of cognition. *For in transcendental apperception necessity is only as form in the individual of experience, and the individual is only in its connection with everything else.* Thus even all theoretical science of the progressive system has to do in its proofs only with subjective groundings, so long as it determines the particular through its superordinate universal.

In these forms of the determination of the object *a priori* through analytic unity we can demonstrate just as systematically

[p. 127]

the resources of Schelling’s philosophy of nature and of his school, as Kant exhibited in the concepts of reflection the source of all Leibnizian principles. In every philosophy that confuses formulas of comparison with judgments, concepts of comparison appear in place of the categories, and we thus obtain light plays of thought in place of laws of nature. The table of these terms of art of the philosophy of nature agrees exactly with the forms exhibited here. We find 1) according to quantity *identity and duplicity*, which also, as homogeneity and heterogeneity, or according to the law of continuity of the logical forms, play their role in every merely comparative philosophy;

2) according to quality the *positive and negative*;

3) according to relation the *relative and absolute*;

4) according to modality the material and formal, now called the opposition of the *real and ideal*. We then also comprehend whence the great convenience of these distinctions or oppositions arises; they must be applicable everywhere in our cognition, in the large or the small, because they contain not forms of the being of things but only forms of the apprehending understanding. For that very reason, however, they are without any significance in the philosophy of nature and a mere imprint of empty logical relations, so that in their now so often attempted applications to physics and history we can recognize nothing more than insignificant arbitrary trifling.

[p. 128]

4) Determination of the Object *a priori* through Synthetic Unity according to the Understanding’s Mode of Combination.

#### §. 112.

The forms of combination show themselves in our mind in manifold ways, according as we regard them from the standpoint of formal apperception merely as condition of the given material of cognition, or from the standpoint of transcendental apperception consider their law as the law of everything whatever that is to be given. The first gives us the unity of the understanding and constitutive principles of the possibility of experience as the nearest immediate mode of combination in our cognition, in that this develops with the aid of sense precisely from the individual manifold. These forms of the unity of the understanding determine for us the highest principles, deducible only, of metaphysical natural science, in which the *legislation of natural necessity* is pronounced.

We can easily derive these systematically from what has been developed so far. Their basic forms are contained in the concepts of the *necessary combination of the given material*, of which we can become conscious only through the forms of synthetic judgments, thus in the concepts of intellectual constitutive combination, i.e., in the Kantian categories and what is derived from them, for the *apodictic* value of a formal determination of material cognition can only be *thought*, thus brought to consciousness with the aid of analytic unity in judgment.

[p. 129]

#### The Table of the Categories.

#### §. 113.

In order to determine these concepts we need only compare the moments of the understanding with the forms of synthesis, §. 107.

1) *Quantity*. Through composition in the forms of pure intuition *multiplicity* is determined as a manifold of the homogeneous, (differing only numerically,) in regard to which a representation of magnitude through concepts becomes possible in *measuring*. For it is only necessary here that for the *unit* or the *measure* some quantum with a determinate denomination be given, and we can then think a *multiplicity* of it to infinity, through its *repetition in the composition*, and through comparison herewith every given magnitude of the same denomination is measured as *totality*. The peculiar thing here is that through the repeated positing of equally large parts of a given kind we think a composite whole, and can continue with this composition without end; this becomes possible for us, however, through the apprehension of pure intuition prior to reflection.

2) *Quality*. Every given manifold of material cognition is apprehended as *real*, the analytic determination of the one through the other gives the *negation* of the one through the other, the synthetic, however, the *limitedness* of everything given through its coinciding, as a part, with others in the same whole.

[p. 130]

3) *Relation*. *World of sense* is the name for the whole of all objects of the materially given cognition; just as this becomes, through the forms of pure intuition, a *mathematical whole of composition* of the given manifold of its *objects*, so through the completed union of everything materially given in the same formal apperception it becomes a *dynamical whole of the necessary connection of all existence of things in it, as nature.* This necessary connection we think through the three relations of inherence and subsistence, of causality and dependence, and of community. The complete determination of the existence of objects through this union, or the form of this dynamical whole, is the *community* of things under the same *order of nature*, which we can think only as interaction of substances. For we first apprehend the given material cognition in formal apperception, where the determination of the existence of the object through the material cognition then becomes only *inherence*, through the apprehension of the same in formal apperception, however, *subsistence*. Only then do we take together a material element of cognition with manifold others in the same form, whence results the connection of the existence of the one with that of the other, the inherences of the one being represented as *dependent* on the other according to its *causality*, and so the community of manifold substances must be thought in an interaction, where the state of each individual is determined through the powers of all the rest.

4) *Modality*. Here it is evident that the determination of the existence of an object is called, only in relation to formal

[p. 131]

apperception, its *possibility*, only in relation to material cognition its *actuality*, in relation to the whole of transcendental apperception, however, its *necessity*.

#### Remark.

In the moments of intuition we think totality immediately through manifold repetition of the unit, limitedness through negation in the real, because the form of combination falls in intuition. In the moments of thinking, on the other hand, the form of connection cannot be apprehended immediately, it shows itself only as I add the one to the other, in the *form of judgment*, through which I express the connection; hence the *correlates*. All dynamical community is thought through the interaction of substances, but I can apprehend subsistence as well as causality not for themselves, but only through the relation to inherences and dependences. Likewise I bring the modal value to the given material only mediately, hence the repetition of the qualitative opposition of comparison for each individual category, possible and impossible, existence and non-existence, necessity and contingency,

[p. 132]

#### The Principles of the Philosophy of Nature.

#### §. 114.

In this table stand only the highest abstractions of those forms of combination of the given manifold. Quite in general, however, we can restrict their sphere still further, in that each and every existence of objects given to us falls in time; more particularly, everything outer, given manifold falls in space, everything inner in pure self-consciousness. There will therefore be found here still other abstractions: of the *pure determination of time* (which Kant calls transcendental schemata,) of the pure determination of space, and of the pure determination of an object of self-consciousness, which stand in necessary combination with the categories, and so form synthetic judgments, which must show themselves as principles of metaphysical natural science.

If we therefore order everything strictly according to the logical system, there must be three divisions, one for the *general metaphysics of nature*, the second for the *special metaphysics of outer nature*, the third for the *special metaphysics of inner nature*.

If we proceed further in the deduction, we seek in the first place for each category its determination of time in general. Here quantity and quality, with the law of their apprehension, always fall in time, so that both extensive and intensive magnitude can be thought only through *successive* repetition of the one into multiplicity, immediately only in *one* dimension, in *number*

[p. 133]

and *degree*. (A plurality of dimensions we can therefore measure against one another only by means of powers of numbers.)

Relation in time becomes *temporal order* in the existence of things, for which every existence determined in relation to formal apperception in general must be *simply persistent*; only the individual material determinations can *alternate*, but their *sequence* too must be determined in a necessary connection of the one with the other as sequence of cause and effect, and finally what is *simultaneously* present must be in interaction.

Modality in time determines all possibility as existence at some time; actuality as existence at a determinate time and necessity as determination of every existence in relation to all time in general.

This then gives the following system of the *laws of natural necessity*, in that we pronounce the validity of the categories for the world of sense, and combine with each its determination of time.

If the individual object of the world of sense is called *appearance*, then the *fundamental law* is: *The world of appearances stands, throughout, under laws of nature.*

#### a.) Mathematical Principles.

These themselves arise from the forms of pure intuition in space, time and number; metaphysical natural science pronounces only the law of their necessary application in the world of sense.

Principle of application: *The law of continuity*: Every appearance is a continuous magnitude.

[p. 134]

#### 1) Axioms of Intuition.

*Principle*: Every given appearance is an extended magnitude, which is measured by a number, below which there are smaller ones, above which there are greater ones.

#### 2) Anticipations of Perception.

Principle: In all appearances the given real is limited by the intensive magnitude of a degree, above which there are greater ones, below which there are smaller ones.

#### b) The Dynamical Principles.

These laws of the necessary connection of the existence of appearances are the purest property of metaphysical natural science, in that they arise from the *only thinkable* determinations of every given material cognition through the original formal apperception.
