Its principle is: The existence of appearances is in thoroughgoing necessary connection.

#### 3) Analogies of Experience.

Principle: All unity in the existence of things is the community of substances through their powers, which is the fundamental law of physical connection.

First: *Principle of the Persistence of Substance.* Beneath all alternation of appearances lies substance, which is simply persistent.

[p. 135]

Second: *Law of Causality.* All temporal sequence of appearances occurs according to the law of the connection of cause and effect.

Third: *Law of Interaction.* All appearances, insofar as they are simultaneous, are in interaction.

#### 4) Postulates of Empirical Thinking in General,

Principle: All existence of things has its necessary determination under universal laws, which is the fundamental law of metaphysical connection.

First: Possible is the existence of an appearance, if it is at some time.

Second: Existence is the existence of an appearance at a determinate time.

Third: The existence of every given appearance is determined with necessity in relation to time in general.

#### §. 115.

These laws are what underlie all our judging of nature; through their deduction we gain, on the one hand, that we demonstrate their unavoidable application in our cognitions, and, on the other hand, that we can show the case to which their use is restricted. The rationality of our cognition gives it, through the law of an original formal apperception, thoroughgoing combination and necessity,

[p. 136]

the sensibility of our reason, however, lets the immediate whole of its cognition arise only through the coinciding of manifold material cognitions in the original formal apperception. In that we now become conscious, through inner sense and reflection, of the necessary combination in the given manifold, we obtain these laws of natural necessity. By means of our deduction we answer, first, those who in an empirical manner will not allow the use of the categories to hold, because they and the principles from them cannot be demonstrated, in that we, to speak with Kant, establish their validity for all objects of experience; for although they do not come into our cognition through intuition, they are yet just as original in cognition as intuition, they arise from a relation under whose condition every intuition to be given to us stands. Second, however, they do not contain the whole law of unity in our cognition, but only the forms of unity in the sensible limitation of our cognizing; we see therefore, against the opinion of those who with these concepts alone wish to fathom the essence of things, that their validity extends only to objects of experience, and can come to sense intuition only as form.

Under these laws the complete necessary connection of the objects of experience is determined through the dynamical principles of the persistence of substance, of causality, and of interaction; it rests therefore ultimately on the use of the categories, substance and cause, in that through substance we obtain an ultimate substrate of being, on which all becoming moves, through cause, however, subject all becoming to the law of

[p. 137]

necessity. Since these categories are in fact what comes to natural cognition through concepts over and above intuition, all dogmatic speculation had to aim properly at them. And so we do in fact find this speculation in a constant struggle, which seeks now to justify their use, now again to avoid it. On the one side their union in the concept of fundamental powers animates the ultimate goal of all theoretical natural science, on the other this very concept is despised as an empty and unfruitful game. We see that every attempt to treat substance and cause according to mere concepts through reflection, or from mere reason through intellectual intuition, must fail, for they belong indeed to the understanding, but only insofar as it is limited in general by sense. Since, however, in the concept of substance the existence of a thing is thought as determined in relation to the immediate cognition of reason in general, and not merely in relation to individual intuition, every philosopher who wanted to set up a new system dogmatically had to come first upon this concept, and seek to ground his system through an exact determination of it. Thus in modern philosophy Descartes began his speculation with an investigation of substance, Spinoza laid at the ground of his whole system the concept of a single and highest substance, Leibniz repeated in his simple, representing monad the same concept, and Schelling likewise laid at the ground of his system that which is everything and in which everything is, as absolute reason. Since, however, there lies in this no condition at all of the manifoldness of what exists, all these attempts had to

[p. 138]

fail through this, that they can never come over from the unity of the understanding to the manifoldness of sense, however much they may strive to avoid the immediate use of the concept of cause. Only through the combination of cause and effect does the necessary union of the one with the other in its manifoldness become possible for us. This form can from the side of the understanding be derived from no other, but without sense can nowhere be applied. We need, for a sensibly conditioned rational cognition of the world, the united use of the two concepts of substance and cause, in order thus to comprehend the unity of a world of sense through the interaction of its substances. Hence skepticism, which likewise knew only in reasoning from concepts a way to the grounding of its judgments, proceeded, namely in Hume and Aenesidemus, from the position that without the concept of cause no necessary combination of the existence of manifold objects could be obtained, but that from mere concepts it would never be possible to see how the existence of one thing could depend as effect on the existence of another different from it, the cause. We, on the contrary, see that there can be no talk at all of a proof with regard to the use of these concepts; but that the moment of deduction, whereby both come into our cognition, lies in the sensibility of our reason.

All these concepts of natural necessity are therefore of grounded unavoidable application in our cognition, but only within a limited field. Their supreme concept is that of an appearance, of an object of the world of sense; insofar as we raise ourselves above this, we raise ourselves at the same time above these laws of nature; this happens

[p. 139]

however, by our grasping unity and necessity immediately for themselves, and not merely as form in the sensibly given material.

#### §. 116.

In order to prepare the judgment of this opposition in the most determinate manner, we still need a closer discussion of some forms of natural necessity.

The supreme concept of the whole system is that of nature, and the highest formula is: The world of sense is a world under laws of nature, i.e., the existence of things in it stands in thoroughgoing physical connection through its metaphysical unification under universal laws, for by nature we understand the existence of things according to necessary and universal laws. *According to the essence of our reason, therefore, no cognition other than cognition of nature can arise for it from sensible intuition,* for it unavoidably adds unity and necessity to every intuition, and so combines the whole of all given sensible cognitions under the same laws. These must present themselves in the objects as the rule of an inviolable mechanism, in which from the given moment of the present the whole past and future can be calculated with necessity, for it is the restricting condition of our essence that we are receptive to no cognition contrary to this. It is in the first place only the unity and originality of my self-activity in cognizing which, as determination of the object *a priori*, projects itself, as it were, out into the world as natural necessity.

[p. 140]

With regard to the individual laws we must here look with particular exactness at the principal difference between the mathematical and the dynamical principles, of which the former express the law of the composition of the given manifold, the latter the law of the connection of the existence of things.

The first thing that reason added to sensation in the cognition of the world of sense was the mathematical delineation, which belongs to the figurative synthesis of the productive imagination. Thereby arises a necessary composition of objects in space and time, of which we become conscious under the laws of continuity, of number, and of degree. In every rule of arithmetic and geometry we become conscious only of a necessary law of this composition. E.g., if I say 3 times 7 = 21, I say thereby that if I put together in one sum three numbers of seven like things, I then have, according to a necessary law, 21 such things; or, two sides and the enclosed angle determine only one triangle, thereby I say: it is a necessary law of the composition of straight lines in space that, if I have put two straight lines together at a determinate angle, the length and position of the third, which with these encloses a triangle, is already determined. The dynamical principles, on the other hand, go beyond this mere composition of things to a necessary connection of their existence, in that they connect the existence of the property with that of its substance, in which it is, or the existence of the effect with that of its cause, through which it is, so that the whole alternation of appearances consists through an

[p. 141]

interaction of substances, in which each, with its power, flows into all the others.

Here the manner of combination is very different in the one case and the other. Space and time are indeed necessary forms of composition, but that things in space stand beside one another precisely as I find them has still something contingent about it, and can also be thought otherwise; the complete necessity, by contrast, is the property of dynamical connection alone. What I think combined as cause and effect, or as substance and property, has no contingency of combination any longer, but is represented as so united in respect of its existence that this union cannot be altered without being annihilated. Water, e.g., flows from one vessel into another, and so alters the relations of its spatial composition; but if I want to take from it a property, e.g., its liquidity in drops, this does not happen by this property being separated from it and transferred into another, but I annihilate this property by bringing about another, conflicting one, e.g., rigidity through freezing, or elastic fluidity through evaporation.

*Thus in our cognition a complete necessary connection takes place only for the existence of things, once their existence is given, but for their mere coincidence only a mathematical composition.* The magnet, e.g., attracts with necessity the iron brought near to it, but it is contingent for both that they happen to come to lie next to one another. There does indeed occur a uniform and thoroughgoing necessity in the determinations

[p. 142]

of things in nature, over which the contingency of composition seems to vanish from experience, for the necessary connection of the existence of things with one another brings everything under its power, in that it makes existence in the following time dependent on that in the preceding. Yet in this, only the existence of things, and not *their being given itself*, is necessarily connected (otherwise no alteration at all would be possible); for each moment of time taken by itself, the relation of composition, e.g., of coordination in space, that sun, earth and moon stand toward one another in this position precisely at this moment, is still only something contingent; each moment here borrows its necessity only from something outside it, namely the preceding one, through the connection of existence in both. And so the composition of things, even in the whole, remains something contingent, since in each moment it derives from the preceding one, but none counts absolutely as the initial moment. Only for calculation does this contingency vanish, in that I regard some present or other as the first given, and can now determine from it with necessity both forward, the future, and backward, the past. Notwithstanding, then, the metaphysical connection of the essence of things under universal and necessary laws, notwithstanding the physical connection of every given thing with every other, and finally notwithstanding the necessary course through time of every event once begun: there still remains to us a contingency in the composition of the one with the other in the same time, which I call the *contingency of mathematical composition*

[p. 143]

*of appearances.* Its ground can easily be demonstrated from the organization of our reason. The law of unity and necessity enters cognition from the essence of reason itself; the manifoldness of objects, on the other hand, we obtain only through the stimulation of sense to intuition, where the law of the excitation and of the ordering of the empirical intuitions beside one another lies not in reason, but in that external thing which acts upon sense; it is therefore subjectively contingent for reason, how in empirical intuition the content of cognition comes together, how the one falls in here beside the other. Whereby precisely the character of the mathematical forms of combination, which we found above, is determined, where indeed everything that is given must stand under the conditions of composition in space and time, but for the coinciding of the one with the other in respect of matter, in an undivided moment of time, no law can lie in reason; rather these forms must be so constituted that in them a progress from one to another remains always further possible, without ever reaching a closed whole, which then expresses itself in the infinity of space and time. Through the laws of natural necessity we thus obtain the form of a complete necessary connection of all objects *actually given* in the world of sense, but under the condition of an always possible greater extension of the sum of this actually given, so that the first composition of objects in this world always remains something contingent.

But what does this contingency actually say? The older metaphysics calls contingent first of all that which only as

[p. 144]

the consequence of another is, then contingency and dependence of a thing are one and the same, a verbal meaning which we do not seek here. In the properly modal opposition to the necessary, by contrast, it was explained: contingent is that existence whose non-being is possible; against this we have remarked that the difference of the possible, the actual and the necessary is only a subjective one of apprehension; for the complete cognition of the object everything is determined with necessity: this concept of the contingent would therefore remain without application. Here, however, it is to receive meaning after all. For us necessity as category is the determination of the existence of an object through the unity of transcendental apperception, contingency as its correlate, on the other hand, the determination of the existence of an object only in relation to the single material cognition. Now every single material cognition, as soon as it is given, falls immediately into the formal apperception and so determines its object with necessity; but if it is not yet given, it determines its object neither contingently nor necessarily; how, then, is the concept of the contingent still to find an application here? Only through the determination of the given material cognition in relation to the original form taking place *only in a restricted manner*, so that a restricted necessity must in another respect be judged as contingency (and the manner of representing it consequently receives only a subjective worth). Such a restriction, however, expresses itself precisely in the continuity and infinity of the purely intuitive forms, so that here the essence of things in nature remains contingent in this, that each single existence in a series without beginning and end stands ever again under the condition

[p. 145]

of another. From each single given point of time the history of the world is determined throughout with necessity, but for time in general it becomes contingent, because in it no first source is found, but always only derivation and outflow. Yet with this we already meet the connecting link of the natural and the ideal view of things.

#### §. 117.

We have not yet come to the end above with the deduction of the principles of metaphysical natural science; rather, besides the general determination of time, the category was to be determined *a priori* in particular for outer nature through the pure form of space, for inner nature through self-consciousness. These relations must be developed more closely here.

The outer intuitions fall together immediately into the purely intuitive form of space; their objects therefore unite into a complete mathematical composition in space. For inner sense, on the other hand, there lies at the ground, as form of the given manifold of inner intuition, only that pure self-consciousness which does not arise from mathematical combination, but occurs immediately as a peculiar material determination of immediate cognition lying at the ground of reflection. This difference between space and pure self-consciousness makes a very significant difference between outer and inner natural science, and compels us to keep the two wholly apart. *The objects of the outer senses fall, as to their content, into space, as to their existence*

[p. 146]

*in time, and are thus subject to a thoroughgoing, complete mathematical combination. My activities, on the other hand, which I intuit inwardly, stand indeed also, as to their existence, under the condition of mathematical composition in time, but as to their matter they are united only in the I of self-consciousness without any mathematical coordination.* Outside me every thing stands regularly beside the other, and its parts are one beside the other in space according to complete mathematical synthesis. For inner sense, however, this form corresponding to space is lacking; the coordination of the simultaneous in my intuiting, thinking, feeling and willing has no mathematical form of pure intuition lying at the ground; hence inner nature is harder to observe and has fewer apodictic laws, but just thereby the inner approaches more closely the ideas, for to these the hostile principle is precisely mathematics.

We must here consider the influence of mathematics in two opposite respects. We found just now that in the law of the mathematical composition of things in space and time there lies a condition of contingency, whereas strict necessity springs only from the dynamical connection of the existence of things. Here, then, the mathematical forms give a restriction of natural necessity, which becomes so important precisely for the idea. On the other side, however, once the manifold is given, the pure forms of intuition in space and time determine the cognition of it through and through with such necessity

[p. 147]

that we can then carry out the cognition completely in relation to the transcendental apperception according to the original relations to reason, without anything merely empirical remaining in it. This then makes the great difference between outer and inner cognition of nature: the former is thoroughly governed by mathematics, the latter only in an incomplete manner.

#### §. 118.

Precisely because for outer intuition both the existence and the given of the objects is comprehended in pure forms, the mathematical principles of natural necessity find strict application here; we obtain here, through the pure determination of objects in space, peculiar constitutive principles of outer nature, according to the following first elements.

First, for the objects of outer nature space is the original form of the given manifold; they stand therefore under the law of extended and continuous magnitude, and fall ever further asunder into divisible parts to infinity. This gives *the law of the divisibility of matter to infinity,* for which, then, the moment of deduction is here exhibited. Every mathematical attempt to prove it runs back in the end always only to the subjective embarrassment of conceiving, without or against it, a filling of space; here we see now how, precisely through this filling, it must unavoidably make itself valid.

Second, everything manifold and real in space must be comprehensible through mere quantitative differences, for cognition here determines itself mathematically and completely in relation to the immediate cognition of reason,

[p. 148]

all empirical qualities of outer sensation must be resolvable, in that they are traced back to mere quantitative relations of the filling of space and of motion in space. The existence of things in space, in their relation to one another, comes back to thoroughly explicable relations of pull and push, so that all empirical qualities of outer sensation that appear at first resolve themselves, in the perfected science of nature, into mere laws of motion.

Third, the real which fills space, the movable in space, we call matter. The properties of matter, of the one relatively to the other, are therefore in our perfected cognition only quantitative differences of motion, pull and push; the existence of matter itself, however, is determined completely in relation to the immediate cognition of reason; we cognize, therefore, *this movable in space as simply persistent substance, whose quantity can in all physical processes be neither increased nor diminished, but whose outer relations only alternate.*

#### §. 119.

Thus outer natural science, as mathematical physics, is a closed whole, capable of being completed in itself, in whose interior everything is thoroughly explicable from universal mathematical laws. Quite different, however, is the relation of inner experience with its incomplete mathematical synthesis, which gives precisely the opposite results.

First, the object of all inner self-intuition is determined as inner activity of the I, and the sub-

[p. 149]

ject of it is the ever self-same, single I. The object of inner nature has therefore no manifold at all outside one another as extended magnitude, but its manifold activities always fall together in the intensive magnitude of one and the same inner action of the I, as we had to presuppose already for the laws of association, and found confirmed again for the spontaneity of cognition in the original formal apperception. The I as substrate of inner activity is therefore a single subject, which cannot be thought as divisible at all, but has no other than the intensive magnitude of the degree of its faculties, so that it is not destructible by division, but can be thought as mortal only by extinction or gradual vanishing of its consciousness.

Second, the inner empirical qualities of cognizing, representing, thinking, feeling and desiring do not fall at all under the purely intuitive forms of a mathematical composition; they too are therefore subject only to the law of intensive magnitude, but otherwise are irresolvable qualities, which cannot be traced back to quantitative differences, make no claim to be explained from relations of magnitude, but remain standing for themselves in a validity of their own. Precisely by this, that the I is withdrawn from the law of extended magnitude, it distinguishes itself in its qualities as *the living* from everything material, the dead. For life we call only activity from an inner principle; in matter everything comes together from outer relations, there is nothing simply inner there; even life in the organism is only the analogue of life, for its activity too flows only from a

[p. 150]

*closed circle* of outer relations; in self-cognition, on the other hand, we refer all activities to the same inner essence of the I to which they belong.

Third, the I or the mind is indeed the object of all inner experience and the single subject which is the substrate of existence in all these appearances, which concern only *its* inner activity; but that peculiar relation, that pure self-consciousness lies at the ground of reflection only as a mere feeling of my existence, without being self-intuition, brings it about that I am able to intuit only my activities, but not myself. Hence it comes that my existence in inner nature is not determined apodictically, through any sensible form of a pure intuition, in relation to the immediate cognition of reason, as that of matter is, but, beside the sensible form, falls immediately into the essence of reason, and so becomes an object of faith, as we shall soon see more closely. For experience, however, and in time, my existence is by no means determined as persistent substance, i.e., the mind as object of inner experience is not cognized, like matter, as imperishable in nature; we do not cognize it in time as immortal, but the simplicity of its essence is only an analogue of an organization, i.e., of a form of changing substances enduring through a time, like the flame of a candle, which has its unity only in the form of the process of combustion, but constantly lets the very thing that burns, through which it subsists, change. Thus the essence of the mind is compared precisely to the most perishable thing we know.

[p. 151]

#### §. 120.

From these three opposed basic elements outer and inner physics each develop for themselves, and it can easily be shown from them how it becomes impossible for us to unite the laws of material existence and the laws of life in one system of nature. Instead of our being thereby able, as some hope, to hold fast the essence of the eternal, everything would rather harden in the forms of the finite, for the existence of matter is in nature far more firmly grounded than that of intelligence. It would succeed more nearly in completing such a system of nature into a deadening materialism than in producing from it a desirable intellectualism. Indifference of matter and mind, however, leads just as little to the goal; deification can succeed not by matter and mind becoming indifferentiated into one another, but only by our freeing the mind from matter.

Our cognition of nature presents itself under the most general laws of natural necessity only in two separate systems, of outer and of inner nature. There is for us a twofold, wholly different manner in which the existence of things appears to us; the one borrows its colors from outer experience, and shows us the material world, the other borrows its colors from inner experience, and shows us the spiritual world. We possess a self-sufficient cognition of outer nature or the material world, wholly subject to mathematics. Beside this our self-cognition forms an inner nature of the spiritual, which, however, only through constant relation

[p. 152]

to the outer acquires stability; yet on the other side self-cognition is again the beginning of all our knowledge, pure self-consciousness was the immediate material determination of our cognition, and thereby we obtain a further transitional stage to the cognition of matter, on which this is cognized only in relation to myself, the mind, thus according to laws of irresolvable qualities. Perfected mathematical cognition shows only one matter in relation to another; the immediate appearance of matter for me in sensation, on the other hand, shows me in color, tone and scent nothing but irresolvable qualities, which can be explained just as little as inner qualities, precisely because this cognition of matter in relation to myself still remains under the conditions of inner perception. This relation of inner and outer physics will develop more determinately if we follow the individual basic elements in comparison.

1) Outer experience has at its ground an original material determination of the formal apperception in space, hence the complete application of the law of the continuously extended; there is here nothing but outer relation of the one to the other without end, whereas inwardly there already lies at the ground the singleness of a material determination of transcendental apperception, so that here the simple, which is not found outwardly at all, is the first.

2) Quality is in general that which withdraws from all explanation, for the real is precisely that which is given immediately in the empirical

[p. 153]

material consciousness is immediately given. Every explanation is a synthetic representation of the one through the other; explanation therefore takes place not at all for qualities, for in the moment of quality there was only the analytic mediate representation of the one through the other under the form of negation. All explanation is therefore composition of the magnitude of a given real, and not explanation of the quality itself. Just now, however, we have set the outer qualities, as resolvable, against the irresolvable inner ones; what is this resolution of quality to mean? Matter appears to me immediately as warm and cold, as sound and color, but I resolve these qualities as subjective relations, and cognize objectively, instead of them, only change of temperature, oscillating and radiating motion; I thus here trace the quality, physically, back only to quantitative difference, I obtain a distinctive view of the world outside me, in which I see phoronomically nothing but outer relations of position and motion in space, dynamically the filling of space by the movable, recognize this as the substance of the world, to which I ascribe the basic forces. Inwardly, on the other hand, cognition proceeds from the qualities of sensing, representing, feeling and willing, and also remains entirely standing with them, without being able to reduce them to relations of magnitude. This difference springs precisely from the complete mathematical determinability of outer experience, for which space contains a quantitative apodictic determination of the relation of everything given in it to everything else. Hence this resolution of outer quality, which however becomes no explanation of it, but where one only places alongside the qualitatively

[p. 154]

different, quantitative differences, without thereby removing the former or really composing them out of the latter. Outer quality retains its full worth as soon as I cognize matter in relation to myself; it is removed only where I seek merely relations of the one in space to the other in it. However much, then, the theory through extensive magnitude, or mathematical physics, may always be sufficient to itself, it can yet never draw into its circle the theory through intensive magnitude, the explanation with regard to qualities, and outer quality remains standing as an irreducible intermediate link of the inner and outer view of the world.

3) Through the three laws of the persistence of substance, of causality, and of interaction, all combination of existence, and thereby all connection of perceptions, comes into our experience. The first condition of such a necessary connection of perceptions is the persistence of substance, for through the category of substance existence in general was first determined in relation to transcendental apperception, i.e., with necessity. But just as little as that something is substance can it be perceived that something is absolutely persistent, for in the latter case I should have had to observe through all time. If, then, I am not in a position to cognize *a priori* of something that it exists as substance, experience as necessary connection of perceptions is altogether impossible for me. Now we have in general only the outer and the inner mode of intuition by which objects are given to us. The inner stand

[p. 155]

only under a pure form of unity, whereby the change in what exists is united, through which only the existence of the manifold is determined as combined, but the given itself occurs in perception only contingently. In outer intuition, on the other hand, the manifold given falls together, as being beside one another, in the pure form of space. Through this space, then, being beside one another is determined in relation to transcendental apperception, and thereby also in relation to time in general, whereby the law must then be formed: that which is absolutely beside one another, or the substrate of outer intuition, exists as persistent substance. In outer experience, then, substance is given, in relation to which all change of appearances can be determined as alteration of mere inherences. The I, on the other hand, as substrate of inner experience, is not intuited at all as subject, but only thought and cognized by means of changeable activities; to it, then, in all its cognizable faculties, an intensive magnitude belongs, which can become greater or smaller and can even be thought as vanishing. There lies, then, in inner intuition no determining ground whether the mind exists as substance or only as inherence in another. Hence the unity of inner experience must be borrowed only from the persistent in the outer, since without this no determination of time would be possible in it. We must first cognize the inner as *simultaneous* with the outer, i.e., as in interaction with it, in order thereby to bring determination of time into it. Thus, then,

[p. 156]

all spiritual view of the world in our reason is bound to the condition of the material, which must lie at its ground, and on which it can subsist only as correlate, as we indeed also find this in the relation of our inner life to the body, and find it there in such a way that every other life may be grasped by us only according to analogies with this relation. (From this moment Kant drew his critical proof for the refutation of empirical idealism.)

[p. 157]

### Second Division.

Deduction of the Principles for the Doctrine of Ideas, or the Unity of Reason in the Essence of Things.

### Introduction.

#### §. 121.

Since Kant gave back to the word idea its old great meaning from Greek philosophy, we can designate by it the whole interest of speculation. In its whole inquiry after truth, beauty and goodness, philosophy is, according to its interest, the science of ideas. We set this idea over against the category or pure concept of the understanding; we find that the latter leads only to insight into the natural view of things, over which we first set a higher ideal view; we then see life in speculation stirred up by the conflict of these two views, in that the idea demands freedom beside nature, recognizes the natural essence of things only as the finite, as appearance for human reason, and sets over this the true being of things in themselves as their eternal essence.

[p. 158]

We have now asserted here that this natural and ideal view of things differ only as two different views of the laws of objective unity in our mind. In our reason there lay unity and necessity of its cognition as its first law; this was to show itself in the laws of the natural view of things as it expresses itself, prior to reflection, in the sensibly given of our material cognition, in the laws of the ideal view, on the other hand, as reflection grasps the law of unity and necessity purely for itself from the immediate cognition of reason, as it lies as the first and innermost principle in transcendental apperception. With regard to the concepts of the understanding we have already made the test, that those forms of combination of the given manifold actually appear in the laws of natural necessity; now we are given the task of showing also how the forms of our ideal conviction develop from that moment of pure unity.

We demand for these forms of the idea precisely as much deduction from the exhibited anthropological moment as for the categories, for only thereby can we justify judgments from ideas, and it must be possible here, just as with the concepts of the understanding, to show the origin of these forms from the essence of our reason. Kant had to restrict himself to a deduction of the categories because by deduction he did not understand quite the same as we do. He took our intuitive cognition as the only one secured for itself, and regarded everything else solely from the standpoint of reflection; here, then, he demanded a ground of justification for every cognition springing from mere reason, in order to hold alongside that

[p. 159]

intuition. This he could indeed exhibit for the categories, since through them that intuition first becomes the whole of experience; but for the ideas it could be shown only very incompletely, since their object is no longer found at all in those intuitions. Our deduction, on the other hand, must apply in the same way to every mode of cognition, because by it we think only a subjective derivation from the essence of reason.

Before we give this deduction of the principles from the idea itself, we wish first to orient ourselves more closely about the standpoint from which it must be conceived. We say, the unity of the understanding and its forms of natural necessity are obtained by our bringing to consciousness the original formal apperception as condition of the given manifold of material cognition, the unity of reason with its ideas, on the other hand, by our grasping the law of the unity of transcendental apperception purely for itself. The one time we proceed, as it were, from the manifold, and set unity over it; the other time, on the other hand, we grasp immediately necessary unity itself. Here we can indeed show that these two views take place for our reason, for on the one hand we obtain the material of our cognition only through stimulating sense; on the other side, however, unity and necessity is the original law of rationality, which, independently of every single stimulation by sense, becomes law for each and all. This, however, we must ask: why do these two views differ? why do they not show the same goal? Why do I find in the pure law of formal apperception not precisely only the formal condition of everything material, and in the formal

[p. 160]

condition of the given that pure law? Whereby do different and opposed forms of the concept and of the idea arise here?

The answer to all these questions is: Every sensible reason recognizes the limitedness of its own essence by becoming conscious how it obtains the content of its cognition only through *a principle alien to its essence*, of outer stimulation to cognize. Unity and necessity is its property and its first law, but the demands of this law can *never completely* be satisfied by cognition initiated only sensibly. Thus transcendental apperception demands, from the first law of our cognition, *a whole of the filled form*; but sensible stimulation can lay at its ground only an *empty form*, in which *the incompletability of the filling of the form* can be taken up. The self-cognition of the limitedness of our reason therefore finds, in the unity of the given manifold, instead of *the totality of a world-whole*, only *the infinity* of the incompletable purely sensible forms in number, time and space; it finds in every given whole only *limited reality* instead of *an absolutely real*; it finds in all relations only *series of the conditioned*, where every conditioned presupposes a higher condition, without ever being able to grasp, in *the unconditioned*, the complete whole of the series; it must therefore finally set the modality of its given cognition, *as appearance* for its limited view, against the *necessary essence of things in themselves*. From this opposition of completed unity to the forms

[p. 161]

of combination of what is given to us we then obtain the opposition of the ideal view to the natural.

With regard to the deduction of the ideas we must therefore distinguish exactly *the positive foundation of our whole ideal view*, and *the forms of the pronouncement of the ideas prior to reflection.* That positive foundation is the faith in reality absolutely, which is the innermost property of every *rational* power of cognition; the forms under which alone we can, prior to reflection, pronounce the ideal view to ourselves spring, on the other hand, only from the negation of the limitation of our sensible knowledge. With the ideas we want to grasp the absolutely positive of our cognition; for human reason, however, this is possible only under the form of a double negation. And herein shows itself the high worth of reflection in our mind: the ideal view of reason *in its difference* from the natural view of the understanding is the mere property of reflection, in which finite reason recognizes its own limits.

For the deduction of the ideas we have, then, to discuss first by way of preliminary: how is self-cognition of one's own limitedness possible? Next: whence does the speculative faith in the reality of things absolutely come to us? And finally: whence do the reflected forms of the ideal view itself come to us?

[p. 162]

#### How Does Reason Cognize Its Own Limits?

#### §. 122.

Kant calls a mode of cognition *immanent* if it relates to objects of experience, i.e., to objects whose existence is given in a sense intuition; *transcendent*, on the other hand, is for him a mode of cognition which with its claims goes beyond the objects of experience. Then he asserts that we possess only immanent cognitions, since all material of our cognition comes to us from sense intuition. In order to designate in this regard the likewise only immanent use of the ideas, he is fond of using the expression that they are of no use to us for an extension of our cognition beyond the limits of experience, but serve us for the *determination of the boundaries* of our faculty in general.

This last view indeed shares his general fault, that here too he sees only what appears first of all before reflection, the negative forms without the positive intention that lies at the ground; but it is nevertheless very apt in this, that we are led to what is peculiar to the ideal view precisely only through the limitation of our own essence. In the Kantian school this determination of boundaries has occasioned many words and many difficulties, especially through the dispute over the thing in itself and the transcendental object. This thing in itself was supposed to be what is altogether neither cognizable, nor thinkable, nor representable; the riddle was only wherein it then still differed from nothing, and how one was nevertheless in a position

[p. 163]

to make words about it. If one could not grasp it itself, then its name had at least to designate an empty place in our power of cognition, about which, however, no one made himself properly clear: not Kant, because he found no difficulty in the matter, everything being self-evident to him; not the pupils, because in sheer difficulties they could no longer find the matter; but this regains its first simplicity when we first orient ourselves about the self-cognition of the limits of our essence. But how is it possible for a being to cognize itself as limited? Is it not an old metaphysical rule: *quodlibet ens est unum, verum, bonum atque perfectum* [every being is one, true, good and perfect], every thing taken by itself has unity, truth and perfection? To this we reply again quite metaphysically: if I think to myself any thing that has its substance in itself, a stone, say, as a crystal, as isolated from all other things, held together only by its inner power, then this, compared only with itself, has without doubt unity and perfection; if, on the other hand, a thing exists only as a form of changing substances, or if its first power, as excitability, is bound to a receptivity from without, then for such a thing isolation from everything external cannot be made even in thought; such a being is only through the external, it is for itself only something limited. But this latter is precisely the case of a sensible reason; this, then, while wholly entangled in itself, will nevertheless feel its dependence on the external, and will cognize itself as a *finite reason*. Hence an inner contradiction of its own essence is clear to every sensible reason: its own form is never filled by the alien content; instead of the closed

[p. 164]

totality of the world it receives only extension without end, and is thus able to recognize the limits of its own essence itself, in the contingency of the mathematical composition of the given in its cognition.

#### 2) Limits of Thinking and Cognizing.

#### §. 123.

The word thinking is determined in two ways: once in opposition to intuiting, and then in opposition to cognizing in general. Intuition was the cognition of which I am immediately conscious again, what was thought was the cognition which I find in myself only mediately through reflection; but besides this we also set the thinkable in general beside the cognizable, in that we set all problematic representation, in thinking and fabricating, as thinking, against assertoric representation, against cognition. In both respects the sphere of the thinkable is the wider. Intuition is only object of inner perception; thinking first completes it into inner experience; through thinking we add to the intuitively given *actual* the forms of *necessity*. Cognition in general restricts itself to this necessary, mere thinking oversteps it in the representations of indeterminate possibilities. In both respects we now use in German the word idea to designate the domain of thinking which reaches beyond intuition or cognition. We call a cognition a mere idea if its object cannot be shown in intuition; we call a representation, a proposal, a plan,

[p. 165]

a mere idea if it is unfeasible, or at least if the means of execution are not yet at hand. Yet we still distinguish the idea, which can lay claim to reality, from the chimera, which has no reality. Indeed, in this sense the faculty of ideas becomes for us precisely the highest and most important in our mind, for to it belongs the pure pronouncement of the self-activity of reason, and this counts with us above everything actually cognized and intuitable, because the inner law of the spiritual becomes the highest in our world.

This faculty of thinking beyond the limits of intuition or cognition, this faculty of ideas, springs from the relation of the original unity of transcendental apperception to the law of contingency in the mathematical composition. (§. 116.)

All thinking and fabricating, all voluntary representing, through which concept, error, etc. became possible, depended in the first place on problematic representation, and this separated itself from cognition through the faculty of schematizing or abstracting. For this kind of representation we saw above already (§. 58) how it springs from the laws of imagination, and maintains its own domain through the faculties of *combining* and *negating*. Here we can give its theory the final completion. The necessary unity of basic consciousness which underlies all our cognition is unavoidably comprehended along with it in every abstraction, before reflection; but the actually given intuition is given in relation to this form not with subjective necessity, but only subjectively contingently with regard to the rule of its composition. Hence here in every case the relation

[p. 166]

of the actually given intuition to the necessary form still leaves a latitude for the voluntary mode of representation, *how it might also be thought otherwise*; this latitude we must therefore be able to show in the moments of the given object, i.e., in our representation of quantity and quality, and there it shows itself in the faculty of combination and negation. Imagination cannot think any new real to the given, but it can well think, in the purely intuitive series of composition, all alterations of the given order and a repetition of the given without end, whereas with regard to quality it can think, to the given, in each case an other in general, *the thing which is not this*.

Just so the reaching-over of thought cognition beyond intuition springs from the same relation. Thought cognition adds nothing to intuition but the forms of universal and necessary laws, which remain empty forms until intuition presents to them the case of application. (§. 98.) Kant was perfectly right to declare all human cognition immanent; though we have thought-forms which go beyond the given of intuition, their application is nevertheless possible only through intuition, and if there is reality in human cognition, this is given only through intuition. The world, then, which is object of our experience, is the only one of which we can even have ideas. Thus the purely intuitive forms serve only to bring sense intuition together, the thought-forms of the category, e.g. of cause and effect, connect only the existence of objects of that intuition, and if the thought-forms

[p. 167]

of the idea do also rise above the given of the individual intuitions, this happens only in order to think a whole of them in general, without ever wholly freeing oneself from them, or, say, cognizing the supersensible as another world; rather the highest is always only that we think an *other order of the same* world. We think in the idea of the soul only the self-subsistence of the spiritual, which is given as object of inner experience; world becomes the whole of all objects of experience, and in deity we think the being which gives this world its law.

The peculiarity of the ideas is therefore here too only the overreaching of the original form beyond the given of its filling. Idea is in general a representation whose object cannot be given in any determinate cognition, and these ideas are either *aesthetic* through combination, or *logical* through negation. In the aesthetic ideas of beautiful forms, namely, we present the form of an intuition as a case under an inexpressible rule as intuition, whose law cannot be expressed through any determinate concept; logical ideas, on the other hand, are concepts of a real which cannot be given in any intuition, which we can therefore think only as the opposite of everything given in general. Beyond the given, then, only the negation of the logical idea leads us, for through combination we can only represent another order of the actually given, or relate an actually given combination as a case to an inexpressible rule, which as such can again be indicated only through the negations of the logical ideas.

[p. 168]

### First Chapter.

### Deduction of the Table of All Transcendental Ideas.

#### §. 124.

*Transcendental idea* I call, with Kant, every particular form of the unity of reason. Which forms of this kind are found in our reason we can show completely from what has gone before. The necessary unity of basic consciousness attaches itself to every excitation of our cognition, but can never be filled, however great or small the extent of the stimulation may be. The first law of unity in our cognition thus becomes a law of completeness simply; the form of unity in the given material, on the other hand, must always show a limitation. Through this completeness the forms of the unity of reason therefore stand over against those of the unity of understanding, but this can, according to what has just been proved, happen only through negations. We can think the completeness of the unity of reason only through negation of the limitations in the categories.

The supreme form of all transcendental ideas is therefore the idea of the negation of the limits, the idea of the *absolute*, and the characteristic of the ideal mode of representation becomes representation of the real through doubled negations.

1) The first moment of the ideas is therefore quality. We seek in the idea reality simply; in

[p. 169]

intuition, on the other hand, we always have only limited realities side by side, so that nothing remains for the ideal quality but the idea of the absolute, or the removal of the limits themselves, in the unlimitedly real.

2) In the moment of magnitude our understanding, as analytic understanding, is limited to this, that it can grasp the necessary only in the universality of formal laws, and not in the synthetic allness of the objects before intuition. We therefore represent magnitude through the category and according to the form of number always as a determinate allness, where the many is measured by unity, and a determinate multiplicity, e.g. of inches, rods, miles, earth-diameters or sun-distances, can always be used again as unity in a higher multiplicity, without ever arriving at an allness that could not again be thought as one in many. For the completeness of the idea we now think this limitation removed; in opposition to every finite allness we demand *absolute totality* of the objects of the world-whole as an allness that could not again be thought as unity in multiplicity, the one and all of completed magnitude.

If we wish to bring the whole opposition of the natural and ideal view to its simplest expression, we find this here in the absolute representation of magnitude, for the law of the contingency of all mathematical composition has only just led us to the separation of concept and idea. Thus the incompletability of every mathematical synthesis in the infinite and the continuous, and totality, stand opposed to one another, and in the contradiction of these two every other contradiction between category and idea is resolved. The idea demands totality,

[p. 170]

but nature can instead of this exhibit everywhere only infinity of the incompletable.

3) From this there follows for the ideal determination of modality that the natural view of things shows, as *absolutely contingent*, only a subjective view of the individual reason as to the essence of things, in which this becomes only *appearance*, to which, however, the idea opposes *absolute necessity as the essence of things in themselves*; for the modal limitation of our cognition is the origin of its empirical truth from the subjective history of our reason; this we must therefore think as removed in the idea, in the law of its transcendental truth.

4) The highest idea of relation is that of *freedom*, for the limitation of all relations according to categories lay in natural necessity; but the idea of the removal of natural necessity is called freedom.

In the categories of relation we think the community of things through the interaction of their substances. For the idea the sum total of all things is called the *world*, and the law of their community the *world-order*. Nature shows us the order of the material world as throughout subject to the law of mathematical synthesis, hence also throughout in contradiction with the idea; we can claim for the idea only an *intelligible world of the living* (according to the view of inner nature), whose substance we can think only as *soul*, whose power, however, as *free will*, and whose order, finally, must be thought as subject to *deity*, as the absolute cause in the essence of things.

[p. 171]

#### §. 125.

With this survey we pronounce for our theory of reason the principle of the *negative origin of the ideas*, which shows the first view of the opposition of our doctrine of ideas to speculative rationalism. This wants to find in the absolute the principle of all its knowledge and the theme of all philosophy, from which its absolute knowledge alone is to proceed. Against this we shall here for the present only adduce the origin of this idea itself. To be sure, the idea of the absolute is the highest form of all transcendental ideas, but that in cognition nothing can be begun with it, that it rather must always relate to something else, on which alone it can be formed, this its negative origin shows us. Far from its being able to be the immediate source of all truth, it is only a mediate product of reflection, which we can produce for ourselves only through the opposition to given reality. In fact, what can be in itself more positive and more freed from negations than the idea of unrestricted, absolute reality, and yet for our consciousness precisely this idea is the most negative that we can think; we reach it only through doubled negations, through negation of the limits. Whatever may become for us a single object of intuition, that is always a real as a limited part of the whole, every positive reality is always bound to the limits of time, where every real of the moment is a conditioned one, whose higher condition lies in the past; if we wish to raise ourselves from this to the idea of the unconditioned, unrestricted, this happens

[p. 172]

only through the negation of the negation in a voluntary reflection without any intuition.

With the idea of the absolute we wish to grasp the unity of all possible experience and the highest reality; but in setting out toward this we abandon everything that intuition brings to cognition, are left solely to free reflection, and so form for ourselves a mere idea of opposition to all limited and isolated reality of intuition. However often it has been attempted to accomplish something in speculation through this idea alone, and to grasp the absolutely real purely by itself without any relation to the limited of common cognition, it is nevertheless already a very bad sign against these attempts that even those who appeal, in the cognition of the absolute, to an intuition of their own, yet have only negative expressions in their language to designate this idea of the absolutely real. If we know an object through intuition and now want to describe it, we shall not determine through exclusions what it is not in order to make it recognizable, but we describe it positively, as we saw it. Of something round we shall not first say that it is neither triangular nor quadrangular, but we say straight out that it is round; if we want to name something green, we shall not describe at length that it is neither red nor black, nor that it does not have some other color, but we say straight out that it is green. Only then, on the contrary, when the determinate intuitive knowledge of an object is lacking to us, do we make use of those negations, and say of a thing that it is neither this nor that, so that, even if we cannot describe it itself, we may yet

[p. 173]

circumscribe the knowledge of it as closely as possible, and so avoid confusion with others. The latter is then also the only means which everyone uses for the cognition of ideas. We say only: their object is the infinite, unrestricted, unconditioned, absolutely real, the neither — nor in every single distinction of determinate things, without ever being able to state what it then properly is. We seek, then, through this idea the highest real of our cognition, as befitted undivided unity and necessity, but we can approach it only by reflection forming the opposition to everything that comes to cognition for us in sensible intuition;

[p. 174]

### Second Chapter.

### The Law of Transcendental Truth, or of Objective Validity.

#### §. 126.

Throughout the whole course of our investigations we have sought to present the doctrine of the objective validity of our cognitions in a new way. Already in the theory of sensation we showed that sense intuition does not receive its object through that which affects in sensation, but that the object is already there with the intuition, sensation giving it only its subjective validity, as distinct from fancy. Afterwards it was found that all grounding of self-active cognitions in judgments is only a subjective grounding according to the rule of an empirical truth, in which we ask only: which cognitions are in our reason? but not immediately: what is their relation to the cognized object? Finally it emerged, moreover, that objective significance in our cognition belongs neither to the necessary form that springs from the self-activity of reason, nor to the actual content that sense supplies, but that the law of objective validity can lay claim only to the *whole immediate cognition of my reason as transcendental apperception*. We called transcendental truth the agreement of cognition with its

[p. 175]

object; of this, then, there can be talk only with regard to the *whole of our transcendental apperception*. Only now were we in a position to seek a judgment about it.

From the whole investigation of our cognizing hitherto there results finally a complete survey of the system of cognitions *which are actually present in my reason*, and together make up the unity of their transcendental apperception. Truth and falsity in the particular is always reckoned subjectively only from the connection of the whole; we prove in mathematics or physics, and we convict ourselves of error in common life, only by comparing the particular with the connection of the whole; the whole of transcendental apperception then has within itself an inner rule of truth.

But precisely this whole, complete transcendental apperception we can now compare further with the idea of transcendental truth, and ask: how do the objects correspond to it, how does it agree with the object in itself?

A reason with its entire cognition and its whole empirical truth can be thought in such a way that to this its cognition there corresponds a being of its objects in themselves, that transcendental truth belongs to it, or in such a way that its whole cognition has only a subjective significance for it, that no object in itself corresponds to it, that it is only *illusion*. Midway, as it were, between these two presuppositions lies then the third, that the objects of the mode of cognition of a reason are only *appearances*. Such a reason cognizes the true essence of things, but not *as they are in*

[p. 176]

*themselves*, but only under certain subjective limitations unavoidable to its essence. Suppose our healthy intuition of things were a cognition of things as they are in themselves, then dream and fancy are mere illusion, the intuition of the jaundiced person, however, who is subjectively bound to the color in his eye, from which he cannot free himself, is appearance; or he who, in Plato’s image, is able to see on the wall of a cave only the shadows of the things which pass by outside it, to him these appear, but he does not see them as they are in themselves.

The question of the objective validity of our cognition can thus be put: does our cognition have transcendental truth or not? and if the former is so, do we cognize things purely according to their essence in themselves, or according to a limited mode of appearance? The answer to this is given most luminously if we first show: our cognition does not show us things immediately as they are in themselves; but afterwards raise the question, is it then illusion, or does it show appearances?

#### §. 127.

The unconcerned presupposition of the first opinion, that a cognition with transcendental truth of things as they are in themselves is at our disposal, was the principle of all speculative dogmatism; to this, for a long time, the doubt of the skeptics was opposed, whether objective validity is found at all in our speculations; Kant, however, was the first who drew attention to the third case, and critically placed the self-cognition

[p. 177]

of the limits of our reason at the head of all his speculations. He showed at length how little we could approach the essence of things in themselves, how much we must content ourselves with appearances, and found much approval with this doctrine; but gradually the successors departed from it again, and Schelling, made secure by the rejection of all reflected speculation, returned entirely to the first dogmatic view. With his very first entry into speculation he overlooks all the difficulties of the skeptics and critics, wants to know in philosophy only of absolute knowledge, of cognition of things in themselves; his first theme is agreement of cognition with the object, and his first proposition an attempt to pronounce the law of this. He calls the relation of cognition to the object that of the subjective and objective, and the first naive presupposition of his whole doctrine is that all is perfectly in order with that agreement (with the eternal copula); he is only concerned to grasp this undoubted agreement in a law, which he at first called indifference of the subjective and objective (*System of Philosophy*, §. 1), but afterwards pronounces: true being and cognizing oneself is one and the same without opposition. (*Relation of the Philosophy of Nature to Fichte’s Improved Doctrine*, p. 50.) To carry this through, he must reject the whole of cognition, with the help of reflection, as voluntariness, above which we might be able to raise ourselves; if he then gives his doctrine itself, it consists only in this: to bring the many of reflection, which is not, to the unity, which alone is; his whole doctrine has only a polemical existence, and if he wanted to say nothing but his most proper, own

[p. 178]

opinion, he would have nothing at all to say to us but *one inexpressible*. Every *word*, then, that he uses will one day refute him. This or any similar way of philosophizing may withdraw, grammatically or logically, as much as it likes from the words theory and explanation; by the common meaning of the words its whole business is nonetheless only an attempt to arrive at a theory of transcendental truth. One begins here always with some hypothesis of the self-positing I, of total indifference, or absolute identity of subject and object, or finally of the absolutely indistinguishable being and self-cognizing, from which the agreement of cognition with its object in transcendental truth is to be *explained*.

But precisely this alleged theme of philosophy is no theme at all for a theory, not at all for a science. Rather, all theory and all scientific form belongs only to the gradations of subjective validity and of empirical truth, whereas that highest modal relation in our cognition cannot be subjected to any theory at all. Our whole investigation hitherto serves as evidence that we arrive at a whole of our transcendental apperception only through subjective relations of the cognitive activities to one another, without ever being able to use the relation of a cognition to its object for explanation. This relation is subjectively a first presupposition in all cognizing, but it is precisely what is capable of no development that belongs at the head of no system. Where cognizing occurs, an object is cognized, that lies in the nature of cognizing; but we can never, as it were,

[p. 179]

set cognition and object side by side for comparison, to judge whether the reality of the one gives truth to the representation in the other or not, but our reason can only compare its cognitive activities subjectively with one another. Even in the simple consciousness: I am, I remains only the object of which I become conscious through my subjective activity, without being able here to overcome the relation of the one to the other. Indeed, it can even be shown that, however we turn, we are not even in a position to think out a reason which, even if it were ever so much more perfect than ours, even if it actually cognized the true essence of things as they are in themselves, would be in a position to assure itself of this. Even the absolutely intuiting reason, before whose gaze its whole universe lay open, could not do that, for it too remains, *however we may think out its organization*, only with its subjective activity in intuiting. And all this for the simple reason that the self-cognition of our reason is *purely inner*. Of cognizing we know only through inner experience; this we obtain through inner sense and reflection, in which, however, our reason is so organized that it can observe for itself only its own inner relations, and nothing external going out beyond the inner activity. For every single cognitive activity, however, the being of the object is such an external, with which we therefore come into contact only through this activity, without ever being able to place it beside the latter for comparison. The whole problem, therefore, to show the objective validity of our cognition only through the agreement of the object with the cognition,

[p. 180]

is wrongly posed, and all this insistence that one should and will hear in philosophy of nothing other than a highest, absolute truth and its law, springs only from ignorance of a theory of human reason.

#### §. 128.

No proof, then, would be possible at all that we cognize things as they are in themselves; conversely, however, it can be shown without much difficulty that *the objects of our cognition, as we intuit them, cannot be in themselves*.

The law of transcendental truth demands agreement of cognition with the object, whereby the being of the object is the first, the validity of cognition however the second, dependent on that (the object is not to be created, but only cognized). The law of the existence of the thing is here the earlier, independent of its cognizability, in respect of how the thing is in itself. If, on the other hand, the existence of the object of a determinate mode of cognition is so constituted that this existence becomes dependent on cognizability, then the object of this cognition is not in itself as it is here represented; unless, which is something we never speak of in human cognition, it were first altered or created through cognition.

Now our cognition consists of the actual of sense intuition under the necessary form of formal apperception, whereby in the unity of transcendental apperception the world of sense with its history

[p. 181]

in space and time is cognized. If we now compare this world of sense and its existence with what was just set up, we find that the existence of things in space and time becomes, through the law of the contingency of all mathematical composition, dependent on the apprehension of the objects before experience, and thus cannot possibly belong to the essence of things as they are in themselves. The contingency of the coming together of one sense intuition with another makes it that our reason is bound to the law of the composition of magnitude, whereby the world of sense itself becomes something incompletable; in magnitude we have a form of the world of sense which cannot be developed at all into a completed whole.

We can always count further in the series of numbers, from one into the indeterminate of the infinite, and when the mathematician has then imagined a completed infinite, nothing prevents him from regarding this again as a unity, and counting further with it, so that he finally even plays with powers of the infinitely great, without ever coming to the end. Just so space and time. In space, beside everything given, there is always still room for the infinite further on, without beginning and end, as is already evidently pronounced in one of the first demands of the geometer, to extend every straight line without end; and time does not itself flow away, but only the events in it; it is only, as it were, a standing form, in which, from every moment, a past and a future without beginning and end, into the infinite, still has room. Every extensive magnitude is a part in the composition of a greater whole, every magnitude in general is a whole which consists through the composition of its parts.

[p. 182]

From the essence of the objects of our intuition, which in number, space and time is subject to the law of magnitude, there is therefore no world of sense at all as an all-embracing whole, but every whole that can be given is only a part of an ever greater one. The objects of sense intuition are consequently, in the incompletability of their magnitude, subject to a law of their existence which has significance only in relation to the way in which they are cognized; they are not for themselves, but only *as objects of a cognition*, i.e., only either illusion or appearance.

This contradiction between the incompletability of the mathematical series of world-magnitude and totality in the idea we can then consider more closely in particular according to the four moments. It shows itself according to quantity in the magnitude of the world in composition. The subjective unboundedness of our experience, the possibility of extending it ever further in space and time, expresses itself, as determination of the objects of our cognition, in the infinity of space and time themselves. Here we can therefore answer completely the difficulty that remained for us at the first view of mathematical intuition (§. 38). If we take up the laws of the continuity and infinity of space, time and number merely mathematically, these belong to the most evident in our cognitions; if, on the other hand, we wish to judge them philosophically, we always run the danger of entangling ourselves in contradictions. The world in space and time has a magnitude, but this cannot be a *finite* one, for then it would be bounded, space and time would run out beyond it, it would therefore be only the magnitude of a part and not of the world-whole, but just as little one

[p. 183]

*infinite* (*quantum infinitum* = ∞), for infinite is that whose magnitude can never be completed, which here however is supposed to be thought completed as an infinite whole. The concept of a *quantum infinitum* annuls itself; infinite magnitude must never be regarded as a whole. (Herein lies a fault of Schulz’s theory of the infinite; if one wants to correct this, all the principal propositions of his theory lose their meaning; what he says can be used only as a critique of mathematical language.) It is only the simply incompletable and indeterminable magnitude, which, taken objectively, therefore belongs to a kind of being which cannot be a being in itself.

Secondly, for the quality of the real we find the same contradiction in the law of the division of a given continuous whole. A continuous magnitude can again be divided further into the indeterminable, so that the actual division of the given whole can be regarded neither in its composition out of simple parts as finite, nor in an imagined composition out of infinitely small differential parts as infinite, as *infinita*. Continuity too is no quality of that which is in itself.

Thirdly, for the moment of relations the series of magnitude shows itself in the chain of events or in the series of the conditioned and its conditions. Here every conditionedness is only through its condition; if, then, this series is to subsist for itself, it would have to be there as a complete whole. But such a whole is not possible under the laws of nature; here we find every cause itself again as a conditioned, in that which determines it to exert its effect precisely in this time, the unconditioned

[p. 184]

can again be reached neither through the *free beginning* of a finite series, nor through the unconditionedness of the whole, for this freedom conflicts with the continuity in the flow of events, and instead of the whole we have again only incompletability.

Fourthly, the modal expression of the series is that of the contingency of the dependent, which could subsist for itself only through the absolute necessity of the simply independent. This independence, however, is in contradiction with natural necessity, for in nature the existence of every moment is indeed necessarily determined for itself, but yet always by means of its dependence as effect of the past, in an incompletable series backwards. Every single existence in nature is, through physical connection, dependent in its states on every other beside it in an *infinite* whole, and, according to metaphysical connection, dependent on the universal laws of nature, which hover over it as commanding fate, but themselves have no essence in themselves. Thus this natural necessity too does not belong to the essence of things as they are in themselves.

We thus exhibit from the law of the contingency of all mathematical composition that every sensible reason which understands itself makes, with the positive cognition from its intuitions, no claim to complete transcendental truth.

(Against this showing, taken as proof that we do not cognize the things in the world of sense as they are in themselves, there now stands the objection: if we in fact do not cognize things in themselves as they are, we have no judgment as to how they may be; we can

[p. 185]

also assert that the world of sense does not correspond to them, for our judgment about them is worth nothing at all.

This objection, first, has caused all the difficulties in the Kantian school when one wanted to determine the idea of being in itself. To remove these we wish to remark the following. Of course our reason must have some standpoint of conviction on which *it trusts itself* with a judgment about being in itself, if it wishes to assert even only this denying judgment against its sensible cognition; what this is, we shall orient ourselves about directly in exhibiting its speculative faith. This matter remained obscure because Kant had not properly developed the distinction between illusion and appearance. We wish for the moment only to get to know the subjective convictions of our reason, and for these we have so far shown conclusively that it must pronounce for itself the judgment on the form of its cognition of nature: to this no subsistence for itself can belong. We can also here still decline all further objective comparisons. Our reason has, with regard to things in themselves, beyond the sole judgment *that they are*, only negative judgments about *what they are not*.

Secondly, the same objection serves also, under the pretext of skepticism, those who busy themselves only with the errors of others’ speculations because they are too sluggish to try something better themselves. The ground of these skeptical objections always lies in the confusion of error with unreason. The business of philosophy is to secure reason in the self-activity of its thinking against error; it has by no means the aim, however, of transforming a madhouse into an academy of sciences.

[p. 186]

All dispute among philosophers presupposes, for the one who wants to take part in it, a rightly organized reason and seeks to warn this against error; error, however, is only a fault of reflection, a fault in the use of sound reason; madness, on the other hand, is a fault of the immediate organization of reason itself, sickness of reason. The game of skepticism now occupies itself constantly with the truth: one cannot prove *a priori* for the individual that he is awake, nor refute *a priori*, for the human race in general, the suspicion that it is afflicted by madness, but about this everyone is left *de facto* to his own conviction. As long as reason has not made itself known, it would not be impossible that madness should be found in its place. This point can make it clearer than any other how no philosophy with its truths purely *a priori* can attain complete evidence if it is not founded on an experiential anthropological investigation.)

#### §. 129.

We have so far taken the first step for our doctrine of ideas, in that we showed, against the view of common life: no being in itself belongs to the nature of things in space and time; we must further answer the question: does our cognition of nature show only illusion or appearances?
