Is there a transcendental truth for our reason, albeit a limited one, or is there none at all? Do we lose ourselves everywhere only in deceit and delusion, or is there a firm law of objective validity in our mind?

[p. 187]

The question in which all the interests of speculation are united is that of the relation of the natural and the ideal view of things, as the relation of their finite and their eternal essence. By these expressions, the finite and the eternal, there is namely asserted the validity of the natural and of the ideal view of the world side by side, yet in such a way that in nature we have only a subjective, limited view of human reason, whereas in the idea of the eternal we raise ourselves above this to the true essence of things in themselves. The difficulty of all speculation then consists in making this coordination of the finite and the eternal count in our convictions. For if we start from the view of common life, nature is for us the nearest and its reality the most evident, but with its laws the laws from the idea, the laws of freedom, stand in direct contradiction, and we find no means of getting across to them; if, on the other hand, we start immediately from the presupposition of the idea and its eternal law, we do indeed stand on the ground of freedom, but cannot find our way back to the finite of nature. The coordination of the two views can become clear only on our path of subjective consideration, in that both views show one and the same essence of things, while the difference between them lies in the subjective conditions of our cognition. If we now wish to undertake this subjective exposition, we find in common consciousness the natural view in secure possession of intuition and its evidence, whereas the ideal view appears as a mere matter of faith with far less secure rights. For us, therefore, the proof just given, that that cognition of nature does not suffice for reason itself to grasp the essence

[p. 188]

of things in themselves, is the entrance into the domain of speculation, in that we thereby lay a transcendental idealism at the foundation of the empirical realism of common life. This first step, however, serves only to prove the natural view of things wrong when it wants to pass itself off as the complete truth; we must take two steps further, namely first to show the well-founded claims of the finite in our mind, and then to secure the rights of the idea itself.

Whoever has once come to know the inadequacy of the finite view of things is easily seduced into reaching immediately for the idea of the absolutely certain and of absolute truth, and into wanting to defend the rights of the ideal on the strength of this alone, in that he rejects the finite entirely as deception and delusion; so proceeds the philosophy which names itself after intellectual intuition or after the doctrine of the absolute simply. Against this we must in turn take the rights of the finite under our protection, by showing that we have at least no truth and certainty at all in us if our finite view of things had no claims upon them.

Our theory of reason showed us that we have no other content of cognition than that from sense intuition; we have no other cognition than experience, all our cognition remains immanent, and what we possess beyond that sense intuition is only the form of necessity and unity, which without that content would be an empty, meaningless form. Sense intuition thus remains unavoidably the source of all reality in our cognition, but it forms itself at first only under the forms of the cognition of nature, and

[p. 189]

whose transcendental truth we have here just called in question, although earlier we were able to exhibit its empirical truth, its well-founded presence in reason. This conditioned reality of our view of nature must therefore after all be the source of all truth in our reason. If we are to be able to speak of an eternal, of a being of things in themselves, we must also arrive at it through the reality of cognition from experience. This points us back to the distinction between illusion and appearance. By denying to our natural view that it shows things as they are in themselves, we must nevertheless not transform it into dream and delusion, if we do not want to give up all truth for our reason as lost; we may rather regard it only as a subjectively conditioned mode of cognition, which indeed, hindered by the limitedness of our sense, does not let us see things as they are in themselves, but yet contains an appearance of these things. Where there is appearance, there must also be something that appears; even if, therefore, we do not cognize in it what it is, we nevertheless cognize that it is, and could we free ourselves from the limitedness of our essence, we would hold fast in the very same cognition the being of things as it is in itself.

If we therefore wish to assert a reality of the ideal view of things, this is possible for us only by laying experience beneath the ideas, as it were as a foil, by not allowing the cognition of the finite to be transformed for us into illusion, but seeking to hold fast in it still an appearance of the eternal. We want, therefore, that the cognition of our reason should indeed go to the eternal reality of being in itself, that this eternal

[p. 190]

reality should appear to us in our cognition from experience only in a limited way, but that in the idea, by negating these limits, we raise ourselves above the limited and so are able to cognize in it eternal being as lying at the foundation of this appearance.

#### §. 130.

How, then, is our standpoint to be chosen in order to show that our cognition of nature is not mere illusion, but that the highest reality lies at its foundation? So much we know, that we are not in a position to cognize the eternal immediately in its purity so as to decide the dispute directly by comparison. We know that it is impossible for our reason, as it were, to step out of itself to the object and so to compare its cognition with it. The objectively intended standpoint of the investigation, the agreement of the representation with the object, helps us here as little as it has been of use to us in any positive investigation of truth. We arrived at cognition from experience, and were able to exhibit the principles of its necessity in the fundamental laws of nature, not by confirming its relation to the things themselves, but by showing that every human reason knows by its nature these and these laws, and must judge according to them. In just the same way, with regard to the validity of the ideas, we shall have to take the same course of deduction, by showing: every finite reason, by virtue of the organization of its essence, necessarily believes in the eternal reality of being in itself.

[p. 191]

Nor can it be with these ideas as it is with the historical things of our cognition of nature, where the one person, for example, believes in the eternity of his essence, the freedom of his will, and the existence of God, and the other does not, just as the one knows that Pallas stands in the heavens and how she moves, while the other lets himself be quite unconcerned about it, or the one knows that oxygen is here on earth and how it shows itself, while the other deals with it and lives with it daily without troubling himself about it. With regard to these ideas nothing can be true that not everyone believes and has in himself; truth here does not depend on the stimulating sense, but springs from reason itself. Our position for the deduction of the ideas is therefore this, that we show that everyone necessarily believes in the eternal reality of the ideas. For this faith lies unavoidably in the immediate cognition of his reason, but of it he becomes aware again only mediately, through reflection; in this he can then commit errors of self-observation, and so himself suppose, and suppose vividly, that he believes nothing of all this, although this faith lies immediately in him as in everyone else. By virtue of this deduction we must therefore undertake to exhibit directly to everyone who denies the reality of the ideas, not merely that they nevertheless really have reality, but that he himself, whatever he may say, in fact also believes in their reality, and in holding the contrary only deceives himself.

And now this important deduction itself! It consists in the single word of the original unity of a rational activity of cognition, which only wants to be properly applied. We have seen that the individual

[p. 192]

forms of the ideas, totality, the absolute, freedom and eternity, arise only from the negation of the limits in the forms of the categories; the question now is, how do they obtain their applicability? Through the fact that in our reason there lies a basic consciousness of the absolute reality of the eternal, which is expressed through these forms of the unlimited in relation to the finite, which is only its appearance. But how can that basic consciousness of being in itself, as lying at the foundation of the finite, be derived in the theory of reason? Quite simply from the supreme relation of the anthropological theory of reason. Every rational power of cognition which has the form of original unity and necessity in its basic consciousness (as we have shown from experience of our reason) must refer every reality of cognition which it recognizes to complete unity and necessity; there forms itself in it, therefore, in every sensibly given material consciousness, however limited, the form of an unconditioned reality of it, through the highest condition of the unity of reason itself. Reason, through its peculiar form, always has the completed unity lying in each of its cognitions; even if, therefore, the content of actual cognition, stimulated only sensibly, has that form of incompletability in itself, it nevertheless falls within the original unity of that basic consciousness, and must therefore be regarded as the appearance of a *reality absolutely*.

It is the supreme relation of the formal basic consciousness of our reason to any material cognition by which the latter at all times the highest reality, albeit only as appearing and not purely as given in itself,

[p. 193]

recognizes therein, and so has in its innermost being a *speculative faith* in the conditionally absolute validity of its cognitions. No more intuitiveness can be given to this deduction, for it is wholly factual, and intelligible throughout only to one who, by exact self-observation, has procured for himself a quite determinate representation of the organization of a reason, and precisely of the form of rationality itself in a cognition.

Precisely by virtue of its rationality there lies in every reason a speculative faith in the being of its objects in themselves and in the transcendental truth of its cognition. This speculative faith is the *first presupposition* of every rational cognition which accrues to it immediately with the consciousness of necessity. Hence the natural realism of common human understanding, which rejects every idealistic assertion as ridiculous. In order, according to our limited idealism, to deny to our natural view of things its full transcendental truth, we must first call speculation to our aid; otherwise the relation from which Kant derived the transcendental illusion of every reason left to itself is the first in every rational cognition. There is only *one* truth, and we absolutely trust ourselves to be in possession of it; we presuppose immediately that we cognize things according to their essence in themselves, and only the conflict between the subjective incompletability of nature and the self-subsistence of the essence of things, which we think in the idea, can draw our attention in philosophical speculation to the fact that a distinction nevertheless lies at the foundation here, that we can let nature count only as appearance

[p. 194]

—a nature above which we want to raise ourselves in the idea.

With regard to the positive significance of the ideas, the idea of *being in itself* is the first in our ideal view of things; but it is only the idea of absolute necessity, namely the being of a thing independently of every manner in which it is cognized, whereas the modal limitation of sensible reason consists precisely in a dependence of the being of its objects on being cognized, so that the absolute contingency in the *appearance* lies before a subjective way of viewing things.

Commonly we oppose to *appearances* (phenomena) the *noumena* or things of thought; the former are objects of sense intuition, things in space and time, the latter are objects in the idea, which only the understanding thinks, like the world-whole or the deity; the world-order of the former we call *nature* as order of the sensible world, that of the others the *order of the intelligible world*, and here these things of thought with their intelligible world do not occur immediately as the things in themselves. Rather we find them in our consciousness at first only by quite voluntary reflections, of which it would still be a question whether they have any significance. For the noumena of the philosophers are those reflected forms of transcendental ideas of which we have shown that we form them voluntarily, by thinking the limits negated in the given relations of nature. Now, however, we can remark that the idea of being in itself is only one of these forms, and that with it we have precisely shown the use of these forms in general and thereby completed the deduction of our ideal view of things.

[p. 195]

The ideas of the absolute are indeed the property of reflection, which forms them only by negation of the limits; but they are of necessary applicability precisely in reflection, because through them we express to ourselves, before inner re-observation, the relations of speculative faith, the innermost law of the truth of our mind.

#### §. 131.

Since it is the first presupposition of every rational cognition that transcendental truth accrues to it, sensible reason with developed reflection can never reject its inadequate view of things as mere illusion, but will always regard it as appearance of the true essence of things, so that if it thinks the subjective limitations of its view removed, the eternal truth then stands before its eyes. We have, therefore, no other than finite cognition of things in nature, but in this we hold fast the law of the eternal essence of things, and need the forms of the absolute in order to become conscious of it before reflection.

The modal principles of our ideal view of things are therefore the following:

1) The sensible world under natural laws is only appearance.

2) At the foundation of appearance lies a being of things in themselves.

3) The sensible world is the appearance of the world of things in themselves.

[p. 196]

The first of these principles is the limiting principle of *knowledge* for the idea, the second is the principle of *faith*, the third the principle of *intimation*, wholly in agreement of these kinds of conviction with their explanation given above (§. 101.). Knowledge was the conviction of the understanding *a priori* with regard to sense intuition, for which we posit precisely as supreme law the law of the limitedness of our mode of cognition. The speculative faith in reality absolutely, stated here, exists only through the opposition which lies in the self-cognition of limits of one’s own essence; through it, however, the supreme place of the purely rational in our mind is designated, and it is therefore the foundation of all pure rational faith. For faith we called the conviction of reason *a priori*, which must arise in our mind through every thoroughgoing material determination of formal apperception, besides the limitation through sense. If, now, reason *acts*, this refers not only subjectively to the object of *its* cognition, but to the being of things absolutely, and thus to the highest positively incomprehensible reality of the eternal. The laws of pure reason for action thus go to the ideal view of things, and we see how speculative faith lies at their foundation.

Finally, the moment of the power of judgment was the contingency of all material consciousness for the immediate cognition of reason, whereby the subordination of it, as the conditioned, under the higher condition of formal apperception was determined; the power of judgment’s own conviction *a priori*, however, was intimation. Here we now find that precisely the last result of the contingency of the

[p. 197]

given material is the mere worth of our cognition of nature as appearance; the recognition of the ideal eternal worth in appearance, or the subordination of nature under the eternal law of faith, can therefore only become the theme of intimation. The proper domain of intimation is thus the subordination of nature under the practical laws of faith.

We know through intuition and concepts of the understanding of the existence of things in nature, we believe according to concepts of reason in the eternal essence of things, but we can recognize the law of faith in nature only in feelings, without intuition and without determinate concept. This doctrine of the ideas has the great advantage over every self-sufficient one that it carries with it the *principle of its own ignorance*, for to the limited mind it is the highest wisdom to recognize its own limits. In the logical doctrine of ignorance one distinguishes material, historical ignorance, whose general ground lies in the always possible extension of our experiences, and which is overcome by learning new truths, from formal ignorance in philosophical and mathematical matters, which is only a lack of cultivation, for the uncultivated man as well as the cultivated has here the same content of truth in himself, one learns nothing new there, but only develops the truth dwelling in everyone and makes it clearer to oneself; beside these two kinds of ignorance one must set the third, which is a union of both, that of the *necessary mysteries* for human reason, which cannot be removed at all. Its domain is the positive cognition of the eternal essence of things.

[p. 198]

This our doctrine of the ideas differs from the Kantian in that he knew no speculative faith, and he could not find it, because of the incompleteness of his doctrine of the grounding of judgments, in which he never went beyond proof. He rejected the speculative validity of the ideas because no proof concerning them can be conducted from speculative reason; he thereby remained standing only at reflection, and did not penetrate to that which is observed through this reflection. He did indeed always speak of a transcendental object of appearance, but to the question: do we cognize things in themselves? he left the answer owing. We, on the other hand, can here wholly complete our subjective theory, and at the same time decline every objective turn of the matter. Every reason believes that it cognizes things in themselves, not at the risk of erring, for in this respect there is no error, but at the risk of not being a fool.

The result of our whole doctrine of transcendental truth is then the highest praise of the critical method in philosophy. Suppose philosophizing be called the voluntary activity in thinking for oneself; and let it be asked: what do you want with this self-active thinking? Whoever enters upon the answer says: truth, the highest truth, agreement of cognition with its object, of the object with the subject! But if we go critically after what you really do, or even only can do, we find that you by no means want this truth, but only the cultivation of your cognition, the closest possible approximation to the ideal of logical perfection in cognizing, which is attained through proving, demonstrating and deducing your propositions. What you, beyond this,

[p. 199]

think to seek, that seems so to you only through confusion of empirical truth, from the relation of cognition to reason, with transcendental truth, from the relation of cognition to its object.

We have brought the logical principle of ground to the formula: every proposition must have a sufficient ground in immediate cognition, for it is only the mediate repetition of something immediately given; one thinks it to oneself secretly according to a transcendental meaning, but actually thus: every true cognition must have its sufficient ground, for the being of the object is the ground, the truth of the cognition after all only the consequence. With this postulate, however, we can do nothing at all; this dependence of cognition on its object is no theme at all for a scientific investigation. Whoever asserts the contrary demands a theory of the possibility of cognizing, he wants to answer how cognizing is possible. But have you then also asked yourselves whether the possibility of cognizing is a theme for any theory at all? Hardly! For otherwise you would find that cognizing occurs only as a quality before inner experience, but for qualities there is indeed no theory at all, and least of all for inner qualities; only quantitative relations can become the theme of a theory, and such a relation is not that of a cognition and its object.

[p. 200]

### Third Chapter.

### The World of Ideas.

#### §. 132.

From the principle of speculative faith set up, as highest ideal principle, our whole ideal view of things develops, in that we apply the forms of the transcendental ideas in order to think the true essence of things as lying at the foundation of our natural view. We can therefore put together systematically all our judgments from speculative ideas if we apply the forms of the transcendental ideas to the modal principles just set up.

Our ideal view of things contains an appraisal of nature according to ideas, in that we think the unconditioned in addition to the conditioned of nature. This happens in accordance with the categories, according to the four moments which we set up above (§. 128.), according to which Kant ordered his antinomies of reason. For if, according to the idea of the unconditioned, we want to think immediately the absolute completeness of a world under natural laws, then according to the four moments we entangle ourselves in the contradictions of the finite and the infinite, the simple and the continuous, freedom and nature, necessity and contingency. An empirical view, which holds with intuition and mathematics, asserts namely infinity,

[p. 201]

continuity, nature and the contingent existence of things; a rationalistic view, on the other hand, demands finitude, simplicity, freedom and necessity, and a skeptical view draws from both the conclusion that each is in the wrong against the other, and that there is therefore no truth in speculative matters.

We understand this dispute very easily; the contradiction consisted only in this, that one wanted to apply the idea to the uncompletable series of mathematics itself, instead of opposing it to these. The rationalists were wrong to apply the idea thus to nature, and the empiricists were wrong to deny all significance of the idea because it did not fit into their nature.

The resolution of this conflict, however, occurs in the different moments in opposite ways. In the mathematical moments, where the finite and the infinite are opposed to one another, both parties are wrong, because neither the finite nor the infinite magnitude can be thought as something absolutely completed, but both fit only into the uncompletability of the mathematical series. On the other hand, the dynamical moments of the contingent and the necessary, of nature and freedom, contain only an apparent contradiction, namely if one includes their application in nature and the sensible world, instead of inferring precisely from this to the opposition of two world-orders. The contingency of all being in the uncompletable mathematical series has precisely taught us that natural necessity is only a subjective condition of my mode of cognition, that therefore very well alongside it, as the contingent, an absolute necessity of eternal being, and in like manner alongside nature

[p. 202]

as the law for appearance, freedom as law for the eternal order of things, can subsist.

For magnitude and quality, as the moments of mathematical composition, the idea therefore contains only contradictions; a significant application can be made only in relation and modality, or the moments of dynamical connection.

#### §. 133.

At the foundation of our whole ideal view of things lies therefore being in itself as *eternity*. We must distinguish this eternal being precisely from the temporal schema of necessity, or being through all time. The true idea of eternity is the idea of an existence independent of the limits of space and time, without space and time, in opposition to space and time. That we cognize things as beside one another in space and as after one another in time depends only on the subjective limitations of our reason; this beside and after one another in its uncompletable series is nothing in itself, but must be thought as removed in eternal being. Positively we indeed have no representation at all of a thing that did not exist in a determinate space and a determinate time; we cannot free ourselves from these forms, for they spring from the peculiarity of our essence. But we can well see that these forms do not fit a being in itself; we think the idea of a being that is not bound to them, and that is for us the idea of eternity. Being through all time, from the first past to the last future, is always still only finitude,

[p. 203]

for time itself is uncompletable and in everything completed only finite; eternal being we oppose to all this, we think therein a being without any where and any when, in opposition to Where and When. How ill time suits an independent being of things in themselves every closer comparison shows. If I want to assume the being of things in themselves as present in time, then actuality belongs only to the moment of the present, i.e. the mere boundary between past and future and not to the smallest duration; this moment thus vanishes compared with the smallest duration, and every duration bordering on it is either past, which is no more, or future, which has not yet become. All reality from the whole of time would then be only as much as a point from an infinite line, i.e. no part of the line at all, but only a boundary of it. We can therefore think eternal being only figuratively as a Now without passing away and coming. Eternal being is thus in no way a supplemented existence through space and time, but we think therein only an existence free of the limits of both, which, as the true being of things, lies at the foundation of all appearances in space and time. In order to bring more content into this representation of eternal being, we may well also choose for it the expressions of a being with God or a being of God’s intuition, not as if we understood by it a being in which one beheld the deity in an enthusiastic vision, but an existence as God intuits things. We think our reason, precisely on account of its finite limitedness, as a merely ectypal reason, whose cognitions are mere ectypes of true being; we then represent to ourselves, however,

[p. 204]

figuratively an absolute mode of cognition in opposition to ours, as the archetypal one, of the intuition of the ideas, whose objects are the archetypes of true being, and since we call such a reason a divine one, it would thus be the mode of intuition of the deity, before which, as it were, the eternal ideas of all things and of our own essence would stand.

#### §. 134.

Upon this modal foundation our ideal view itself then develops in the moment of relation. The positive in our representation of the eternal is always nothing but the empty idea of the real absolutely; otherwise only the negative touches the eternal itself, while the positive, which we still retain in an idea of the unconditioned, is always in part still the property of appearance. For only in appearance is being itself given to us; the separation of the three modal principles for the idea is a mere abstraction; in the original unity of our cognition they are always all three together, and the whole of the representation according to ideas belongs here properly each time to intimation, which wants to approach the representation of the eternal through the finite, but can do this always only in feelings, whereas in the always incomplete concept only the negative belongs to faith.

We therefore form the world of ideas only by stages, in accordance with our finite representation of the world, in nature by negation of the limits. Since the law of magnitude is properly in contradiction with the idea, we think the absolutely real in that we the quality of our experience, as freed from the law of magnitude,

[p. 205]

represent, whereby we thus first of all raise ourselves above the merely material view of things in nature to what is living in the mind; we oppose to finite material substance an intelligible substance of the soul, give freedom to it, and so constitute the interaction of an intelligible world among free beings.

But this intelligible world, too, is only an idea of the eternal modeled on appearance; this world also cannot, as we represent it to ourselves, be in itself, but we need it only as a regulative for our actions in appearance, in that we subject ourselves in accordance with it to the laws of the end in the essence of things. We therefore raise ourselves secondly in our ideas also still above this intelligible world, and find only in the idea of the deity the completeness of our ideal view.

For our understanding has no other forms for thinking to itself the existence of things according to relation than the categories of substance, power and community. We think the existence of things in their dynamical whole under the laws of interaction in the world. This law is the form of the world for our reason; we call it the order of things in the world, and then speak of a lower world-order of nature and of the finite, and of a higher intelligible world-order of freedom and of the eternal.

This highest unity of our world is thus always only combination of manifold substances under universal laws. We have in nature material substance as the absolutely persistent with its moving fundamental powers, whereby the interaction in nature is produced, and in it natural necessity shows itself as the world-order of this material finitude. Just

[p. 200]

so we form for ourselves in the idea, for the intelligible world, the idea of the soul, as personal intelligence, as substance; its power is the free will, and the order of this world consists in the laws of the interaction of free persons, or in the laws of the realm of ends.

But in this world, too, the community of things consists through a law of order as the highest unity of this world; to this mode of representation also clings the limitedness of the analytic determination of the object *a priori* in the relation of the universal rule *in abstracto* to the subordinate case, and of the synthetic determination of the object *a priori* in the composition of single individual intelligences to infinity. Hence at its foundation, too, there still lies, beyond the idea of unlimited community, a higher idea, namely the idea of the deity, in which this order of things subsists eternally, and which we can think only through the idea of a highest absolute cause.

Our whole cognition thus raises itself, with regard to the ideas, through three stages. At the foundation lies the *natural view of things* according to matter and mind, in outer and inner physics. On the second the idea develops into the *moral view of the intelligible world*, above which finally intimation still ascends to the *religious view of things* according to the idea of the deity.

[p. 207]

### Fourth Chapter.

### The Idea of the Soul.

#### §. 135.

The nature of things shows itself to our reason in a twofold manner, in the material and the mental view of the world; above nature, however, we raise the absolute essence of things in themselves in the idea. Hereby there arises the riddle of all speculation, the relation of the absolute essence of things to matter and to mind. Speculation without critique, which does not know the correct relation of appearance to the absolute, therefore always tries anew a philosophy out of one piece, in which all our knowledge is to be united in the absolute. But since this is undertaken wholly against the law of our reason, the first presuppositions of every such doctrine become arbitrary fictions; there arises the philosophical novel of the eternal essence of things, which each tells in his own way, whose chief elements, however, must always be matter, mind and their union in the absolute.

The simplest and most natural telling of it is that of common *dualism* without cultivated speculation; here material substances and soul subsist independently beside one another, and above them is the creating deity. More cultivated speculation, on the other hand, demands unity of principle, and seeks a philosophy of identity instead

[p. 208]

of this dualism, whose purest subspecies are: 1) material existence is the absolute in *materialism*, 2) mental existence is the absolute in *spiritualism*, and 3) the indifference of matter and mind is the absolute in *pure fatalism*.

If one wants to make materialism probable, one must hold to mathematical evidence and the natural prejudice for conviction from intuition. In the greatest consistency that this system permits, it is godless, irreligious, without idea; it can therefore find approval only in a spirit of the age of violent opposition to enthusiasm, or among those who interest themselves one-sidedly in mathematical physics; to others the absurdity is equally clear which lies in this: wanting to explain life from death. Its purest presentation is the atomistics of older physicists; otherwise it passes through hylozoism, which confounds the *invisible* (the gas) with the mental, and the one-sided doctrine of the world-soul, into spiritualism.

Spiritualism justifies itself through the prejudice of unity in reason, in that it appeals to the simplicity of what thinks, and the identity of subject and object in self-cognition. Here only the existence of the living is recognized, the novel develops very variegatedly, its purest shape shows itself in Leibniz’s Monadology, more murkily it appears in common idealism, egoism, further in the doctrine of the emanation of souls from the deity, and through Spinoza’s pantheism and Schelling’s philosophy of identity it passes over into pure fatalism.

[p. 209]

The motto of pure fatalism would be: neither death nor life, in that the essence of things is subordinated to a supreme fate, through the prejudice of natural necessity. This doctrine is in itself capable of no development, wherefore those who in their first presuppositions assert something similar, like Spinoza or Schelling, in the execution always incline back again to spiritualism.

We shall not engage in any of these arbitrary attempts, for we know that all cognition of nature belongs only to appearance, but that in matter and mind two modes of appearance of the highest reality show themselves, which we may in no way squeeze together into one physical theory, since we can explain neither the death of the one through the life of the other nor life through death. Our cognition follows unavoidably the successive stages of the cognition of matter, of mind and of the eternal. At the foundation lies the material view of mere laws of motion; through this we arrive at the mental view of the world according to mere analogies with our own inner life, and from this finally to faith in the eternal, in that we think the mental absolutely.

We must appreciate the necessity of each one of these views of the world in order to learn to understand the organization of our reason.

We cognize from the principle of our speculative faith the eternal essence of things, in that in our finite view of the world we think the limits of our subjective view negated. If now from mere reason (according to §. 101. and 131.) there is given in the laws of the final end of things a law of eternal being, then there must

[p. 210]

under this also show itself the existence of the appearance as absolute substance, in that we lay an eternal reality at the ground of the empirical reality of the appearance. But since the completed mathematical composition of outer experience wholly contradicts the idea, the material for this idea can lie only in the object of self-consciousness. For if we wish to think the being of matter as absolute, we obtain a mere negation of limits without any content; if, on the other hand, we wish to think the I or the mind as absolute, there still remains something for us to think in the idea, because the inner qualities are not annihilated by any mathematical composition.

We found above, in the comparison of outer and inner physics, that the relation of matter to matter must be thoroughly intelligible and explicable according to mathematical laws, since the cognition of matter is determined, as to its content, with full necessity in space, and as to its existence in time. We therefore cognize matter as an absolutely persistent substance in space, whose properties can be resolved into mere relations of motion, and whose qualities are altogether resolvable, so that we must be able, e.g., to explain the essence of the organism from itself alone, according to material laws, without any aid from inner life. Thus matter is given against matter with completely closed necessity in space and time and is subject to mathematics. But it was precisely this necessity of the mathematical series that we have now come to know, in a higher relation, as the contingency of the finite. This mathematical cognition of matter is therefore the foundation of the finite, but

[p. 211]

it is also wholly enclosed in the finite. The finite is, to be sure, the appearance of the eternal, but precisely this mathematical cognition of matter, which is the surest and firmest thing in nature, belongs wholly to the subjective limitation of our mode of cognition; if we wish from this to think the limits of the finite as negated, then there remains for us in the representation of the eternal only the blind idea of eternal reality without any content. All properties of matter in space and time and through motion would thus have to be thought as removed in the eternal, and nothing more would remain to be thought in this matter. The mass, then, which is the properly real and the foundation of all being in nature, is, with respect to the eternal, the true nothing, the *οὐκ ὄν*, to which no existence at all belongs in itself, whose existence belongs only to my subjective way of viewing the world.

On the other hand, the I, as the individual object of my inner self-cognition, is the thinking and acting mind, a faculty with reason and will, which, to be sure, cognizes its own existence only under the limits of a mathematical composition in time, and perceives its outer relations only mediately through matter in space; but this mind nevertheless cognizes those qualities of reason and of the will, and even the qualities of matter in relation to itself, not under those mathematical forms, but as irresolvable properties (§. 120.) which do not vanish with those forms. If, then, we relate the cognition of ourselves to speculative faith, that an eternal being lies at the ground of all appearance, and if we now think our own essence through the idea of the negation of the limits according to its eternal significance, then self-consciousness does not shrink away for us

[p. 212]

together into the empty formula that something is, as into a blind representation of the absolutely real, but we retain in the idea of the soul a determinate content of inner qualities, which leaves us something determinate still to think in the eternity of our essence.

The true relation of outer and inner physics in our reason is therefore this: that the inner view of nature alone supplies our ideas with a positive content, while the outer wholly vanishes before the idea; immediately, however, for the natural view only the outer material view has its subsistence for itself, while the inner remains thoroughly dependent on it. (According to §. 120.) The organization of our mind therefore necessarily demands both views in combination: the true essence of things appears to us only through the living, but immediately the appearance of nature consists for us only through matter.

Only through the relation to material substance did we obtain a firm rule of existence, only through the persistent in matter did inner experience become possible; we would therefore have no hold or firmness at all in our reason without the thoroughly finite cognition of matter, but we would also have no positive relation of appearance to the idea at all if the object of pure self-consciousness did not remain independent of the complete mathematical composition, and precisely thereby leave inner experience in the finite incomplete, whereby a necessary relation of this object of pure self-consciousness to eternal reality is given to us in the basic consciousness of reason.

[p. 213]

#### §. 136.

Through this we now obtain the following system of *psychological ideas*, which gives application to all our ideal convictions.

The singularity of the subject in our inner consciousness, which we designate by the word I, becomes for us, before the idea, an independent individuality, as an *immaterial substance*. For the individuality of our self-consciousness remains for us in the idea of the *soul*; the dependence of its existence on matter vanishes of itself, because matter is nothing for the idea; we must therefore think it as an independent substance, which is at the same time immaterial, whose schema, however, is not persistence in time, but the eternity of being without any time.

Independent individuality we call *personality*, and an immaterial personal substance is called a *spirit*. We therefore think our eternal being in the idea of the soul as a spiritual existence, for which the perfected inner qualities then remain as content. These, however, are reason and will. The complete idea of the soul is therefore that of a rational, willing spirit, which we call *intelligence*.

If, then, we raise ourselves in the idea above the mind as object of inner experience, and think the limitation of our temporal view of our own essence as removed, there remains for us, for faith in our eternal being, this idea of the soul or of intelligence, the idea of a rationally willing spirit whose existence is not bound to space and time. The faith in the eternity of our individual rational will is therefore

[p. 214]

necessarily grounded in every human reason by the fact that to it belongs, in the innermost essence of its basic consciousness, faith in the absolute reality of its cognitions, and that it consequently attributes to everything that has reality for it in appearance the worth of an appearance of the eternal. If it thinks to itself the limitation of appearance as removed, then it is the eternal being itself that it holds fast in the idea. The blind man, to whom I tell of the color of a body, which he knows only through feeling, will be able to take from it nothing but that quite other properties belong to the object than those which he perceives in it; so it goes with us with matter in regard to the ideas. If we wish to think its eternal reality, there remains for us only the idea of a *wholly different* constitution than its appearance gives to us. He, on the other hand, who has seen a region only through fog can think this away; he has no perfected view of it, but much still remains to him standing in its outline, which he can supplement to a clearer view. So also our self-cognition in relation to the idea: this too is clouded by sense and thus bound to space and time; but if we think these limits removed, then the whole appearance does not vanish for us in our eternal being, but a part of the outline remains standing for the perfected, clearer view, which we hold fast in the representation of a personality with reason and will, without, however, being able positively to separate the share of the idea from the subjective limitations.

Here, then, we have our ideal convictions of the nullity of the material view of things, according to mere laws of motion, and of the eternal being of the

[p. 215]

reason shown; but thereby no proof whatever has been furnished for these convictions. We had to hold solely to subjective deduction. These convictions exist as *ideal principles* in our mind, and cannot even be regarded as proved from the principle of speculative faith. Just as little as we could prove the individual principles of natural science from the supreme principle: the world of sense is a world under laws of nature, since we first learned from the progressive deduction what content of supreme laws of nature is to be found in our reason, so little is the subordination of individual ideal convictions under the principle of speculative faith a proof, for here too the deduction must first show the individual content in our reason, and this we have done here by comparing the supreme forms of the outer and inner view of nature with the supreme ideal relation of appearance and of being in itself. With regard to the proofs for the persistence of the soul, we remain wholly with the same results that Kant already found. Such proofs, first, never reach our eternal being beyond the limits of space and time, but have only the immortality of the mind, its continuance through all future time after the death of its body, in view; and secondly, if we strip them of all poetic decorations, we can lay at their ground as ground of proof nothing but the empty formal determinations of an object of pure self-consciousness: the I is the *subject* of all its thinking, and the I is the same *single* subject in all its thinking. But from these grounds nothing follows for the temporal persistence of the mind.

[p. 216]

First, that which exists only as subject and not as predicate of another would, to be sure, be substance and absolutely persistent in time: but so much we do not cognize of the object of pure self-consciousness. We cognize, to be sure, all thinking only as activity of the I, but the I itself does not become for us, for itself, an object of intuition (§. 25.); through pure self-consciousness we do indeed cognize *that it is*, but not *What* and *How* it is; it could therefore, in another relation than that to its thinking, nevertheless be determined as the predicate of another.

Secondly, if we wished to infer with Mendelssohn from its singularity to its simplicity and indestructibility, then against this it holds, first, that its singularity by no means necessarily has to be the simplicity of a thinking monad, but that it can just as well be compared with the singularity of an organic form, e.g., that of its body, where it would then indeed be destructible; and then, even if simplicity were granted, there would still inevitably belong to the thinking monad in time a degree of strength in all its properties, which can increase and decrease; even though it could therefore not be destroyed through division of an extensive magnitude, it could still be extinguished through annihilation of its intensive magnitude.

#### §. 137.

We here distinguish the idea of the eternity of our essence from the persistence of our mind in time as immortality. This relation we must still consider more closely.

The assertion of the continuance of the mind after the death of the body goes upon a being in time, thus

[p. 217]

upon finite relations, and is a matter of experience. The decision of this question does not at all have, for a rightly understood philosophical speculation, the interest it appears to have, for in regard to it what matters to us is eternity and freedom, in which alone the dignity of our essence can be maintained, and which precisely is not to be found in any time. In order to call ourselves free, we must raise ourselves above all time; the rights of death and of rigid natural necessity in time, on the other hand, are the surest and greatest. The material substance is here certainly imperishable through all time, and thus precisely the mere nothing for the relations of the eternal; our own inner being, however, retains its reality in the world of ideas, and for that very reason attaches itself only for a few moments to these embodiments.

Faith, then, finds place only in the eternity of our existence; the continuance after death, or the mortality of the mind, is on the other hand a theme for inner physics, about which we must have knowledge, or about which one can be advised according to probabilities. This region of inner natural science and its relation to the outer is, however, very likely that about which clear concepts are hardest to obtain. A splendidly prepared field of wilder or tamer hypotheses, as of healthy or sick children of fantasy, offers itself to us here in the questions about immediate communion of spirits, spirit-seeing, generation of the souls of children from the souls of the parents, metempsychosis, and life before birth. What are we now to do with these mysterious investigations of higher physics? About the outer relations of spirit to spirit it is easy for us to answer, in that we reject all efforts of those who would, with their secrets,

[p. 218]

enrich us. In regard to all outer spiritual relations, namely, the principle stands firm that, according to the organization of our reason, no spiritual community is possible for it at all except through material mediations; with immediately spiritual contact nothing at all remains for us to think. For the spiritual appears to us only in inner self-cognition; the cognition of it is bound to inner sense and can show me only my own life, but every foreign life only through spatial mediations, through analogies with the relation of my inner being to my bodily organization. Here, then, everything depends on the judgment of the relation in which mind and body stand to one another. It may have been remarked less definitely that whoever once assumes the immortality of the mind is thereby compelled, without any image, to engage also with opinions about transmigration of souls and life before birth. In regard to this, Socrates makes in the *Phaedo* a very important discovery: to dying life is not opposed, but becoming-born. What can be born must in nature also be mortal; what can arise in nature can also pass away in it. For nature can also run through the course of every process in it backwards; every process can also take place reversed, but dying is precisely the reversed process of becoming-born; the possibility of both is therefore the same, and if the possibility of the birth of a spirit were comprehensible to me, the possibility of its dying would also lie before my eyes. Thereby we are then, if we wish to assume the immortality of the soul, burdened at the same time with the thought of our earlier existence before birth, which, since it enters into that beginningless

[p. 219]

past reaches back, at first glance has something shuddersome about it, with which one does not gladly engage; afterwards, however, when one has once become familiar with it, it turns out that this lets itself be depicted quite agreeably for the history of transmigrations of souls. There are then principally two kinds of representation: the one kind lets us serve our way up from below and have already attained in man a quite considerable degree, the other, on the contrary, takes us for degraded court-servants of the Deity. Scientifically, the first view, about which one can get adequate instruction among us from Lavater and Herder, is favored in physics, in order to lay spiritual meanings beneath the gradations of organized formations of the earth; the other, on the contrary, makes itself felt more in the mysteries of the doctrine of religion, where, in accordance with the consciousness of our inclination to evil, one draws it out into the history of the Fall or of the defection of the ideas from God. Both kinds of representation, of the growth or decrease of our worth, are images from nature, like the growth of youth and the aging, of which the former pleases the sanguine, the other the melancholic temperament more; they become adventurous in their application when I apply them to the transmigration of souls in time itself, and so make the image again into actuality. If, on the other hand, we keep the image and apply it poetically to the idea, then it gives us the opposite views of intimation.

But here we wished to speak of our existence in time, as it shows itself in inner experience, and to ask whether we are to think it as limited to this life, or not. The correct comparison is the following: The presupposition that to my mind, independently of the

[p. 220]

body, an existence of its own in time belongs, is in any case an unusable, empty thought, and, as we have just seen, even a very burdensome one, in that it forces us to hold opinions about transmigration of souls. In order to arrive here at a determinate judgment for ourselves, everything rests on the manner in which the relation of outer and inner physics must be thought toward one another, on the community between body and mind. The dualism of the common school metaphysics proposes here, between two hypotheses, the choice: either to admit an immediate physical influence between mind and body, both, though things of different kinds, standing in interaction, the nerve-activities working on the sensation of the mind and the will of the latter working back on them, or merely to assume a pre-established harmony, only the ordering hand of the Creator of the world having placed both natures so that they play alongside one another in a necessary parallelism, though as things of different kinds.

Neither of the two satisfies, however. The pre-established harmony repeats only in other words the inexplicability of the matter, for to let the will of God intervene means only to acknowledge the end of our insight; the natural influence, however, is contrary to every sound physiology, in that we here ascribe moving forces to an immaterial substance which consequently itself fills no space—and why precisely only in the center point of the organism, why not everywhere else? We thereby give up all our laws of physics to ghosts, elves, fairies, genii, ethereally winged angels of light and of darkness, or to any other child of inventive fantasy. Higher speculative views

[p. 221]

let, on the contrary, either (materialistically) thinking subsist only through matter, or (spiritualistically) matter only through the thinking being; but here too neither of the two fits into our world under laws of nature.

For these two attempts follow the idea of drawing outer and inner physics together into one system of natural science, against which we have already spoken above (§. 72. and 120.). Materialism makes false pretensions, for (according to §. 118.) there is for outer natural science a mathematical theory of the movable, in which, however, only the relation of matter to matter can be comprehended, whereas both the constitution of matter according to representations of sensation, such as color, sound and scent, in its relation to the cognizing reason, and still much more reason itself, withdraw here from all explanation. Spiritualism, however, according to our natural view of things, can serve still much less for an all-sufficient physical theory, for independently of the persistence of material existence in space we would have no inner experience at all; only through the interaction with the history of my body do I obtain any rule of ordering for the inner alterations, thus without the intuition of things outside me in space my self-cognition, according to the organization of my reason, would not even be possible.

How, then, are we to judge the relation between body and mind? We need only ask the common judgment of life in order to obtain the correct answer; artificial speculation errs easily here, but at the ground of the natural, non-speculative reflection of common life there always lies the presupposition: *that*

[p. 222]

*I and my body are one and the same*, so that, as soon as it is a matter of acting, we make no difference any more. For this assertion I do not wish to adduce the common point that in sleeping and waking, health and sickness, we depend on the body and are bound up with it down to our innermost consciousness, for this too could be thought through a mere interaction between the two, but I appeal to this, that everyone in every action called voluntary takes, and necessarily must take, *his will and the life-process of his body* for one and the same.

#### §. 138.

According to the law of causality every occurrence in nature has a determinate, complete cause, from which it flows; but I cannot, according to the law of all composition of magnitudes, assume for the same occurrence two different causes, and apparently two causes which have the same effect must in fact be one and the same. Let this, however, not be misunderstood. Different causes do indeed work together to a composite effect; then to each belongs a part of the effect, but the same part, which belongs to the one, I cannot then ascribe to the other; there cannot be, alongside one another, two sufficient causes of the same phenomenon. Thus, e.g., the movement of the hand of a clock is the result of the force of its moved springs and of the relations of all its wheels, where each has its part in the effect. I can

[p. 223]

also, to be sure, combine with the clockwork such a compensation, which, when it stands still or is wound up, works in its stead, and moves the hands according to the same rule. But to lay two clockworks on the same hands, so that each of them moved them in the same way, would not go; it would then run either twice as fast or not at all. Let us apply this to the voluntary movement, e.g., of the hand, and we shall see that we declare our will and the life-process of our body to be altogether one and the same. The thoroughgoing mathematical explicability of material appearances makes it necessary that the organism too must let itself be explained completely from laws of material physics, which do not rise above motion, pull and push. Thus it must also be an outer process, mediated by moving forces of matter, through which the vital appearances of my body subsist. We know very little of this as yet; but in order to give the thing a name, I will assume that the life-process of my body in regard to muscle-movement is a heightened electric process, then it is mediated galvanic shocks, which spread downward along the connection of my nerves, contract my muscles and so bring about the movements of my hand. The occurrence of this movement would then be explained wholly materially, yet I nevertheless call it a voluntary one, and say: I move my hand only because I will to move it. I give, then, here two complete causes of the same occurrence, side by side, according to two different views, in two ways: once I say from inner perception, my will is the cause of the movement of my hand, and then according to the physiological explanation, the movement follows according to the material

[p. 224]

laws of the life-process in my body. If there can therefore be only one sufficient cause of an occurrence, then the life-process of my body and my will are one and the same, and one sees easily that this proposition can be extended also so far: *my mind in general, as object of inner experience, is one and the same with the life-process of my body as the object of outer experience.*

And is this assertion neither contradictory nor materialistic? We need only compare our exposition of the ideal view of things in order to find the moment of deduction precisely for this relation of inner and outer nature. Neither in inner experience do I cognize my mind as it is in itself, nor even in outer experience in my body something as it would be in itself, but both are only appearance. It is therefore only a *different mode of appearance* of the one and same reality, which shows itself to me once as my mind inwardly, and then as the life-process of my body outwardly; my material view remains here only the auxiliary representation of my sensibly limited reason, and loses all significance toward the eternal; the inner living view, on the other hand, lets the true essence of things themselves appear to me more closely, even if still in a limited way.

#### §. 139.

Yet we must illuminate this object still more fully. How do we stand now with the mortality of the mind according to its inner mode of appearance in time?

[p. 225]

It depends on what we judge the same to be with regard to the body. We posit the reality of the mind as one and the same with the reality of its organization—with what, then, are we actually comparing the mind? With the substance which today or yesterday constitutes my body as matter, that is not possible, for this material substance is in the organization the daily altered, ever changing, the abiding in it is only the form of the organization, the form of the life-process itself. Thus with this enduring form of changing substances in the organization alone can I compare the mind. It would be equivalent to that wherein life in matter actually consists; this, however, is only the form arising from the conflict of the material forces in an organic process, and with this the most perishable thing that is to be found in matter, which is so easily extinguished, like the little flame on a candle.

Precisely from the fact that the mind corresponds to the life in matter, one has indeed wished to infer the very opposite, by saying: the mind is the principle of life in matter, it is the vital force through which an organization actually lives, a little flame from the universal essence of the world-soul, which can indeed also pass over from form to form, and escapes when a formation is destroyed, or is lost again in the universal life of the world-soul—or whatever similar expressions one may choose. But in all this the relation of the living to matter is thoroughly misunderstood; we may not actually speak of any principle of life in matter, for every life is for us only an inner thing; life can indeed appear *through* matter, but never *in* matter. We know no true

[p. 226]

life other than cognizing, desiring and willing of our reason. Life means to determine oneself from an inner principle to action, and for this we have no other case of application than the inner activity of the mind. In matter everything comes about only from outer relations, so too in the organism, which consists only through the counteraction of its parts against one another under a determinate form. In matter there is only an analogue of life through the form of the organizations; to this corresponds the inner life, but we may not introduce this life itself, neither through interaction of the mind nor as a life-force of its own, into the material relations. To want to let the inner living thing, the mind itself, act on matter is contrary to the principles of a sound physiology, since the complete mathematical construction of matter pushes out every such foreign aid of the immaterial from itself, and in addition it becomes a quite idle hypothesis. The nerves, excited to sensation, act in an inconceivable way on the mind, and give it the sensation; this mind then acts again in an inconceivable way through its will on other nerves, and so moves the muscles. To what purpose these two inconceivabilities? Let one rather leave the play of the nerves among themselves, and one obtains without aid of the mind the same result. A life-force of its own in matter as something material, as property of a particular kind of organizable matter, or as a particular kind of matter itself, we may, however, in no way presuppose either; the analogue of life in matter, to which the appearance of our inner life corresponds, is not material *substance as mass*, however finely one may dissolve it into vapor, gas

[p. 227]

or ether, nor an *outer force*, for that goes only upon pull and push, but *the form of a physical process*. Process in nature is the result of the interaction of forces, and its law is the form of such an interaction and not the essence of a force. The unity of an organism, through which it lives, is therefore not a vital force, which can be added to it or withdrawn from it, but solely the form of the combination of the material forces in it, the peculiarity of the life-process. The universal organism of nature too can be regarded not as world-soul, but only as the universal law of the cycle in the occurrences of the world.

The common modes of representation of the relation between matter and mind make either the kinship between the two too great, in that they wish to unite in one mode of appearance that which, according to the opposed modes of appearance of things, is the same reality, or they strive to make the separation quite sharp, from fear of materialism, in that they will not admit that unity even according to opposed modes of appearance. All hypotheses of the first kind, which presuppose a natural influence between mind and matter, or a material vital force, are a more or less concealed hylozoism, where one confuses the materially invisible, vapor, gas, ether of life, ethereal fluid, nerve-spirit, with the spiritual, under the pretext of a finer, higher, nobler material substance, or even of an intermediate thing between matter and mind. This helplessness is shared by almost all theories of comparative anthropology with the most unskilled representations of the alchemists.

[p. 228]

On the other side, when someone makes keener attempts with comparative anthropology, and seeks out in the organization the parts corresponding to the individual functions of thinking and willing, as Gall, say, has attempted with the structure of the brain, we hear from many philosophers protests, in the name of the freedom of the will, as if this were thereby endangered, which is by no means the case. In general you must indeed admit the dependence of the mind on the history of the body in growing up and growing old, sleeping and waking, health and sickness, magnetic exaltation, fever-dream and raving—where, then, are we to find the boundary? No; on the contrary, the cultivation of comparative anthropology must, whether we may now understand much or little of it, one day show us, down to the smallest detail, the correspondence of the organic functions with the inner life, and all this has nothing at all to do with the idea of freedom. The freedom of the will is indeed not to guarantee the independence of the *inner* nature from the *outer*, but solely the independence of the *mind* from *all nature* in general, and in this our insight will become only so much the clearer, the more determinately we recognize the *natural* agreement between the organization and reason.

Thus to the most perishable thing which may be found in the material world, to the life-process of an organization, we must regard the *temporal* existence of the mind as equal; but in order to give to this matter a clarity sufficient for all necessary consequences, we shall still have to subject the general concepts of material physiology to a new critique.

[p. 229]

#### §. 140.

It is an old task of speculation to explain how the infinite becoming is related to being. In our world the becoming of the inherences is only through and in the being of the substance and its power, but becoming is for us higher than being; only to becoming do we deem the living bound, so that motion and life become for us of equal meaning, while infinite rest would be a rigid being of death. Being for itself in substance would be for us, in its unchangeable rest, the annihilation of the world before our eyes, a vanishing of its actuality into the empty unity of the understanding, in which nothing would be distinguishable; only in becoming does the world step before our sense, only in becoming is it for us appearance, and its actuality as a world of sense consists solely in the *history* of the world through all time. How, then, is such a becoming of the world through all time possible?

We grasp this task here only for the standpoint of explicability, for the material view of the world. In the material world the given determinable is the mass as movable substance; the form in it, on the other hand, is figure in space and motion in space and time; the becoming in it is the change of figures through motion, in this consists the history of the world; we call it the formation of matter. This formation, however, is only the mathematical (phoronomic) form of the world, which must first have a dynamic form of the community of things lying at its ground (§. 113. 3)), through which it subsists. This dynamic form is the form of the interaction of material forces, which we call a *physical process*. What, then, is the formative principle of the

[p. 230]

material world? Not a formative force of nature, but a *formative drive* from the relation of the material fundamental forces in the process. The formative principle in nature is not the law which determines the *effect*, not the law of the fundamental force, but the law which gives the *community* of things, the law of their interaction, which contains only the rule of the *world-order* for given substances and forces, and this is the rule of physical processes.

The fundamental forces of every mass are an *original expansive force* in inverse ratio to its respective volume, and an *original attractive force* in all distances according to the inverse ratio of the spherical surfaces whose radius is the corresponding distance. The supreme forms of physical processes are, on this basis, *processes of restored equilibrium*, in which the forces engaged in conflict put one another to rest, in that each indifferentiates the effect of the other, and *processes of the cycle*, organizations, where the history of the change runs out from one state of alterations, and leads back again to the same alteration, so that the process always repeats itself periodically.

Which of these two laws, then, determines the form of the course of the world, which becomes the formative principle in the whole of nature? Striving toward equilibrium or cycle? In particular cases we perceive now processes of indifference, now organizations: the movements of the planets about their sun; the water—from heaven it comes, to heaven it rises and again down to earth must it, ever changing, or the formations in animals

[p. 231]

and plants follow the law of the cycle; every chemical dissolution, however, and every fermentation ends with the rest of equilibrium, when the interpenetration or separation of the heterogeneous is evenly completed, just as every counteraction according to the law of specific gravity, according to the law of temperature changes or of excited electricity. But all these observed indifferentiations or organizations have only a subordinate subsistence; every individual process leads only to a relative equilibrium or to a relative cycle, for the inner law of each such process is always overpowered in the infinite whole of the course of the world by a still higher sphere. Every individual process whose inner forces accord with the organization can be brought to rest and destroyed by outer influences from a higher equilibrium, as, e.g., the life of the animal and of the plant, which subsists through the daily cycle of its vital functions, maintains itself ever more firmly in struggle with outer nature as it grows to maturity, but then, aging, declines again to complete dissolution; here the organization is overpowered in the progress from youth to age, to death, by the law of equilibrium. Just so, however, there is on the other side also no dissolution which could not be parted again, no separation which could not be reunited through new outer influence. Which, then, is the supreme law of the course of the world, to which at last every individual process succumbs? Is it dissolution in rest or renewal of motion into the infinite?

Our more recent mathematical physics has more or less unconsciously given itself the prejudice: that in nature everything strives toward equilibrium, that becoming is, as it were,

[p. 232]

a foreign state forced upon nature, against which it struggles, in order to rigidify in eternal rest, and thereby the law of death was set as the mechanism of nature as supreme, even though the already acknowledged law of equality of action and reaction, or the law that the sum of all motions in the world can be neither increased nor diminished, ought to have proved the contrary. Schelling has the merit of having first recognized among us, against this, the highest law of organization and of its life, and so made nature living in itself.

We can here, first, show with ease *indirectly* that only under the presupposition that the law of the cycle is the supreme one in nature is a history of the world through infinite time possible at all; if we take the law of equilibrium as the supreme, we always obtain only a finite history of the world. Either we assume that in primeval time the created or uncreated chaos once lay in complete rest of an even interpenetration of all its elements, into this rest there entered the formative principle foreign to it, the first mover, and gave the first beginning of motion; this began at once to spread further, the history of the world began, it evolved up to the wildest fermentation of the disunion of all elements, but with this it had to reach a highest point, the motion sank again, and must at last lose itself back into the rest of the first equilibrium: or we begin at once with chaos, in which its forming principle wholly resides, with chaos as a fluid in the highest, wildest fermentation, which, however, overpowered by the law of equilibrium, gives a history of the world only by this, that it

[p. 233]

gradually, growing ever calmer, rigidifies into the dead rest of a firm crystallization. In any case we obtain here, then, only a finite history of the world. The law of the cycle, on the other hand, corresponds to the course of occurrences through all time, in that the appearance of the world through all time and through all space becomes the development of the cycle in the interaction of all material substance with each; in ever greater spheres the history renews itself through the epochal self-reproduction of each organism; if the one goes to ruin, it is only by the whirls of a higher sphere that it is carried away, until at last every subordinate cycle loses itself in the infinite of the interaction of all with each, similar to the passage of all elliptical circles over one axis into the infinite arc of the parabola.

Beside this indirect showing we can, however, also place a direct proof. We ask: what is the highest law of physical processes in the world? and we can find the answer ourselves, since we know the fundamental forces of the material world, if we only investigate the forms of their conflict. Every mathematical theory arises through continued combination of its simplest elements, and these contain its sole fundamental laws. All changes of the material world are therefore only compositions from the relation which shows itself in the reaction of two masses according to the law of their fundamental forces. For two such masses we can think in general four forms of their reaction; reaction *from a distance* or *only in contact*, and in each case either with preponderating force of attraction or of repulsion. Here now there results from every original reaction from

[p. 234]

a distance a process of the cycle, but from that in contact, on the other hand, first of all a process of equilibrium.

First, in the action at a distance a play will arise between the original attraction and elasticity, as soon as both masses move toward one another, whether at rest or also in rectilinear approach or recession. Here at last the original attraction from a distance will decide the outcome; both masses will plunge together toward the centre of their gravitation with determinate velocity, and collide there. In the impact both are pressed together against one another; thereby their original elasticity is brought into play, which will annihilate their motion at the highest degree of compression. But now, left to their elasticity alone, they are driven apart again, and, because the expansive force stands in direct proportion to the compression, when they come out of contact they will recede from one another with the same velocity with which they approached one another at the initial moment of the impact. This receding motion, however, is gradually overcome by the attraction; they come again toward one another into rest, and the process begins anew.

But if at the initial moment the one mass has toward the other a moment toward oblique rectilinear motion, then only the original attraction enters into relation with the spatial relation; if we regard this with respect to the relative space in which the one mass rests, then this lies in a centre of forces to which the attraction belongs, in inverse ratio of the square of the distance, as central force, and around which the other therefore describes a curved line of the second order.

[p. 235]

If, namely, the attraction is strong enough to give the distance in an oblique line a maximum, the motion passes over into the cycle through an ellipse; but if this is not the case, it remains with a mere onset of a cycle into the infinite, in parabola or hyperbola.

Secondly, processes in contact, where repulsion preponderates, ensue according to the mechanical relation of the surfaces of contact as mere motions according to the relation of specific gravity, but where attraction preponderates, as chemical dissolutions, both of which therefore come to rest once equilibrium is attained. Yet these actions in contact alone always stand under the condition of an earlier action at a distance, and can show themselves only where opposed actions at a distance maintain themselves in relative equilibrium. The relation of the action at a distance is therefore alone the original one.

Herewith we have established two things. First, the formative principle of nature is a universal law of organization in it; every process out of free motion carries with it a law of its own self-reproduction; every original, independent organization (such as that of the *astronomical motions*) is a *purely dynamical* one; *chemical* organizations, on the other hand, such as those on the surface of the earth, whose cycle is determined by an alternation of dissolutions and secretions, have only a dependent subsistence through a superordinate dynamical organization (hence e.g. the power which the periods of the earth’s axial rotation and annual revolution have over *every vital motion on its surface*), and are therefore in every case

[p. 236]

subject to the law of a continual stimulation from without (the highest of which, for the earth, is its *illumination* by the sun.)
