Secondly, this universal law of organization in nature subsists, however, not through a supreme formative being in matter as world-soul, but the fundamental forces of motion become organizing forces only through *reciprocal relation* in space and to space, so that a mathematical proof for the universal organization of nature can indeed be given, but this highest law of unity in the material world (of the form of its community) falls under the condition of the contingency of all mathematical composition. It therefore has only a regulative worth for application, in that, in accordance with it, we are indeed entitled to expect organized forms throughout the whole of nature, but can nowhere specify the form itself for the individual case. For this reason material life always appears to us as a free play of organic forms.

#### §. 141.

What, then, is our ideal view of things in general under the idea of the soul?

Underlying all our convictions is the material view of things, which, however, has only a finite worth for the human view of things. Not to the substance in this world, but only to the change of its history, does the second, spiritual view of the inner living then attach itself. By mere analogies, according as the form of its

[p. 237]

organization corresponds to the inner life of our own reason, we form a spiritual view of the world of nature, which proceeds from the recognition of reason in others in human society as its brightest point, but from there spreads in ever more and more indeterminate relations over the whole of nature, as far as we find the motion of organic forms in it, so that in just that proportion we wish to recognize again in nature too the highest law of our inner life, the law of the end.

This spiritual view of the world then attaches itself more closely to the idea, and thereby becomes for us the cognition of an intelligible world and of its higher order of things, in that we have faith, for the eternal essence of things, in the self-subsistence of intelligence, deem human society united under spiritual laws of virtue and of right, and have faith in the law of the end as the highest in the existence of things, to which therefore nature also, in its organizations, submits through the law of its sublimity and of beauty in the free play of its forms.

With this we cast deep glances into the innermost of the organization of our convictions. What meets us in life as a light play of intuitive forms becomes after all the object of the purest satisfaction in its mysterious beauty. Here we see how this transition and this union is grounded in the deepest interior of our mind: to those merely material forms corresponds the inner life, and in this the idea grasps the eternal essence of things itself.

All theoretical outer physics proceeds in its explanations from the existence of mass or of material substance; this domain of theory, however, is the one

[p. 238]

which retains no significance at all for the ideal view. In relation to the inner living, by contrast, we cognize matter in heat, light, sound, etc., not as mass, but from the forms of physical processes, from the *forms* of the conflict of mass according to figure, motion, change of figures, history and becoming in general; to all this the law of beauty then attaches itself, and so far reaches the ideal interpretation of our knowledge.

[p. 239]

### Fifth Chapter.

### Of the Idea of Freedom.

#### §. 142.

The idea of the world finds a tenable application only in the *relation* of appearance to the intelligible world of being in itself, only through the relation of the lower world-order to the higher; for in nature the incompletability of all composition of magnitudes contradicts the very idea of a world-whole. The sole cosmological idea is therefore the independence of eternal being from nature, which we call freedom.

The idea of the soul gives us in intelligence the substance of the intelligible world; the idea of freedom, on the other hand, must determine for us absolutely the cause, the power of the same, through which a community of intelligences becomes possible in it. Now the external causal relation of rational beings is for us determined as voluntary action; the power of the intelligible world, through which its community arises, becomes therefore the rational will, and its ideal determination the freedom of the will. From the premises so far given we shall be able to develop our doctrine of freedom easily.

Freedom stands opposed to nature; it is the idea of an existence for which the limits of natural necessity are removed, and so in particular also the necessary concatenation of events in time. Freedom is

[p. 240]

therefore possible, and is thought as necessary, as soon as we have grasped the distinction between appearance and being in itself. The concatenation of events in time, and the whole of natural necessity, are for us, with regard to the eternal being of things, only something contingent, in that it belongs not to their being itself, but only to our manner of representing it. For being in itself there is no time at all; it is therefore a being absolutely free. Now we have faith in the eternity of our own essence as an intelligence, and so place the will of the intelligence under the law of nature only for our limited view of things, but in itself necessarily in the eternal order of things, in which it must take part in their free being.

#### §. 143.

The idea of freedom is applied in two cases: once in the inquiry after the ground in the being of things in general with regard to the creation of the world, and secondly in the investigation of how I am able to impute to myself my actions, which yet ensue according to the universal necessity of nature. In both relations the application of the idea has been much misunderstood, in that one let it enter into nature or into time itself, which turns out unavoidably contradictory. The first view then gives the idea of the creation of the world in time through a free creating power, or the idea of miraculous interventions of the creating power in the midst of the particular course of events. Both with contradiction. The creation of nature is a wholly idle concept, for the past

[p. 241]

has no other reality than the recollection of it in the present; this recollection, however, leads the thread of history back beyond every arbitrary beginning in the same series, ever still further backward, in that the development of each state of nature becomes comprehensible from the preceding one; history evolves itself backward beyond every alleged point of beginning. Secondly, miraculous actions of the creating power in the course of history itself are to be compared to the knot which the weaver ties in his warp because the thread has broken, which ill befits the Creator. But still more: those laws of natural necessity are not prescribed to us by nature, but our reason prescribes them to a world that is to be able to become appearance for it; for our reason, therefore, the thread can never break; nature may be whatever it will for the senses, for us it must always fit under those laws. This whole use of the idea is faulty; the relation of freedom to nature is found only in the relation of the intelligible world in general to the sensible. The in-itself of the eternal order of things lies, in general, at the ground of the whole unviolated series of events in time, and appears to us through it. If we wish to cognize it according to its free essence, we need only think the limits of our subjective view as negated; the free does not hover as creator above nature, but lies at its ground as the sole true being.

#### §. 144.

The other was the imputability of the human will. The difficulty here is this: I myself

[p. 242]

fall, through birth and education, wholly into history; I am myself only a product of nature; I am, as I appear in nature, necessarily through the occasioning causes in birth, situation and education, which have produced me at all in appearance. Notwithstanding this, I nevertheless make in conscience claims upon myself, in which I impute to myself my actions as good or evil, and give myself, in virtue and right, necessary precepts for my actions, as if it depended on me what I will do or leave undone, and I judge each single one of my actions commonly always as if it stood in my free election whether I could also have left it undone. We resolve this difficulty thus. If we call the constitution of our will with regard to its virtue the character of it, then we can first ascribe to it an empirical character, which falls into inner nature and with it into history and into time. But this empirical character is only the appearance of an intelligible character, which lies at its ground in the being of things in themselves and according to the eternal order of things, and contains its true being. This intelligible character then falls into the world of freedom, and through it I judge my will as free. I can then also relate it, as free cause, to the whole appearance of my empirical character, i.e. to the whole history of my life, and here judge myself as free in each single one of my resolutions. This relation of my freedom to my actions takes place, however, not properly on the detached single deeds in election, but on each single one only through the connection of the whole. According to the same fundamental law of the will according to which I acted yesterday,

[p. 243]

I shall necessarily act also today and throughout my whole life; but this fundamental law itself is the freely adopted principle of my character. The freedom of the intelligible character relates to the whole connection of the voluntary actions of my life, in which my empirical character appears, and thereby I judge myself also as free author of each single one of my deeds. If, e.g., someone says: what can I do about it that through birth and education I have become precisely such a human being? the answer to this is: if you were not, in your intelligible character, by disposition such a human being, you could never have come to appearance in such a life. The necessary concatenation of events in nature, which produces you in nature, belongs only to the form in which you become conscious of your deeds; the deeds themselves, however, are free deeds of your intelligible character.

The conviction of the freedom of our will is inherent in reason immediately, from the principle of speculative faith together with the consciousness of the eternity of our essence, as the second principle from the idea, in which we think the power of the intelligible world absolutely. How this conviction expresses itself in life, however, we shall make clear to ourselves when we compare the claims of the law for willing from pure reason with the law of nature in general. All conflict of idea and nature springs from the incompletability of magnitude; in this we shall also find the simplest expression for showing the character of freedom in our will.

The will forms resolutions inwardly, and acts in accordance with how it has resolved. But in order to determine its

[p. 244]

resolution, there works on one side the command of duty from pure reason, e.g. to fulfil my promise, on the other side, however, often the sensibly determined inclination, which, in accordance with its interest, seduces me to act contrary to duty. Now in the demand of my conscience I presuppose that it is possible for me always to remain true to the necessary requirement of what I ought to do, however strong the impulse of inclination against it may become. I assume in conscience that those impulses, however strong they may be, can always only affect my will but not bend or determine it, unless I freely yield to them. Here, then, for the resolution, is my virtue, i.e. the strength of my good disposition, in struggle with inclination, and I maintain before conscience that my free will never lets its virtue be overcome by compulsion, but only through its free resolution, for otherwise I could not impute the opposite to myself, since I should have been compelled by outer nature. Such a demand on the will, however, contradicts the laws of nature, and such a virtue is not possible in nature. The virtue of the human being is an inner power of disposition, which with regard to the resolution can come into conflict with the inclinations aroused from without in the mind. In nature, however, my resolution will always be determined by the strongest impulse. Every power in nature has a determinate degree, which can be thought smaller or greater without end, so that above every given power, however great, a still greater is always possible. Accordingly, to the virtue of a human being there belongs at any time a determinate degree of its power to work toward the resolution; above this there must in each case be a still greater degree

[p. 245]

possible, which would overcome it in this conflict, and thus for every human virtue in nature a degree of sensible impulse is possible to which it would have to succumb. In nature, therefore, the property of the will of letting itself be determined by no external impression, however strongly it may work, is impossible; every virtue in nature is only a surmountable finite virtue. By contrast, that presupposed property of the will, of letting itself indeed be affected by sense but not determined, would demand an infinite power of resistance, which contradicts the law of magnitude in nature. A will, consequently, which can never violate the command, a holy will, could not appear in nature at all, for it would have to enter into it with infinite power; only to an unholy, human will can it happen that it becomes appearance to itself, in that its imperfect virtue, as a finite power, alone fits into nature. But even this finite will assumes in conscience that every impulse, however strong it may be, can only affect it, but never determine it to action, but that every such determination is an inner self-determination; in this presupposition, then, conscience expresses the faith in its own freedom, raises its own existence above the limits of nature, but can then make up the imperfection of human virtue, as against the infinity of its intelligible character, only through the consciousness of an original propensity to evil.

[p. 246]

#### §. 145.

In order to give this doctrine more distinctness, we must seek to free it from the usual confusions. Freedom presupposes voluntariness, contingency and self-subsistence, but must not be confused with any of these; we must determine the differences exactly.

The first confusion is that between relations of inner nature and relations of the eternal order of things. I ought to keep my promise, I ought to respect others, I ought to safeguard my honor, without my having to do this always. To *must* something is the natural necessity of my action, to *ought* something is the practical necessity of it, in which something is demanded of me with necessity, without its following necessarily, as a must, according to laws of nature, rather so that in nature very often the opposite follows. This demand of the ought is made on my will; but it presupposes not merely that I have will, or can act voluntarily, but assumes besides in this will a property which cannot be thought in nature, but contradicts the law of nature, for in nature there happens only what must happen; if, therefore, the ought is required of my will, this demand goes beyond the limits of nature. My will is now the inner determining ground through which I act in inner nature; through it my inner life comes into conflict with the outer; its possibility demands a law of its own, through which inner nature subsists, according to which voluntary acting is distinguished from mere relations of outer nature

[p. 247]

and in accordance with this we presuppose in choice already a so-called *psychological or juridical freedom*, that of having inner determining grounds for action, which is however wholly different from the *metaphysical freedom* of the idea, in that through the latter choice is not constituted, but a kind of it, free choice, is distinguished from animal choice.

If, e.g., the judge imputes a law-violating deed for punishment, he has not to ask *with what intention* I did the deed, but only *whether* I did it. I must not have been compelled to an action; it must have been my intentional, i.e. free deed, if it is to be imputable to me, for otherwise it is not really I at all who acted, but another or nature through me. *My deed* is not straightway what happens through my body, but what happens through my will. If someone falls unluckily and thereby injures another, what happens through his body cannot be imputed to him; if, on the other hand, a tutor knowingly leaves his ward alone with a loaded gun, and the child does harm with it, then the deed of another will nevertheless be imputed to him as neglect. *What I do*, therefore, is always reckoned through the opposition of inner living nature against outer nature; an action which follows only according to laws of outer nature is for me a compelled action, whereas I am free in all my voluntary actions, in that I bring them forth through my inner life. If we speak, then, of psychological or juridical freedom, we set

[p. 248]

here not freedom and nature, the finite and the eternal, against one another, but we remain wholly in nature, and distinguish only the laws of the efficacy of inner and outer nature. To justify this concept, therefore, presents no difficulty at all; all that is asserted in it is that I am capable of acting from inner determining grounds, the external may then always have its influence in it too; enough if my will only stands in the series of causes of an action, whether it be the led or the leading. I act according to the external circumstances which are given to me, but enough that I acted with will; so I am in this always psychologically free. Freedom in the idea, on the contrary, was quite another thing; it presupposed choice, but went much further with its demand, in that it asserts that external circumstances can indeed affect my will, but can never determine its infinite power; it demands, therefore, not merely a living power of the will in inner nature, but besides the infinity of this power beyond all nature, in the eternal essence of things.

By this confusion the sphere of freedom in our mind is commonly assumed far too great. One distinguishes a domain of freedom and a domain of necessity in the human mind, ascribes sensibility and the affection of the mind from without to natural necessity, but calls all voluntary activities in acting, thinking, in reflection, already part of the domain of freedom. This then utterly destroys all inner natural science, and lets one nowhere arrive at a secure boundary between the domain of the idea and the domain of nature. Herein lies the subjective error in Jacobi’s, as in Fichte’s, theory of freedom. One then thinks

[p. 249]

with voluntary inner activity, with consciousness, to enter already the domain of ideas, and all voluntariness in thought, poetry and character is withdrawn, contrary to right, from the explanation of nature as an expression of freedom. In fact, however, all this ensues just as much according to an explicable inner mechanism as I move my muscles according to an outer one. The idea of freedom, in its opposition to nature, shows its claims not in this, that it wants to give the human being character, but in this, that it undertakes to interpret his empirical character through the eternal essence of his intelligible character.

Secondly, the confusion between freedom and contingency touches more closely the idea of freedom itself. Contingency stands opposed to necessity, and the error lies in setting freedom over against not nature but necessity, with which it in fact does not at all conflict. This confusion arises because it readily appears that for duty and conscience freedom is unavoidably presupposed, but it is harder to show in what the demand of freedom here properly consists. The matter presents itself at first thus. If someone is imputed an action, e.g. that he has broken his word, as wrong, one presupposes thereby that he could just as well have kept as broken his word, for if an external impossibility shows itself, this will excuse him. It is therefore assumed that the resolution to keep his word, which he did not have, was equally possible to him as the resolution to break his word, which he had. Now this resolution is his action, consequently his effect; one presupposes therefore that here, although the cause is given, the effect is nevertheless something contingent. A free action must therefore, notwithstanding

[p. 250]

that it ensues in nature with necessity, in some respect nevertheless allow itself to be judged as contingent. It could indeed still be said: as the human being is, so too necessarily is his action. In the case mentioned it was not contingent whether the human being would break his word or not; rather, had he been an honest human being, he would have kept his word; he is not, so he does not keep his word either. But thereby that contingency would not be removed, but only pushed back, for here we nevertheless presuppose, in order that the imputation may take place, that it was equally possible to him to be an honest human being as the opposite; consequently we always assume his constitution, necessary in nature, for the sake of freedom, as something in another respect contingent. This reflection is indeed correct, but it touches only a subsidiary determination of freedom, as can already be gathered from this, that this contingency shows itself only in the evil deed, but not so immediately in the good. The absolutely good, i.e. the holy will, would act, according to a necessary law, throughout as it ought, wholly without that contingent determination of him who is now with the law, now against it. That contingency, namely, belongs only to the faculty of election, and in a higher meaning to the faculty of free election. To have the election between several equally possible actions always presupposes a relation of contingency, yet at first in such a way that this can well subsist in nature. For election belongs only to the finite will, insofar as it is determined as an excitable power, where through its own inner law the stimulating moments themselves are not yet given along; it is here therefore subjectively contingent for its own essence, though necessarily determined for outer nature, which single stimulations

[p. 251]

happen to strike it, and which among them will give the decision in the electing resolution. Here, however, in nature the strongest stimulation will in each case prevail; against which we further assert that for free election even this is still contingent, and only the will itself decides from its inner law. This required contingency in free election now indeed breaks through the law of natural necessity and raises itself above nature. If, therefore, a free will nevertheless appears in nature, and its intelligible character expresses itself through an empirical one, its intelligible character does indeed demand a contingency of election, which in nature would be a contradiction. But precisely for nature and in nature it is not demanded to unite necessity and contingency, but precisely in opposition to nature.

Freedom in general does not consist in the freedom of election, but free election is only the expression of freedom for the finite, unholy will, whose essence becomes appearance to itself only in a nature, whereas the holy will must be thought as raised in its freedom above all election and above all nature. It must be possible to think that an action necessary in nature is in another respect only contingently determined, otherwise the freedom of the human will would be unthinkable; but freedom itself is not this lawlessness and contingency, but in the removal of natural necessity it becomes precisely the condition of an absolute necessity of the eternal. Our manner of acting in nature must be able to be regarded as contingent for the sake of freedom; this, however, happens not by our ascribing to it freedom as contingency, but by this, that we determine its necessity itself, that we determine natural necessity

[p. 252]

only as contingency. Natural necessity is not an absolute necessity of the being of things themselves, but a mere form of appearance, unavoidable indeed for the power of comprehension of finite reason, but for the true essence of things precisely the absolutely contingent.

The third was the relation of freedom to self-subsistence. Freedom is independence from nature and its law of magnitude. This, however, shows itself in the infinity of the world-whole through time and space, first according to the determination of the object through synthetic unity, through the forms of the physical connection of the existence of things, and secondly in the infinity and contingency of the sphere under every concept, according to the determination of the object through analytic unity, through the forms of metaphysical connection. Now according to the rule of physical connection the dependence of a thing is determined thereby that it exists either only as predicate of another, and has no substance in itself, or that at least its states subsist only as effects of the other parts in the same dynamical whole, where then in the interaction of nature every being is at least subject to the second dependence. For the idea we have now freed our own spiritual essence from these two dependences, first in that we have faith in the merely finite worth of material substance, and by contrast in the intelligible substantiality of the soul, whereby its existence as self-subsistent substance is therefore presupposed; secondly in that we believe that the free will in the infinite power of its choice can indeed be affected by sense but not be overcome,

[p. 253]

whereby its dependence in interaction is therefore thought as removed.

Here the one-sided pursuit of this or that self-subsistence has already produced false theories of freedom; but, what is most important, we ourselves have thereby not yet taken into account independence according to metaphysical connection, the independence of the single being from universal and necessary laws, or from fate, under which it stands. With our negative ideal view of things it succeeds quite well so long as we set our ideas only against those forms of physical connection, in that we thus still retain in the idea a positive content in the free will of intelligence. We think to ourselves thus human society united into an intelligible world under a higher order of things according to laws of community of freely-willing beings, and form for ourselves a legislation of virtue and of right. But when we then confidently surrender ourselves to this manner of representation, and now consider the relation of the individual to the eternal order of things, we suddenly become aware that freedom is again annihilated by this just as before by nature. For we have again thought this eternal order of things after the analogy of a natural whole as a world under universal laws, where therefore the existence of the individual just as well loses its self-subsistence against the dependence from the metaphysical connection of things. The ought of nature becomes an *intelligible must* in the eternal order of things. We presuppose in faith a rule of the final end in the existence of things as the law of their eternal order

[p. 254]

to which every single thing is subjected, what have we thereby done other than put, in place of the empirical fatalism in nature, an *intelligible fatalism* of the eternal, to whose omnipotence every single existence again succumbs? Or if we wish to set Deity above even this intelligible fate, and to recognize it itself only as the will of Deity, the same difficulty returns, in that we wish to save our own self-subsistence against our being in, through or with God. How are we now to resolve this difficulty? Through the right of human ignorance, through the solely negative determination of the idea! The form of metaphysical connection or of the subordination of existence under laws is the last, without which nothing at all would remain for us to think in regard to the world; if therefore we wish to free our ideal view of things from this analytic limitation too, then nothing remains to us but the mere idea of its absolute relation, and in the case of freedom nothing more to think than independence of the absolutely necessary from all forms of nature in general. If anyone, then, makes objections against our representation of the eternal order of things, as though it contradicted freedom, we shall fully approve his objections, but answer him that only the negative share of the idea counts, and that here the idea of that which is independent of nature, freed from all contradiction, is the idea of the eternal essence of things itself, even though we still always retain a part of the mere relations of nature in our representations, as soon as we seek, for the intimation, to recognize the eternal in the finite.

[p. 255]

As soon as we apply the presupposition of the freedom of the will not merely negatively to the absolute determination of our essence, but attempt, in any positive way, an explanation, even if only of relations of the intelligible world-order, by means of it, there must unavoidably show itself the contradiction of our individual self-subsistence with the totality of the world-whole, which will warn us to refrain from every positive use of the ideas, and to recognize in this our unavoidable ignorance.

[p. 256]

### Sixth Chapter.

### Of the Idea of the Deity.

#### §. 146.

Our ideal view of things can develop only by stages upon the given finite of appearance, for since only negative forms are at its disposal, it wins a determinate shape only through a gradual representation of the removal of the subjective barriers in the human view of things.

Thus we first form for ourselves an intelligible world raised above time and space, whose eternal reality appears to us only through the world of sense. We compare the finite of nature with this idea, and then matter vanishes for us into nothing as regards true being, whereas the view of the world according to the laws of inner experience is enlivened for us by the eternal ideas. In that we believe our own existence to be eternal and recognize ourselves as eternal intelligence, the whole manner of appearance of things according to relations of inner nature becomes for us a property of the higher order of things. We recognize, as ourselves, so also every other human being as intelligence, and so it comes about that we must judge the society of human beings according to the laws of the eternal order of things, in that we regard it not merely as appearance, but as really belonging to the intelligible world. But this rational community

[p. 257]

of human beings under the laws of duty and of right is only the summit of this way of representing, according to relations of inner nature, in that we judge the history of humanity according to the ideas of science, art and right; but the same way of representing spreads gradually over the whole of outer nature as well; in a similar manner we realize to ourselves, through the aesthetic ideas of the beautiful and the sublime, precisely this higher order of things in everything that speaks to us as living in nature, for we cognize according to the same analogy the living through all forms of organization, through color, sound and fragrance, and so judge nature according to wholly different laws than those of the dead play of motions, according to laws which have only an ideal significance.

Taking all this together, then, we properly relate the appearance of nature to the eternal ideas, and that way of expressing the world of ideas as an intelligible world of rational beings in their community is still always only a partial, incomplete expression of the idea; for on the one hand the relation of appearance to being in itself, according to relations of inner experience, goes beyond that representation, in that we relate to the idea not only the rational but, in countless gradations, everything living and every beautiful thing in general; on the other hand, however, in our representation of the intelligible world a part of our sensible limitations always remains standing, in that we think in it the incompletability of the mathematical series as completely abolished neither for the physical nor for the metaphysical connection in the existence of things. For first, in the relation of intelligence to intelligence the mathematical

[p. 258]

relation of the composition of the manifold, which is nothing for eternal reality, nonetheless remains. Likewise this world becomes no absolute whole, in that the manifoldness of intelligences does not limit itself but, by analogy with a being-beside-one-another in space, runs on beyond all bounds. In this the further application becomes at once chimerical, or a mere playing of fantasy, as soon as under that order of things we think not only the community of human beings on earth but wish to extend the law in like manner over all life in nature. Secondly, the idea of the eternal order of things in the commands of duty itself gives the unity of the intelligible world only in laws of interaction, which appear in abstract forms and are empty laws, containing no existence unless an existence that stands under them is given from elsewhere, according to a relation merely contingent for them. The ought, to be sure, holds as a necessary law for every free rational will that appears in nature; but it is for this law merely contingent whether anywhere such a free will is met with, to which the law can be superordinated.

In this way we represent to ourselves in the intelligible world only the appearance of the rational in relation to eternal reality, always still according to limited forms of sensible cognition. In the completion of our ideal view of things we must consequently think these limits too as negated, in order to approach, through a completed representation of the Absolute, the idea of the eternally Real as far as is possible to human reason. Through this idea of the abolition of the limits of the intelligible world, or through the idea of the absolutely

[p. 259]

thought eternal order of things there arises for us then the speculative idea of *Deity*, as the highest idea of reason.

#### §. 147.

Thus, then, there finally develops the necessary conviction of the existence of God from the principle of speculative faith. The idea of Deity springs for us from the supreme relation of the unity of all cognition in the immediate cognition of reason, whereby in the concept of community all contingent manifoldness of things with regard to eternal being is thought as abolished, and so only the idea of a highest cause in the being of things remains to be thought.

With no idea has so much been attempted as with this highest idea of the pure ideal of reason, to put together something Real out of mere negations, in that the concept of the most real being should at least be something immediately positive. But we see that all such attempts must lose themselves in the void, for we can determine this idea of an absolute object of reason, like every other, only through double negation, through the denial of all limits of our cognition. It presents for us no difficulty to elaborate this idea according to all individual determinations possible for our speculation; the positive ground we can borrow from nothing else than the relation of the concepts of the understanding to nature, in which we need only, for the elevation to the idea, think the whole contingency of the given as abolished.

[p. 200]

In this way we find four attempts to arrive at the speculative idea of Deity. We think Deity

1) as to magnitude, as the *Ideal of Reason*, the absolute object of transcendental apperception according to the idea of absolute unity in the being of things.

2) As to quality, as the object of the highest concept, *the most real being*, with regard to which, for every concept out of the sum total of all possibility, the judgment is determined as affirmative.

3) As to relation, as *the absolute ground in the being of things*, through which all community of things subsists.

4) As to modality, as *the being of all beings*, the absolutely necessary being, from which the necessity of the higher world-order, i.e. of the practical legislation, proceeds.

According to these four ideas we must elaborate the idea of Deity further, in order thus to determine the individual negative relational concepts through which alone we are in a position to express the highest thought of our being.

1) For the first idea all manifoldness comes to us only from sense, and for reason there remains merely the empty idea of unity in general. The absolute object of reason must therefore here, in opposition to all composition, be thought as one and simply simple, in whose unity divisibility in general must be excluded, whereby we obtain the idea of an *absolute unity*, which is neither analytic nor synthetic, contains neither under itself nor in itself a manifold of parts, but is in general

[p. 261]

opposed to this. This highest idea leads us, then, not merely to a general concept of objects of reason, which, like the idea of the soul, would still admit a plurality of its objects, or which, like the idea of the world, would comprehend a manifold as a whole, but the object of this idea becomes a single one, the highest being, the Ideal of Reason. We think here not merely the concept of eternal things in general, but the single object of reason; yet we can frame this representation only in opposition to the divisible manifold in general, for the unity of our reason is in itself a wholly empty form, to which we can procure no content without the given manifold. Here, then, we think only the negation of composition in a possible content in general, and this idea must necessarily first be determined again, through the concept of cause, backwards toward the manifold given, in order to think anything at all in connection with it. This quantitative idea therefore designates nothing but the empty place of a highest unity in the essence of things.

2) The qualitative expression of the idea is just as devoid of content. We think here the Ideal of Reason as the most real being. We determine its concept against the absolute All of reality in general. This is the empty speculative idea of Deity, as Kant had borrowed it from the Wolffian school, a God from pure logic, of whom it was formerly believed that he carries his existence already in his concept. We can, namely, think an object of reason in general only through concepts, and so obtain, through the form of representation through concepts, a mode of determination of the most real being, which at first can have the semblance of a positive

[p. 262]

representation. According to the principle of determinability, namely, every thing must have either a given concept or its opposite; I can therefore think each thing as determined with respect to all concepts, i.e. with respect to the sum total of all possibility; so that of this whole sum total of all possibility each single predicate belongs to it either affirmatively or negatively. Any single object would only then be completely determined according to concepts if I had actually determined it with respect to the whole sum total of possibility according to the law given. If we now think here, in the sum total of all possibility, every predicate as determined as reality, then, it is said, there will be an object as the most perfect, most real being, to which all reality is ascribed affirmatively, of whose reality that of every other single being would then be, as it were, only a partial emanation; this would be the Ideal of Reason, Deity. Logic would thus give us here seemingly a form for distinguishing Deity from every other thing. In every other thing a part of all reality is affirmed, another denied; in God alone all reality is affirmed without negation. Many have long toiled in vain over this idea; we need only consider it more closely in order at once to see its emptiness. First, the whole idea of the most real being arises only through a confusion of negation with limitation, and secondly, we can think out positively no single reality that could serve to determine this idea. The whole proposal, to unite all affirming concepts in one idea of the most real being, holds only under the presupposition of the metaphysical rule: realities do not conflict with one another; all realities let themselves be

[p. 263]

united in one being. But this principle is only surreptitiously obtained through confusion with the analytic proposition: realities do not contradict one another. Contradiction is the logical opposition of a concept and its negation or its opposite. We have shown above (§. 111. 1)) that first *the one and the other* of limited realities must be given to us before we can apply the concept of negation, in that through it reflection merely thinks the one through the other, without insight into the way in which one is other than the other. The reality of the one and of the other we represent only in positive concepts side by side, and here the conflict of concepts is earlier than the contradiction. I cannot perceive that a reality does not belong to a thing but its opposite does; rather I infer this only from becoming aware of its being something else, where this other is in positive conflict, according to a real division of concepts, with the former. I see that an object is not red, not by perceiving no color in it, but by perceiving, say, a green color in it actually, which conflicts with that. Thus a conflict of limited realities is the first thing we find in order to be able to make use of negation; this conflict, however, is wholly different from logical contradiction. The task for the idea is now to think the limitation as abolished in the Absolute; this, however, does not happen through my merely thinking away all negations, but it would happen only by my thinking that Positive of which no negation could be spoken, that would be the unlimited Positive. The realities of our cognition are limited, and thereby often in conflict with one another, in that

[p. 264]

two coordinate concepts in the same division can never occur as predicates of the same being, although both are positive. Two parts in a whole, the two halves of a sphere, are both equally real and positive, but the one cannot for that reason be the other. I therefore may not set the task at all of thinking the All of reality united in one being. Rather, if we wish to think reality for the idea, we get back at first only the idea of the Absolute, empty, in that every reality in our cognition is a limited one, and it is then in the end all the same on which one I wish to make present to myself the negation of these limits. Thus also, seen from this side, this qualitative idea of the Most Real remains empty, in that we can name absolutely no reality of our mind whose positive element would not vanish, were we to wish to think it unlimited. Is God, e.g., darkness or light? Darkness he cannot be, that is only lack of light; but light? if only this did not stream from place to place and spring from its sources. Thus not light either, but perhaps the primal source of light, the sun? Suns are divided, of them there are many, they are afflicted with the finitude of space. If we therefore wish to find an absolute reality, we must seek it in our inner consciousness. Here sensation and sense are no attribute for Deity, they are only limits; but everything else in our inner being is only cognition and will of intelligence. Thus God would be the highest absolute intelligence, the highest living spirit. Here we at least retained, on the first stage of idealization in the idea of the soul, a positive content, in that the self-consciousness withdrew from the complete mathematical composition. But

[p. 265]

even in this, after all, only the form of the Absolute of the idea served; we retained the content, in that we related the *given object* of inner nature to the Eternal for intimation. From this relative we were to free ourselves here in the highest thought too; the object itself is given in the idea of Deity only through the idea, and therefore even the reality of the rational will leads us, for this idea, no further than any other. Will consists only through cognition, it is acting reason; but cognition too is assailed by finite relations, if not wholly dominated by them; its reality too is annihilated in that we wish to think it wholly absolute. In cognizing, the finite is the relation to its object; we can think Deity only as absolute reason, where again only the negative part of the idea belongs, and then we may just as well say absolute light, or whatever else. Every representation of divine attributes is only figurative; we borrow the attribute itself from the finite, and then, through the addition of the Absolute, withdraw from it again a part—we know not how great, and know not which part of its content—as belonging only to appearance. Everything positive is attained here only through feeling, without any concept.

#### Name is sound and smoke,

#### Beclouding heaven’s glow.

3) As with every idea, so also here the moments of magnitude and quality remain for us without significance; of more determinate application for speculation can only be the third and fourth idea. According to relation we must, in the idea of Deity, think the unity of the existence of all things

[p. 266]

absolutely, in that we think the mathematical incompletability in the community of things as abolished. This can now, first, not happen by our thinking an absolute completeness in the composition of the things themselves in their community, as the All and One of the world, for every allness turns out for us only as infinity, which contradicts totality; and here, moreover, the order of things itself would hover over them as an empty form that was to give them the law, without yet bearing in itself a being of its own. We think therefore in Deity the being through which this eternal order of things over them subsists. Second, this cannot happen by our uniting all being of things in it as one highest substance, for then we should again compose it mathematically of parts, which cannot be thought absolutely but contradicts the idea. There remains for us rather, thirdly, only to add in thought, in Deity, the idea of a highest cause over the essence of things and their world-order, as the primal ground in the being of things.

4) With this the modal idea then connects, which sets above this eternal order of things the being of beings as absolutely necessary being, in comparison with which every other existence can be determined only as contingent, in that the eternal order of things itself flows from Deity. But since this order is given to us only through the ideas of the commands of duty, the modal determination can be completed only through relation to them. We think the eternal order of things in the principle of the best world, which is the highest in our faith, as the reality of the eternal Good; we think in Deity, according to the full

[p. 267]

idea, the eternal goodness itself, i.e. a holy will as primal ground in the being of things.

#### §. 148.

But in the speculative idea of Deity the most important thing is that we consider only its relation to the eternal order of things, whatever this may be. We must, namely, chiefly remark that every speculative elaboration of this idea is faulty in which it is not thought as ground of the eternal order of things.

In the inwardness of our religious conviction this idea lives only in feelings, and shows itself through the intimation of the divine in all life of nature, (which a more helpless logic is wont to express as the physico-theological proof for the existence of God,) however the one or the other may then express this highest feeling, that is merely a matter of science. Here, however, in the idea of Deity everything through which it is expressed is subject to a voluntary reflection, which is easily carried out one-sidedly, so that apparently the one thinks this, the other that, at the first thought of our being, which yet is necessarily one and the same in every reason. According to the common view among the people Deity is thought as highest cause of the world, and as the holy ground of the highest order of things, and all speculation will be able to bring to this way of representing no further correction than that, through its distinction of appearance and eternal essence of things, it makes this idea clearer to itself. Philosophers sought, in order to refine

[p. 268]

more subtly, to raise themselves above this idea, but have instead always remained only beneath it. All such one-sided attempts at elaborating the idea of Deity we can reduce to two purely speculative basic forms. Once, one forms the highest unity in the being of things not through the concept of cause but through the concept of substance, in that one unites all being in the being of Deity. Secondly, on the other side, one has sought to gain by representing Deity not as ground of the eternal order of things but as this order itself.

Every carried-out speculation which wishes to proceed from the Absolute and credits itself with a positive cognition of the Eternal loses itself in the former view, in that it becomes pantheism; for only through the stepwise character of our *oppositions* do we raise ourselves above the world to the idea of Deity, those, by contrast, retain only the choice whether the world itself, or a part of it, (its form, order, bond of unity) is to become Deity, where the latter obviously contradicts itself. Spinoza agrees with many an old and several of our present German philosophers on this idea, even with Leibniz, if we regard the world as the thought and not as the object of the thought of its creating monad. But this way of representing does not fit at all into the human co-ordination of the finite and the eternal; it can please only one who does not distinguish appearance and eternal being, and presupposes that he holds in his cognition of things immediately eternal being itself. With no idea is the great exception of criticism of so much help to us as with this highest idea of reason, that we namely here at the

[p. 269]

limits of our field of view appeal to our positive ignorance, and everywhere show how only the negative share of the idea properly speaks. Just for this reason we can think Deity only as ground by which the unlike is united, and not as substance for an equating of everything in One. Every attempt at application can make plain to us the contradictions of a substantial union of all being in the being of Deity. If we think Deity only as the ground of the eternal order of things, then we restrict ourselves, as is fitting, since we are able to cognize positively only appearance, to our ignorance with regard to the true relation of eternal being to itself, and of the completed relation in which our view of things stands to their true being; we recognize the rights of a mere intimating feeling from the judging of the beautiful, in order to grasp the relation of the finite to the eternal. If we wish, on the contrary, to unite all being positively in the one substance of Deity, then nothing is outside Deity, all is One. Then, however, the co-ordination of the finite and the eternal would remain wholly unthinkable; we could not only give no reality to appearance in relation to the Eternal, but it would itself, as semblance, not even be possible before the educated eye. For since here all being is only the one and highest, there is nothing to which anything could appear; there is possible only an in-itself, but no changing image of appearance. This view shows itself only as a physical hypothesis for the explanation of the possibility of cognizing, and yet the actual human cognition can never be derived from it. The idea of such a pantheistic being is unthinkable for our cognition, because it introduces absolutely positive determinations

[p. 270]

into the idea, and so makes ignorance impossible for him who would bear it in himself. We obtain therein an absolute unity in the being of things in relation to which no manifoldness at all could be thought, not even for appearance.

And yet on the other side we should have to, through this same idea, since there would be only the one idea of the reality of the highest substance, assume the reality of appearance as equivalent to it; it would be the highest being itself which stepped into appearance. Here, however, it can be thought only of an imperfectly good, unholy will that it becomes appearance to itself, in that the Holy can not at all enter into nature; and consequently this idea of Deity as a substance comprehending all loses itself wholly in its insufficiency, if we wish to give it practical significance.

The supreme modal relation of our cognition was that of the metaphysical connection in the being of things (§. 114. and 145.), in that we can comprehend the necessary determination of all existence only in its dependence on universal laws. The eternal order of things is a universal of necessary laws, to which, however, no being for itself can belong; if we do not wish to regard it as a higher Nature, as the form of an infinite whole, then it remains for us in the idea an incomplete thought, a condition for a given conditioned, the world, without a conditioning, which would prescribe that condition. The thought of the higher world-order is thus completed solely by our thinking in addition, indeterminately, an absolute ground, through which it holds, and this ground is the Ideal of eternal Goodness, or Deity. We see from this that the reduction of the ordinary

[p. 271]

concepts of God to more subtly thought-out ones, where one wishes to believe only in an eternal order of things or a providence, is precisely only a less complete utterance of the idea. The intention of the philosophers who devised such refinements was to present the common faith as freer of images; they did not notice, however, that they merely altered the image. All expression of this idea is figurative; the worth of an image, however, can be judged not according to philosophical truth but only aesthetically according to its beauty. Every such doctrine which calls the eternal order of things Deity is fatalism, and rises at most to an intelligible fatalism; its fault is that it always frames its idea of the true being of things in themselves after a schema of nature, so that a fate as mere law becomes the highest, as this is indeed possible with a subjective way of viewing things, where the subjective constitution of the individual reason prescribes the law, which for the being of things in themselves is a clear contradiction. The idea of an all-ruling providence is properly the idea of a living fate, and thereby a very imperfect expression for Deity itself, in that it contains in the eternal order of things only an empty formula of a universal law without a being of its own. As regards its aesthetic worth, however, this fate loses, precisely through its becoming living, its epic or tragic effect. (It is historically remarkable that this idea of an eternal order of things was so violently turned into atheism against Fichte, since it is entirely one and the same with the idea of providence, against which his opponents after all have little to object.)

[p. 272]

We shall later develop more closely the important distinction between a religious and a physical use of the ideas; this much, however, already results easily here, that the lyrically sublime must stand in art above everything dramatically sublime, and that, if we wish to express our reverence for Deity not merely in hymns or dithyrambs, we shall inevitably obtain a fate over Deity as soon as we mythologically animate our Olympus with several distinguished figures. For the only positive representation of absolute necessity that we can make for ourselves is that of an inviolably ruling law, and such a law will thus become the highest in every completed mythology. It would, to be sure, be more philosophical to subject even fate itself to the highest Deity, but thereby the whole fable acquires no stability, the realm of the gods becomes a lawless despotism. Indian mythology has retained many philosophical basic ideas; thus in it too fate is actually subject to Vishnu, it obeys at his incarnation as Krishna his commands; a mythological inconsequence, which often enough afterwards punishes itself through a certain absurdity in the invention of most Indian myths.

#### §. 149.

Our speculation will champion none of all this; our idea of Deity is only *one*, the idea of the holy primal ground in the being of things, which lets itself be expressed speculatively for our reason according to three relations, which then have their only speculative development

[p. 273]

contained in them. We think, namely, first, in the relation of transcendental apperception, in Deity the pure Ideal of Reason, the absolute self-subsistence of the highest being; secondly, in the relation of formal apperception, Deity in relation to the world, Deity as Mediator, i.e. as the being through which the world is; thirdly, in the relation of material consciousness, Deity in relation to nature, as the holy spirit, from which all light and life of nature proceeds. It is therefore each time the same idea of the divine being that is presented only according to the three supreme *subjective* relations of the power of comprehension of a finite reason, without this admitting any, as it were, physical development into a theological or cosmological scientific system. We must therefore by no means confound this merely subjective threefoldness of view with the now usual natural-philosophical oppositions of *natura naturans* and *natura naturata*, or with similar oppositions of the finite, infinite and eternal, e.g. according to Schelling’s presentation in the *Bruno*. All these ideas are wrongly physical, in that this triunity embraces not merely the divine being but always at the same time the world. Thus in Schelling the eternal Father is only the idea of Deity itself, the infinite maternal principle is nothing but the form of the world, and the eternal Son is the world itself under its form; in Schelling’s latest presentations, however, God appears, just as formerly in Fichte, only as the eternal bond of all things, i.e. as the form of the world. All of which misconceptions arise from the same source of the misunderstood highest physical task of our mind, of which more further below.

[p. 274]

The dead word of our speculative idea is thus solely that we think Deity as highest cause in the eternal being of things, through which the higher order of things subsists; life and warmth come to it only from the innermost of our acting being. In speculation this idea is the last that we can pronounce, for living faith, on the other hand, it is the first and innermost in our being, as the faith in the reality of the highest Good, from which all ideal life proceeds, and to which it returns again, after it has spread itself, in the living play of beauty, over nature and the individual life in the history of humanity.

#### Remark.

#### §. 150.

Concerning the attempted proofs for the existence of God we have no need to be lengthy, since we have already decided in general that no inference can lead to an ideal principle. For this particular case the following still holds:

Among the logical forms of inference only the hypothetical serves to prove an existence; but then, first, an existence must be given from which I proceed, and secondly, a rule of ground and consequence which leads me over from the one to the other. Here, however, in purely hypothetical form, affirmatively only from the ground to the consequence is inferred, which for Deity has no application

[p. 275]

Since Deity is thought as the highest ground, we should therefore have to infer from its consequences to it; here, however, purely hypothetically only the *modus tollens* holds, so that we could perhaps prove its non-being, never however its existence. For the affirmative there would be only the hypothetical induction: if all consequences of a thing are, so is it itself. But how are we to come to all consequences? There would thus remain to us only probability from an incomplete induction. So the outcome too then shows that every attempted proof is a circle in the inference, where one presupposes as already given either speculatively the absolutely necessary being or practically the highest end.

1) The ontological proof: To the most real being every reality must belong, consequently also absolutely necessary existence—this is not even hypothetical, and thus confuses existence with the problematic determination of a mere concept, which must precisely be opposed to it. Without the circle in the inference, which already presupposes this existence, it says nothing at all.

2) The cosmological proof from the contingent existence of things in nature to an absolutely necessary being is hypothetical, but infers unlawfully *modo ponente* from the consequence to the ground. It holds good only through the circle that here the highest reality is presupposed which one wished to prove.

3) The physico-theological proof, from the purposiveness in nature to a highest reason that has ordered all this, is at most an inference of probability,

[p. 276]

in that we can show only single forms as purposive, and supplements itself again only through the circle that we bring the representation of purposiveness rather first from the idea to nature, instead of finding it in it.

4) The moral proof: The ought and all claims of conscience, from which we cannot disengage ourselves, would be a clear contradiction if we did not presuppose the existence of God, etc.—this contains the same circle, for this contradiction entitles us to the inference only under the presupposition of an absolute purposiveness in the arrangement of the world, which we believe precisely in the idea of Deity.

[p. 277]

### Third Division.

### Deduction of All Regulative Principles for Finite Reason.

### Introduction.

#### §. 151.

The law of the transcendental power of judgment in the organization of every finite reason was the separation of matter and form in its cognition, the contingency of the stimulation through sense, whereby the content comes to it, and the emptiness of pure rational form for itself. This expressed itself for the logical power of judgment in the separation of the case from the rule, so that we could always find the rule for the given case of application only with the artificial aid of reflection. The last business of the power of judgment should properly be the subordination of the case under a given rule, but in our self-cognition there appears at first always only the individual element of the case for itself, and it becomes only then the task of the *reflecting* power of judgment to seek out the rule over the case in

[p. 278]

addition. This happened in two ways: through speculation, if the rule already presupposed in our cognition needed only to be brought out for reflection, or through induction, if we seek to divine the rule first from given cases.

Here, however, we saw (§. 83.) already that even with induction neither the case nor the multiplicity of cases gives itself the rule, for immediately the inference from many cases to the rest under a rule counted for nothing, but only the *presupposition of a rule in general* for all cases entitled us to induction. Law and rule are thus at all times for the reflecting power of judgment the presupposed; speculation and induction differ only according to a peculiar relation to this rule.

Every universal and necessary principle shows itself to our mind through speculation. I call a principle, however, *constitutive* when, as soon as it is given, it itself determines the case of its application, so that the *subsuming power of judgment* is in a position to develop science from it in theoretical form; *regulative*, by contrast, a principle is called when the *reflecting power of judgment* must first seek for it the case of application and its constitutive determination. Regulative principles therefore are superordinated to induction, they are mere maxims of the reflecting power of judgment, which guide it in seeking, and are called *heuristic maxims* when they serve positively to guide inductions for a given manifold,

[p. 279]

thus, e.g., the philosophical doctrine of language gives us such maxims for historical study of language, thus mathematics gave us heuristic maxims according to which we were in a position, after the first discovery of new planets, to find them again in the heavens, to predict their distance and the laws of their motion, and just such maxims guide all experimental observation of nature in general.

From §. 72 we can determine further for this distinction: every mathematical principle is immediately constitutive, in that it already carries with it the law of its development, every philosophical one, on the other hand, remains at first a regulative one, and becomes constitutive in general only thereby that we are in a position to determine it mathematically.

First, then, beyond the domain of mathematics there are in general no constitutive laws of a theory possible, and secondly, within it a constitutive part of science distinguishes itself in every natural science from another that is ruled only by heuristic maxims. We can namely in every mathematical system develop forward from the supreme principles the system, in that we compose every complexion itself from its elements, but with these evolutions we come always only to a certain limit, where the composition of complexions becomes too great. Here we take the reverse path of observation, grasp the composite as a whole, and attempt

[p. 280]

only to arrange the complexions in the large in an involution, without completing the evolution down to the particular. The latter procedure of induction demands as exact a development of constitutive laws as possible, in order to obtain determinate heuristic maxims, but it remains indispensable in its own sphere, in that all theoretical compositions nevertheless always treat only general rules, without being able to find their way to the individual history.

[p. 281]

#### First Chapter.

#### Survey of All Regulative Principles of the Power of Judgment.

#### §. 152.

The power of judgment is the logical self-activity of our mind; from its standpoint, as the point of view of method, we would therefore have to repeat all the previous laws of speculation once more for induction, but we wish to dwell only on the most general moments. The law of the power of judgment was the contingency of the given manifold for the necessary form of unity, the separation of sense and understanding in finite reason. The whole interest of the regulative principles therefore concerns the dispute between *empiricism* and *rationalism* and its reconciliation through *criticism*. At the basis of all development of science through reflection lie three first maxims of the power of judgment, of which one, as the *maxim of unity*, defends the claims of the understanding, the second, as the *maxim of manifoldness*, the claims of sense, but finally a third, as the *maxim of combination* or of the limitation of all theory, balances both claims against each other, in that it guarantees to sense the ever-possible extension of its content,

[p. 282]

the claims of unity, however, it restricts only to a form empty in itself, above all content, according to the law that for finite reason all significant unity is combination and not absolute unity.

The dispute between empiricism and rationalism is to be decided quite clearly from all that has been said so far. The origin of our cognition is, *in the eyes of inner re-observation*, but not *for immediate cognition*, either the intuition of inner sense, which gives the manifold content, or the concept and judgment of reflection, which supplies the unity of necessary form. The scientific development of our mind now aims at this: in the eyes of this inner re-observation, to determine completely the subjective validity of our cognitions in relation to one another, and so to comply with the rule of their empirical truth.

Every one-sided speculation, however, confuses this task of subjective grounding with the theme of transcendental truth, or the objective grounding of cognition. It is then driven to empiricism by the prejudice that only through sense intuition does our cognition hang together with the object, and that from this all truth spreads in our mind; it is driven to rationalism by the prejudice that only the apodicticity of the forms of unity in our cognition gives it objective validity. The error is thus the same on both sides: one misunderstands the whole business of the scientific development of our mind, in that one confuses the *subjectively immediate validity* of intuitive evidence, or the *subjective universal validity* of the apodictic laws, with objective validity, thus in each case empirical

[p. 283]

truth with transcendental truth. If we abstract, however, from this mistaken aim of speculation, then at the basis of what really happens on the one side and on the other lies in each case a quite correct maxim of the power of judgment, which is merely pursued one-sidedly: for empiricism, namely, the maxim of the extension of our cognition, for the goal of its materially ever greater perfection; for rationalism, however, the maxim of theory, for the goal of formal perfection (§. 68.); so that we need only unite both critically in order to understand ourselves about the whole business itself.

The dispute between these two maxims must be repeated twice, on the large scale, for speculation, once for the natural and then for the ideal view, where in one case it is to be settled in exactly the opposite way from the other, as was already indicated in the first Introduction.

For the *natural view of things* the dispute is the more easily understood and often discussed one, which concerns only science, where for natural science in general theorists and empiricists, and for natural description a systematic and a merely historical treatment of the science, stand opposed to one another. At the basis of the former here lies the *maxim of an ever-possible application of the logical forms*, at the basis of the latter the *maxim of the insufficiency of all logical forms by themselves on account of their mediacy*, and the reconciliation is effected (according to §. 63.) by a *maxim of objective validity*. All our cognition stands under the form of experience, where for us according to the first maxim

[p. 284]

apodictic laws are given as the condition of all possible content, of which we become aware only through the systematic forms; according to the second maxim, however, all historical content, as the conditioned, lies in intuition by itself, independently of the logical forms; according to the third maxim, finally, the conditioned must be necessarily determinable through the condition, so that for the completion of our cognition of nature the *law of the cognition of everything particular from its universal* (for speculation and against induction) holds: the universal law is always the apodictic condition under which the particular and individual is given only as the conditioned; thus only in the union of everything particular under its universal in theory can we relate cognition of nature to its objective validity.

More important, but also more difficult for the development, is the conflict of these very maxims for the *ideal view of things*. Here the one-sidedness of the former maxim is the basic error of every higher rationalism, which may be called *demand for a hyperphysical theory*, confusion of the doctrine of religion with physical theory, *mythological philosophy of religion*. The one-sidedness of the other maxim yields the *idealized empiricism* designated in the Introduction, as protector of all superstition through rejection of all theory and all speculation in favor of a blind doctrine of faith. The reconciliation, however, is effected through the critical coordination of a natural, ideal and religious view of things according to the relation of our three modal principles from the idea (§. 131.)

[p. 285]

which contain the highest cathartic of all human speculation. These are transformed here, namely, into the following three regulative principles.

1) For the natural view of things the demands of theory must be recognized, solely as conditioned by the incompletability of the mathematical series, as fundamental law.

2) Alongside nature there subsists the freedom of the eternal order of things, for a doctrine of faith without any theory.

3) The union of these two laws is effected through the religious appraisal of nature according to laws of the beautiful and the sublime, which arise for us only from feelings of intimation, in that here (for induction and against speculation) the highest law of unity is recognized only through the individual of aesthetic judgments (in opposition to all theory). The speculative principle of aesthetics, free composition of intuitive forms into unity without determinate concept, is demanded, namely, *a priori*, in that, according to the idea of Deity itself, the contingency of the manifold coinciding in mathematical composition is subjected to the law of unity, according to a principle quite peculiar to the power of judgment.

#### §. 153.

The correct and unavoidable application of all these regulative principles demands a case where the reflecting power of judgment remains wholly left to mere induction itself, without extending itself to pronounced constitutive

[p. 286]

laws of speculation. We find this, both in the natural and in the ideal view of things, in the use of the third regulative.

At the head of the system of every theoretical natural science stands a mathematical physics, which develops itself out of constitutive laws. But however far we may continue this development, we always remain with it at a science of universal laws, without ever reaching the individual of a single history (e.g. of our solar system, of the earth). If, therefore, conversely, we want to recognize, according to the third physical regulative, everything individual in history as conditioned by the universal laws, then all those constitutive laws hover only as heuristic maxims of indeterminate application over the whole of observation, and the wealth of empirical science unfolds itself only in a procedure of induction, which attaches itself to the individual observation and history itself, whereas speculation always remains dry and empty, although it fancies that it governs all history. In outer physics, e.g., every speculative procedure retains an atomistic character, in that it lays at its basis only the inner unity of the being of substance and mass, while the unity of the heuristic maxims, which really holds in experience, is always only the derived outer unity of the forms of physical processes. It is Schelling’s great merit for the philosophy of nature that he has guaranteed to it, on the large scale, the scientific worth of induction, in which our best physicists, though often involuntarily driven toward it, could nevertheless place no confidence. Unfortunately he has confused precisely these heuristic maxims with constitutive laws, and especially with the basic laws of the ideal view of things.

[p. 287]

In a similar way, as an analogue of these heuristic maxims, there hovers over our whole judging of nature the inexpressible principle of all judgments of taste, as the speculative foundation of intimation, according to which we demand free harmony of intuitive forms throughout the whole of nature, without being able to anticipate its application at all before the individual case itself is given to intuition. This principle of the power of judgment corresponds in aesthetics only to the empty principle of speculative faith; to both the law of the end must then still be added, in order to bestow life on it.

[p. 288]

#### Second Chapter.

#### The Heuristic Maxims of Natural Science.

#### §. 154.

Against the one-sided theories of a merely sensible or purely rational power of cognition we have led our speculation on, by way of the subjective history of human cognizing, to a theory of finite reason, and have opposed this, as the system of criticism, to empiricism and rationalism. In this way, however, our composite speculative system has been set in contrast only according to its methodical points of view (whose moments admittedly lie hidden everywhere at its basis, but which very few want to enter into in the dispute); in another way it will, according to its bare results, frequently arouse displeasure, in that it takes up into its composition every one-sided result, but precisely thereby pleases no one, because the opponent too is heard.

We easily survey from the organization of our reason about which objects results are demanded of purely speculative investigations, and can divide these according to the four moments of speculative cognition.

[p. 289]

1) Empirical intuition: matter and mind.

2) Pure intuition: completion and incompletability.

3) Logical thinking: intuition and idea.

4) Transcendental thinking: nature and supernature.

Here, then, according to one-sided results, the following stand opposed to one another:

1) materialism, dualism and spiritualism; 2) determinism and fatalism; 3) realism and idealism; 4) naturalism and supernaturalism.

We take into our system the whole positive content of each of these doctrines, and reject, on the other hand, the negative of each.

1) Our doctrine is complete materialism, for we demand a self-sufficient theory of outer nature for our material view of the world, in which everything, down to the most intricate processes of organization, and down to the innermost correlation with mental activities, is to be materially explicable. But our doctrine is also dualism, in that, independently of this theory, we demand a theory of its own of inner natural science; and finally it is, in a more eminent sense, spiritualism, in that in those two theories we only expound the finite view of things, but relate this finite to the eternal only through the inner view of life.

2) Our doctrine, in the whole of its ideal view of things through the ideas of Deity and of its eternal order of things, is complete determinism, which subjects the speculatively closed totality in the essence of things

[p. 290]

to a law of the end; but it is also, for theoretical natural science, a fatalism, whose blind necessity springs from the contingency of all mathematical composition, and which prescribes to nature, for theory, only laws of a self-sufficient mechanism (in opposition to a theory of final causes).
