3) In the opposition of realism and idealism, the former signifies the doctrine of the objective significance of a given mode of cognition, the other, however, the doctrine of a merely subjective significance of it. Here, then, our doctrine of the natural view of things is an empirical realism but a transcendental idealism; conversely, on the other hand, our doctrine of the ideal view of things is an empirical idealism but a transcendental realism, in that what holds for nature only as idea is, for the true essence of things, what is properly real.

4) Our doctrine is naturalism of knowledge and supernaturalism of faith, e.g. an empirical atheism, in that all *theory* of nature is to keep itself unmixed with ideas, but an ideal theism, in that all nature is to be judged *aesthetically* according to ideas.

Finally, if we methodologically still oppose skepticism to criticism, we grant skepticism too its due in its basic assertion. Skepticism asserts that in speculative matters no firm truth is to be attained by human reason, but by the rule of truth it understands an objective grounding of cognitions. Its principle is thus precisely ours too: an objective grounding of cognitions does not take place,

[p. 291]

only that the skeptic falsely confuses this with the rule of empirical truth.

But just as we are here in agreement, in like manner, with all the contending parties of the philosophers, so we are, on the other hand, in conflict with all of them on *one* ground; our whole undertaking will be rejected by every one-sided view, and despised by the eminent and the dilettantes of every school as syncretism and eclecticism. For whether individuals solve a speculative problem or reject it as insoluble, they are nevertheless all agreed that if one is once to set up a speculative system, this demands *a theory in one piece*, a theory that embraces the whole system of our convictions. To this we oppose a principle of the *recognition and limitation* of all theoretical claims of our reason, as lies in the ideal regulatives of our convictions just set forth. By a closer development of the regulatives of our reason we shall have to make the rightful claims of theory and its limitations still more clearly evident.

#### §. 155.

The result of the whole Kantian *Critique of Pure Reason*: there is no speculative cognition from pure reason, really meant for him as much as our ideal regulative: *There is no theory from ideas.* But as he treats the regulative principles in the Appendix to the Dialectic of Pure Reason, he misunderstands this law, in that he mixes the maxims of the systematizing reason

[p. 292]

with ideas. These maxims contain the claims of unity upon *every actually given* manifold, thus according to a moment of the power of judgment, whereas the idea springs from the highest demand of unity for *every manifold that is ever to be given*, according to the moment of reason. The speculative use of ideas is therefore reduced, with Kant, to a mere aid to theory by a so-called relative supposition of its objects. But for precisely this they cannot be used at all. For this reason we have kept the heuristic maxims of the systematizing power of judgment entirely separate even from the ideal regulatives.

Also what Jacobi says, with the expression which we borrow from him, against philosophy in one piece, aims at our principal regulative: There is for the human mind no theory in one piece, and in general no theory from ideas. The highest in our theoretical science is the doctrine *of the ideas*, as we have just derived them. A science *of the ideas* we possess, in which their negative forms are evolved, for reflection, on the positive forms of the cognition of nature, but further *from* these transcendental ideas of speculative reason as principles no science is possible any longer, but only faith, in that their merely negating expressions refuse all evolution. We can nowhere set them up above as grounds of explanation, in order to understand from them the essence of things; rather, we must only think them inevitably in addition to the given essence of things, in order to understand ourselves.

[p. 293]

#### §. 156.

The system of the regulative principles of the power of judgment contains two parts, the ideal regulatives and the heuristic maxims of the system for nature. Of these the former are the highest, all-embracing; the rules of the systematizing power of judgment first subordinate themselves to the first ideal regulative. This first ideal regulative demands mathematical theory for the whole natural view of things, and only in the sphere of this rule do the heuristic maxims of the systematizing power of judgment come into opposition with one another. Every logical system demanded a system of concepts in definitions and divisions, and a system of judgments in every theoretical science through proof. According to these two forms of the system, therefore, the heuristic maxims come into opposition according to classification of concepts and the claims of proof. In all natural science there stand opposed to one another systematists and historians, theorists and empiricists.

First, for the classification of concepts, in empirical anthropology, experimental physics and natural history, the two maxims of the homogeneity of everything heterogeneous and of specification into the infinite assert their rights side by side, in that, given the continuous unity of our cognition (according to §. 111, 2), every manifold given at all must lie under the rule of systematic unity, but the individual of the single form can never be reached by a descriptive composition out of concepts, and each time requires intuition beyond these. If, therefore, Buffon and Linnaeus quarrel over the claims of classification upon natural history,

[p. 294]

so this dispute does not belong to science; rather, for science both are agreed: in science both opposed procedures stand necessarily side by side for every part of natural science that does not lend itself to a constitutive theory. The maxim of a ladder of beings, however, according to the third rule (§. 111, 2), that of the continuity of all logical forms, belongs properly only to the Leibnizian metaphysics, from its idea of the All of realities in God and its representation of other beings through successive negations from this All of reality. Since we must reject this mode of representation according to (§. 147, 2), that maxim of arrangement into *one* series of gradations has no worth; we shall rather, under the rule of logical continuity, have to expect, in Batsch's expression, a net-like connection in the transition from species to species, in that the ramifications of every stem of concepts cross one another in manifold ways in what is actual in nature. The consequence of this is: there is only one system of physiological theory, but many kinds of systems of arrangement of its concepts can subsist side by side. (According to Linnaeus and Jussieu, according to Lavoisier and Winterl.)

Secondly, for proof in the system of judgments, the theorists demand, according to the one maxim, that everything particular be true only through its superordinate universal, and so must be comprehended from this; the empiricists, on the other hand, according to the other maxim, place all worth in the pure fact, which each time can be ascertained only through perception, because of the insufficiency of merely mediate logical cognition by itself. Here we have already spoken at length of the rights of proof, and know also the true essence of theory

[p. 295]

for natural science, namely in that it gives a form which governs all experience, but for itself always remains an empty form of universal laws. For use in common life the strict application of mathematics will determine the boundary beyond which the empirical procedure always maintains the preference over the rational; the rational, however, will then wisely restrict its interest to the science through which alone it can react mediately upon life. For as long as rational natural science really forms inductions according to heuristic maxims, it acknowledges (secretly or consciously) empirical inquiry as its teacher, and it is able to raise itself above it again only when it is put in a position to elevate its results, in part, as constitutive laws above the experiences, in subordinate theories grounded through inductions. The difference between the theoretical and the empirical procedure in the natural sciences will become clearer to us still if we compare the essence of theory, from what was developed above, yet more closely. All theory formed itself either through speculation or through induction; to speculation belonged then constitutive theory from given universal laws, but induction too grounded its claims not merely on the multitude of cases under a rule, which would give only a universality of habituation, but on the presupposition of the rule itself according to heuristic maxims. It is this relation of the heuristic maxims to observation, in order to obtain correct inductions, by which one-sided empiricism and false theorizing are distinguished from the correct procedure. Pure empiricism, which, apart from all theory, only collects and narrates facts, deserves

[p. 296]

no censure; the faulty empiricism is at bottom already theoretical, it seeks inductions, but without guiding maxims; its rules are therefore gathered only from the plurality of cases and according to habits, without any principle. Thus, e.g., the physician censures the method of cure of a mere empiricist, who applies his remedies at random, because they have already often done good service, or because in these individual symptoms they have often done good service; but the empiricist can answer him in turn: You rational physicians proceed, after all, precisely so; what help are the many words about theory, you explain as little by it as we do, and you apply each remedy in turn only because its healing power has been tested by experience. The true difference lies, namely, not in this last use of induction itself, which is the same on both sides; the gain, however, which the rational physician draws from his theoretical science consists in guiding maxims, which give his induction security, although he is not in a position to elevate them to constitutive laws of a theory from which one could see why precisely here this, there that remedy is the best. Conversely, the false theory, which stands opposed to sound empiricism, errs in this, that instead of contenting itself with guiding maxims for induction it wants to seize violently the place of induction through arbitrary hypotheses of constitutive laws which would make all further inductions from experience dispensable for it, in that it fancies it already comprehends from them the true course of the matter. It strikes the eye how this hits precisely the false theorizing of the atomistic philosophy of nature with the arbitrary basic form of its absolutely hard first corpuscles, the

[p. 297]

Cartesian theories or Euler's theory of the magnet, just so all common hypotheses about the formation of our planetary system, or finally the theories of humoral and nerve pathology. The correct procedure, therefore, is not to follow mere empirical compilations, and yet also not to presuppose constitutive hypotheses, but only, reflectively, to hold to guiding maxims. Here, however, the talent of the investigator of nature is not mere learned skill, but a gift of genius or at least a natural talent, if he is to combine with success.

#### §. 157.

On account of what follows we must illuminate this distinction more closely with regard to the particular relation of Kant's dynamical philosophy of nature and Schelling's heuristic one.

Kant opposed to the atomistic mathematical physics, which was founded on the metaphysical prejudice against an *actio in distans* and on the mathematical one of the absolutely hard, his philosophical dynamics, in which the law of continuity in mathematical physics first came into its own. This very promising doctrine, so convenient for mathematics, found approval in part, but was almost universally misunderstood, in that some could not wholly rid themselves of their atomistic prejudices, while others confused this doctrine with Schelling's dynamical philosophy of nature, which is nevertheless of a wholly different tendency. Kant's mathematical physics is the beginning of a theory of nature which develops regularly from constitutive laws; Schelling's philosophy of nature, on the other hand, uses only the most universal forms of its

[p. 298]

laws as heuristic maxims, and forms itself under these only by inductions on experience itself (as this shows itself most purely and richly in his work on the World-Soul, in which he first made known all those combinations from experience on which our philosophical physics has since had to live). The difference between the two is therefore precisely the most general one, of which we are speaking here: the fully developed laws of the Kantian dynamics stand only as guiding maxims above Schelling's merely phenomenological philosophy of nature. Hence arises the appearance as if the second treatment were not aimed at theory at all; one has even, precisely because the old atomistic, mathematically hypothetical or even Kantian dynamical procedure was definitely aimed at theory, sought the opposition of the new doctrine just in this, that it wants to explain nothing at all, to give no theory. But this is a mere misunderstanding. In its completion it aims at theory just as well; it contains in itself, in part, constantly, individual theories of heat, of the life-process, etc., and it appears as a whole not as theory only because, according to its main business, it seeks first of all to prepare theory; for only after its combinations with the help of its heuristic maxims are completed do there show themselves the beginnings of the theories which are won by this procedure, from which one, as usual, explains the course of individual processes of warming, electricity, assimilation, irritability, etc.

It lives in the inductions which are brought about by its highest guiding maxims; it sets up for us, for the natural history of the earth, as supreme guiding maxims its astronomical relations, the actions of its

[p. 299]

living organism and the light of the sun, and its first business is, in experimental physics and in the physiology of the organism, to subject all individual facts to these guiding maxims and to arrange them in accordance with them. But where these inductions have attained, or will attain, a certain completeness, there they turn back again, explaining, to the individual phenomenon, and thus show what the function of induction for the theory of nature should properly be. It is to proceed, as was demanded above, in the regions at first inaccessible to mathematics, from the individual of observation, and to subject this part of science to theory. To remove this misunderstanding was essentially necessary for us, so that what we have to say more closely about the ideal regulatives and their reciprocal relation may be understood.

[p. 300]

#### Third Chapter.

#### The Ideal Regulatives.

#### §. 158.

In the doctrine of ideas we obtained the three modal principles (§. 131): the world under natural laws is only appearance; at the basis of appearance lies a being in itself for faith; and the world of sense is the appearance of the world of things in themselves for intimation. These three principles now give us the following regulatives.

1) The goal of science for every natural view of things is theory.

2) Every theory is mathematical, and aims at an incompletable whole, so that all explanations, without a first beginning, are given only for the developments of a continuing history. Every such theory divides into a constitutive mathematical part and an empirically regulative one according to heuristic maxims.

3) There is a complete theory of outer nature, and inwardly a complete theory of the individual reason.

4) The ideal view of things is without any theory; from speculative ideas no theory is possible.

[p. 301]

5) To all theoretical judging of nature from concepts stands opposed the aesthetic judging from mere feelings, as the property of the religious view of things.

The separation of this *theoretical* and *ideal* domain in our mind is then the proper last goal of all speculation; the mixing and confusion of theory and idea, on the other hand, is the first source of all mythological doctrine of religion, from the first poetry to the most sublime metaphysics; it is the source of all hyperphysical theory and of all positive doctrine of the Absolute. In this confusion lies the ground of all disputes about ideas, and of all errors of common life about these and about religion.

Whoever is unwilling to give up his faith here to any theory hates, as ideal empiricist, all speculation, but delivers himself up thereby to superstition. Whoever has more courage to venture on theory then makes wholly false demands upon it, in that he regards the religious view of things as the apex of all theory, as the theme of the supreme physical problem. This mistake lies in the whole common Protestant religious instruction just as much as in the most artificial philosophical system of dogmatics. If you ask after the ideas of the eternity of your essence and the freedom of your will, it is not enough for you to see faith in these established alongside all theory, but you demand further to be permitted to use these ideas again as beginnings of a higher theory, in which you, e.g., from the idea of freedom the whole history of your actions, the organization of your character, the theory of the Fall and of the reconciliation with God explanatorily derive

[p. 302]

you want to, just as the lightning from the laws of electricity. You do not cease to attempt images about it, and although you admit that all these are mysteries of religion, you nevertheless think you have still said something about them with your images. Whoever, finally, takes it still more speculatively, wants even to have us comprehend the true essence of things with Spinoza from the idea of deity, or with Fichte and Schelling from the idea of the world.

We have, on the other hand, first to take under our protection the rightful claims of mathematical theory, and then to separate definitely all idea from theoretical expositions. This will present itself most intelligibly polemically, against a still prevailing speculative system. I choose that of Schelling.

#### §. 159.

Because nature properly *is* only in the whole of its community of things, Schelling, in his aversion to the separating formulas from the law of causality, has rejected all proper explanation and theory from his philosophy of nature, and instead of them has chosen other formulas, of a reduction of everything differing to absolute identity. I have already censured the misunderstanding herein. To be sure, his philosophy of nature is not theory, but it is in the service of theory, a preparation of it according to heuristic maxims. As long as it does not come again to theory, the whole is nothing but a classification of physical concepts, as they let themselves be ordered under the concepts of gravity, light, organism, or magnetism, electricity and chemism, etc.; it is the

[p. 303]

same for chemistry and physics in general that Linnaeus's system was meant to be for natural history. But if it is to acquire, as in Schelling's work on the World-Soul, a deeper significance, it must descend from its lofty philosophical tripod again to individual experience, recognize forces and their effects, in short attempt physical theories in competition with our earlier physics. But in order no longer to hide the whole of the errors behind words, and behind the one-sidednesses of a theory that systematizes now only concepts, now only judgments: what, then, is the essence of all theory, in the strictest, most scientific expression? Evolution of individual cognitions from a given involution of a whole in our knowledge. And this, after all, is Schelling's philosophy of nature in all that it does.

But this is not yet the worst difficulty: Schelling confuses the ideal with the natural properly in this, that he takes the heuristic maxims which hover before him, which are nevertheless all mathematical, or even merely empirically physical, for purely philosophical. We can divide his schemata of the philosophy of nature into the three of duplicity, triplicity and quadruplicity, of which he believes that he has derived them, in the Spinozistic beginning of his system of identity, from the highest laws of the in-itself of things. He believes he has derived the law of duplicity from the highest opposition of the subjective and the objective in the absolute identity of the self-cognition of absolute reason. In his actual philosophy of nature, however, it is not at all of so lofty a descent, but there it is only the schema of the *mathematical* opposition of positive and negative magnitudes in the image of the opposed directions on

[p. 304]

a straight line, and receives a *physical* meaning quite empirically through the opposition of two such magnitudes, through the conflict of two opposed forces in light, which confront one another now as + M and — M, now as + E and — E, now as + O and — O.

He further believes he has derived in Bruno the schema of triplicity from the highest law of the finite, the infinite and the eternal, which presents itself at the top as world (God the Son), as law and form of the world, and as deity (God the Father). In his actual philosophy of nature, however, there lies at the bottom of all triplicity of the Keplerian laws, of magnetism, electricity and chemism, of sensibility, irritability and reproduction, etc., nothing but the *mathematical* schema of the three dimensions in space, which has nothing to do with that philosophical one, but is used in physics wholly arbitrarily.

He believes, finally, that he has philosophically derived the schema of the quadruplicity of the compass card through the expression of the union of an absolute and a relative opposition. In his actual philosophy of nature, however, there lies at the bottom only the *mathematical* schema of the axial rotation of a sphere, with the direct opposition of its poles and the indirect opposition in the direction of its rotation, which *physically*, through the axial rotation of the earth, is applied map-fashion and with the greatest arbitrariness now to philosophical systems, now to medicines.

In fact, all such philosophical schemata are for the philosophy of nature only empty forms, which concern subjective moments in the history of our cognizing (according to §. 111.) and for the most part can be used only logically for the method

[p. 305]

used, but all that is significant and capable of development belongs to mathematics. The error in Schelling’s philosophy of nature lies precisely in that in which he has lately sought its highest worth, in the higher significance which is supposed to remain hidden behind the mathematical forms, but which, for all theory, simply is not there.

The great conveniences in judging nature which this new, allegedly dynamical physics claims to have over the traditional attempts at mathematical theories spring from an advantage that is no better than the introduction of faith in miracles into physics under the pretext that before God no thing is impossible—indeed, it is one and the same with this. If, e.g., animal magnetism astonishes us by unexpected reactions across great spaces and according to unaccustomed temporal relations, this philosophy says boastfully: space and time are only the finite bond of appearance; whoever raises himself to the true essence of things raises himself above them, and what according to that mathematics seems impossible and contradictory is here easily comprehended by us from the world-soul as the true bond of things. This is nothing but that reasoning of lazy reason, as Kant called it, which sets a far too early goal for all theory. What was observed according to spatial and temporal relations must also be explicable according to these, and it is precisely from the laws of appearance that everything is here to be explained; let no one, then, appeal here to the higher true essence of things in order to show greater insight. Rather, for your finding those appearances mathematically and materially inexplicable, the fault lies only with you; only in this, that you cannot rid yourselves of the traditional

[p. 306]

atomistic forms and their doctrine of pores. Warmth, light and sound travel unhindered into the distance according to similar laws, and these your masters themselves still recognize as material; or if you do not conceive this so, the same fault lies at the bottom there as well: you cannot comprehend how the material world can give itself figure and unity, since you attempt the explanation only from the being of its mass, its inertia and impenetrability, from which it cannot succeed. The forms of the processes in which the mass moves you ought to have constructed for yourselves; then you would learn to see how everything spatial and temporal can also be subjected, in space and time, to its determinate material explanation. Schelling himself is still wholly in error here. However exactly he has understood Kant’s *Metaphysical Foundations of Natural Science*, he has nevertheless not succeeded in completing Kant’s view for himself without error; he chose guiding maxims that were too general; colors, tones and inner life constantly play before his eyes, so that he cannot arrive at any completion of materialism in itself, and thereby, in the end, becomes an atomist himself once more. In his work *On the World-Soul* (p. 168.) Schelling says of the material community of things: “In the world generally no dynamical connection can be thought without assuming an original homogeneity of all matter. We are compelled to regard the positive matter that reveals itself in light and warmth as the *universal solvent* (which is afterwards called *Menstruum universale*, *aether*, *world-soul*).” This view of things is nothing but a modified, as it were chemical, atomism. Let us compare that

[p. 307]

with what we had to establish in the doctrine of ideas, under the idea of the soul, with regard to material community, and Schelling’s error will become quite clear to us. Schelling’s aether, as solvent, is unavoidably a chemical kind of matter; we understand, according to his exposition, how, through Kant’s concept of a complete chemical penetration, a *chemically composed* mass can nevertheless be thoroughly *homogeneous*. Through the appropriating oxygen in calcination, e.g., silver is combined with hydrochloric acid, so that now a thoroughly homogeneous muriate of silver is given down to its smallest parts, in which no part is either oxygen, or silver, or hydrochloric acid, but each is the chemical union of these three. Here there is neither oxygen, nor silver, nor acid, but only the unity of horn silver. But with this chemical combination the first thing, the mechanical possibility of a material unity, is not yet explained at all. How, then, is a mass possible, e.g. of horn silver, or indeed a crystal? In the mass every part lies next to the other as divisible into parts, so that each part, in the merely mechanical composition, is only for itself, and none in unity with the other. To this Kant answers with the chief proposition against atomism: Matter fills its space not merely by *being* in it (occupying it, having a volume, being a geometrical body), but only through the repulsive force that belongs to its substance, through the elasticity of all material substance. I.e., in general: unity and combination of material existence is to be comprehended only in the community of substances through the interaction of their forces. (§. 113.) That which properly *is*, the substance of matter, is the

[p. 308]

mass, which, however, is only a many without any unity, something divisible to infinity, where nevertheless every whole is supposed to subsist only through the parts. But this substance is in itself a mere abstraction; in nature every substance has its power, and through this power the form of a physical process, as form of an interaction, through which alone unity and combination come into material being. This law, that in all material existence unity and combination come not from *what is* by itself, but only from the form of the physical process in which the substance in each case is and moves—this Schelling has not seen. He says in another work (against Fichte, p. 125.): “Physics has attained science concerning the course of events in the chemical process only since it recognized that what *actually is* in the chemical appearance is not matter as such, the combined as the combined, but the living bond or copula of the two electricities.” We remark on this, first, that the false element in Winterl’s system, namely his shallow philosophy of nature, has influenced Schelling’s language only too much. According to Winterl, the dead atoms of the mass lie at the bottom of the being of matter as the figureless and differenceless, as it were the bearer of the bond and of the animating principles, through which latter alone figure and process are there. Schelling unites this bond with the animating principles in his living copula, and then makes the fundamental correction of Winterl’s philosophy that he recognizes this bond alone as that which *is*, but denies being to those atoms or to the figureless mass. But since the mass nevertheless always remains the many that *is not*, as the many

[p. 309]

remains, of which, as the mere limit, one nevertheless sometimes comes to speak, this *non-being* will surely remain only a polemical turn of linguistic usage, for of what truly and in fact is not one is not accustomed to speak either, except *apagogically*. But if, in one way or another, the being of this dead mass had its correctness after all, then this view in Winterl and Schelling would be only a new turn of that old doctrine of Ahriman and Ormuzd, or of the figureless chaos, which is dead, and a vivifying form-principle that joins it. (§. 111. 4)) This doctrine, however, we already know: it arises when one ascribes to abstracted forms an essence of their own for themselves, and so sets them over against their own content, instead of first uniting form and content in the same whole before one speaks of the being of it. So it is indeed found in fact: the chemical properties of the mass thought *in abstracto*, as something self-subsistent, are Winterl’s bond, and the forms of the physical processes under which the mass enters into community, substantialized, are his animating principles. Schelling too has taken this false path, and if he pursued it further would lose sight again entirely of the goal toward which he always strove, the annihilation of that separation of abstracted forms. Examples will make this quite clear. What, according to Schelling, is that which *actually is* in the animal, in the plant?—not the nourishment it has taken into itself, not the mass with which it falls upon the scales, but the living unity of the organism, the copula in it, the unity of the life-process. Or in an easier example: What is the Rhine? A stream that flows down from the Alps to the North Sea; it is

[p. 310]

not properly the water in it, which is daily a different one, not the bank, which merely confines it, but the unity of the physical process, whereby water is constantly flowing, confined to its bed. In other words: what we call animal, plant, the Rhine, is not something that *is*, but a history, a *becoming*, a life. Thereby the matter becomes clear: Schelling ought, above and elsewhere very often, to have said, instead of that which actually *is*, the *actual becoming*, and everything would be right. The unity and combination of the material world comes not immediately through that in it which is, through its substance—that is precisely the many in it—but through the becoming at the substance; in this becoming each is not for itself, but the state of the one substance is mediated through that of all the others by means of the interaction of their forces, and the unity and combination of this world consists only in the community of its substances under the forms of physical processes. Schelling’s error is therefore this, that he wants to give a being again, *in abstracto*, to the mere forms of becoming, the physical processes, and his aether, his world-soul as the material principle of the community of all things, is not the being of a first matter, but the original attraction, or rather the law, exhibited by us, of the highest form of all physical processes as the form of an organism. And so it is confirmed here too, as in all theoretical science, that all theory becomes clear to our mind only after experience. Through mere induction from experiences Schelling confirmed his basic law of the universal organism; only afterwards did we succeed in finding those simple mathematical moments whereby the necessity of this law is theoretically derived.

[p. 311]

It is the form of a magnetic, electric, chemical, mechanical or organic process in which we comprehend the unity in outer nature. Schelling says (against Fichte, p. 129.): “The basic law of my physical view is that I regard nature not mechanically but dynamically. If one could only convince me that it consists in mere mechanism, my conversion would be accomplished at once; then nature is undeniably dead, and every other philosopher may be right, only I not.” Here he does not understand the difference of the mechanical and the dynamical, in that he equates it with that of the living and the dead. It was the fault of the doctrine of atoms in the narrowest sense, as a merely mechanical physics, that it hoped to understand the essence of matter without any power, without any dynamics; the dynamical view, by contrast, demands above all an exertion of power from matter through original attraction and repulsion. But this exertion of power is not yet life in the more eminent sense; this attracting and repelling is a thoroughly outer reaction of the one against the other, but life is only there where inner activity is, hence immediately in matter nowhere. Schelling is indeed right that nature is a living whole, and must be cognized as such, but this is the theme of no science, hence also not of outer natural science. The living view of nature outside us we obtain only according to ideas, hence for a merely aesthetic judgment beyond all theory. But of course the doctrine of ideas developed by us must be presupposed, in order that this distinction may become intelligible. For him who, like Schelling, once for all and without investigation will allow only one way of conviction of the absolutely true to count, our distinction

[p. 312]

of appearance and of being in itself, and hence also our distinction of a material and a spiritual view of things, has no meaning. But once this rectification has been given in the doctrine of ideas, the rest too will become clear of itself.

#### §. 160.

We demand, then, theory in the strictest sense of every natural view of things, but precisely in its opposition to the ideal view. The highest perfection of physical theory we possess so far in Laplace’s *Mechanics of the Heavens*, to which, however, the chemical and physiological counterpart, to which science has an equally just claim, is still lacking.

The whole of outer nature is to be subjected to the consistency of a strict theory, in which every phenomenon must be explicable from its superordinate laws, but always only in a mathematical theory, which presupposes historically the particular of every fact and recognizes the incompletability of its series in their infinity and continuity. This is the point on which the ideas are commonly, and erroneously, appealed to. Every physical theory must restrict itself to explaining the relations of individual parts from an infinite history; it may never lay claim to a totality of its whole. This totality we think only according to ideas, but ideas are precisely of no use at all in physics. In nature there is given only the finite, limited, dependent and contingent in an *incompletable whole*, for which totality, the absolute, freedom and eternity have no meaning. It is the *most general*

[p. 313]

*meaning of the atomistic procedure* in physics, from which we are to free ourselves, that one attempts to derive one’s theory from a first beginning (e.g. in cosmology), from the simple (in monadology and atomism in the narrower sense), from freedom and absolute necessity, instead of restricting oneself to seeing in every history only a part taken from the midst of a greater whole. To this belongs, e.g., besides the well-known doctrine of atoms, every attempt to want to invent an absolute initial state of its history and so to evolve this history not from its One but from its Zero, as one begins in physics, say, with a quiet chaos, or as Kant evolves his history of the solar system from a homogeneous quiet fluid, and Schelling from the chemical absolute rest of an original dissolution of all materials in the aether.

Most generally this error shows itself in the use of the ideas of the soul, of the world and of deity, which even Kant wrongly acknowledges again as physical regulatives, after he had at first denied them all claims to be constitutive. Here, however, he did not understand the nature of the systematizing maxims; otherwise he would have seen that every regulative maxim for the natural view of things differs from the constitutive law only in degree in its application, and actually itself underlies theory as a still unknown constitutive law. (§. 86.) To all theory, however, we oppose the ideal regulatives generally, which may be referred to nature only aesthetically. There is no legitimate physical use of the ideas soul, world and deity.

[p. 314]

We must let the incompletability of the mathematical series stand as law for the observation of nature, and may never hope to supplement them theoretically by presuppositions from the idea, since in nature this would be sheer contradiction. We shall therefore, first, not concede that the incompletable finite reality of the mind in inner experience be supplemented, according to the idea, through the immortality of the soul; rather, for nature we remain only with its laws of the finite.

Second, we shall likewise not approve that nature be judged according to the idea of an absolute totality and identity of things in the world, and thus, e.g., outer and inner experience be forced together into one system. We saw, rather, that we must thereby entangle ourselves in contradictions with mathematics, and according to this idea, instead of the living change and the fullness of figures in nature, obtain only an empty unity, in which nothing individual could be distinguished.

Equally little shall we, third, suppose that he has explained anything in nature who shows us with what unattainable artistic genius the deity knew how to arrange this or that so purposively; we see, rather, that every appeal to creation, power and will of the Creator does not fit nature at all, that here rather only that is explained whose origin we comprehend from the mechanism of natural necessity.

#### §. 161.

What matters most to us here is to release the idea both from the slight service of a mere supplementary aid for theory

[p. 315]

and, on the large scale, to free it from all intermixture with theory. Thereby we then finally enter, in the proper domain of the ideas themselves, both for faith and for intimation, into conflict both with ordinary religious instruction and with all higher speculative attempts undertaken without critique. Here too we shall carry out the closer development again in opposition to Schelling and those who philosophize similarly to him.

We can set our doctrine of ideas in contrast with these higher rationalistic attempts in a fourfold way, according to the four moments of speculative cognition.

1) Empirical intuition. Our doctrine of the negative origin of the ideas for faith stands opposed to the positive cognition of the absolute from intellectual intuition.

2) Pure intuition. Schelling wants to cognize the true essence of things from the absolute unity; thereby the manifoldness is incorrectly made into the nothing of the finite, which nothing in fact shows itself only in this, that form and content of our cognition are not congruent.

3) Logical thinking. Instead of the correct opposition of appearance and being in itself, the finite view of things is rejected as a mere product of a deceiving imagination, above which the philosopher is supposed to raise himself, in order to cognize the eternal itself and to understand nature from it.

[p. 316]

4) Transcendental thinking. Instead of the religious view of things, the whole system of philosophy is here united into a physical view.

All these four moments repeat ever the same error, the confusion of the unity of understanding of theory with the unity of reason of the idea, precisely in that one wishes to free oneself wholly from the understanding.

The ground of this whole doctrine is the absolute unity, the Εν καὶ Πᾶν, the absolute identity and totality, which is presupposed as the constitutive principle of all our knowledge. But this happens only by failing to recognize the emptiness of the basic consciousness of unity and necessity in finite reason, and thus placing absolute knowledge in the mere form of our cognizing, without having a content. This presentation succeeds at first, because historically all speculation, both theoretical and according to ideas, develops only in conflict with the first crude empiricism of common life, and thus appears only polemically, and so supposes itself to possess in the ideal forms of the absolute a content of its own, until one discovers that this is in fact composed only of negations, and so can be of significance only in opposition to something else. Since this doctrine now recognizes absolute truth only in the highest unity and necessity, it must inevitably, in one way or another, for nature always reject the plurality and manifoldness of the objects before the sense as mere illusion of the finite; it can indeed explain everything, but always only by reduction of the opposed to zero; it can designate its First only figuratively as an eternal abyss from which all life wells forth, or similarly describe

[p. 317]

it, but thereby transforms the All of things into the eternal emptiness of an absolutely transparent unity. For here the opposition of the finite and the eternal is thoroughly misunderstood in that one supposes that reason must be freed from the content of the manifold, in which, however, the limitedness of our finite view in fact does not at all consist. Not the opposition of unity and manifoldness, but that of totality and incompletability to infinity shows us the merely subjective worth of appearance. In the fact that the form of our unity cannot be fulfilled by the manifoldness of the given, we recognize the limits of our view. We shall raise ourselves to the idea of the eternal, not by thinking the unity of things without manifoldness, not by placing the eternal essence in a law of identity, but in that we represent to ourselves unity and manifoldness both as wholly congruent in a closed allness. Neither the manifoldness nor the unity may be rejected, but only the empirical, inadequate combination of the mathematical forms. These alone are the finite, but to them precisely belongs all theory and all system.

With this error there appears at once also the other (through which all advantages of the critical doctrine of the distinction of appearance and being in itself are lost again), namely that the philosopher, in his absolute knowledge of identity, supposes that he attains in science the in-itself of things; whereby one places their eternal essence precisely in theory, i.e. in the laws of the necessary unity in the essence of things. Since this doctrine now wants to cognize that unity immediately,

[p. 318]

and finds in this all its wisdom, there is unavoidably lost to it, for the idea, the distinction between world and deity; for it cognizes the absolute unity in the things themselves, deity becomes the eternal being of the things themselves, or, in Schelling’s latest expression, the eternal bond of things, hence the order of the world, but in no way a being above the world, and the latter is nevertheless, as we have seen, our true demand for this highest idea.

The doctrine of absolute unity asserts itself at first in the history of philosophy, beside every other speculative system, only as a hypothesis, which wishes to insinuate itself through its serviceability for explaining, without any effort being made to lay a positively firm ground for it. The latter question, in what it immediately secures its own truth? has only recently been taken up. One sought at first in various ways to ground it logically, but finally, after rejection of all reflection, in opposition to this, through intellectual intuition. We have already shown above (§. 53. and 54.) that this thought is an empty evasion of a concept that logically does not contradict itself, but which for finite reason wholly lacks application, since it can be formed only in opposition to its essence limited by inner sense and reflection. Here what was there only indicated can be surveyed still more clearly, namely that Schelling too, with this his organ of philosophy, means only the empty formal apperception of our reason, but confuses this with the whole of transcendental apperception and especially with the basic consciousness of speculative faith

[p. 319]

through disregard of the distinction of our three modal principles from the idea. (§. 53. §. 95. and §. 131.)

With regard to the exposition of the history of our cognizing we are basically almost wholly in agreement with Schelling, so that the merely historical observer might readily pass off the whole dispute between us as a mere dispute about words, when he notices that we recognize in like manner and with the same ideas the opposition of the finite and the eternal as the highest theme of speculation, both rejecting the merely mathematical mode of cognition as the finite. He might say: if each of them only understood the language of the other, they would see that the one only carries out what the other demands. Schelling namely calls the subjective view of nature in its mathematical incompletability something merely imagined, to which no reality belongs, and which does not concern philosophy, which ought to recognize it precisely in its nullity and rise above it to the sole knowledge of the idea. Do we not now say the very same with altered words? What he calls imagining we call finite cognizing and subjectively valid knowledge; what he calls knowledge, on the other hand, we call faith? Certainly! But these words are here not mere designations, but carry their determinate claims with them. The merely imagined is for him, as much as for us, dream and error, a way of representing through which nothing is cognized, whereas intuition alone leads to cognition. Knowledge, however, means for him, as for us, a conviction through intuition and inferences, hence a conviction that permits theoretical evolutions; faith, on the other hand, is again for us both a conviction

[p. 320]

which is receptive to no theory. Hence those propositions express quite properly the main dispute between us. Schelling rejects the finite view of things as mere imagination, which it is not, and demands science, i.e. theory of the eternal, which is impossible. We, on the other hand, restrict ourselves to the scientific cognition of the finite, from whose empirical reality no finite reason can detach itself, and oppose to this the ideal view only in faith. Hence it is precisely the theoretical use of the idea that separates us.

#### §. 162.

Schelling once makes use against Fichte of the turn: what is true in the end must also have been so from the beginning; if you began with that which only becomes clear to you at the end of your philosophical reflections, you would first see things according to their true essence and life. This objection holds against very many philosophers, who confuse the course of thought of their subjective self-clarification, where only at the end they learn how they really stand with the matter, with the system of a mathematical science, in which every theorem becomes true only at its place through its demonstration. But it is only to the doctrine of ideas that it cannot be applied. The ideal view is indeed true only at the end, if at the outset the truth of the natural view is presupposed; for it does not give the latter its theoretical apex, but is possible only *in opposition to it*, through the union of faith in highest reality with the consciousness of the inadequacy

[p. 321]

of our view of nature. Every positive doctrine of ideas entangles itself, as we have already shown, in a mythological system, at whose apex above all stands the empty law of a fate; moreover, it must be able to answer all questions from its absolute knowledge; it is without ignorance in speculative matters, and thereby in clearest contradiction with human nature. It may declare itself against theories as much as it will, yet it will only ever change the word, and possess a science of God’s relation to the world and to the individual fallen ideas, and also a theory of how God or the All comes to self-cognition.

Against all this we set the merely aesthetic use of ideas for intimation in a religious view of things, and so we finally make our doctrine of ideas quite clear by comparing the religious view of things with the physical, in that we set against all theoretical reason the merely aesthetic judging of the last ideal regulative.

Schelling’s philosophy of nature, as so-called doctrine of the All, doctrine of the universal organism, or whatever else, ought to restrict itself to a system of outer nature; instead of this, however, it presumes to dominate the whole of our convictions precisely from the idea, and so inevitably meddles with a mythological doctrine of religion, in that, as Schelling expressly demands, it wants to grasp the true essence of things physically and so to understand it from the eternal essence of deity. More or less this is then also the error of all our ordinary

[p. 322]

religious instruction, in that we fancy we possess determinate religious science as theoretical insight. Against this our third regulative from the idea, the true speculative principle of intimation, declares itself determinately. The transcendental forms of ideas are formed only from the negation of limits; nothing positive is therefore cognized in them from concepts, but they serve only to think the true essence of things as an *other* than the limited essence of nature. So that cognition from them admits of no further exposition than the thought of an absolute view of things beside the limited view of our reason. The positive laws of the eternal order and the relation of the eternal essence to the finite view of our reason are, on the other hand, *insurmountable mysteries* for finite reason, which it is unable to clear up without first being wholly transformed in its organization. Speculative faith gives us in these negative forms only a basis of intimation, that is, of a way of conviction opposed to all theory, from mere feelings.

What we call *aesthetic* in the most determinate sense is the property of feeling in opposition to all theory, and thereby the free property of the power of judgment, whose speculative principles we seek here. Quite peculiarly its own is this third regulative of the religious view of things, or of the recognition of the eternal essence of things in nature according to the third modal principle from the idea, as theme of taste and of devotion. Here we do not wish to go into detail about this speculative basis of the aesthetic in our mind

[p. 323]

since it is precisely that which is without all theory, and the details must first occur in the practical determination of the ideas in their full connection. What matters most is, in general, the opposition of aesthetic and theoretical judging, of the physical and the religious view. The free judging of taste, which recognizes the laws of life throughout the whole of nature, places itself precisely in contrast with all theoretical science and all explanation. I *explain* nature in its life by demonstrating in the forms of the organized the evolution of that mathematical law of the universal cycle; this is a matter of science and theory; but if through the same forms I have an intimation of life itself and of the divine spirit, this is not a matter of natural science, but aesthetic judging of religion.

We see here the most determinate relation between knowledge, faith and intimation. The perfection of reflective knowledge is *science*, which becomes theory through explanation and proof, in that inference is added to intuition and determines the given actual physically through the necessity of universal laws. But above all laws of knowledge there rises, through the self-cognition of our reason’s own limits, the conviction of faith, and gives us in the ideas a new principle for judging nature and the essence of things, which appears to us through nature and its intuition. This principle, however, remains for us unavoidably a positively *unspeakable law of unity*, which cannot be positively grasped in determinate concepts. The ideal law is therefore a

[p. 324]

principle which in the strictest sense remains only a guiding maxim, without ever being able to become a constitutive law for human reason. Thus the domain of *aesthetics* or of feeling separates itself from all science and theory. In place of the *theoretical subordination* of all intuition under the mathematical laws of physics there steps an *aesthetic subordination* of the same intuition under the ideas, in which the power of judgment, in its feelings, can be guided only by *unspeakable concepts*. There is therefore certainly in our mind a region of conviction beyond all science, but it is not the cognition *of* the ideas, but the cognition *from* the ideas, as principles.

The highest distinction for the use of the power of judgment is therefore that of the theoretical and the aesthetic. The case of theory is wherever, according to determinate concepts, positively universal laws are given, where therefore only subsuming power of judgment is required in order to subordinate the case to the rule. This now applies to the whole natural view of things. In this there form themselves through the category positive universal laws, to which the particular in nature, as to its condition, is with necessity subjected. For the execution of science there is indeed here too a domain of induction, in which the reflecting power of judgment remains the sole ruler, but there the guiding maxims are nevertheless only such heuristic maxims, of which it is generally well understood how they hold for nature as constitutive laws, under which a theoretical subordination certainly takes place, only that the individual combinatorial complexions

[p. 325]

turn out too composite for us to be handled with ease by the mathematical imagination, wherefore we content ourselves with the attempt to evolve from the given involution, e.g. of the natural history of the earth, whole classes at once, without being able to write out the individual complexions in each class. The ideal view of things, on the other hand, contradicts all theory from its highest principle. Principles from ideas are infinite judgments, with whose negative forms the subsuming power of judgment can do nothing at all. Here all subordination is left to the reflecting power of judgment, and thus it sets its own aesthetic law of taste over against all theory in general; its rules are capable of no logical development, but must be left to the feeling of each individual himself. So is determined the subjectively conditioned universal validity of our judgments of taste, in that it is only the unspeakable rule in which we must necessarily agree, whereas for the individual subordination each is left only to his subjective feeling; where, therefore, only from the validity of the indeterminate principle is derived the limited objective validity of the laws of the beautiful for a distinct aesthetic view of the world.

We see now how Schelling’s and similar old speculations must at first ingratiate themselves, through the fusing of philosophy and poetry, among the speculating folk (but by no means among those of mere rude health), and whence their self-conceit and airs of distinction come; they let their handicraft pass for art, their physics for poetry, and when they then find the world they have described

[p. 326]

great and beautiful, some of the splendor of the world-spirit falls also upon them, its prophets. In its outcome, however, this doctrine must work just as detrimentally upon science as upon taste. With regard to taste such a consistent philosophical aesthetics will despise the pure beautiful and seek only the philosophically sublime; metaphysical mythology and deep, heavy physical allegory will seem to it the truly significant. The theoretical forms of science become leaden wings, whose weight crushes genius; in science, on the other hand, one will, in false, distinguished conceit, demand an analogue of poetic prose, where, after the manner of the old alchemists, the physicist is ashamed to speak of his experiments otherwise than in unintelligible images.

The need of our social cultivation is precisely the reverse. You scold an age of Enlightenment, of which you suppose that it is passing. What else was the fault of this age than an unbounded craving for theory, which did not understand itself? To whom else do we owe our Protestant coldness and lack of religiosity than to the desire to dominate even the religious with theories? This showed itself as pure reflection; now you give the blame to reflection itself, which belongs only to its false application, and want to improve yourselves by casting reflection from you. You are gravely mistaken! In that way one does not overcome it. Whoever has once begun to follow it does not recover health until he has carried its work purely to its end, and thereby has comprehended which is the domain of science in our mind, and which that of the idea.

[p. 327]

If you hope to secure taste and devotion again for a healthier coming age, then do not let these ingratiate themselves with it, as if with a bad conscience, through the splendor of adorned presentations, but recognize the importance of a reflective cultivation, and hand over to it completed theoretical science wherever it is at all possible, so that the same never-completed work may not clumsily be begun anew over and over again, or even be patched together from old ruins, but that at last a whole may appear in solid perfection.
